concepts/bank-charter-act-1844.title: The Bank Charter Act of 1844
concepts/bank-charter-act-1844.content:
The Bank Charter Act of 1844
The Bank Charter Act of 1844 — 7 & 8 Vict. c. 32, carried through Parliament by Sir Robert Peel and passed in June 1844 — was the legislative embodiment of the currency principle: the doctrine that the note circulation of a country should vary exactly as a purely metallic circulation would, expanding and contracting with the bullion held against it. Its two great provisions separated the issuing department of the Bank of England from its banking department, and froze the right of issue throughout the United Kingdom at a fixed maximum, so that no new bank of issue could be created and no lapsed right revived. The Act answered, in the language of its day, the standing charge of excess — that over-issue of paper by the Bank and by country bankers had fed speculation and brought on panics. Peel took the power of issue out of the play of competition and made it a privilege fixed once and for all.
The currency principle and the Bank’s structure
The Act of 1844 was the triumph of a school of monetary thought built up since the Bullion Report and the resumption of cash payments. Its essential idea was that paper money, if it were to be safe, must be nothing more than a certificate for gold: every note in circulation must represent either a corresponding sum of bullion in the vaults or a fixed authorized amount sanctioned by law. Peel defended the measure on this ground in the debates of May 1844, insisting on a fixed metallic standard as the only sure regulator of the currency. He drew a sharp distinction between money — the medium of exchange — and mere paper credit, the fabric of deposits, bills, and accommodation that rests on confidence but does not itself circulate as coin. The error of confounding paper credit with paper money, Tooke argued, lay at the root of the currency principle and of the evils its disciples hoped to cure.
To enforce the principle, the Act divided the Bank of England into two departments. The Issue Department held the entire stock of bullion and issued notes against it — one pound of gold for every pound of notes beyond the fixed fiduciary maximum. The Banking Department kept the Bank’s ordinary assets and liabilities — deposits, discounts, advances — exactly as any joint-stock or private banker would. Henceforward the note circulation of the Bank rose and fell with its gold reserve, mechanically and without reference to the wants of trade. This was the celebrated “separation of the issue from the banking department,” long urged by Samuel Jones Loyd and the currency school as the way to make the Bank’s paper follow gold as surely as a metallic circulation would.
The fixed maximum for English country issues
For the country banks the Act imposed a maximum where no effective legal limit had existed. No bank of issue might be newly established anywhere in the United Kingdom. Each existing English bank’s right of issue was fixed at the average of its circulation for the twelve weeks ending 27 April 1844; weekly averages were thereafter to be returned to the Stamp Office and the London Gazette, and any bank whose circulation exceeded its maximum for four consecutive weeks paid a penalty equal to the excess. The certified totals settled near £5,150,000 for private banks and £3,500,000 for joint-stock banks — 205 private and 72 joint-stock banks in all. The right of issue was extinguished forever by increasing partners beyond six, by certain unions, by bankruptcy, or by ceasing to issue.
The choice of the April 1844 base was a compromise between interests. Peel first proposed a two-year average; the private bankers asked for five years; the joint-stock banks preferred the maximum of the two years, lest an average-turned-ceiling shrink their issues still further. What the Act did not do, Gilbart was careful to insist, was compel country issues to move with the Bank’s gold. In October 1844 gold stood near £12,150,000, in October 1847 near £6,750,000, and in July 1852 near £21,850,000 — yet the legal country maxima neither contracted nor expanded with these swings. The Act answered the charge of excess; it did not impose the metallic rule on the provinces as strictly as on the Bank itself.
Operation through the crisis of 1847
The Act received its first great test in the commercial pressure of 1847, when a drain of gold on the Bank, following the railway mania and the failure of the harvest, brought the country to the verge of a suspension of payments. Tooke subjected the operation of the Act from September 1844 through the close of 1847 to an exhaustive historical review. His conclusion was that the currency principle rested on a false analogy and that the Act, far from averting the crisis, aggravated it by denying the Bank the power to relieve the pressure of the discount market when the banking department’s reserve ran low. The Act’s defenders answered that its operation had prevented a complete suspension of cash payments and that but for it the panic would have been total. Peel himself, defending the measure on 3 December 1847, maintained that its machinery had saved the convertibility of the note. The government finally sanctioned the Bank to exceed the statutory limit — an act of suspension in all but name — and the crisis passed; Tooke’s argument that the Act had needlessly intensified the difficulty remained the classic indictment of the currency principle.
The permanent freezing of the issue
Most durable was the Act’s treatment of the right of issue as a fixed and depleting privilege. Because a lapsed issue could never be revived, the ceiling itself eroded year by year. Gilbart’s statistics of 1854 recorded that since 1844 thirty-seven private country banks had ceased to issue — eleven inside the sixty-five-mile circle around London and twenty-six outside, with a combined fixed issue of about £536,793 — and seven joint-stock banks, about £169,589, among them houses at Devonport, Ipswich, Stockton, Leeds, Sheffield, and Newcastle. The original certified issue of about £8,650,000 had thereby fallen to about £7,940,000. When an English bank’s issue lapsed, the Bank of England might take up to two-thirds of the extinguished amount; the Bank of Ireland might take the whole — a disparity Gilbart noted without defending. If the long policy were gradual extinction of country issues toward a single issuer, the non-revival of lapsed rights served that end; but Gilbart doubted that the Bank of England could replace in a remote district notes extinguished there, and he rehearsed the older evidence that depriving country bankers of the profit of issue would raise the charges on accommodation and close marginal rural offices.
The Act, the seasonal laws, and later debate
The Act set a ceiling on the wave of circulation; it did not rewrite the calendar of the tide. Gilbart’s tables showed the same seasonal “laws of the currency” still governing English country issues after 1844 as before — the English country circuit lowest about the end of August, rising through November to a peak in April and falling again; the Scottish circuit with its high points in May and November; the Irish circuit swelling with the harvest toward a January peak. The Act capped the height of these waves but left their rhythm untouched. Its legacy, by freezing the issue and barring new banks, was a slow, steady concentration of the note circulation toward the Bank of England, a process that Gilbart’s recommendations — a twelve-month average in place of four weeks, restoration of lapsed rights to banks that had circulated Bank notes under expiring agency agreements, permission to exceed the maximum against gold or Bank notes held, and the union of issuing banks — were designed to soften and direct, though Peel’s statute left little room for them.

concepts/bank-of-england.title: Bank of England
concepts/bank-of-england.content:
Bank of England
The Bank of England, founded in 1694 as the government’s lender and the privileged joint-stock issuer of notes in London, stood at the head of the English monetary system throughout the period 1800–1865. By the beginning of the nineteenth century its notes had superseded the goldsmiths’ notes and formed the standard against which the country circulation was measured; by the middle of the century, after the Bank Charter Act of 1844 divided it into an Issue and a Banking Department, it had become the great national reserve of gold on whose convertibility the whole fabric of credit rested. Every question of the currency — restriction, resumption, the bullion controversy, the country banks, the panics — turned on the Bank and on the duty of its directors to maintain the exchange and the convertibility of the note.
Foundation and the Restriction of 1797
The Bank was incorporated in 1694 on the model of the chartered companies, advancing a loan to the government and receiving in return the privilege of issuing notes in the capital. Its establishment displaced the goldsmiths as the great London issuers, and its charter was periodically renewed in exchange for fresh loans to the state. By the end of the eighteenth century the Bank’s notes, payable in gold on demand, formed the central currency of the commercial metropolis and the reserve in which the country banks kept their balances.
The Bank Restriction Act of 1797 — forced by the strain of the French war, when a run on gold threatened to empty the vaults — suspended the convertibility of the note and made the Bank’s paper inconvertible for the duration of the war and after. This suspension of cash payments opened the bullion controversy: whether the depreciation of the note against gold was the cause or the effect of the high price of bullion, whether the Bank’s issues were excessive, and whether the exchange fell from over-issue or from the extraordinary foreign expenditure of war. The Bullion Committee of 1809–11 reported that the exchanges were governed by the amount of the circulation and that the Bank had over-issued; the government rejected the recommendation to resume. The Imlac tract of 1817, applying Hume’s essay on public credit to the postwar situation, drew the darkest conclusions from the Pitt system of paper money and funded debt, holding that a perseverance in the paper system must eventually produce national bankruptcy. The notes circulated at a discount against gold until the resumption of cash payments in 1819–21 re-adjusted the values of gold and paper.
The Bank, resumption, and the provincial branches
The resumption of cash payments in 1819 committed the Bank to the metallic standard and made the maintenance of convertibility its first duty. From 1826, in response to the panic of 1825 and the collapse of weak country banks, the Bank was drawn into the provinces by the establishment of branches — at Manchester, Liverpool, and elsewhere — which brought Bank of England notes and London credit directly to the manufacturing districts. The country circulation fell as the branch circulation rose: Gilbart recorded the country issues at about £11,700,000 with branch circulation about £3,500,000 in 1836, against country about £7,700,000 with branches about £6,500,000 in 1846. The Bank’s branches, and the joint-stock banks that took Bank of England paper at a preferential discount, displaced much of the Lancashire bill-of-exchange circulation and drew the note issue gradually toward the Bank itself.
The Act of 1844 and the division of the Bank
The Bank Charter Act of 1844 remade the Bank’s constitution. It separated the Bank into an Issue Department, holding the entire stock of bullion and issuing notes against it — one pound of gold for every pound of notes beyond a fixed fiduciary maximum — and a Banking Department, keeping the ordinary assets and liabilities of deposits, discounts, and advances exactly as any other banker would. Henceforward the Bank’s note circulation rose and fell with its gold reserve, mechanically, without reference to the wants of trade. This was the currency school’s design, urged by Samuel Jones Loyd and embodied by Peel: to make the Bank’s paper follow gold as surely as a metallic circulation would. As the great issuer, the Bank now held a fixed fiduciary issue — and when a country bank’s issue lapsed, the Bank might take up to two-thirds of the extinguished amount, a provision that slowly concentrated the note circulation in its hands.
The Bank as lender and the “law” of its circulation
The Bank’s own note circulation obeyed a law peculiar to itself, derived by Gilbart from the monthly averages: four tides in the year, following the public dividends. The circulation was higher in January than in February and March, in April than in May and June, in July than in August and September, in October than in November and December — because the Bank alone paid the dividends, and the great mass of interest money passed through its notes into the hands of the fundholders before settling back into the banking system. This was the pattern of a metropolitan and financial circulation, in contrast to the country banks’ single agricultural circuit and the Scottish and Irish rhythms.
The Bank’s duty, in the management of this circulation and of its reserve, was the subject of constant dispute. In the pressure of 1838–39 Tooke examined the regulation of the Bank’s issues and vindicated it against groundless charges, arguing that the Bank was not bound to accommodate trade but to maintain the exchanges. In 1847 the Bank’s conduct under the Act was the pivot of the crisis: the drain of gold, the exhaustion of the Banking Department’s reserve, and the eventual government sanction to exceed the statutory limit. Tooke’s history of prices from 1797 was in large part a history of the Bank — its advances to government, its issues, its management of the exchanges, and the successive doctrines of its duty, from the accommodation doctrine of the early years to the currency principle of 1844.
The Bank and the wider credit system
The Bank stood in relation to the whole credit fabric. Carey’s comparative study of credit placed the Bank and the London money market at the centre of English confidence, contrasting English banking with the scarcity of banks and low confidence of France. The Imlac writer, in the opposite vein, regarded the Bank’s inconvertible paper and the funded debt as twin instruments of a national bankruptcy that only parliamentary reform could avert. Between these poles lay the practical question that occupied Tooke, Gilbart, and the committees: whether the Bank could and should be the sole issuer, whether its notes could replace in a remote district the country notes extinguished there, and whether the note circulation was the true regulator of prices at all. The Bank’s answer, embodied in the Act of 1844, was to make itself the fixed and sole standard of issue — the one circulation whose amount was governed by gold and not by trade.
In the Sources

concepts/chartism.title: Chartism
concepts/chartism.content:
Chartism
Chartism was the great working-class movement of the 1830s and 1840s — the political expression of the industrial working class, organised around the six points of the People’s Charter, which demanded the reform of the representation and the enfranchisement of the working classes. It was, at once, a political movement, a social protest, and a class movement — the attempt of the excluded and distressed working classes to secure, by political means, the redress of the grievances that the Reform Act of 1832 had left unaddressed. Chartism rose in the dark times of the late 1830s, reached its height in the monster meetings and the great petition of the early 1840s, collapsed as a mass movement after 1848, and left its six points as the programme of later reform.
Origins and programme
Chartism grew out of the disappointment of the working classes with the Reform Act of 1832. The Act had enfranchised the middle-class householder and left the town workman and the agricultural labourer without a vote; the working classes, excluded from the reformed constitution, drew the lesson that only the political power of the franchise could secure the redress of their grievances. The People’s Charter, published in 1838, demanded universal suffrage (for men), equal electoral districts, the ballot, annual parliaments, the abolition of the property qualification for members of Parliament, and the payment of members. The six points were the programme of working-class radicalism, and the Charter united its various strands.
The movement
Chartism organised itself through the National Convention, the monster meetings, the torchlight processions, and the great National Petition with its millions of signatures. It was led, in its various phases, by men of very different temper — the moral-force Chartists, who trusted to agitation and petition, and the physical-force men, who spoke of armed resistance. In 1839 came the Newport rising, the march of the Welsh Chartists on the Westgate Hotel, the dispersal by the military, and the transportation of the leaders. The movement revived in the early 1840s under Feargus O’Connor, the most powerful of the Chartist orators, whose Northern Star was the organ of the movement and whose Land Scheme promised to settle the poor upon the land. The final and most famous episode came in 1848, in the year of the continental revolutions: the monster petition was prepared, and the great meeting was to be held at Kennington Common on 10 April 1848; the government organised its special constables, the meeting passed off quietly, the petition was found to contain a vast number of forged signatures, and Chartism collapsed.
Chartism and the working class
Engels, writing of the condition of the working class, treated Chartism as the political form of the working-class movement — the counterpart, in the political sphere, of the trade unions in the economic sphere, and the inevitable product of the class antagonism of industrial England. To its supporters the Charter was the means of every reform; to the government and the propertied classes it was the threat of revolution. Martineau placed Chartism in the economic conditions of the age — the state of the crops, the distress of the working classes, and the near-revolutionary atmosphere among them — and she blamed, not the poor, but the blindness of the men who attributed the commotions to the innate wickedness of the lower orders while missing entirely the economic roots of the unrest.
Significance
Chartism failed in its immediate object: Parliament never enacted the Charter, and the movement collapsed as a mass force after 1848. But its significance was lasting. It was the great political apprenticeship of the English working class — the demonstration that the working classes would not be permanently excluded from the constitution, and the means by which their claim to the franchise was kept alive through the decades when it was most unfashionable. Its six points were gradually realised in the course of the century — the ballot in 1872, equal districts in 1885, and the successive widening of the suffrage by the reform acts. Chartism belongs to the making of the democratic state, and its history is the history of the entry of the working classes into English politics.

concepts/church-of-england-and-oxford-mo.title: The Church of England and the Oxford Movement
concepts/church-of-england-and-oxford-mo.content:
The Church of England and the Oxford Movement
The Church of England was the established Church of the three kingdoms, and its condition and its controversies ran through the whole of the period. At the opening of the nineteenth century the Church stood at a low-water mark — weakened by the effects of the French Revolution and the long war, its clergy often non-resident, its revenues unequally distributed, and the cry of “the Church in danger” heard from its defenders as popular attacks multiplied. Through the first third of the century it underwent a steady revival and reform — the growth of the Evangelicals, the improvement of the clergy, the building of churches, the spread of schools and missions — and then, from 1833, it was convulsed by the great religious movement of the age: the Oxford Movement, which sought to recall the Church of England to its Catholic heritage and which divided and enlivened the Church for a generation.
The condition of the Church
The Church of England at the beginning of the century, as Overton’s history records, was in a state of neglect and decline. The effects of the French Revolution and the war, the low state of morals and religion, the abuse of pluralities and non-residence, and the unequal distribution of the Church’s wealth were the standing evils of the establishment. Yet Overton, writing from a sympathetic High Church standpoint, insisted that the period from 1800 to 1833 was one of substantial revival and preparation rather than stagnation — a steady improvement from the low-water mark of the late eighteenth century, in Church life, doctrine, education, missions, and relations with the State. Three great parties divided the Church: the Orthodox or High Churchmen, the Evangelicals, and the Liberals. The Evangelical revival, with its zeal for missions, education, and the reform of manners, was the most active force in the earlier period; the High Church party, though diminished, preserved the tradition of the Catholic and apostolic character of the Church; and the Liberal party looked to reform and to the rational reconstruction of the establishment.
Church and State
The relation of the Church to the State was the great constitutional question of the establishment. The Church was bound to the State by the royal supremacy, the union of the temporal and spiritual, and the exclusion of Dissenters and Catholics from the full rights of citizenship. Catholic Emancipation in 1829, which admitted Catholics to Parliament, and the Reform Act of 1832, which remade the political order, struck at the old assumptions of the establishment and raised the question of the Church’s place in the new constitution. The reform of the Church itself followed — the Ecclesiastical Commission of 1835, the commutation of tithes, the reform of pluralities and non-residence, and the redistribution of the Church’s revenues. It was in part as a protest against the state’s treatment of the Church — against the suppression of the Irish bishoprics and the Erastian spirit of the age — that the Oxford Movement arose.
The Oxford Movement
In 1833, with the publication of the Tracts for the Times from Oriel College, Oxford, began the Oxford Movement — the great religious revival led by John Keble, John Henry Newman, Edward Pusey, and Richard Hurrell Froude. Keble’s Assize Sermon of 1833 is commonly taken as its origin. The Tractarians taught the apostolic succession, the divine character of the Church, the reality of the sacraments, and the Catholic heritage of the Church of England as a branch of the universal Church — reformed of medieval abuses but in continuous succession with the primitive and medieval Church. The movement aroused the most violent controversy: the Tractarians were accused of Romanism, their doctrine was examined and condemned in Parliament and the courts, and the celebrated Tract XC of 1841, which sought to reconcile the Thirty-nine Articles with Catholic doctrine, brought the movement to a crisis. The secession of Newman to Rome in 1845, followed by others, seemed to break the movement; but under Pusey it continued as the High Church or Anglo-Catholic party, and it transformed the Church.
The consequences
The Oxford Movement was the decisive religious event of the century. It revived the Catholic and sacramental life of the Church of England, transformed its worship, its ritual, and its sense of itself, and produced the High Church revival that ran through the later nineteenth century, with its ritual controversies and its conflicts over the Eucharist and the ornamentation of the churches. It divided the Church — the Evangelicals and the Low Churchmen opposed the Tractarians, and the secessions to Rome marked the limits of the movement — but it gave the Church of England a new energy and a new sense of its character. Wakeman’s history, written from the Anglo-Catholic standpoint the movement created, carries the story into the late nineteenth century, tracing the High Church revival, the Eucharistic controversy, and the widening of religious conflict through the 1850s and 1860s. Within the period 1800–1865 the Church and the Oxford Movement form one of the great subjects of the age — the religious counterpart of the political and social transformation of the century.
In the Sources

concepts/city-of-london.title: The City of London
concepts/city-of-london.content:
The City of London
The City of London was the ancient municipal territory at the heart of the metropolis — the square mile that had its own municipal corporation, its own courts, its own police, and its own form of government, distinct from every other town in England. The Corporation of London, with its Lord Mayor, its Court of Aldermen, its Common Council, its Livery, and its body of freemen, was the survival of the medieval constitution of the capital into the nineteenth century: a corporate body founded on charter and custom, exempt from the Municipal Corporations Act of 1835, and governed by a system that the two great Royal Commissions of 1837 and 1854 examined in minute detail. The City was, in the words of the 1837 Report, “a province covered with houses” — the commercial heart of the greatest metropolis in the world, whose wealth and whose peculiar institutions set it apart.
The territory and its limits
The municipal territory of the City of London was the area comprehended within the outer frontier of the Liberties — the districts into which the City’s franchises and privileges extended. The ancient distinction between London within the Walls and London without the Walls, or the Liberties, existed in the nineteenth century only in name; the whole was under the like municipal jurisdiction, and residence in either portion conferred the same municipal privileges. The position of the bars and gates, and the line of the ancient walls, defined the boundary between the Liberties and the county of Middlesex. The whole of the ancient London Bridge was within the City, maintained by the City officers, who claimed that the present structure retained the rights of the ancient bridge, including the small plot of the “Bridge Foot” on the Surrey shore. The City lay at the centre of a metropolis whose growth had left it a constantly smaller portion of the whole — 723 acres and a nearly stationary population of 129,128 against a metropolis of 78,029 acres and 2,362,236 people in 1851.
The governing bodies
The Corporation of London was governed by a body of institutions whose roots lay in the medieval constitution of the capital. At its head stood the Lord Mayor, elected annually, the chief magistrate of the City and of its courts. The Court of Aldermen — the twenty-six aldermen, one for each ward, holding office for life — exercised both judicial and elective powers: the admission of brokers, the appointment of officers, and a share in the government of the City. The Common Council, the popular and representative body, consisted of the aldermen and of 240 common councilmen, elected annually in different proportions by the several wards, by the same electors as elected the aldermen. The Court of Common Hall consisted of the freemen of the Corporation who were Liverymen of the several companies. The whole system rested on the wards and their assemblies, the wardmotes, in which the citizens of each ward chose their representatives.
The Livery and the freemen
The franchise and privileges of the City rested on the distinction between the freemen and the liverymen. The freemen of the Corporation were those admitted to the freedom of the City — and no one could become a freeman except by previous admission into one of the companies or guilds. The Liverymen were a certain number of the freemen’s bodies, who, under the name of Liverymen, enjoyed in the Corporation privileges which other freemen did not possess. The freemen were thus divided into two classes: those who were, and those who were not, Liverymen in their respective companies. The object of making the Livery an element in the franchise appears to have been the establishment of something in the nature of a property qualification — an order of the Court of Aldermen of 1697 required an estate of £1,000 for the clothing of the twelve great companies. The Livery, assembled in Common Hall, had a part in the election of the Lord Mayor and of the sheriffs.
The companies and the exclusive privileges
The body of the Corporation comprised the trading companies or guilds — the 1837 Report counted 89 municipal companies or guilds in the Corporation, of which a few were practically extinct or nearly so. No one could become a freeman of the Corporation but by previous admission into one of these companies. The rise and progress of the guilds formed a distinct and important part of the inquiry, and the Report examined their constitution, their privileges, and their relation to the Corporation — though it candidly recorded that in the case of the Companies information was in some instances refused and in others furnished only under restrictions, so that its account was far from complete. The freemen enjoyed exclusive privileges of trading and exercising a handicraft within the City — restrictions that the 1854 Commission was to recommend abolishing as mischievous restraints upon trade and industry.
The courts and the police
The City possessed its own courts and its own administration of justice. The Lord Mayor’s Court and the Sheriffs’ Courts (with the custom of Foreign Attachment) were the great courts of the City; the Court of Hustings, the court at St. Martin’s-le-Grand, and the jurisdiction of the Recorder and the Common Sergeant completed the system, which had its connexion with the newly established Central Criminal Court. The City also maintained its own police, distinct from the metropolitan police of the surrounding districts, and its own prisons. These jurisdictions, and the City’s conservancy of the river Thames, its markets and their tolls, its metage duties and the coal duties, and the management of its property — the Bridge House estates, the tolls of London Bridge, the markets — formed the substance of the Corporation’s government.
The two inquiries and the reform question
The peculiar position of the City was the subject of the two great official inquiries of the period. The Second Report of the Municipal Corporations Commission (1837) — the fundamental investigation of the Corporation’s constitution, limits, governing bodies, courts, freemen and liverymen, Companies, and Southwark connexion — explained why London had been excepted from the Municipal Corporations Act of 1835 and examined the whole system in detail. The Royal Commission of 1854 returned to the subject, surveyed the state of the Corporation a generation later, and set out the reform programme: a new charter consolidating the preservable charters and customs, the election of the Lord Mayor by the Common Council, the election of the aldermen by the burgesses of the wards for six years, the abolition of the Court of Aldermen, the reform of the wards, the £10 occupancy franchise, the abolition of the freemen’s exclusive trading privileges, the incorporation of the City police with the metropolitan police, and the City’s part in the proposed Metropolitan Board of Works. Neither inquiry denied the value of the Corporation — the 1854 Commission found nothing to affect injuriously the honour and integrity of its officers — but both pressed the application of the recognized municipal policy of the country to the ancient City.

concepts/command-of-the-sea.title: Command of the Sea
concepts/command-of-the-sea.content:
Command of the Sea
Command of the sea — the dominance of a navy over the waters that connect the nations — was the foundation of British power in the nineteenth century and the central idea of its naval and strategic thought. It was the command of the sea, established through the wars of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries and confirmed decisively at Trafalgar, that made Britain an island secure from invasion, that opened to its commerce the markets of the world, and that enabled it to sustain the alliances and the warfare that defeated Napoleon and preserved the balance of power. The concept received its classic theoretical statement in the work of Captain Alfred Thayer Mahan, who argued that control of the sea is the decisive factor in the rise and fall of nations, and it shaped the understanding both of British naval supremacy and of the strategy by which it was maintained.
The elements of sea power
Mahan’s theory, developed in The Influence of Sea Power upon History (1890), set out the conditions on which the sea power of a nation depends. He identified six elements: geographical position — whether a nation is insular or continental, commanding the trade routes or divided by land frontiers; physical conformation — the length and character of its coastline, its harbours and rivers; extent of territory — the length of coast relative to the land borders; size of population — the numbers available for maritime service and naval recruitment; national character — the commercial instinct, the adventurousness, the aptitude for seafaring and colonisation; and character of government — whether the institutions of the state encourage or hamper maritime enterprise. On each of these grounds Britain was peculiarly favoured: its insular position, its deep harbours, and the commercial character of its people gave it structural advantages over France, whose continental commitments and divided coasts were structural limitations. The history of the naval wars, Mahan argued, was in large part the history of these advantages working themselves out.
The establishment of British command
The command of the sea which Britain enjoyed in the nineteenth century had been built up through the wars of the previous centuries. The decisive victories of the sailing-ship era — the defeat of the French at La Hogue, the successes of the Seven Years’ War under Pitt, in which Hawke’s victory at Quiberon Bay destroyed the French invasion fleet and the navy carried the conquest of Canada and India, and the naval supremacy of the wars against Napoleon, sealed at Trafalgar — established the Royal Navy as the dominant force of the seas. Trafalgar in particular destroyed the combined Franco-Spanish fleet and ended any serious threat of invasion; after 1805 the sea was open to British commerce and closed to the enemy for the rest of the war. James’s naval history records the campaigns and the battles by which this command was won; Clowes’s history of the Royal Navy traces the administration and the operations of the navy through the century.
Command of the sea and the existence of Britain
The command of the sea was not an ornament but the condition of Britain’s existence. As Alison insisted in surveying the effects of free trade, the maritime superiority of Britain was necessary to the very existence of a free-trading nation — the command of the sea that allowed the importation of food and the export of manufactures, that kept the island secure while its armies fought abroad, and that preserved its commerce and its colonies. The whole structure of Victorian prosperity — the free trade, the empire, the industrial supremacy — rested on the security that the navy provided. The blockade, the convoy, the ability to transport and supply armies across the globe, and the protection of the trade routes were the daily working of the command of the sea.
The principle and the changing means
Mahan drew from this history a permanent lesson: that the principles of naval warfare remain constant even as the means change, and that the destruction of the enemy’s fleet, the concentration of force, and the protection of commerce are the enduring objects of naval strategy. The principles of the sailing-ship era, he argued, yielded lessons of permanent value for the steam era — precedent might be obsolete, but principle endured. The transition of the 1850s and 1860s, from wooden walls to the ironclad and from sail to steam, tested the navy’s command of the sea under new conditions; the command itself, and the idea that it was the foundation of British power, were the enduring inheritance of the age. Within the period 1800–1865 the command of the sea, won at Trafalgar and maintained through the peace and the Crimean War, was the great fact of British naval and imperial existence.

concepts/corn-laws.title: The Corn Laws
concepts/corn-laws.content:
The Corn Laws
The Corn Laws were the protective duties on the importation of foreign grain — the system of agricultural protection that stood at the centre of English political economy from the end of the Napoleonic wars until the repeal of 1846. They were the bulwark of the landed interest and the emblem of protection; they kept the price of bread high, in the eyes of their opponents, for the benefit of the landlord; and they became the great question on which the manufacturing and commercial interest of the country made its stand for free trade. The Corn Laws, and the long struggle over their repeal, fixed the terms of English politics through the first half of the century, and their abolition in 1846 was the pivot of the age’s political economy.
The Corn Law of 1815
The immediate origin of the classic Corn Laws lay in the end of the Napoleonic wars. During the wars the high prices of the wartime corn trade had enriched the agricultural interest; with the return of peace and the prospect of foreign importation, the landlords sought to protect their rents by excluding the foreign corn. The Corn Law of 1815 prohibited the importation of foreign wheat until the domestic price reached eighty shillings a quarter — a measure that, in the eyes of its opponents, maintained the high price of bread for the benefit of the landed interest and at the expense of the poor. The Act was carried against the violent opposition of the manufacturing and working classes, and it opened the long controversy over protection that was to run for thirty years.
Protection and its effects
The operation of the Corn Laws was the subject of a perpetual contest. Their defenders — the agricultural interest, the landlords, the farmers — argued that they secured the independence of the country in its food supply, sustained the agriculture and the rural population, and maintained the prosperity of the land. Their opponents — the manufacturers, the merchants, the economists, and the working classes — argued that they raised the price of provisions, depressed the wages and the standard of living of the people, discouraged the commerce and manufactures of the country, and enriched the landlord at the expense of the community. Tooke’s history of prices examined in detail the influence of the corn laws on prices, the seasons and the crops, and the state of the circulation; Martineau traced the agricultural distress, the Corn Bill debates, and the standing burden of the duties. The sliding scale, adopted in the 1820s, which varied the duty with the price of corn, mitigated but did not end the controversy.
The Anti-Corn-Law League and the repeal
In 1838 the Anti-Corn-Law League was founded in Manchester, and under Cobden and Bright it turned the demand for repeal into a great popular agitation — raising funds, registering freeholders in the manufacturing districts, and propagating free-trade doctrine through lectures, pamphlets, and the Economist. The League made the corn laws the central question of English politics. The potato blight in Ireland in 1845 supplied the decisive occasion: Peel, convinced that the free importation of food was a national necessity, carried the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846 — a measure that split the Conservative Party and destroyed his government. The repeal, effected with a measure of compensation to the landed interest, was the triumph of free trade and the end of the protective system.
Significance
The Corn Laws were the emblem of the old order, and their repeal the great turning-point of the century’s political economy. They embodied the dominance of the landed interest and the principle of protection; their abolition embodied the ascendancy of the manufacturing and commercial interest and the principle of free trade. The struggle over the Corn Laws — the Corn Law of 1815, the sliding scale, the League’s agitation, and the repeal of 1846 — determined the direction of English policy for the rest of the century, and the repeal fixed free trade as the settled policy of the British state. Within the period 1800–1865 the Corn Laws are, with parliamentary reform, the great subject of the age’s political contention.

concepts/country-banks.title: Country Banks
concepts/country-banks.content:
Country Banks
The country banks of England were the note-issuing bankers of the provinces — the private houses and, from 1826, the joint-stock companies that supplied the greater part of England outside London with its paper circulation. Their notes were the ordinary money of the shopkeeper, the farmer, and the manufacturer; their solvency and their amount were the standing anxiety of English monetary politics from the late eighteenth century to the Bank Charter Act of 1844 and beyond. The country bank stood between the single national issuer and the local economy, drawing up the surplus capital of one district and releasing it for trade and industry in another, expanding and contracting as local business required — a “beautiful system,” in Gilbart’s phrase, that the currency reformers distrusted and eventually shackled.
Goldsmiths, Restriction, and the multiplication of banks
Country bank notes began as goldsmiths’ notes. After Charles I seized merchants’ deposits in the Tower mint in 1640, and after apprentices proved unsafe custodians during the Civil War, merchants lodged their money with goldsmiths, who borrowed and lent, took rents, advanced on the taxes to the Crown, and issued receipts that passed from hand to hand. Statutes long spoke of “bankers’ or goldsmiths’ notes”; Irish acts of 1709 and 1729 treated such notes like inland bills and punished forgery. After the Bank of England’s foundation in 1694 its notes gradually superseded the goldsmiths’, and banking separated from the goldsmith’s craft, though many London bankers still belonged to the Goldsmiths’ Company at mid-century.
Authentic continuous statistics of country banking are scarce for the early period. Few country banks existed before the American war; they multiplied after it, suffered heavily in the panic of 1793 (twenty-two bankruptcies), and expanded rapidly after the Bank Restriction Act of 1797 suspended cash payments. From 1808 note-issuing banks took annual licenses; stamp duty on notes dated from 1804 and was raised in 1808 and 1815. Parliament had barred notes under twenty shillings in 1775 and under £5 in 1777; Restriction reopened £1 and £2 issues, which continued toward the 1833 expiry of the Bank’s charter, until after the panic of 1825 the government stopped stamps under £5 and required existing small notes to cease by 1829. The speculation before 1825 was laid at the country banks’ door; the legislative answer was to abolish the small note, to allow banks of more than six partners beyond sixty-five miles from London, and to draw the Bank of England into provincial branches.
Lancashire and the special case of bills of exchange
Lancaster — above all Manchester and Liverpool — formed a province apart. Little country paper and few Bank of England notes circulated there; trade ran mainly on bills of exchange endorsed from hand to hand. Large notes for customs duties and small notes for wages came from London; manufacturers and dealers settled among themselves on London-payable bills. After 1826, Bank of England branches at Manchester and Liverpool, and joint-stock banks that took Bank of England paper at a preferential discount rather than issuing their own, displaced much of the bill circulation. With the weak private banks gone or merged, and notes under £5 abolished, a “secure” country circulation seemed at last achieved — until the later panics shifted the indictment from safety to excess and to regulation.
Excess, ill-regulation, and the bankers’ defence
In late 1836 another panic produced a charge, aimed especially at the new joint-stock banks, not of unsafety but of excess. Unlike 1825, when circulation could only be guessed from stamps, Lord Althorp’s Act of 1833 forced quarterly averages of weekly circulation into the Stamp Office and the London Gazette. Those returns showed the country circulation up by early 1836, and contemporaneous speculation and year-end panic were blamed on the notes. In 1839 the complaint changed again: the country circulation was ill-regulated — it did not move with the Bank of England’s gold, nor even with its notes, as the political economists required. A Commons committee on banks of issue sat in 1840–41; its practical fruit was the weekly returns of 1841.
The country bankers answered that London failures were relatively worse; that the great fluctuations began with influential merchants in the great cities and with the Bank of England’s own issues, not in country channels — the Liverpool failures of a few houses ran to seven or eight millions where country notes never circulated; that country issues promoted domestic production and had less power to throw the exchanges; and that to force miners and manufacturers into direct contact with exchange-regulating operations, without the cushion of local circulation, would be hazardous. Gilbart repeated their case with evident sympathy, noting that the charge of excess in 1836 and of ill-regulation in 1839 had each, in turn, been made to answer political ends.
The Act of 1844 and the fixed maximum
The Bank Charter Act of 1844 answered chiefly the charge of excess. It forbade any new bank of issue; fixed each existing English bank’s maximum at its average for the twelve weeks ending 27 April 1844; required weekly averages; and imposed a penalty equal to the excess for any four-week excess. Increasing partners beyond six, certain unions, bankruptcy, or ceasing to issue extinguished the right forever. The certified totals settled near £5,150,000 for private and £3,500,000 for joint-stock banks — 205 private and 72 joint-stock banks of issue in all.
The country circulation had already fallen sharply between 1839 and 1843, from about £11,700,000 to about £7,700,000. Bankers blamed dull trade and low corn prices; Gilbart added lasting causes: banks swapping their own notes for Bank of England paper under advantageous contracts; railways returning notes faster; the penny post of 1840 and letter registration speeding the return of rivals’ notes to London; and the spread of deposit accounts and cheques instead of pocket notes. Even without the Act, he thought, actual issues would not have recovered their former peaks — a hard maximum on a seasonal series forces the average below the ceiling, the maximum is sliced among many banks each keeping a safety margin, and a penalty equal to the whole excess made prudence keep issues well under the line.
Deposit banking and the economics of the note
Restriction showed itself in attempted evasions — a circular under Sir Charles Wood, note-like cheques on penny stamps later stopped by stamp law; in fourth-week dips when banks pulled in their own paper and fetched £5 and £10 Bank notes from London to hold their averages; and in joint-stock banks that issued only at some branches and used Bank of England notes elsewhere. Branch Bank of England circulation rose as country issues fell — country about £11,700,000 with branches £3,500,000 in 1836, against country about £7,700,000 with branches £6,500,000 in 1846. Yet the deposit system softened much of the pressure: once notes lodged with bankers and payments moved by cheque and clearing, transfers replaced note circulation. London joint-stock deposits had already passed £22,000,000 while the Bank of England’s private deposits rose from about £5,000,000 to £12,000,000; Gilbart believed similar deposit growth was general in the provinces without extinguishing the private banks.
The country “laws of the currency”
From the monthly averages Gilbart derived what he called the “laws of the currency” for each circulation. The English country note obeyed a single annual circuit — lowest about the end of August, rising through November (with a slight December reaction) to a peak in April, then down again to August — governed by the agricultural and local trade seasons, not by dividend dates. This was the pattern of a circulation rooted in the country’s own business: harvest payments, fair and market weeks, the local round of debt and credit. It was a law peculiar to the country banks, and Gilbart’s central argument was that these several laws could not be forced into one amalgamated system without wrecking the local machinery that moved capital from district to district as trade required. The Act of 1844 capped the height of the country wave; the tables of 1854 showed the same seasons still governing it.
Extinction and the eroding privilege
Because lapsed issues could not revive, the fixed maximum eroded. By 1854 thirty-seven private banks and seven joint-stock banks had ceased to issue, cutting the certified issue from about £8,650,000 to about £7,940,000. Topographically, inside the sixty-five-mile London circle there was no joint-stock bank of issue and no provincial Bank of England branch of the type under discussion; forty-seven private banks there held about £1,300,000 authorized issue; outside, 120 private banks held about £3,310,000 and sixty-five joint-stock banks about £3,330,000. The average authorized size of private banks was nearly the same inside and outside the circle, near £27,700. For actual circulation in 1853 the private banks ran further below authorization than the joint-stock banks, and private banks inside the circle further below than those outside — the joint-stock actuals often in the high eighties or low nineties per cent of authorization in peak months, the private banks inside the circle nearer the mid-seventies. Gilbart’s recommendations for redress — twelve-month averages, restoration of lapsed rights under expiring agency agreements, permission to exceed the maximum against gold or Bank notes, and the union of issuing banks — were designed to arrest a process he thought needless and damaging.

concepts/currency-vs-banking-school.title: The Currency School and the Banking School
concepts/currency-vs-banking-school.content:
The Currency School and the Banking School
The currency controversy of the 1830s and 1840s divided British monetary thought into two great schools, whose contest produced the Bank Charter Act of 1844 and the debate over its operation that lasted through the crisis of 1847 and beyond. The currency school, led by Samuel Jones Loyd (Lord Overstone), Robert Torrens, and in Parliament by Sir Robert Peel, held that the note circulation ought to vary exactly as a purely metallic circulation would — that every note in circulation should represent either bullion or a fixed legal maximum. The banking school, led by Thomas Tooke and William Newmarch and joined in practical spirit by James William Gilbart, denied that the note issue was the cause of price movements and panics, insisted on the distinction between money and credit, and held that the convertibility of the note was the sufficient safeguard. The Act of 1844 was the currency school’s victory; the history of prices was the banking school’s long answer.
The currency principle
The currency principle rested on a simple and compelling analogy. If the whole circulation were metallic — gold and silver coin alone — its amount would vary only with the influx and efflux of bullion: the country could never pay out more than it had, and a drain of gold would automatically contract the money in circulation. Paper money, the currency school argued, ought to imitate this exact behaviour, or it would become the engine of over-issue, rising prices, and speculative panic. Every note beyond the fixed fiduciary maximum should therefore be covered pound for pound by bullion in the Bank’s vaults, and the note circulation should rise and fall mechanically with the reserve. Peel, in the debates of May 1844, insisted on the fixed metallic standard as the only sure regulator, and the Act embodied the principle by dividing the Bank into Issue and Banking departments and by fixing the country issues at their April 1844 averages. Tooke’s objection was fundamental: the analogy was false, because the note was not the only or the chief medium of exchange, and because the amount of the circulation did not govern prices but was governed by them.
The banking-school critique
The banking school denied the premise. Tooke distinguished sharply between money — the medium of exchange, of which the note was part — and paper credit, the vast fabric of deposits, bills of exchange, and bank accommodation that rested on confidence but did not circulate as coin. The error of confounding paper credit with paper money lay, he argued, at the root of the currency principle and of the evils its disciples hoped to cure. The amount of the note circulation was not an independent cause of prices; it was the effect of the state of trade, of prices, and of the exchanges. Money flowed into circulation when trade wanted it and drained away when it did not, and no law of issue could or should reverse that order. A metallic circulation, so far from being the type of perfection, was itself subject to drains, and the attempt to make paper imitate it mechanically served only to aggravate pressure in a crisis.
The history of prices supplied the evidence. From the Restriction through resumption and the successive panics, Tooke traced the concurrence of prices, circulation, and the rate of interest, and found that the note issue expanded and contracted with the state of trade rather than leading it. The drain of gold in 1847, he argued, arose from the state of the exchanges and of trade — the railway mania and the failure of the harvest — not from over-issue of notes; and the Act of 1844, far from averting the crisis, intensified it by denying the Bank the power to relieve the discount market when the Banking Department’s reserve ran low. He compared the crisis of 1847 with that of 1825, and traced the difference to the working of the new law. Peel, defending the Act on 3 December 1847, maintained that its machinery had saved the convertibility of the note; the government’s sanction to exceed the statutory limit was, in the banking-school view, an admission that the principle would not work in a real emergency.
The practical, statistical position
Gilbart’s position was the statistical and practical one of the banker rather than the theorist. He welcomed the transfer of the currency question from faction to statistics, and he set out, in the seasonal “laws of the currency,” the evidence that each circulation — the Bank’s dividend tides, the English country circuit, the Scottish and Irish rhythms — obeyed laws peculiar to itself and could not be forced into one amalgamated system without wrecking the local machinery of country banking. The currency school’s remedy, a single national issue governed mechanically by gold, ignored the real work of the note in moving capital from district to district as trade required. Gilbart did not defend over-issue; he accepted the need for the Bank’s convertibility and for the country maximum. But his reforms — twelve-month averages, restoration of lapsed rights, permission to exceed the maximum against gold or Bank notes held, and the union of issuing banks — were the amendments of a man who believed the Act had overshot its mark, capping the height of the seasonal waves without serving the country’s circulation. Tooke supplied the theory of that amendment; Gilbart supplied the statistics.
The issue and its legacy
The controversy was never wholly resolved in the period. The Act of 1844 remained on the statute book and the currency principle remained the official doctrine, vindicated by its defenders in 1847 and reaffirmed at each subsequent test; the banking-school critique survived as the classic indictment, revived whenever the Bank’s machinery proved too rigid for the wants of trade. The contest fixed the terms in which all later discussion of the currency, the country banks, and the management of the Bank of England was carried on — the distinction between money and credit, the question whether the issue or the rate of interest is the regulator, and the rival claims of a single national issuer and of the local banks of the provinces.

concepts/engineering-and-steam.title: Engineering, Steam, and the Industrial Revolution
concepts/engineering-and-steam.content:
Engineering, Steam, and the Industrial Revolution
The industrial transformation of Britain rested on the work of its engineers — the builders of the canals, the roads, the bridges, the harbours, the lighthouses, and the steam engines that remade the face of the country and powered its industries. Samuel Smiles’ Lives of the Engineers recorded these men and their works, and from his volumes the history of British engineering in the century can be traced: from the earliest drainage and canal works, through the great civil engineers who built the roads and bridges and harbours, to the invention and perfection of the steam engine and the locomotive. The engineer, the self-taught man of mechanical genius, was the type of the age, and the works he built — the canals and railways, the bridges and harbours, the engines of the mills and the mines — were the physical foundation of Victorian prosperity.
The earliest engineering: drainage, water, and canals
The history of British engineering, as Smiles traced it, began with the works that reclaimed and watered the land. Vermuyden drained the Fens; Myddelton brought the New River to London; Perry repaired the Dagenham Breach; and Brindley, the first of the great canal builders, cut the canals that bound the industrial Midlands and the north together and opened the inland commerce of the country. These early engineers, many of them self-taught, established the profession and the methods on which the later works were built. The canal system, above all, was the first great transformation of inland communication — the means by which coal, iron, and goods were carried from the producing districts to the markets and the ports, and the indispensable foundation of the early industrial revolution.
The great civil engineers: Smeaton, Rennie, Metcalfe, and Telford
The age of the civil engineers followed. Smeaton built the third Eddystone Lighthouse and carried out numerous harbour, canal, and bridge works; Rennie built Waterloo, Southwark, and London Bridge, the London and Liverpool docks, and the fen drainage works, and developed the dredging machine and the hollow quay wall. Metcalfe, the blind road-builder, and Telford, the greatest of the road and bridge engineers, transformed the communications of the kingdom — the roads, the bridges, the Highland works, the Caledonian Canal, the Menai and Conway bridges, and the Holyhead road. These men were the builders of the infrastructure of the age, and their works — the harbours, lighthouses, bridges, and roads — carried the commerce and the travellers of the growing nation.
The steam engine: Boulton and Watt
The central invention of the age was the steam engine. Its history, as Smiles traced it, reached its climax in the partnership of James Watt and Matthew Boulton. Watt, the mathematical instrument maker of Glasgow, invented the separate condenser and made the steam engine a practical and economical source of power; Boulton, the Birmingham manufacturer, founded the Soho Manufactory and carried the condensing engine into the Cornish mines and, with the rotary engine, into the mills of the country. The partnership defended the patent against infringers, established the steam engine as the motive power of the industrial revolution, and produced, through William Murdock and the Soho works, the beginnings of gas-lighting. From the condensing engine of Watt and Boulton descended the steam power that drove the factories, the mines, the ships, and the locomotives of the nineteenth century.
The locomotive and the railways
The steam engine reached its most celebrated application in the locomotive. George and Robert Stephenson, carrying forward the work of Trevithick, Blenkinsop, and Hedley, perfected the locomotive, built the Stockton & Darlington and Liverpool & Manchester railways, and created the railway system that bound the country together. The railway, the great engineering and commercial phenomenon of the age, was the culmination of the work of the engineers and the means by which the industrial revolution transformed the whole of society. From the canals of Brindley to the locomotives of the Stephensons, the engineers remade the country.
The engineer and the age
The significance of engineering and of the engineers lay in the transformation they wrought. The works of the engineers — the canals, roads, bridges, harbours, lighthouses, steam engines, and railways — were the physical foundation of British industrial and commercial supremacy, the means by which the coal and iron of the country were exploited, its goods carried, and its power developed. And the engineers themselves, many of them self-taught men of the people, were the type of the age — the embodiment of the industry, perseverance, and mechanical genius that Smiles celebrated and that the Victorians prized. Within the period 1800–1865 engineering and steam stand at the centre of the story of industrial revolution, the work of the hands and minds that made the modern world.

concepts/free-trade.title: Free Trade
concepts/free-trade.content:
Free Trade
Free trade was the great economic doctrine of the Victorian age — the principle that the commerce of nations should be left free of protective duties, and that the prosperity of England was best served by the unrestricted exchange of its manufactures for the food and raw materials of the world. From the liberal Tory reforms of Huskisson in the 1820s, through the great fiscal reforms of Peel, to the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846 and of the Navigation Laws in 1849, the cause of free trade triumphed in the middle decades of the century and fixed the commercial policy of England for the rest of the Victorian age. Free trade was at once a doctrine of political economy and a popular movement — the creed of Cobden and Bright, the Manchester School, and the Anti-Corn-Law League — and its triumph marked the ascendancy of the manufacturing and commercial interest over the landed interest of the old order.
The liberal Tory beginnings
The movement toward free trade began within the liberal Toryism of the 1820s. Huskisson, as President of the Board of Trade under Liverpool, reduced the Navigation Acts, carried the Reciprocity Bill for reciprocal tariff arrangements with the maritime nations, and reduced the duties on a range of raw materials. The principles of political economy — the doctrines of Adam Smith and his successors, that commerce left free would enrich all parties — began to make their way into legislation. The trend was interrupted by the long dominance of protection, but it was never wholly stopped, and it prepared the ground for the great reforms of the following decades.
Peel and the fiscal revolution
The decisive progress came with Sir Robert Peel’s great ministry of 1841–46. Facing a country in deep financial difficulty, Peel revived the income tax to meet the deficit and set about a vast reduction of the tariff — remitting duties on raw materials and manufactured articles, and simplifying the whole fiscal system. His successive budgets of 1842, 1843, and 1844 showed the gradual conversion to free trade; the tariffs were purged — glass, auction duty, cotton, wool, sugar — and the principle of protection was abandoned in the details of taxation long before it was abandoned in the Corn Laws themselves. The conversion of Peel, and of the Conservative party, to free trade was the great political event of the mid-century.
The repeal of the Corn Laws and the Navigation Laws
The triumph of free trade came with the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846. The Anti-Corn-Law League, founded in Manchester in 1838 and led by Cobden and Bright, had made the cause of free trade a great popular movement; the potato blight in Ireland made repeal a national necessity; and Peel carried the abolition of the protective duties on grain against the mass of his own party. The repeal fixed free trade as the settled policy of the state. It was followed by the repeal of the Navigation Laws in 1849, which opened the British carrying trade to foreign shipping, and by Cobden’s commercial treaty with France in 1860 — the Anglo-French treaty that reduced the tariffs between the two nations. Alison, surveying the effects of free trade, traced its consequences for the prices of food, for national progress, and for the independence of the country, and insisted on the necessity of maritime superiority to the existence of a free-trading Britain.
Significance
Free trade was the creed of the Victorian age, and its triumph transformed the economy and the politics of England. It broke the power of the landed interest and the protective system, opened England to the commerce of the world, and made the country the workshop of the world and the entrepôt of its trade. It was the doctrine of the Manchester School and of the economists, the policy of Peel and Gladstone, and the settled principle of English commercial policy for the rest of the century. Within the period 1800–1865 the triumph of free trade is, with parliamentary reform, the great achievement of the age — the establishment of the commercial and liberal order on which Victorian prosperity rested.

concepts/ironclad-transition.title: The Ironclad Transition
concepts/ironclad-transition.content:
The Ironclad Transition
The ironclad transition was the great transformation of naval warfare in the middle decades of the nineteenth century — the replacement of the wooden line-of-battle ship and the sailing navy by the armoured, steam-driven ironclad, the ancestor of the modern warship. From the Warrior of 1860, the first British ironclad, through the development of armour, guns, turrets, and rams, the navy that had won its command of the sea under sail was remade under steam and iron. The transition was the most fundamental change in naval construction since the sailing-ship era began, and it tested the principles of sea power under entirely new conditions.
The coming of steam and iron
The command of the sea which the navy had won under sail was, by the middle of the century, being transformed by the two great inventions of the age: the steam engine and the iron hull. The Crimean War had shown the value of steam in the operations before Sebastopol, and the introduction of the screw propeller and the development of marine engines made steam a practical motive power for warships. The use of iron in shipbuilding, at first for the hulls of merchant ships and the smaller vessels, was extended to the great ships of war, and the French navy, in particular, began the construction of ironclad or cuirassé ships. Britain, whose naval supremacy rested on the wooden line of battle, was compelled to meet the challenge, and in 1860 the Warrior — the first British ironclad — was launched.
Reed’s survey of the ironclad fleet
The classic account of the British ironclad navy is Edward J. Reed’s Our Iron-Clad Ships (1869), written by the Chief Constructor of the Royal Navy (1863–1870), who was responsible for most of the designs he described. Reed surveyed every class of British ironclad from the Warrior through the Devastation-class monitors then under construction, defending the ironclad programme and providing detailed comparative data on armour, guns, speeds, handling, and cost. He traced the principal changes since the Warrior: from partial to continuous armour belts, from uniform to graduated armour thickness, from broadside-only fire to all-round fire, from long to short hulls, from V-shaped to U-shaped sections, and from overhanging to upright stems. He defended his ships against contemporary criticism, arguing that armour was not yet obsolete, that the gun-and-armour contest was still undecided, and that the navy was adapting to changing armour and guns.
Armour, guns, and the turret
The ironclad transition was driven by the contest between armour and guns. Armour thickness increased progressively — from the Warrior’s four inches through the Bellerophon’s six, the Hercules’s belt of nine, the Hotspur’s eleven, to the Glatton’s turret of fourteen — while the guns grew from the four-and-a-half-ton pieces of the Warrior to the twenty-five-ton guns of the Monarch and Captain and the thirty-ton guns of the Thunderer and Devastation. The central controversy of the transition was the turret versus the broadside: whether the guns should be carried in the broadside, as in the old ship of the line, or in revolving turrets, as in the monitors of the American Civil War and the designs of Captain Cowper Coles. Reed discussed the turret controversy at length, weighing the advantages of the small port and great training against the vulnerability of the turret ports and the risk of jamming, and comparing the Captain and the Monarch. The ram, revived as a weapon of war, and the conversion of the old line-of-battle ships into ironclads completed the transformation.
Significance
The ironclad transition marked the end of the old navy and the beginning of the new. It was the most fundamental change in naval construction since the sailing-ship era, and it carried the navy from the wooden walls that had won Trafalgar to the armoured, steam-driven ships of the modern era. The command of the sea which the navy had won under sail had to be maintained under steam and iron, and the ironclad transition was the means by which Britain preserved its naval supremacy through the transformation. Within the period 1800–1865 the transition belongs to its closing years — the introduction of the ironclad in 1860 and the beginning of the armoured fleet that would dominate the later Victorian Navy — but its principles, and the contest of armour and guns it set in motion, were to shape naval warfare for the rest of the century.
In the Sources

concepts/london-street-folk.title: London Street-Folk and the Labouring Poor
concepts/london-street-folk.content:
London Street-Folk and the Labouring Poor
The London street-folk and the labouring poor of the capital formed the great social subject of the mid-century — the vast population of the street-sellers, the costermongers, the casual labourers, the vagrants, and the criminal and destitute classes whose condition was laid open to the world by Henry Mayhew’s investigations. Mayhew, as Special Correspondent of the Morning Chronicle in 1850 and then in his encyclopaedic London Labour and the London Poor (1861–62), recorded the trades, the earnings, the habits, and the miseries of the London poor with a combination of first-hand testimony, statistics, and analysis that made his work the foundation of English social inquiry. The London of the 1840s and 1850s, one of the richest cities in the world, contained within itself a population living in conditions of poverty and insecurity that shocked and fascinated the age.
The Morning Chronicle survey
Mayhew’s investigation began in the Morning Chronicle in January–March 1850, in a series of letters by him as Special Correspondent. The letters explored the casual wards and the vagrancy of the metropolis — the evils of uncertain labour, the system of casual wards in the workhouses, and the class of habitual vagrants the system created; the geographical history of vagrancy and the effect of the Irish famine upon it; the causes of depredation, vagrancy, and mendicancy, drawing on the Constabulary Commissioners’ Report of 1839; the boot and shoe trade, slop work, and the sweated trades; the toy-makers and the doll manufacture; and the low lodging-houses in which the poor herded together. The letters were the raw material from which Mayhew built his greater work, and they established the method — the personal interview, the exact statement of earnings and expenditure, the statistical table — that made him the founder of the English social survey.
The street-folk
In London Labour and the London Poor Mayhew organised his investigation around the street-folk — the people who earned their living in the streets of London. The first volume covered the costermongers, the street-sellers of fish, fruit, vegetables, game, flowers, green stuff, eatables and drinkables, stationery and literature, and manufactured articles, together with the women and children who sold in the streets. The second volume continued the subject: the street-sellers of second-hand articles and live animals, the street-buyers, the street Jews, the street-finders and collectors, and the sanitary trades of the streets — the dust-yards, the sewers, the night-soil, the chimney-sweeps and the crossing-sweepers. The third volume carried the survey into the street trades and labour of the poor: the destroyers of vermin, the street-exhibitors and performers, the street-musicians and vocalists, the garret-masters and cheap cabinet-makers, the coal-heavers, ballast-men and dock-labourers, the cheap lodging-houses, the watermen, the omnibus and cab drivers, the carmen, the vagrants, and the ticket-of-leave men.
Those who will not work
The fourth and final volume turned to the criminal and destitute classes — “those that will not work”: the prostitutes, the thieves, the swindlers, the beggars, and the vagrants, with contributions by Bracebridge Hemyng on prostitution, John Binny on thieves and swindlers, Andrew Halliday on beggars, and the Rev. William Tuckniss on the charitable and reformatory agencies of London. Here Mayhew’s inquiry passed from the honest poor struggling for a living in the streets to the underworld of the metropolis — the women, the criminals, and the mendicants whom the philanthropists sought to reform and the police to control.
The condition of the labouring poor
The significance of Mayhew’s work lay in what it revealed about the condition of the labouring poor. It showed a population living in constant insecurity — dependent on casual and uncertain labour, at the mercy of the seasons and the trade, crowded into foul and disease-ridden districts, and separated by an abyss from the prosperity of the city that surrounded them. It recorded, with a precision never before attempted, the exact earnings of the trades, the cost of living, the diet, the lodging, and the habits of the poor; and it placed on record the testimony of the poor themselves, in their own words, as no earlier inquiry had done. The work stands at the head of the great Victorian social investigation — the inquiry into the condition of the people that fed the reforms of the century and that remains the indispensable record of what mid-Victorian London was really like.
