concepts/parliamentary-reform.title: Parliamentary Reform
concepts/parliamentary-reform.content:
Parliamentary Reform
Parliamentary reform in the United Kingdom between the Union and the mid-century meant the remaking of the House of Commons — the destruction of the rotten boroughs, the transfer of representation to the new manufacturing towns, and the widening of the franchise from the narrow body of electors of the old system toward a larger, and eventually a mass, electorate. It was the central constitutional question of the first half of the nineteenth century, agitated in the 1790s and again after the war, denied by the long Tory ascendancy, and at last carried by Earl Grey’s ministry in 1832 in the teeth of a national crisis. The Reform Act of 1832 settled the borough franchise on the £10 householder, opened seats to the industrial towns, and left the working classes — as Chartism was to insist — still outside the pale of representation.
The unreformed constitution
The House of Commons that entered the nineteenth century was the creation of an older England. The distribution of seats had been fixed in an age when the South, the agricultural counties, and the old corporate towns had carried the weight of population and wealth; by 1830 the industrial revolution had shifted population and commerce to the North and the Midlands, yet the representation had not followed. Nomination boroughs — seats owned outright by a patron — survived almost untouched: Old Sarum, a grassy mound with no inhabitants, still returned two members; Gatton was the standing example of a “pocket borough” bought and sold with the soil. Meanwhile Manchester, Birmingham, Leeds, and the other great manufacturing towns sent no member at all. The franchise itself was an incoherent patchwork of ancient customs — freemen, burgage-holders, potwallopers, scot-and-lot payers, £10 householders in some boroughs and resident householders in others — with no principle of uniformity behind it. Molesworth’s opening survey traced the long history of the question, from the Long Parliament and Cromwell through the elder and younger Pitt’s abortive schemes and the repressive legislation of the 1790s, and closed with the distress of 1829–30 that made reform a national demand.
The long denial and the prelude to crisis
Reform had been demanded and denied for a generation. The French Revolution had discredited it in the eyes of the governing classes and brought on the repression of the 1790s and the Six Acts after the war. The long Tory ascendancy under Liverpool had resisted every motion; the liberal Tories — Huskisson, Canning, and their school — had reformed commerce and administration but left the constitution untouched. Catholic Emancipation, wrung from Wellington’s ministry in 1829, broke the old alliance against change: it proved that the constitution could be altered when the crisis was sharp enough, and it alienated from the government a section of its own supporters. The death of George IV in June 1830 and the accession of William IV brought a general election; the July Revolution in France frightened the timid and encouraged the reformers; and agricultural distress, rick-burning, and the machine-breaking of the “Captain Swing” riots spread alarm through the southern counties. When Wellington declared in November 1830 that the existing system possessed the full and entire confidence of the country, and that he was not prepared to bring forward any measure of reform, his ministry fell, and Earl Grey — who had advocated reform since the 1790s — was summoned to form a government.
The Reform Bill crisis, 1830–32
Grey made reform a Cabinet question, and on 1 March 1831 Lord John Russell rose to introduce the first Reform Bill. The details of the scheme — the disfranchisement of the rotten boroughs, the enfranchisement of the new towns, the £10 householder franchise in the boroughs — were debated through a crisis that brought the country to the verge of convulsion. The Bill passed its second reading by a single vote, 302 to 301, on the night the strangers’ gallery was crowded with the people; it was then defeated in committee on General Gascoigne’s wrecking amendment. The ministry dissolved Parliament, and the general election of April–May 1831 returned a great reform majority. The second Bill passed the Commons by large majorities, only to be rejected by the Lords in October 1831 by a majority of forty-one, the bishops voting almost solidly against. Popular fury followed: riots at Derby and Nottingham, the burning of Nottingham Castle, the destruction of the Mansion House and the Bishop’s Palace in the Bristol riots, the breaking of the windows of anti-reform peers. The Political Unions — disciplined reform organisations that had spread from Thomas Attwood’s Birmingham Union across the country — threatened to march on London.
The crisis came to a head in the “Days of May” 1832. The third Reform Bill was introduced; the Lords, under Lord Lyndhurst’s lead, carried a motion to postpone the disfranchising clauses. The Grey ministry resigned, and the King sent for the Duke of Wellington — who failed to form a government, unwilling to take office on a reform basis and unable to command the support even of his own friends. Grey was recalled with the King’s reluctant promise to create enough peers to carry the Bill. The threat of the new creation was enough: the Tory peers abstained in great numbers, the Bill passed the Lords, and the Reform Act received the royal assent on 7 June 1832. Molesworth noted the mass abstention of the peers and the decisive force of the threatened creation; the “leap” had been made, and the constitution was remade.
The Reform Act of 1832
The Act disfranchised fifty-six rotten boroughs and reduced thirty more to a single member; it enfranchised forty-two new towns and extended the county representation; and it established the £10 householder franchise in the boroughs — the occupier of a house rated at £10 a year became an elector. The result was a wholesale redrawing of the electoral map of Britain and a decisive shift of power from the landed and closed boroughs to the middle classes of the towns. The first Reformed Parliament assembled in January 1833 with the reformers triumphant — the Conservative party (as the Tories now called themselves) reduced to about 150 members. Martineau’s account of the passage stresses both the revolutionary danger narrowly averted and the moderate character of the settlement: the Act enfranchised the middle-class householder and the substantial tenant, but left the town workman and the agricultural labourer without a vote. The agitation that had carried the Bill had been in part a middle- and working-class alliance; the settlement rewarded the one and disappointed the other.
The consolidation of reform
The years that followed consolidated the change. The first Reformed Parliament, against the background of the cholera epidemic and the financial difficulties of the government, carried the great measures of the reform era: the abolition of slavery in the British colonies (1833, with the £20,000,000 compensation to the owners), the Factory Act of 1833 limiting the hours of children, the New Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834, the renewal of the Bank of England and East India Company charters, and the Municipal Corporations Act of 1835, which swept away the corrupt self-perpetuating oligarchies of the old borough corporations and established elected town councils for 178 boroughs. The parties reshaped themselves — Tories as “Conservatives,” Whigs as “Reformers,” with a distinct Radical or “Destructive” section — and Peel, in the Tamworth Manifesto of 1834, accepted the Reform Act as final and promised moderate reform. The old order of the Pittites was literally dying off, as Martineau’s great necrology of the volume observed, and a generation of reformers was taking its place.
The unfinished settlement
The Reform Act was not the end of the question. The working classes, excluded from the £10 franchise, drew from the settlement the lesson of Chartism: that the Reform Act had transferred power from the landed aristocracy to the middle class and left the workman still unrepresented. The People’s Charter of 1838 demanded universal male suffrage, equal electoral districts, the ballot, annual parliaments, the abolition of the property qualification, and payment of members. The Chartist movement, with its monster meetings, its National Petition, the Newport rising of 1839, the Kennington Common meeting of 1848, and its eventual collapse, kept the demand alive through the 1830s and 1840s even as the reformed Parliament refused it. The £10 settlement of 1832 stood, in Martineau’s and Molesworth’s common telling, as the great constitutional turning-point of the age — the moment when the old constitution was broken and the long argument over who should vote, and how, entered its Victorian phase. Further widening — to the borough workman in 1867, the county labourer in 1884, and the women and mass electorate of 1918 — lay beyond the horizon of this period, but the Reform Act of 1832 set the direction of the whole.

concepts/public-credit-and-national-debt.title: Public Credit and the National Debt
concepts/public-credit-and-national-debt.content:
Public Credit and the National Debt
The national debt and the funding system were the great financial facts of the age — the vast accumulation of debt contracted in the wars of the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, and the system of government borrowing by which it was sustained. The debt, and the taxation required to service it, stood at the centre of the political economy of the period: to the state it was the foundation of public credit and the security of the fundholder; to its critics — from Hume to Cobbett and the radicals — it was the instrument by which the many laboured for the few, and the standing peril of national bankruptcy. The controversy over the debt, the funding system, and paper money ran through the whole period, and the writing of the age — from the Imlac tract of 1817 to the currency debates of the 1840s — was filled with its anxieties.
The growth of the debt
The national debt had grown through the wars of the eighteenth century and to an enormous height during the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars, when Britain borrowed on an unprecedented scale to carry on the struggle. The funding system — the borrowing of money on long-term annuities and the gradual redemption of the principal — had been the means of financing the wars, and by 1815 the debt stood at a colossal figure. The interest on the debt, and the taxation required to meet it, formed the great burden of the postwar state: the income tax, the assessed taxes, the duties on every article of consumption, and the standing weight of the taxation that pressed on the people. Martineau’s account of the postwar years records the enormous war debt, the challenge of demobilisation, and the state of the finances with which the Liverpool ministry had to struggle.
The critique of the funding system
The funding system and the debt were the subject of a powerful and continuing critique. David Hume, in his essay Of Public Credit (1752), had argued that national debts, if they grew too large, must eventually cause national bankruptcy — that the paper credit of the state would at last prove unable to bear its own weight. The Imlac tract of 1817, reprinting Hume’s essay with commentary, applied these principles to the post-1815 situation, and argued that a perseverance in the “Pitt and paper system” — the borrowing policy of Pitt and the paper money of the Restriction — must eventually produce a national bankruptcy, and that only parliamentary reform could avert the calamity. Cobbett and the radicals took up the same theme: the funding system was the means by which the fundholders, the placemen, and the pensioners battened on the labour of the people, and the “Old Corruption” of the state was built on the debt. The paper money of the Restriction — the inconvertible notes of the Bank of England — was denounced as the instrument of the system.
The resumption and the currency
The settlement of the currency after the war was bound up with the question of the debt. The resumption of cash payments in 1819–21 restored the convertibility of the note and re-adjusted the values of gold and paper, and the debates over the currency — the bullion controversy, the return to gold, and the later currency principle — turned on the relation of the note issue to the public credit and the state of the exchanges. Tooke’s history of prices traced the Bank of England’s advances to the government and the relation of the currency to the national finances. The management of the debt, the reduction of the interest, and the maintenance of public credit were the standing duties of the Treasury, and the public funds — the great market in which the debt was bought and sold — were the emblem of the country’s credit and the barometer of its fortunes.
Significance
Public credit and the national debt were the foundation and the anxiety of the Victorian state. The debt was at once the security of the fundholder and the burden of the taxpayer, the basis of the state’s borrowing power and the standing peril denounced by the critics of the funding system. The controversies over the debt and the currency — the fears of national bankruptcy, the defence of the funds, and the debates over the standard — ran through the whole period, and they shaped the financial policy of the age. Within 1800–1865 the question of public credit is central: it was the fiscal inheritance of the wars, the ground of the postwar taxation and discontent, and the frame within which the great currency and free-trade debates of the century were conducted.

concepts/responsible-government-colonies.title: Responsible Government in the Colonies
concepts/responsible-government-colonies.content:
Responsible Government in the Colonies
Responsible government was the great reform of the British colonial system in the middle decades of the nineteenth century — the extension to the colonies of the principle that the executive should command the confidence of the elected assembly, in the same manner as the British cabinet is responsible to the House of Commons. Advocated in the wake of Lord Durham’s Report on the affairs of British North America (1839), and expounded with the greatest force by Charles Buller, the doctrine of responsible government transformed the government of the self-governing colonies, reconciled them to the empire, and laid the foundation of the later Commonwealth. It was the application of the Westminster model of cabinet government to the colonies, and the answer to the chronic conflict between the colonial legislatures and the executive that had threatened to drive the colonies, as it had once driven the American colonies, into separation.
The problem of colonial government
The British colonies in the early nineteenth century were governed, in their internal affairs, by a system that combined a representative assembly with an executive responsible not to that assembly but to the governor and, through him, to the Colonial Office in London. The result was chronic conflict: the assembly and the executive vied for power, the assemblies used the power of supply to wrest control, the real authority rested in an irresponsible governor and his clique, and the system, as Buller argued, produced nothing but paralysis and discontent. The Canadian rebellions of 1837–38 brought the question to a crisis, and Lord Durham’s mission to Canada — to which Buller was secretary — produced the famous Report on the Affairs of British North America (1839), which recommended the reform of the colonial government.
The doctrine of responsible government
Buller’s Responsible Government for Colonies (1840) expounded the doctrine that Durham’s Report had recommended. He defined responsible government as requiring that the colonial executive should be composed of persons enjoying the confidence of the majority in the representative assembly, with the governor selecting his advisers accordingly. He insisted that this was the English constitution transplanted — not republicanism, not an elective executive on the American model — and he answered the objections to it: that it would lead to republicanism (it was merely the English system), that it would weaken the governor’s authority (it would strengthen it by placing him above party), and that it would dissolve the imperial tie. He argued, on the contrary, that responsible government was the surest means of keeping the colonies within the empire, and that the American Revolution itself was the proof that attempting to govern colonies without local responsibility led to separation.
Colonial dependence and imperial supremacy
A central point of Buller’s doctrine — and of the practice that followed — was that responsible government was compatible with imperial supremacy. There were certain affairs on which the Imperial Government must have the final voice: foreign relations, war and peace, the regulation of trade, and the disposal of the public lands. These reserved powers were compatible with full local responsibility in internal affairs. The distinction between imperial and local matters, and the reservation of the former to the mother country, was the key to the working of the system: the colonies governed themselves in their own affairs, while the empire retained the control of the questions that affected the whole. This was the principle that made possible the reconciliation of colonial self-government with the continuance of the imperial connection.
The establishment of the system
The doctrine of responsible government, carried into practice in British North America in the 1840s and gradually extended to the other self-governing colonies, transformed the colonial system. The colonies of Canada, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island, and later the Australian and New Zealand colonies, obtained the right to govern themselves in their internal affairs, with the governor acting on the advice of ministers who commanded the confidence of the assembly. The chronic conflict of the old system gave way to orderly self-government, and the colonies, reconciled to the empire, remained within it. The constitutional theory of the relation — imperial supremacy reserved, local responsibility conceded — became the basis of the later Commonwealth.
Significance
Responsible government was the greatest reform of the colonial system in the century, and it stands at the head of the history of the modern Commonwealth. It solved the problem that had destroyed the first British empire — the attempt to govern colonies without local responsibility — by conceding to the colonies the self-government in their own affairs that they demanded, while retaining the imperial connection. Within the period 1800–1865 it belongs to the middle years, when the lessons of the Canadian crisis and Durham’s Report were put into practice; and it represents the liberal and constitutional side of the British empire, the principle that the colonies were to be governed not by coercion but by consent.
In the Sources

concepts/socialist-thought-communist-man.title: Socialist Thought and the Communist Manifesto (1848)
concepts/socialist-thought-communist-man.content:
Socialist Thought and the Communist Manifesto (1848)
The middle of the century saw the first great statement of modern socialism in the Communist Manifesto of 1848, the work of Karl Marx and Frederick Engels, written as the programme of the Communist League on the eve of the European revolutions. The Manifesto — with its declaration that the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles, its analysis of the bourgeoisie and the proletariat, and its closing summons to the working men of all countries to unite — was the most influential political tract of the modern age. It grew directly out of the observation of the industrial working class and its conditions, of which Engels’ Condition of the Working Class in England (1845) was the classic study, and it stood in the stream of the working-class movements — Chartism above all — that the English radical and labour agitation of the 1830s and 1840s had produced.
The condition of the working class
The intellectual foundation of the socialist critique was laid by the observation of the condition of the industrial working class. Engels, in his Condition of the Working Class in England (1845), written from his two-year observation of Manchester and the English industrial towns, described the factory system, the great towns, the Irish immigration, the mining and agricultural proletariats, and the attitude of the bourgeoisie, and argued that the condition of the working class was the inevitable product of the class antagonism of industrial capitalism. He treated Chartism as the political expression of the working-class movement and the trade unions as its economic form. The book, with its statistical and descriptive power, supplied the empirical foundation for the socialist theory that Marx and Engels were to announce.
The Communist Manifesto
The Communist Manifesto was commissioned at the November 1847 Congress of the Communist League in London, and its manuscript was sent to London for printing a few weeks before the February Revolution of 1848. Its first chapter, “Bourgeois and Proletarians,” opens with the famous declaration that the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles, and traces the rise of the bourgeoisie, its revolutionary role in destroying the feudal order, and the creation of its own gravedigger, the modern working class or proletariat. The second chapter, “Proletarians and Communists,” sets out the relation of the Communists to the working class and their programme — the abolition of private property, the centralisation of credit and production, free education, and the rest. The third chapter, “Socialist and Communist Literature,” attacks the rival socialist schools of the age; and the fourth, “Position of the Communists in Relation to the Various Existing Opposition Parties,” closes with the summons, “Working Men of All Countries, Unite!” The later prefaces of 1872–1893 added the lessons of the Paris Commune and the record of the Manifesto’s worldwide circulation.
The significance
The Manifesto and the socialist theory it announced stood, in the English context of the period, in a definite relation to the movements of the age. It was the intellectual statement of the class antagonism that Engels had observed in England and that Chartism had expressed politically; it was addressed to a workers’ movement, the Communist League, and to the revolutionary year 1848; and it announced, in its closing summons, the international unity of the working class. Within the period 1800–1865 the Manifesto belongs to its closing years, the product of the observation and the agitation of the English and European working classes, and the first great statement of the socialism that was to transform the politics of the later nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Its immediate effect in England was small beside the collapse of Chartism in 1848; its lasting effect was immense, as the classic programme of modern communism.

entities/babbage-charles.title: Charles Babbage (1791–1871)
entities/babbage-charles.content:
Charles Babbage
Charles Babbage (1791–1871) was the mathematician, inventor, and scientific reformer whose Reflections on the Decline of Science in England (1830) was the most influential attack ever made on the condition of English science, and whose Difference and Analytical Engines made him one of the founders of the modern computer. A man of extraordinary mechanical and mathematical genius, Babbage devoted his life to two great causes: the advancement of science by the reform of its institutions, and the construction of calculating machines that would do the work of the human computer without error. His criticism of the Royal Society, though it made him enemies, helped to modernise the organisation of English science; his calculating engines, though never completed in his lifetime, were the true ancestors of the computing machines of the twentieth century.
The critique of English science
Babbage’s Reflections on the Decline of Science in England, and on Some of Its Causes (1830) compared the state of English science with that of France, Germany, and Italy, and found it wanting. He attacked the Royal Society for its administration, for the abuse of its fellowship elections, and for its neglect of science; he criticised the learned societies and the universities of Oxford and Cambridge for their failure to teach and encourage science; and he denounced the lack of government patronage compared with the Continent. The work, grounded in statistical tables of scientific publications and the membership of the Royal Society, was a polemic for the reorganisation and public support of science — a reform manifesto for the scientific institutions of England. It made Babbage the leading spokesman for the advancement of science, and its influence was lasting, even where its specific accusations were disputed.
The calculating engines
Babbage’s greatest and most characteristic work was his lifelong attempt to construct calculating machines. The Difference Engine, a machine to compute and print mathematical tables by the method of differences, occupied him through the 1820s and 1830s; the Analytical Engine, a far more ambitious machine designed to perform any mathematical operation on punched cards — the true ancestor of the programmable computer — was his later and still grander conception. Neither machine was completed in his lifetime, defeated by the immense difficulty of mechanical precision and by the limits of the engineering of his age; but the designs, and the labour Babbage devoted to them, established the principles of the modern computer. The failure of the government to continue its support of the Difference Engine was one of the grievances that embittered him, and it fed his conviction of the neglect of science in England.
Significance
Babbage’s significance in the period is double. As the author of the Decline of Science, he was the great critic and reformer of the scientific institutions of England, the man who forced the country to confront the inferiority of its scientific organisation and who prepared the way for the reform of the Royal Society and the growth of government support for science. As the inventor of the calculating engines, he was a figure of extraordinary originality and foresight — a genius whose ideas were before his time, and whose unfinished machines were the ancestors of the computers of the future. He stands, with the scientific reformers and the engineers of the industrial age, among the men who made modern science, and his life was the type of the brilliant, embattled, and insufficiently supported English scientific genius.
Sources

Babbage, Charles. Reflections on the Decline of Science in England (1830). The critique of the Royal Society and English science.

entities/canning.title: George Canning (1770–1827)
entities/canning.content:
George Canning
George Canning (1770–1827) was the most brilliant and original statesman of the liberal Tory school — the minister who transformed British foreign policy in the 1820s, broke with the Holy Alliance, and gave the age its celebrated doctrine of recognising de facto governments. His career was a long and bitter struggle against the prejudices of the old Tory party and the enmity of men like Eldon and Wellington; he was long kept out of the highest office by the hostility of the King and his rivals, and when at last he became Prime Minister in 1827 he held the post only a few months before his death. He stood, in the words of the age, for the liberal and progressive side of Conservatism — for the New World called into existence to redress the balance of the Old.
The long struggle and the rise
Canning entered Parliament as a follower of Pitt, and made his name as an orator of extraordinary brilliance — eloquent, witty, and combative. He held office under the Tories, serving as Foreign Secretary and as President of the Board of Control, but his liberal opinions and his personal unpopularity among the more rigid Tories long excluded him from the leadership to which his talents entitled him. In the years after the war he stood apart, distrusted by the old guard, while the Liverpool ministry ran its course. His opportunity came with the retirement of Lord Sidmouth and the suicide of Lord Londonderry (Castlereagh) in 1822, when he at last became Foreign Secretary and entered the cabinet.
The transformation of foreign policy
As Foreign Secretary from 1822, Canning broke decisively with the policy of the Holy Alliance — the concert of the continental monarchies which, under Metternich’s guidance, suppressed liberal movements across Europe. When the French invaded Spain in 1823 to restore the Bourbon monarchy, Canning refused British participation and opposed the intervention; his great speech on the Spanish question proclaimed the principle that England would not join in crushing a nation’s liberties. His most celebrated stroke was the recognition of the South American republics — Argentina, Colombia, Mexico — which had thrown off Spanish rule. With the British navy keeping the European powers from intervening in the Americas, Canning declared that he had “called the New World into existence to redress the balance of the Old.” He protected Portugal from Spanish invasion, asserted British commercial interests, and made British foreign policy, for the first time since the war, independent and distinctly liberal.
The premiership and death
The culmination and tragedy of Canning’s career came in 1827. When Lord Liverpool was struck down by a stroke, Canning was summoned to form a ministry — but the old Tories, led by Wellington, Eldon, and Peel, refused to serve under him, and the Tory party split. Canning formed his government with the help of the Whigs, but the strain of the political warfare and the immense labour of office destroyed his health. He died in August 1827, after only a few months as Prime Minister. His death, at the height of his powers, was a national loss; Lord Goderich briefly headed the ministry he left, but it fell apart, and Wellington succeeded. Canning’s significance in the period is that of the statesman who turned British policy in a liberal direction — away from the Holy Alliance and toward the support of constitutional and commercial liberty — and whose brief, brilliant career pointed the way from the old Toryism to the liberal conservatism of the later age.
Sources

Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vols. II–III. Canning’s foreign policy, his premiership, and his death.
Alison, Sir Archibald. History of Europe, Vol. II. Canning and the diplomacy of the 1820s.

entities/carlile-richard.title: Richard Carlile (1790–1843)
entities/carlile-richard.content:
Richard Carlile
Richard Carlile (1790–1843) was the most resolute and the most persecuted of the English radical publishers — a man who spent the greater part of his adult life in prison for the cause of the freedom of the press. The publisher of The Republican and of the works of Thomas Paine, Carlile carried the fight for the liberty of publication through the repression of the postwar years, defying the government, the Society for the Suppression of Vice, and the courts. His gaol-written numbers of The Republican, produced from Dorchester Gaol while his wife and sister suffered imprisonment in the same cause, made him the emblem of the radical press — a man who would not be silenced, and whose prisons became the platform from which he wrote.
The radical publisher
Carlile began as a tinplate worker who was converted to radical politics by the agitation of the postwar years, and who became a bookseller and publisher in Fleet Street. His shop became the centre of the radical and freethought press, the place where the works of Paine and the radical journals were sold in defiance of the government. In 1819, in the aftermath of the Manchester massacre, Carlile’s The Republican carried the first extended radical response to the killings — his letters of 30 August and 1 September to the Prince Regent and Lord Sidmouth, denouncing the “Magisterial and Yeomanry Assassins of Manchester” and printing in full the Sidmouth–Derby letter in which the Regent thanked the magistrates for their “prompt, decisive, and efficient measures.” For these letters, and for the broader campaign of the radical press, Carlile was prosecuted and imprisoned.
The long imprisonment
Carlile’s imprisonment for publishing Paine’s theological works and related tracts began in 1819 and continued for years, much of it at Dorchester Gaol. From prison he continued to write and publish: the numbers of The Republican were produced in gaol, and his shop in Fleet Street, kept open by his family, continued to sell the prosecuted works. His wife and sister were imprisoned in the same cause — his sister for twenty-one months. The Republican of 1823, written from Dorchester in the fourth and fifth years of his confinement, was dedicated “To Spaniards in Exile,” after the collapse of the Spanish constitution, and carried his war against the Vice Society, his addresses to the Methodists, the Church clergy, the Quakers, and the Swedenborgians, and his advocacy of materialism and of “morality uncontaminated with religion.” Through it all he defied his persecutors, challenging the Vice Society to raise prosecutors as fast as he could raise defendants.
The freethinker and republican
Carlile’s radicalism was at once political and religious. He was a republican — urging the Spanish exiles to aim at an avowed republic rather than constitutional monarchy — and a freethinker, denying the supernatural and advocating a morality independent of religion. His Republican was not only a political journal but a campaign for the liberty of thought and speech, a campaign conducted, as he insisted, as “Christianity’s Prisoner.” His constructive programme, in the later numbers, pointed toward the Mechanics’ Institutes and the “temples of science” as the substitutes for public worship — the education of the people in place of their indoctrination.
Significance
Carlile’s significance in the period lies in his place at the centre of the struggle for the freedom of the press. Where others fled or yielded, he resisted — accepting imprisonment, enduring it, and continuing to publish from within the prison walls. His trials and imprisonment, and the open sale of the prosecuted works in London throughout his confinement, made him a standing demonstration of the limits of the government’s power and a rallying point for the radical and freethought movements. He died in 1843. Within 1800–1865 he stands, with Cobbett and Hone, as one of the three great martyrs and makers of the English radical press.
Sources

Carlile, Richard. The Republican, No. 2, Vol. I (3 September 1819), in the Harrison-bound miscellany. The Peterloo letters.
Carlile, Richard. The Republican, Vol. VIII (1823). The numbers written from Dorchester Gaol.
Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. II. The prosecution of the radical press.

entities/cobbett-william.title: William Cobbett (1763–1835)
entities/cobbett-william.content:
William Cobbett
William Cobbett (1763–1835) was the greatest radical journalist of his age — the son of a Surrey farmer who rose, through his own energy and genius, to become the most powerful writer of popular political prose in England. His Weekly Political Register, carried to a huge readership by its cheap “twopenny trash” edition, was the voice of the rural and working poor against the funding system, the corn laws, the boroughmongers, and the “Old Corruption” of the postwar state. A man of paradoxes — at once a conservative of the old English stock and a radical reformer, a lover of the country and a scourge of the town — Cobbett made himself the tribune of the disinherited and one of the decisive forces behind the great reform agitation of the age.
The self-made man of letters
Cobbett was born at Farnham in Surrey, the grandson of a day-labourer, and passed his boyhood in the fields his family worked. He was a soldier, then a writer in America, where he made his first reputation as a controversialist under the name “Peter Porcupine,” and returned to England to become a journalist of prodigious energy and combative power. His genius lay in his prose — plain, racy, concrete, and charged with an extraordinary force of conviction — and in his identification with the common people of the English countryside. The autobiographical Life of William Cobbett, written in America, traced his rise from the day-labourer’s cottage, insisting on his humble origins against the family pretensions of others, and became the classic statement of his self-made career.
The Political Register and the “twopenny trash”
From 1802 Cobbett published the Weekly Political Register, and in 1816 he transformed it into the organ of the poor by issuing it at twopence instead of the expensive price of the ordinary journals. The “twopenny trash,” as its enemies called it, reached the working classes and the labouring poor as no political writing had done before, and made Cobbett the most widely read political writer in England. Its leading themes were the national debt and the funding system — the burden of taxation that, in Cobbett’s argument, fell on the labour of the people to support the fundholders, the placemen, and the pensioners of the state; the corn laws; and the corruption of the unreformed Parliament. His agitation helped create the politically conscious radicalism of the postwar years, the mass movement that the government answered with repression.
The postwar crisis and the flight to America
In the years after Waterloo Cobbett stood at the head of the radical press, and the government watched him with hostility. When the repression of 1817 came — the suspension of Habeas Corpus and the prosecution of the radical publishers — Cobbett, rather than face imprisonment, fled to America. From there he continued to write, and in 1819, from America, he ridiculed Bentham and the philosophic reformers; his absence left the leadership of the London radicals to younger men. He returned to England in 1819, resumed the Register, and took up again his great causes. In the 1820s and 1830s he continued his agitation — for reform, against the funding system and the game laws — and his Rural Rides gave a classic picture of the condition of the English countryside.
Significance
Cobbett’s part in the making of the age was twofold. He was the great popularizer of radical politics, the writer who gave the working classes and the rural poor a language in which to name their grievances and a program for their redress; and he was the representative, in his own person and in his writing, of the England of the small farmer and the labourer that the industrial and financial revolution was destroying. His agitation fed directly into the reform movement that carried the Reform Act of 1832 — a measure Cobbett, returned to England and elected to the reformed Parliament, lived just long enough to see. He died in 1835. Within the period 1800–1865 he stands as the founder of English popular radical journalism and one of the decisive voices of the reform age.
Sources

Carlile / Hone / Cobbett, Harrison-bound miscellany. The autobiographical Life of William Cobbett and the 1817 run of the Weekly Political Register / Political Pamphlet.
Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. II. Cobbett’s “twopenny trash,” the rise of the radical movement, and the postwar agitation.

entities/derby.title: Edward Smith-Stanley, 14th Earl of Derby (1799–1869)
entities/derby.content:
Edward Smith-Stanley, 14th Earl of Derby
Edward Smith-Stanley, fourteenth Earl of Derby (1799–1869) was three times Prime Minister and the leader of the Conservative Party during the long opposition years of the 1850s and 1860s. He was a statesman of extraordinary gifts — an orator of the first rank, the finest natural speaker of his generation after Gladstone — who had begun his career as a reforming Whig and had crossed to the Conservatives over Ireland. His three short ministries, particularly the third of 1866–68, were marked by the great paradox of his career: it was Derby’s Conservative government, with Disraeli as leader in the Commons, that carried the Reform Act of 1867, a measure far more democratic than anything the Whigs had dared to propose.
The young Whig and the crossing
Derby, as Lord Stanley, was a brilliant young Whig in the 1830s, a member of Grey’s reform government and of the ministries that carried the great measures of the reform era. He was, in those years, one of the ablest of the younger Whigs, a man of commanding ability and fiery oratory. His defection came over the Irish Church question: in the 1840s, as the Whig party moved toward the appropriation of the surplus revenues of the Irish Church, Stanley refused to follow, and he crossed to the Conservative side. For the rest of his career he was a Conservative — a man of aristocratic, sporting, and independent temper, whom many regarded as the natural leader of his adopted party.
The Conservative leader
In the years after the fall of Peel, the Conservative Party split between the followers of Peel and the Protectionist majority under Lord George Bentinck and Disraeli. Derby succeeded to the leadership of the Protectionist Conservatives and led them through the long years of opposition in the 1850s. He formed his first ministry in 1852 — the celebrated “Who? Who?” ministry, so called because the aged and deaf passed the names of the new ministers around the House — and a second short-lived ministry in 1858–59, both of which fell quickly in the unstable politics of the decade. Throughout, Derby remained the head of a party that was a minority, unable to command a stable majority, but which he held together by his personal authority and his great ability in debate.
The Reform Act of 1867
Derby’s third ministry, formed in 1866 after the fall of Lord Russell’s government on a reform measure, proved the great opportunity of his career. Resolved that the Conservatives should not again go out on reform, Derby and Disraeli carried the Reform Act of 1867 — a measure which, in its final form, established household suffrage in the boroughs and added about a million voters to the electorate, a far more democratic settlement than the Whigs had proposed. Derby called the undertaking a “leap in the dark,” the phrase he made famous. The Act split no Conservative party and carried the government, but its passage was followed almost at once by Derby’s retirement, broken in health, in 1868. He died in 1869.
Significance
Derby’s career embodied the transformation of Conservatism in the middle of the century. He began as a Whig reformer and ended as the Conservative Prime Minister who carried the greatest reform of the age; he led his party through the long wilderness of the 1850s and brought it, under Disraeli, to the commanding position it would hold in the later Victorian age. His significance in the period 1800–1865 lies in his leadership of the Conservative opposition, his three premierships, and his part in the Reform Act of 1867 — the act that closed the mid-Victorian chapter and opened the era of mass politics.
Sources

McCarthy, Justin. A History of Our Own Times. Derby’s place in the mid-Victorian political story.

entities/disraeli.title: Benjamin Disraeli (1804–1881)
entities/disraeli.content:
Benjamin Disraeli
Benjamin Disraeli (1804–1881) was the great rival of Gladstone and the maker of the modern Conservative Party. Of Jewish descent, a novelist before he was a statesman, and the most brilliant parliamentarian of his age, Disraeli rose from unpromising beginnings to lead the Protectionist revolt that destroyed Peel, to carry the Reform Act of 1867 as a Conservative measure, and to become Prime Minister. His career in the period 1800–1865 — the years of his obscurity, his rise, and his struggle for the leadership — was the making of a political figure whose full triumph lay beyond the close of this period but whose methods and ambition were already unmistakable.
Early career and Young England
Disraeli entered Parliament in 1837 after early failures, and made his way by a combination of audacity, literary fame, and political calculation. He was associated in the early 1840s with the “Young England” movement — a group of young Tory members who, in reaction against the materialism and commercialism of the age, preached a romantic conservatism of crown, church, and aristocracy, and who were lampooned and patronised by the more practical politicians of the day. Disraeli’s novels — Coningsby, Sybil — gave the movement its intellectual expression and made him a figure of note in the literary as well as the political world. But his real opportunity came with the great question that was to dominate the 1840s: the Corn Laws.
The attack on Peel
When Peel resolved, in 1845–46, upon the repeal of the Corn Laws, Disraeli placed himself at the head of the Protectionist revolt against his own leader. His speeches against Peel in 1846 were among the most brilliant and savage of the century — the caustic attacks in which he accused the minister of betraying the party and the principles for which it stood. Rallying the Protectionists around Lord George Bentinck, Disraeli fought the repeal measure through Parliament, and when the ministry fell on the Irish Coercion Bill, it was Disraeli who had supplied the invective that helped bring it down. The Conservative Party was shattered and split by Peel’s conversion; Disraeli became the leader of the Protectionist remnant, and the long years of opposition that followed were the school in which he learned the arts of party leadership.
The long opposition and the road to power
Through the 1850s Disraeli led the Protectionist Conservatives — a minority party — against the succession of Whig and coalition governments, and struggled to revive his party’s fortunes. The era of ministerial instability, the “everybody against everybody” period, gave him repeated but brief opportunities: he served in Derby’s ministries, and made himself the indispensable parliamentary lieutenant of the Earl of Derby. His great opportunity came in 1866–67, when the fall of Lord Russell’s ministry on a reform measure brought Derby and Disraeli to power. Disraeli, resolved that the Conservatives should not again go out on a Reform Bill, carried the Reform Act of 1867 — a measure far more democratic than anything the Liberals had proposed — in what Derby called a “leap in the dark.” He had “dished the Whigs,” and the Conservative Party had carried a reform greater than its opponents had dared to attempt.
Character and significance
By the close of the period in 1865 Disraeli stood at the head of the Conservative Party, the acknowledged rival of Gladstone, and the most striking and original figure in English politics. His ascendancy was built on parliamentary genius — an oratory of wit, paradox, and audacity that made him the delight of the House — and on a patient strategy that had turned the shattered Protectionists into a disciplined and hopeful party. His premierships, the empire policy, and the rivalry with Gladstone that dominated the later Victorian age lay beyond the horizon of this wiki; but within 1800–1865 he had already made himself the man of the future, the Conservative who understood that a party of resistance to change could not endure, and who would remake his party to carry change itself. Disraeli’s career is the proof, within this period, that parliamentary genius and long patience could raise a man of foreign and plebeian origin to the summit of English political life.

entities/grey-charles.title: Charles Grey, 2nd Earl Grey (1764–1845)
entities/grey-charles.content:
Charles Grey, 2nd Earl Grey
Charles Grey, second Earl Grey (1764–1845) was the Whig statesman who carried the Reform Act of 1832 — the great constitutional change that remade the House of Commons and opened the Victorian age. A reformer from the 1790s, when as a young Whig he had moved the reform motions of the 1790s, Grey waited more than a generation for his opportunity. When it came, in the crisis of 1830–32, he formed the first genuinely Whig government in more than forty years and carried reform through the teeth of the Lords and the danger of revolution. His ministry, having accomplished the great change, went on to carry the abolition of slavery and the other reforms of the age, and he retired in 1834, leaving a reformed Parliament and a remade constitution behind him.
The long apprenticeship
Grey had advocated parliamentary reform since his youth, when he was the rising hope of the reform party in the Whig opposition of the 1790s. The French Revolution and the war discredited reform for a generation, and Grey passed the long years of the Tory ascendancy in opposition, the leader of the section of the Whigs that held to the reform principle. His patience and his consistency made him, by 1830, the natural head of any reform government, the man to whom the country looked when the old system at last broke down.
The ministry and the Reform Bill
When Wellington’s ministry fell in November 1830 on its declaration against reform, William IV sent for Grey, and he formed a government with reform as a cabinet question. His cabinet was a strong one — Brougham as Lord Chancellor, Lord John Russell as the champion of reform in the Commons, Althorp, Durham, Melbourne, Palmerston. On 1 March 1831 Russell introduced the Reform Bill, and the crisis that followed tested Grey’s nerve and his mastery. The Bill passed its second reading by a single vote, was defeated in committee, was re-introduced and passed the Commons, and was rejected by the Lords in October 1831. Through the riots, the Political Unions, and the danger of revolution, Grey held the government together; in the Days of May 1832, when the Lords again refused, he resigned, and returned only with the King’s promise to create enough peers to carry the Bill. The Reform Act received the royal assent on 7 June 1832 — the triumph of Grey’s life.
The consolidation and the fall
Grey’s ministry went on from the Reform Act to the other great measures of the age — the abolition of slavery in the British colonies in 1833, with its £20,000,000 compensation, and the beginnings of the reform of the Irish Church. But the ministry was already weakening; the Irish Church question and the divisions within his own government undermined it, and in July 1834 Grey resigned, worn out and unable to hold his colleagues together. He retired from public life and died in 1845. Grey’s place in the period is fixed by a single, decisive achievement: he was the minister who, in the crisis of 1830–32, carried the great Reform Act — the turning-point of the constitutional history of the century — and who thereby opened the age of reformed, democratic, and party government in England.
Sources

Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. III. Grey’s ministry and the Reform Bill crisis.

entities/hone-william.title: William Hone (1780–1842)
entities/hone-william.content:
William Hone
William Hone (1780–1842) was the bookseller and political satirist whose acquittal at the three Guildhall trials of December 1817 was one of the decisive victories of the freedom of the press in England. Prosecuted on three separate ex-officio informations for political parodies on the Catechism, the Litany, and the Athanasian Creed, Hone defended himself without counsel before three special juries and was acquitted on all three counts — the government, which had hoped to crush the radical press, was “laughed out of Court,” and Hone became a national hero of the liberty of the press and trial by jury. In the years that followed he produced the great series of illustrated political pamphlets — The Political House that Jack Built, the Queen’s Matrimonial Ladder — that made him, with Cruikshank’s cuts, the chief pictorial satirist of the Queen Caroline era.
The trials of 1817
In the repression of 1817, when the government was prosecuting the radical press and Habeas Corpus was suspended, Hone was arrested on a warrant from Lord Ellenborough for publishing three parodies on forms of Church of England worship: The Late John Wilkes’s Catechism, The Political Litany, and The Sinecurist’s Creed (a parody on the Athanasian Creed). He was tried at Guildhall on three successive days, 18–20 December 1817, before Mr Justice Abbott and then Lord Chief Justice Ellenborough, on informations brought by the Attorney-General, Sir Samuel Shepherd. Hone conducted his own defence, in speeches lasting many hours, and based it on a historical parade of scriptural and liturgical parodies — Luther and the church dignitaries of past ages — to prove that the practice was customary and that the prosecutions were political, aimed not at protecting religion but at crushing a man who had exposed ministerial delinquencies and stifling the press. Three special juries, in three successive days, returned Not Guilty.
The triumph of the press
The acquittals were received with extraordinary rejoicing — crowds estimated at twenty thousand filled the Guildhall and its approaches, and the City of London Tavern meeting of 29 December 1817, under Mr Waithman, adopted resolutions declaring the liberty of the press inseparable from the purity of trial by jury and Hone’s acquittals a demonstration of that right. The prosecutions had been an attempt to crush an individual and to uphold abuse; their failure was a landmark of the freedom of the press. Hone’s own report of the trials, with its account of the three defences and of the public meeting, became a primary document of the struggle.
The pamphlets and the Every-Day Book
Hone followed the trials with the great series of political pamphlets that carried his satire into the Queen Caroline years. The Political House that Jack Built (with the “Thirteen Cuts” by Cruikshank, and the Doctor Slop dedication), the Queen’s Matrimonial Ladder (“A National Toy, with Fourteen Step Scenes”), Non Mi Ricordo!, the Miraculous Host, and the other squibs of 1820–22 lampooned the ministry, the placemen and pensioners, and the proceedings against the Queen, and were collected in the Chidley volume of 1830. Hone’s later years took a different turn: the Every-Day Book (1826) and its companions, illustrated almanacs of popular amusements, customs, and antiquities, made him a respected antiquarian, and he was reconciled to the Church and to a quieter life. He died in 1842.
Significance
Hone’s significance in the period is double. His acquittals of 1817 were the great judicial victory of the radical press — the moment when the government’s attempt to use the law of blasphemous libel against political parody was decisively defeated by the jury, and when the freedom of the press and the integrity of trial by jury were vindicated before the whole nation. And his illustrated pamphlets made him the chief satirical voice of the reform and Queen Caroline years, the man who, with Cruikshank’s cuts, gave the political satire of the age its most telling and most popular form. He stands, with Cobbett and Carlile, among the three great makers of the English radical press.
Sources

Hone, William. Pamphlets and Parodies on Political Subjects (Chidley collection, 1830). The nine illustrated squibs.
Hone, William. The Every-Day Book, Vol. I (1826). The antiquarian sequel.
Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. II. The trial of Hone and the repression of 1817.

entities/liverpool.title: Robert Banks Jenkinson, 2nd Earl of Liverpool (1770–1828)
entities/liverpool.content:
Robert Banks Jenkinson, 2nd Earl of Liverpool
Robert Banks Jenkinson, second Earl of Liverpool (1770–1828) was the Prime Minister who presided over England through the Napoleonic wars and the long and troubled peace that followed. His ministry, formed in 1812, lasted until 1827 — one of the longest continuous administrations in British history — and carried the country through the postwar depression, the radical agitation and Peterloo, the repression of the Six Acts, the Queen Caroline affair, and the gradual liberalisation of the 1820s. A careful, capable, and moderate administrator rather than a brilliant orator, Liverpool governed by holding together a cabinet of difficult and gifted men — Castlereagh, Canning, Wellington, Eldon, Peel — and his long tenure gave the postwar Tory ascendancy its stability and its character.
The long premiership
Liverpool came to the premiership in 1812, in the midst of the war, and remained in office for fifteen years. He was a Tory of the moderate, administrative school, a man of business and of the Treasury rather than of the platform, and his great gift was the management of men. His cabinet was a coalition of the ablest talent of the Tory party, and its internal divisions — over the Catholic question, over currency, over the measures of repression — were constant; Liverpool’s art lay in preventing them from breaking the ministry. After the war he faced the immense problems of demobilisation, debt, and distress, and the rising tide of radical agitation that culminated in Peterloo and the Six Acts. Martineau’s account of the period presents him as the head of a government divided within itself, unpopular with the King and with large sections of opinion, yet enduring through a mixture of caution and conciliation.
The postwar crisis
The years after Waterloo were among the most difficult in English history. The collapse of wartime prices brought agricultural distress; demobilisation flooded the labour market; taxation and the burden of the national debt pressed on the people; and the radical movement, fed by the cheap press of Cobbett and Carlile and the agitation for reform, rose to a height that terrified the government. Liverpool’s ministry met the agitation with repression — the suspension of Habeas Corpus in 1817, the prosecution of the radical press, the force that dispersed the Manchester meeting of August 1819, and the repressive legislation of the Six Acts. These measures, and the ministry’s conduct after Peterloo, made it the emblem of the reaction; yet within the same administration the seeds of a milder policy were already present, in the liberal Tories who were to succeed the old guard.
The liberal transition
In the 1820s the character of the ministry changed. The retirement of Sidmouth, the death of Castlereagh, and the accession of Canning as Foreign Secretary and of Huskisson and Peel to the Board of Trade and the Home Office marked the transition from the old Tory repression to liberal conservatism. Under Liverpool’s presidency this reconstructed ministry began the great work of commercial and fiscal reform — the reduction of the Navigation Acts, the Reciprocity Bill, the reform of the Combination Acts, the reduction of the tariff, and the sliding scale for corn duties — which prepared the way for the free-trade era. Liverpool himself, cautious and unwilling to commit the government to the dangerous Catholic question, held the balance among his brilliant subordinates. In 1827 he was struck down by a stroke and resigned; Canning succeeded him, and the long Liverpool era closed.
Character and significance
Liverpool died in 1828, a few months after leaving office. He left the memory of a prudent and successful war-and-peace minister, the man who had governed England through the greatest crisis of the century’s opening decades without revolution and without the total reaction that the radicals had feared and the ultras had hoped. His significance in the period is that of the steady hand at the helm — the Prime Minister whose long tenure held the Tory party and the state together through war, postwar crisis, and the beginnings of reform, and whose government, repressive in its first phase and liberal in its last, bridged the age of Pitt and the age of Canning and Peel. He stands, with Pitt and Peel, as one of the founders of the modern Conservative tradition of strong and moderate administration.
Sources

Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. II. The Liverpool ministry and its long tenure through the postwar decade.
Alison, Sir Archibald. History of Europe, Vol. I. England from 1815 and the Liverpool government.

entities/melbourne.title: William Lamb, Viscount Melbourne (1779–1848)
entities/melbourne.content:
William Lamb, Viscount Melbourne
William Lamb, second Viscount Melbourne (1779–1848) was the Whig statesman who led the governments of the later 1830s, and the Prime Minister under whose tutelage the young Queen Victoria learned the arts of constitutional kingship. Twice Prime Minister — for a few weeks in 1834 and again from 1835 to 1841 — he presided over the transition from the Reform era to the early Victorian age, governing a weak and divided party with a combination of indolent charm, sharp wit, and political skill. His ministry carried the consolidation of the reform settlement — municipal reform, the new Poor Law in operation, the removal of Irish grievances — and his character, at once easy and shrewd, made him one of the most distinctive figures of the age.
Early career and the first ministry
Melbourne was a Whig of the old school, the husband of the celebrated and unfortunate Lady Caroline Lamb, and a man whose political opinions were moderate, worldly, and sceptical. He held office as Chief Secretary for Ireland in Canning’s ministry, and rose to be Home Secretary under Grey, in which post he was responsible for the maintenance of order during the Reform Bill crisis. When Grey resigned in July 1834, Melbourne formed a short-lived ministry, but it was dismissed by William IV within a few weeks — the King, offended by the Whig government’s handling of the Irish Church question, suddenly dismissed the ministers and sent for Peel. The episode, the last exercise of the royal prerogative of dismissal, was itself a sign of the constitutional changes the age was working.
The second ministry, 1835–1841
Peel’s brief “Hundred Days” ministry fell in April 1835, and Melbourne returned to power at the head of his second and long administration, which lasted until 1841. It was a ministry of difficulty: dependent in the Commons on the support of the Irish members and the Radicals, blocked in the Lords by a hostile Conservative majority, and weakened by the early deaths and defections of its ablest men. Yet it carried the great consolidation of reform — the Municipal Corporations Act and the reform of the Irish Church, and the measures of the reformed era. The years of the Melbourne ministry were also years of gathering storm — the Canadian rebellions and Lord Durham’s mission, the Chartist agitation, the dark times of 1839–40 — and Melbourne’s government, criticised and weak, held on through them with a kind of fatalistic composure.
The Queen’s Prime Minister
The most celebrated aspect of Melbourne’s career was his relation to the young Queen Victoria. On her accession in 1837, Melbourne, as the Whig Prime Minister, became the guide of the eighteen-year-old sovereign; he attended her daily, instructed her in the working of the constitution, and formed a bond of genuine affection and dependence. Martineau’s account of the early reign dwells on the Queen’s devotion to her first minister and on Melbourne’s part in shaping the young monarch. The Bedchamber Question of 1839 showed the strength of the tie: when Peel, on coming to office, demanded the dismissal of the Queen’s Whig ladies-in-waiting, Victoria refused, and Peel resigned — Melbourne returned, and the Whigs continued, the incident a celebrated proof both of the young Queen’s will and of the position Melbourne held in her confidence.
Fall and character
The ministry at last fell in 1841, defeated at the general election on the free-trade question, in which the Whigs had staked their tenure on a fixed duty on corn and been rejected. Melbourne retired, and died in 1848. He left the memory of a singular political figure — a statesman of great ability who governed almost by negligence, a man of the world who regarded politics with a sceptical detachment, and the kindly tutor of a young Queen. His significance in the period lies in the two great services of his career: the consolidation of the Whig reform settlement in the difficult years after 1835, and the education of the young Victoria in the constitutional monarchy she was to embody for the rest of the century.
Sources

Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. IV. The second Melbourne ministry and the accession of Victoria.
Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. III. Melbourne’s first ministry and its dismissal in 1834.
Molesworth, William Nassau. History of England from the Year 1830, Vols. I–II. Melbourne’s ministry and its fall in 1841.

entities/palmerston.title: Henry John Temple, Viscount Palmerston (1784–1865)
entities/palmerston.content:
Henry John Temple, Viscount Palmerston
Henry John Temple, third Viscount Palmerston (1784–1865) was the most popular British statesman of the mid-century, twice Prime Minister, and for a generation the very type of the vigorous, patriotic, and self-confident English minister. His long career spanned the whole period from the Napoleonic wars to the eve of the Reform Act of 1867. As Foreign Secretary and then Prime Minister he conducted the foreign policy of the country with a boldness, a willingness to assert British interests, and a sense of national pride that made him the idol of the middle classes and the terror of foreign courts. His last ministry, from 1859 to his death in 1865, presided over the settled years of mid-Victorian prosperity and the close of the Palmerstonian age.
Early career and the long apprenticeship
Palmerston entered politics as a young Irish peer, holding minor office under the Tories before crossing to the Whigs over the Catholic question. He served as Foreign Secretary in the ministries of the 1830s and 1840s, and there built the reputation on which his later ascendancy rested. His foreign policy — robust, interventionist, and confident — was directed to the maintenance of British interests and the support of liberal causes abroad where they served those interests. He conducted the Eastern Question with a firm hand, supported Belgian independence, and earned the hostility of the continental autocracies. His methods were summed up by his own conduct of the affairs of his age — the dispatch of British fleets, the assertion of British rights, and the readiness to speak for England in the councils of Europe.
The “Civis Romanus sum” and the Don Pacifico affair
Palmerston’s foreign policy reached its most characteristic expression in the Don Pacifico affair of 1850. Don Pacifico, a British subject and a Jew of Gibraltar, had had his house plundered in Athens by a mob, and the Greek government had refused him redress; Palmerston, to compel satisfaction, ordered a British fleet to blockade the Greek coast. The affair provoked a great parliamentary debate in which the Whig government was attacked for bullying a small state. Palmerston’s defence, in a speech of immense effect, claimed for every British subject, wherever he might be, the protection of the British flag — the famous “Civis Romanus sum” — and the House sustained him. The speech was the embodiment of Palmerstonian policy: the assertion that a British subject, like a citizen of Rome, carried the power of his nation with him, and that the government would not be trifled with in the treatment of its people.
Fall and return
Palmerston’s very vigour brought him down in 1851. In the excitement of Louis Napoleon’s coup d’état in France, Palmerston — as Foreign Secretary — gave his approval to the act without the authority of his colleagues, and was dismissed by Lord John Russell. He revenged himself by defeating the government, and the years that followed were a period of ministerial instability — the “everybody against everybody” era, in Molesworth’s phrase. When the Aberdeen coalition, formed at Christmas 1852, broke under the disasters of the Crimean War — the mismanagement exposed by the Roebuck committee — Palmerston was called in February 1855 to form his first ministry, the man the country trusted to conduct the war. He carried the war to its conclusion, the fall of Sebastopol and the Peace of Paris of 1856, and remained the dominant figure of English politics.
The last ministry and the Palmerstonian age
Palmerston’s second ministry, formed in 1859 in the “union of the Whigs and Radicals” with Lord John Russell as Foreign Secretary, lasted until his death in 1865 — a long and settled administration in an age of peace and prosperity. He met and defeated the attempts at further parliamentary reform, resisting the extension of the franchise with the instinct of a man who distrusted democratic change; he presided over the country during the American Civil War, steering between the cotton famine and the Alabama claims; and he managed the perennial questions of the day with a steady, popular hand. His last triumph was the general election of 1865, in which the country returned him with a decisive majority — the last victory, as McCarthy recorded, of the Palmerstonian system.
Death and the close of an age
Palmerston died on 18 October 1865, in his eighty-first year, and with him, as contemporaries felt, died the whole character of the age he dominated. McCarthy’s account of his death marks it as the end of an era: the Palmerstonian ascendancy — the rule of the bluff, vigorous, conservative-liberal statesman who trusted the middle classes and the constitution and disliked great changes — closed with its author. His death opened the way for the reform agitation that produced the Reform Act of 1867, a change he had spent his last years resisting. Palmerston stood for the confident, insular, prosperous England of the mid-century — at once liberal and conservative, patriotic and shrewd — and his long rule gave the period its settled, self-satisfied character. No statesman of the age was more representative of the England of his time, and none left so clear an image of what the Victorians meant by a great English minister.
Sources

Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. IV. Palmerston’s foreign policy, the Don Pacifico affair, and his fall and return.
McCarthy, Justin. A History of Our Own Times, Vol. II. Palmerston’s last victory and death.

entities/peel-robert.title: Sir Robert Peel (1788–1850)
entities/peel-robert.content:
Sir Robert Peel
Sir Robert Peel (1788–1850) was the dominant Conservative statesman of the middle years of the century, twice Prime Minister, and the author of the two great administrative and legislative achievements that remade the British state: the establishment of a uniform and disciplined police in London and the tariff and currency reforms that culminated in the repeal of the Corn Laws. His career was a long march from the rigid Torism of his early years to the free-trade liberalism of his last — a progress that split his party and ended in his fall, but that fixed the direction of English policy for a generation. Peel governed, as his contemporaries observed, less by the arts of party than by the power of his own mind and the authority of his administrative mastery.
Early career and the character of the minister
Peel entered public life as the heir of a manufacturing fortune, the son of a Lancashire cotton baronet, and rose rapidly under the old Tory system. He was Chief Secretary for Ireland, Home Secretary under Liverpool, and the author of the reform of the criminal law and of the metropolitan police — the “Peelers” of the new London police force that bore his name. His early politics were those of the post-war Tory ascendancy: hostile to parliamentary reform, and the mover of the repressive legislation of the postwar years. His conversion to Catholic Emancipation in 1829 — carried against his own past and his own party — first showed the pattern of his career: the statesman who would sacrifice consistency and party to what he conceived to be the necessity of the country. He resigned rather than oppose emancipation, and for years afterwards was a figure of suspicion to the men he had deserted.
The Tamworth Manifesto and the reformed era
After the Reform Act of 1832, Peel set himself to reconcile the Conservative party to the new constitution. His Tamworth Manifesto of December 1834, issued on forming his first, short-lived ministry, accepted the Reform Act as final and promised a policy of careful, moderate reform — a declaration that fixed the character of Conservatism for the Victorian age. His “Hundred Days” ministry of 1834–35 fell quickly, defeated on the ecclesiastical questions of the day, but Peel had established himself as the leader of a reconstructed party — the Conservatives, as the Tories now called themselves — capable of governing in a reformed Parliament. In opposition through the later 1830s he watched the Whigs struggle, and prepared himself and his party for power.
The great ministry, 1841–1846
Peel’s second ministry, formed after the general election of 1841, was the greatest administration of the period. He inherited a country in deep financial difficulty — annual deficits, deepening distress, and a revenue that would not meet the expenditure — and he addressed himself to the whole body of the country’s difficulties. Martineau’s account of the ministry emphasises the union of financial and commercial reform with the determination to apply principle to the state of the economy. Peel revived the income tax (abandoned since 1816) at sevenpence in the pound to meet the deficit, and set about a vast reduction of the tariff — remitting duties on raw materials and manufactured articles and simplifying the fiscal system. In Ireland he attempted to “kill Home Rule by kindness,” through the Maynooth grant, the new colleges, and the Encumbered Estates legislation. His government carried the Factory Act reforms, the Mines and Collieries Act, and the great legislative work that crowded the session.
Peel’s financial and commercial policy rested on the currency settlement as well as the tariff. In 1844 he carried the Bank Charter Act, separating the issue of the Bank of England from its banking department and fixing the note issues of the country at a legal maximum — the embodiment of the currency principle that every note beyond the bullion should be covered by gold. His speeches of May 1844, as Tooke recorded, insisted on the fixed metallic standard as the only sure regulator of the currency. The Act was the deliberate work of a minister who believed that sound money and free trade were the twin foundations of national prosperity.
The repeal of the Corn Laws
The culminating act of Peel’s career was the repeal of the Corn Laws. For years he had been moving toward free trade in private, convinced that the protective duties on grain benefited the landed interest at the expense of the people and impeded the commercial greatness of the country. The decisive occasion was the potato blight of 1845, which threatened Ireland with a terrible famine and made the free importation of food a national necessity. Peel, unable to carry his Cabinet and unable to secure the formation of a Whig ministry, returned to office resolved upon repeal. In January 1846 he announced his conversion, and carried the repeal of the Corn Laws in June with the support of the Whigs and Radicals against the mass of his own party. Disraeli rallied the Protectionists, and the ministry fell immediately afterwards on the Irish Coercion Bill. Peel’s final speech — in which he declared that he left a name “perhaps to be remembered in the pages of history” — closed the great administration, and the Conservative Party was split, not to recover a majority until the 1870s.
Retirement, death, and legacy
Peel spent the few remaining years of his life in the quiet authority of a statesman above party, giving his support to the Liberal governments that carried on his free-trade policy. He died on 2 July 1850, thrown from his horse on Constitution Hill, and the country gave him a funeral worthy of a national minister. Martineau’s closing tribute to his last position in the British legislature called it “the noblest that, in our period of time, could be held by any man” — the position of the statesman who had governed against his own party for the good of the country. Peel’s legacy was double: the administrative and fiscal reconstruction of the British state — sound currency, free trade, a reformed tariff — and the lesson, learned and resented by his own party, that a minister might be greater than his following. He was the architect of the settled free-trade and gold-standard policy that the Victorian age inherited, and his name stood, with Gladstone’s, as the founder of the modern Conservative tradition of fiscal and administrative reform.
Sources
