entities/russell.title: Lord John Russell, 1st Earl Russell (1792–1878)
entities/russell.content:
Lord John Russell
Lord John Russell, first Earl Russell (1792–1878) was the Whig statesman who introduced the Reform Bill of 1832 and who, in the long middle years of the century, was the indefatigable advocate of parliamentary reform, of religious liberty, and of free trade. Twice Prime Minister — from 1846 to 1852 and again in 1865–66 — he stood for a quarter of a century at the centre of English liberal politics, the small, sharp-tempered, fearless champion of reform whose career was one long service to the causes of the age. He was, with Palmerston, the other great Whig leader of the Victorian decades, and the man whose commitment to reform outlasted the caution of his colleagues.
The champion of reform
Russell was a younger son of the Duke of Bedford, a Whig of the reforming school, and entered politics with a passion for the reform of the representation. It was he who, as Paymaster of the Forces in Grey’s ministry, rose in the House of Commons on 1 March 1831 to introduce the Reform Bill — a speech Molesworth called one of the most remarkable ever delivered in the House. He carried the Bill through all its stages in the Commons, through the dissolution of 1831 and the Days of May crisis, and became the man of the Reform Act. His name was henceforward inseparable from the cause of parliamentary reform, and through the 1830s and 1840s he pressed for its extension — the ballot, the removal of the remaining disabilities, and the widening of the franchise — often in advance of his own party.
The ministry of 1846–1852
Russell succeeded Peel as Prime Minister in 1846, at the head of the Whig ministry that followed the split of the Conservative Party over the Corn Laws. His administration had to govern through the terrible years of the Irish Famine, the commercial crisis of 1847, and the European revolutions of 1848. Its record was mixed — the famine relief measures proved tragically inadequate, and the ministry fell in 1852 after its conduct of the Ecclesiastical Titles Bill, its response to the Papal Aggression, and the dismissal of Palmerston. Yet it was under Russell that the repeal of the Navigation Laws was carried in 1849 and that the country passed through the crisis of 1848 without revolution.
The later career
Russell returned to office under Palmerston, serving as Foreign Secretary in the duumvirate of 1859, and succeeded him as Prime Minister on Palmerston’s death in 1865 — only to see his government fall within a year on his own reform measure. The failure of his moderate Reform Bill in 1866, defeated by the “Adullamites” under Lowe, brought down his ministry and opened the way for Disraeli’s Reform Act of 1867. He retired to the Lords as Earl Russell and died in 1878. Russell’s significance in the period lies in his long and consistent championship of the great liberal causes — parliamentary reform, religious liberty, and free trade. He was the man who introduced the Reform Act of 1832, the persistent advocate of its extension, and the Whig leader whose belief in progress and reform never flagged through half a century of English politics.

entities/stephenson-george.title: George Stephenson (1781–1848)
entities/stephenson-george.content:
George Stephenson
George Stephenson (1781–1848) was the father of the railway locomotive and the man who, more than any other, created the modern railway system. Born in the colliery village of Wylam in Northumberland, the son of a colliery fireman, he raised himself from herd-boy and labourer to be the most famous engineer in England — building the first public railway to use steam locomotives, and carrying the locomotive from the obscurity of the northern coal-fields to the triumph of the Rainhill trials and the opening of the Liverpool & Manchester Railway. His life, as told by Smiles, is the great example of self-education and the rise of the engineering class — the type of the industrial age in which the son of the labouring poor could remake the world through his own genius and perseverance.
The self-made engineer
Stephenson was born at Wylam in 1781, and spent his boyhood as a herd-boy and labourer in the poverty of the colliery districts. He worked as a fireman and engineman at various collieries, and his determination to master the principles of the steam engine — learning to read and write as an adult to do so — marked the beginning of his rise. He married, worked at Willington Quay and Killingworth, and, as his circumstances allowed, he educated himself and resolved that his son Robert should have the education he himself had lacked. His early work at Killingworth included the improvement of the locomotive, the primitive form of which he took up and made practical, and the invention of the “Geordie” safety-lamp — a device for the firedamp of the northern mines invented contemporaneously with Sir Humphry Davy’s, and the subject of a famous and bitter controversy over priority.
The Stockton & Darlington and the locomotive
The decisive moment came with the Stockton & Darlington Railway. Appointed engineer of the line, Stephenson surveyed and constructed the railway, which opened in 1825 as the first public railway to use steam locomotives for freight and passengers. The project established the railway as a practical means of transport and Stephenson as its leading engineer. He then undertook the far greater task of the Liverpool & Manchester Railway — a line made necessary by the commerce between the two great towns, opposed by the canal and landed interests, and the occasion of the famous parliamentary battle in which Stephenson was cross-examined on the technicalities of his own invention. The construction presented immense difficulties, above all the crossing of Chat Moss, the great peat bog west of Manchester, which Stephenson drained and filled by his own methods.
The Rocket and the Rainhill trials
The triumph of the locomotive came at the Rainhill trials of 1829, when the directors of the Liverpool & Manchester Railway offered a prize for a locomotive that could haul a given load at a given speed. Stephenson’s son Robert had returned from three years as a mining engineer in Colombia, and together they designed and built the Rocket, which outran all its rivals and decisively established the steam locomotive as the motive power for railways. The Liverpool & Manchester Railway opened on 15 September 1830, with the fatal accident to Mr Huskisson, and its immediate success inaugurated the railway age. Stephenson was engaged as engineer for numerous new lines; his son Robert constructed the London & Birmingham Railway, the largest engineering work of its day, and the tubular bridges at Menai and Conway.
Later years and significance
In his later years George Stephenson retired to Tapton House near Chesterfield, engaged in coal-mining, addressed working men at the mechanics’ institutes, and travelled — visiting Belgium at the invitation of King Leopold and Spain. He died in 1848, and was buried with public honours. His significance in the period is immense: he transformed the steam locomotive from an imperfect colliery curiosity into the motive power of the world, and he created the railway system that bound England together and remade the economy and society of the age. The son of a colliery fireman, he became the type of the self-made engineer — the embodiment, as Smiles presented him, of the virtues of industry, perseverance, and self-education that the nineteenth century prized.
Sources

Smiles, Samuel. Lives of the Engineers: The Locomotive — George and Robert Stephenson. The full lives of father and son and the railway revolution.

entities/victoria.title: Queen Victoria (1819–1901)
entities/victoria.content:
Queen Victoria
Queen Victoria (1819–1901) ascended the throne on 20 June 1837, in her eighteenth year, and reigned for the greater part of the nineteenth century. Her accession marked the beginning of a new era — the transition from the old world of the Regency and the Reform crisis to the settled Victorian age. A young and popular sovereign, she brought a freshness and a gaiety to the throne that contrasted with the age of her predecessors, and her reign, particularly through her marriage to Prince Albert and the long years of her maturity, gave its name to the age. Within the period of this wiki — from 1800 to 1865 — her story runs from her girlhood and accession through her coronation, her marriage, the crises of her early reign, and the establishment of the monarchy as the settled centre of the constitution.
The accession
Victoria was the only child of the Duke of Kent, the fourth son of George III, and came to the throne at the death of William IV on 20 June 1837. The country received the new sovereign with universal goodwill and, as Molesworth recorded, an “almost romantic interest.” After the “feeble old man” William IV, the youth and gaiety of the girl Queen were exhilarating; her delight in being seen, her drives through thronged parks, her command that her people should see her, made her at once the most popular figure in the nation. Her accession was accompanied by a general election, which returned the Whigs under Melbourne with their majority maintained, and the young Queen formed a close dependence on her Prime Minister. The crown, which had played a contentious part in the Reform crisis under William IV, passed into hands that were to make it once more the unifying centre of the state.
The coronation and the early reign
Victoria was crowned on 28 June 1838, in a coronation at once magnificent and, by the standard of the age, comparatively economical. The early years of her reign were crowded with difficulty — the Canadian rebellions and Lord Durham’s mission, the Bedchamber Question of 1839, the rise of Chartism, and the dark times of 1839–40 — but the Queen’s popularity, and the devotion of the people to the young sovereign, carried the monarchy through them. In February 1840 she married Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha, and the birth of the Princess Royal in November 1840 began the family that was to give the Victorian age its domestic character. The Bedchamber Question — when Peel, on coming to power in 1839, demanded the dismissal of the Queen’s Whig ladies-in-waiting, and the Queen refused — had established that the Queen would not lightly surrender the personal arrangements of her court; Melbourne’s return kept the Whigs in office, and the episode became a celebrated instance of the young Queen’s will.
The monarchy and the constitution
Through the great events of the middle years of the century — the Peel ministry, the repeal of the Corn Laws, the revolutions of 1848, the Papal Aggression, the Crimean War — Victoria reigned at the centre of a constitution in which the Crown, though no longer a governing power, remained a real and respected influence. Her marriage to Albert, who became her trusted adviser, gave the court a seriousness and a domestic virtue that harmonised with the temper of the age. The monarchy was being transformed from the personal, sometimes arbitrary, force it had been under her predecessors into the emblematic and constitutional crown of the Victorian state — popular, respectable, and above party. Victoria herself, though she held strong opinions and disliked the revolutions that disturbed the continent, generally kept within the constitutional limits of her power.
The close of the period
By 1865, the year of Palmerston’s death, Victoria was a settled and beloved sovereign, the mother of a large family and the centre of the national life. The period of this wiki closes with her still only in mid-reign; the long decades of her widowhood and her later transformation into the imperial matriarch lay in the future. Within 1800–1865 her significance is that of the young Queen who gave her name and character to the age — the sovereign whose accession opened the Victorian era and whose steady, constitutional popularity carried the monarchy through the great transitions of the Reform, free-trade, and Crimean decades. Her reign would run for another thirty-six years beyond the close of this period, but its foundations were laid in these early years of youth, marriage, and the consolidation of the modern crown.

entities/wellington.title: Arthur Wellesley, Duke of Wellington (1769–1852)
entities/wellington.content:
Arthur Wellesley, Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, first Duke of Wellington (1769–1852) was the greatest soldier of his age, the victor of the Peninsular War and of Waterloo, and, after a lifetime of military glory, a statesman of the first rank — Prime Minister from 1828 to 1830, and thereafter the permanent counsellor and “faithful servant” of the crown through the middle years of the century. Within the period of this wiki his story runs from the close of the Napoleonic wars through his ministry and the surrender on Catholic Emancipation, his opposition to reform, and his long and honoured old age. He personified, more than any other man, the old Tory England — aristocratic, military, and unbending — and his reluctant concessions marked the passing of that England.
The hero of the war
Wellington’s reputation was made in the wars. As commander in the Peninsula he had driven the French from Spain and Portugal and won the victories that made him the national hero; at Waterloo, on 18 June 1815, he commanded the allied army that finally overthrew Napoleon. He returned to England covered with honours, the most popular man in the country, and entered political life as a figure of immense authority in the Tory interest. In the postwar years he held high office and served at the Congress of Aix-la-Chapelle in 1818, where his influence helped smooth the evacuation of the allied army of occupation from France. He was a member of Lord Liverpool’s cabinet, and by the late 1820s the natural leader of the party of order.
The ministry and Catholic Emancipation
In January 1828 Wellington became Prime Minister, at the head of a Tory ministry that included Peel at the Home Office. The great question of his administration was Catholic Emancipation. In Ireland the agitation of O’Connell and the Catholic Association, brought to a crisis by the Clare election of 1828 — in which O’Connell, though a Catholic, was elected to Parliament in defiance of the law — forced the question upon the government. Wellington, who had long opposed emancipation, became convinced that it could no longer be resisted without civil war, and in 1829 he carried the Catholic Relief Act with Peel’s aid, breaking with his own party and alienating a large part of the Tory interest. The Duke, as Martineau observed, was deserted by half his friends; the Protestant backlash organized the Brunswick clubs; but emancipation was carried, and Ireland was for the moment tranquillized.
The opposition to reform and the fall
Wellington’s ministry did not long survive the measure. In 1830, with the country agitated by distress, the French Revolution, and the rising demand for parliamentary reform, Wellington declared in the House of Lords that the existing system of representation possessed the full and entire confidence of the country, and that he was not prepared to bring forward any measure of reform. The declaration was the death of his government: it fell in November 1830, and Earl Grey’s reform ministry took its place. In the crisis that followed Wellington led the Tory opposition to the Reform Bill, and in the Days of May 1832 was sent for by the King to form a government — only to fail, unable to take office on a reform basis and unwilling to carry the measure he had so long resisted. The great Duke, the hero of the war, had become the emblem of the old order against which the country had risen.
The elder statesman
Wellington never again held the premiership, but he remained a commanding figure. He commanded the armies in the field of politics with the same stolid authority he had shown in war; he led the Tory opposition, served in Peel’s governments, and stood by Peel in the crisis of the Corn Laws, supporting repeal and, as Martineau records, making his great speech in the House of Lords for the measure. In his old age he became the beloved “Iron Duke” of the national imagination, consulted by successive sovereigns and ministries, the guardian of the army, and the personification of the nation’s greatness. He died in 1852, and was buried with the highest honours in St. Paul’s. Within the period 1800–1865 his significance is double: the soldier who won the wars that made Britain supreme and the statesman whose ministry carried Catholic Emancipation, and whose resistance to reform marked the end of the old Tory world.
Sources

Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vols. II–III. Wellington’s ministry, Catholic Emancipation, and the Reform crisis.
Alison, Sir Archibald. History of Europe, Vol. I. Wellington and England from 1815.
Molesworth, William Nassau. History of England from the Year 1830, Vols. I–II. Wellington’s ministry and its fall in 1830.

events/abolition-of-slavery-1833.title: The Abolition of Slavery (1833)
events/abolition-of-slavery-1833.content:
The Abolition of Slavery (1833)
The Slavery Abolition Act of 1833, carried by the first Reformed Parliament, abolished slavery throughout the British colonies — the greatest humanitarian triumph of the age, and the fruit of a generation of agitation by the abolitionists under Wilberforce, Clarkson, and their successors. The Act, effective from 1 August 1834, emancipated the slaves of the British West Indies and the other colonies, and accompanied the emancipation with a compensation of £20,000,000 to the slave-owners and a system of apprenticeship. The abolition of the British slave trade in 1807 had attacked the traffic; the Act of 1833 destroyed the institution itself, and it set the example that the other powers were gradually to follow.
The long agitation
The movement against the slave trade and slavery had been the great humanitarian crusade of the age. The British slave trade had been abolished in 1807, after the long agitation led by Wilberforce and the abolitionists; the movement then turned to the institution of slavery itself, and through the 1820s pressed for the emancipation of the slaves in the British colonies. The agitation was carried on by the Anti-Slavery Society, by the churches, and by a great popular movement in the country, and it was powerfully reinforced in the 1820s by the government’s resolutions on the amelioration of slavery and by the revelations of its cruelties — the Smith the Missionary case and the condition of the colonies. By 1830 the abolition of slavery had become a demand that the reformed Parliament could not refuse.
The Reform and the Act
The first Reformed Parliament, which assembled in January 1833 after the triumph of the Reform Act, was the parliament that carried abolition. The ministry of Earl Grey, in which the abolitionists had strong supporters, brought forward the measure, and the Slavery Abolition Act was passed in 1833, to take effect on 1 August 1834. The Act emancipated the slaves throughout the British colonies, and it did so with a compensation of £20,000,000 paid to the slave-owners — the immense sum that was the price of the great act of justice. It accompanied the emancipation with a system of apprenticeship, by which the emancipated labourers were to pass through a transitional period of forced labour; this system, attacked by the abolitionists and marked by abuses, was brought to an end in 1838, two years before its appointed term.
The post-emancipation condition
The aftermath of emancipation was watched with anxiety and with hope. Martineau’s account of the years that followed dwelt with admiration on the quiet and orderly conduct of the former slaves, contrasting it with the behaviour of their former masters, and on the difficulties of the colonial legislatures and the planters in adjusting to the new order. The economic troubles of the West Indies, the hostility between the colonial legislatures and the executive, and the problems of labour and production followed emancipation; but the great fact stood — the institution of slavery had been abolished throughout the British dominions, and a whole race had been set free. The example of Britain, and the pressure of British opinion, contributed to the gradual abolition of slavery by the other colonial powers in the course of the century.
Significance
The abolition of slavery was the greatest humanitarian achievement of the age, and it fixed the moral character of the century. It was the triumph of the religious and philanthropic movement that had grown up since the 1780s, and it demonstrated the power of a great popular agitation carried on in the name of justice to move the state. Within the period 1800–1865 it stands as the culminating act of the reform era — the measure, carried by the reformed Parliament alongside the Factory Act and the Poor Law, that showed what the new constitution was for. And it set the pattern of British moral leadership in the world, the example that the other nations were to follow, and the memory that was to shape the later struggle over the slave trade and slavery beyond the British dominions.
Chronology

1807: Abolition of the British slave trade.
1820s: Agitation for the amelioration and then the abolition of slavery.
1833, August: The Slavery Abolition Act passed; to take effect 1 August 1834.
1834, 1 August: Emancipation throughout the British colonies; the apprenticeship system begins.
1838: Abolition of the apprenticeship; full freedom.

Sources

Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. III. The Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 and the £20,000,000 compensation.
Molesworth, William Nassau. History of England from the Year 1830, Vols. I–II. The abolition of slavery in the first Reformed Parliament.
Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. IV. The post-emancipation condition of the colonies.

events/accession-of-victoria-1837.title: The Accession of Queen Victoria (1837)
events/accession-of-victoria-1837.content:
The Accession of Queen Victoria (1837)
On 20 June 1837, on the death of her uncle William IV, the eighteen-year-old Princess Victoria succeeded to the throne as Queen — the beginning of the longest and most famous reign in English history. The accession was received with universal goodwill and “almost romantic interest,” as Molesworth recorded: after the feebleness and contention of the old reign, the youth and freshness of the girl Queen seemed to open a new era. It ended the long Regency and post-Regency age, gave the Melbourne ministry a new lease of life, and fixed the crown once more as the unifying centre of the state. The accession of 1837 is the great boundary-marker of the period — the moment the Victorian age began.
The succession and the new reign
Victoria was the only child of the Duke of Kent, the fourth son of George III, and had been born in 1819, in the scramble of the royal dukes to produce an heir after the death of Princess Charlotte in 1817. She came to the throne in her eighteenth year, a young woman of remarkable character and vitality. The country received her with enthusiasm; her accession was followed by a general election, which returned the Whigs under Melbourne with their majority maintained, and the young Queen formed a close dependence on her Prime Minister. The crown, which had played a contentious part in the Reform crisis and the Queen Caroline affair under the preceding reigns, passed into hands that were to make it once more the popular and constitutional centre of the nation.
The popular Queen
The accession opened a period of extraordinary popularity for the monarchy. After the “feeble old man” William IV, as Martineau observed, the youth and gaiety of Victoria were exhilarating; her delight in being seen, her drives through the thronged parks, her Guildhall dinner, and her command that her people should see her made her the darling of the nation. Her coronation followed in June 1838, and her marriage to Prince Albert in February 1840, with the birth of the Princess Royal in November 1840, gave the young reign its domestic character. The popularity of the Queen shored up the failing Melbourne ministry through the difficult years of the late 1830s, and the young sovereign became, as Lord Lyndhurst said, the “ray of comfort” of a dispiriting political landscape.
The significance of the accession
The accession of Victoria marked the end of one era and the beginning of another. It closed the age of the Regency and the Reform crisis — the age of George IV and William IV, of Peterloo and the Six Acts, of the old Tory and Whig contention — and it opened the settled Victorian age, in which the crown, popular, respectable, and above party, would become the emblem of the nation. Within the period 1800–1865 the accession is the central turning-point: the reign of the young Queen, with her marriage to Albert and her steady constitutional popularity, carried the monarchy through the great transitions of the Reform, free-trade, and Crimean decades, and gave its name and its character to the age.
Chronology

1819, 24 May: Birth of Princess Victoria.
1837, 20 June: Death of William IV; accession of Victoria.
1837, late: General election on the demise of the crown; Melbourne continues in office.
1838, 28 June: Coronation.
1840, 10 February: Marriage to Prince Albert.
1840, 21 November: Birth of the Princess Royal.

Sources

Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. IV. The accession of 1837 and the opening of the reign.

events/american-civil-war-alabama.title: The American Civil War and the Alabama (1861–1865)
events/american-civil-war-alabama.content:
The American Civil War and the Alabama (1861–1865)
The American Civil War of 1861–1865 was the great foreign event of the closing years of the period, and for Britain it raised in acute form the questions of neutrality, of the cotton supply, and of the Alabama. The war between the Northern and Southern states of the American Union convulsed the world’s greatest trading nation and bore directly upon England: the blockade of the Southern ports cut off the cotton on which the Lancashire mills depended, causing the great cotton famine; the seizure of the Confederate commissioners from the British mail packet Trent brought Britain and the North to the brink of war; and the escape of the Confederate cruiser Alabama, built in a British yard, let loose a commerce-raider that preyed on American shipping and gave rise to the Alabama claims that were to be settled by international arbitration. The war, and Britain’s part in it, tested the neutrality of the greatest maritime power and left a legacy of claims and grievances that the later settlement was to resolve.
The cotton famine and the British attitude
The war brought immediate distress to the manufacturing districts of England. The blockade of the Southern ports cut off the supply of cotton, and the cotton mills of Lancashire, dependent on American cotton, fell idle; the destitution of the operatives — some 500,000, in the estimate of the age — was relieved by the relief committees, and was borne, as Molesworth noted, with remarkable patience and order. The attitude of the governing and commercial classes in England was divided: sympathy with the Confederacy was strong among the aristocracy and the commercial interest, while the working classes and the radicals, opposed to slavery, inclined to the North. The British government, under Palmerston, professed a strict neutrality, and the recognition of the Confederacy, pressed by some, was withheld.
The Trent affair
The danger of war with the North came with the Trent affair of November 1861. Captain Wilkes of the United States sloop San Jacinto stopped the British mail packet Trent on the high seas and removed the Confederate commissioners, Mason and Slidell, who were on their way to Europe. The act, a violation of neutral rights and an affront to the British flag, roused a storm of indignation in England; the British government demanded the surrender of the commissioners and prepared for war. The crisis was averted when the United States, unwilling to fight a second enemy, released the commissioners; the affair was settled peacefully, and the immediate danger of an Anglo-American war passed. But it had shown how near the two nations had come to conflict, and it left its mark on the relations of the two countries.
The Alabama
The most lasting grievance was the Alabama. The Confederate cruiser Alabama had been built in the yard of Messrs. Laird at Birkenhead, had escaped to sea, and had then preyed upon the commerce of the United States, capturing and destroying a great number of American merchant ships. The American government held that Britain, by permitting the fitting out of the cruiser in its ports, had failed in the duty of a neutral, and it claimed compensation for the losses inflicted. The Alabama claims became the standing grievance of Anglo-American relations, and they were at last settled by the Treaty of Washington (1871) and the Geneva arbitration, by which Britain accepted the “three rules” of neutrality and paid an award of £3,250,000. The Alabama affair was the classic case of the obligations of neutrality, and its settlement by arbitration was a landmark of international law.
Significance
The American Civil War closed the period 1800–1865 in a sense of change and of anxiety. It tested the neutrality of Britain, the greatest maritime and commercial power, in the face of a war that divided its own opinion and cut off its essential supply; it brought the cotton famine upon the manufacturing districts; and it produced, in the Alabama claims, a grievance that was to be settled only by the arbitration of the next decade. Within the period the war stands as the great foreign event of its closing years — the event that showed the interdependence of the Atlantic world, the perils of neutrality, and the beginnings of the Anglo-American understanding that was to grow out of the settlement of the Alabama.
Chronology

1861: The American Civil War begins; the blockade of the South; the cotton famine in Lancashire.
1861, November: The Trent affair; the crisis and its peaceful settlement.
1862–64: The Alabama preys on American commerce.
1865: The end of the war.
1871–72: The Treaty of Washington and the Geneva arbitration; the award on the Alabama claims.

Sources

McCarthy, Justin. A History of Our Own Times, Vol. II. The American Civil War and the Alabama from the British side.
Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. IV. The United States and the closing of the period.

events/bombardment-of-algiers-1816.title: The Bombardment of Algiers (1816)
events/bombardment-of-algiers-1816.content:
The Bombardment of Algiers (1816)
The bombardment of Algiers, on 27 August 1816, was the naval expedition in which Lord Exmouth’s British fleet destroyed the Algerian fleet and forced the Dey to release the Christian captives and abandon the practice of Christian slavery — the crowning blow against the Barbary piracy that had preyed on the commerce of Europe for centuries. It was a demonstration of British naval power in the Mediterranean in the years of peace, a humanitarian triumph over the slave trade of the Barbary coast, and one of the most celebrated naval actions of the postwar period.
The Barbary piracy
For centuries the Barbary States of the north African coast — Algiers, Tunis, Tripoli — had maintained a warfare of piracy against the commerce of the Christian nations, seizing the ships and enslaving the crews of Europe. The traffic in Christian captives, held for ransom or condemned to slavery, was one of the standing evils of the Mediterranean, and the Barbary powers, nominally under the suzerainty of the Ottoman Empire, had defied the repeated efforts of the European states to suppress them. After the Napoleonic wars, in which the European navies had been otherwise engaged, the Barbary pirates had renewed their depredations with impunity, and the demand for a final settlement had grown in England.
Lord Exmouth’s expedition
In 1816 a British fleet under Lord Exmouth — who had already conducted a first expedition against Algiers in the previous year — was sent to the Barbary coast to compel the release of the Christian captives and the abandonment of Christian slavery. Exmouth demanded the release of the captives from Algiers and Tunis and Tripoli, and when the Dey of Algiers temporised, he attacked. On 27 August 1816 the British fleet bombarded the mole and the town of Algiers, silenced the batteries, and destroyed the Algerian fleet in the harbour. The Dey was forced to capitulate: the Christian captives were released, the practice of enslaving Christians was abandoned, and treaties were concluded with Algiers, Tunis, and Tripoli. The bombardment was a striking proof of the power of the British navy in the Mediterranean, and of the readiness of the British government to use it in a humanitarian cause.
Significance
The bombardment of Algiers was the great triumph over the Barbary pirates, and it marked the effective end of the Christian slave trade of the Barbary coast. It was, at once, a naval action of the first order, a demonstration of British power in the Mediterranean in the years of peace, and a humanitarian achievement in the suppression of slavery and piracy. Martineau placed it in the years of peace and social improvement that followed the war, as an example of Britain’s Mediterranean power projection and of the international effort against piracy. Within the period 1800–1865 it stands as the type of the postwar naval action — the use of the navy, in the years between the great wars, to suppress piracy and slavery and to assert the peace of the seas.
Chronology

1815: Exmouth’s first expedition against the Barbary States.
1816, 27 August: The bombardment of Algiers; the destruction of the Algerian fleet.
1816: The treaties with Algiers, Tunis, and Tripoli; the release of the Christian captives.

events/catholic-emancipation-1829.title: Catholic Emancipation (1829)
events/catholic-emancipation-1829.content:
Catholic Emancipation (1829)
The Catholic Emancipation Act of 1829 — the Catholic Relief Act carried by the Duke of Wellington’s ministry — admitted Catholics to Parliament and to most civil offices, sweeping away the last great penal disability under which the Catholic majority of Ireland had laboured since the Reformation. It was the crowning act of the long struggle for religious liberty, wrung from a reluctant government by the agitation of Daniel O’Connell and the Catholic Association in Ireland and the crisis of the Clare election. The measure broke the old Tory alliance against change, destroyed the unanimity of the government and its party, and opened the way to the reform era that followed.
The long disability and the Catholic question
Since the Reformation, the Catholics of the three kingdoms had been excluded from the full rights of citizenship — from Parliament, from the higher offices of state, from the universities — by a body of penal legislation that the eighteenth century had only partly relaxed. The Treaty of Limerick and its violated guarantees, the penal laws under Henry VIII, Elizabeth, and the Stuarts, and the disabilities of the Catholic subjects of Ireland were the standing grievance of the age. The movement for relief had grown through the eighteenth century and had revived in the 1820s: the Catholic claims were debated year after year, with Mr Canning advocating relief and the Duke of York declaring his unalterable opposition to the last hour of his life. The argument turned in part on the coronation oath, which, it was said, forbade the sovereign to assent to the admission of Catholics to the legislature.
O’Connell and the Clare election
The decisive force was the agitation of Daniel O’Connell in Ireland. In 1823 O’Connell organised the new Catholic Association, with its “Catholic rent” of a penny a month, and turned the demand for emancipation into a great popular movement, financed by the mass of the Catholic people and organised throughout Ireland. The crisis came with the Clare election of 1828: O’Connell, though a Catholic and therefore ineligible, stood for the county and was elected by a triumphant majority — a demonstration, both of the power of the Catholic organisation and of the absurdity of the law, that compelled the question upon the government. Wellington, who had long opposed emancipation, and Peel, his Home Secretary, became convinced that it could no longer be resisted without civil war.
The Catholic Relief Act of 1829
In 1829 the government carried the Catholic Relief Act. Catholics were admitted to Parliament and to most civil offices, and the political disability was removed; the measure was accompanied by the suppression of the Catholic Association and by provisions designed to diminish the number of Irish electors. The bill was carried against the furious opposition of the Protestant interest — the Brunswick clubs and the militant Orangemen — and Wellington and Peel, deserted by half their friends, broke with their own party to carry it. The Duke was hanged in effigy and Peel had to fight a contested election on his re-appointment; but emancipation was carried, and Ireland was, for the moment, tranquillized.
Significance
Catholic Emancipation was a turning-point of the age. It proved that the constitution could be altered when the crisis was sharp enough, and it broke the old alliance of Protestant and Tory opinion against change; the government that carried it had conceded to agitation what it had refused to argument, and the lesson was not lost on the reformers. It opened the way for the reform of Parliament itself — for the great Reform Bill of 1832, which the political revolution of 1829 had made possible. And it established O’Connell and the Catholic Association as a power in the state, the beginning of the great Irish agitation that was to run through the century. Emancipation stands, with the Reform Act, as one of the two great constitutional surrenders of the age — the moment the old exclusive constitution of the eighteenth century began to break up.
Chronology

1823: O’Connell organises the Catholic Association.
1828: The Clare election; O’Connell elected though ineligible.
1829: Wellington and Peel carry the Catholic Relief Act; the Catholic Association suppressed.

Sources

Molesworth, William Nassau. History of England from the Year 1830, Vol. I. The Catholic question and the crisis of 1828–29.
Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. II. The Catholic question in the 1820s.

events/corn-laws-repeal-1846.title: The Repeal of the Corn Laws (1846)
events/corn-laws-repeal-1846.content:
The Repeal of the Corn Laws (1846)
The repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846 — the abandonment of the protective duties on imported grain — was the great free-trade triumph of the age and the measure that split the Conservative Party and destroyed Sir Robert Peel’s government. For a generation the Corn Laws had been the bulwark of the agricultural interest and the emblem of protection; against them the manufacturing interest had organised the great agitation of the Anti-Corn-Law League, and the potato famine in Ireland in 1845 finally convinced Peel that the duties must go. Peel carried the repeal through Parliament against the mass of his own party, which, under Disraeli and Lord George Bentinck, turned him out of office on an Irish Coercion Bill immediately afterwards. The repeal fixed free trade as the settled policy of the age and remade the terms of British politics.
The Corn Laws and the League
The Corn Laws, which imposed duties on imported wheat and other grain, had been renewed and adjusted through the postwar years to protect the home agricultural interest. To the manufacturers and the working classes they were the emblem of a system that kept the price of bread high for the benefit of the landlord. The Anti-Corn-Law League, founded in Manchester in 1838 and led by Richard Cobden and John Bright, turned the opposition into a great popular agitation — raising funds, registering freeholders in the manufacturing districts for the county vote, and propagating free-trade doctrine through lectures, pamphlets, bazaars, and the Economist. By the mid-1840s the League had made the Corn Laws the central question of English politics and had prepared the ground for repeal.
The crisis of 1845 and Peel’s recantation
The decisive event was the potato blight. In 1845 the potato crop — the staple food of Ireland and of a large part of England — was struck by disease, and it became clear that a terrible famine impended. Peel, who had long doubted the Corn Laws in private, was convinced that the duties must be suspended or repealed to allow the free importation of food. In December 1845, unable to carry his Cabinet with him and faced with the refusal of Lord John Russell to form a ministry, Peel resigned; but Russell could not form a government, and Peel returned to office resolved to repeal. In January 1846 he announced his recantation of agricultural protection, and the announcement was published in the Times; the repeal of the Corn Laws was brought forward, with a measure of compensation to the landed interest, and passed in June 1846 after a struggle in which Disraeli rallied the Protectionists around Lord George Bentinck and delivered his brilliant speeches against the minister.
The fall of Peel
The passing of the repeal destroyed the government. Peel’s own party, the Protectionist majority of the Conservatives, voted against him; the repeal was carried only with the support of the Whigs and the Radicals, and the ministry fell immediately afterwards on the Irish Coercion Bill, defeated by the coalition of Protectionists and Whigs. Peel’s final speech, in which he declared that he left a name “perhaps to be remembered in the pages of history,” closed his great ministry. The Duke of Wellington, who had supported repeal, remained loyal; but the Conservative Party was shattered and split, and did not recover a majority until the 1870s. Lord John Russell formed the Whig ministry that followed.
The free-trade settlement
The repeal fixed free trade as the settled policy of the British state. Alison, surveying its effects, traced the consequences for the prices of food, for national progress, and for the independence of the country, and insisted on the necessity of maritime superiority to the existence of a free-trading Britain — the command of the sea that allowed the importation of food and the export of manufactures. In the same spirit the repeal of the Navigation Laws followed in 1849, opening the British carrying trade to foreign shipping. The repeal of the Corn Laws was the pivot of the age’s political economy: it marked the triumph of the manufacturing and commercial interest over the landed interest, the acceptance of the free-trade doctrines of Cobden and the League, and the beginning of the era of unqualified free trade that lasted into the twentieth century.
Chronology

1838: Foundation of the Anti-Corn-Law League in Manchester.
1845, autumn: The potato blight; the prospect of famine.
1845, December: Peel’s resignation; Russell’s failure; Peel’s return.
1846, January: Peel announces his recantation of protection.
1846, June: Repeal of the Corn Laws passes.
1846, June–July: Peel’s government falls on the Irish Coercion Bill; Russell forms a ministry.

Sources

events/crimean-war-1853-56.title: The Crimean War (1853–1856)
events/crimean-war-1853-56.content:
The Crimean War (1853–1856)
The Crimean War was the great European war of the mid-century — the conflict in which Britain and France, with the Ottoman Empire and later Sardinia, fought Russia over the Eastern Question, and in which the allied armies besieged and at last took the Russian fortress of Sebastopol in the Crimea. It was the first great war of the age of steam and the electric telegraph, the war in which the incompetence and suffering of the armies were exposed by the war correspondent and the nurse, and the war that ended the “forty years’ peace” and marked the opening of the second half of the century. The war carried England from the settled prosperity of the Exhibition era into a conflict whose mismanagement destroyed a government and whose lessons — of Balaclava, Inkerman, and Scutari — remained with the age.
The causes and the outbreak
The war grew out of the Eastern Question — the perennial dispute over the decaying Ottoman Empire and the ambitions of Russia. The conflict over the holy places and the Russian claims to protect the Orthodox Christians of Turkey led, in 1853, to the Russian occupation of the Danubian Principalities and the declaration of war by Turkey; the British and French, alarmed at the Russian advance, joined the war in 1854. The British government, the Aberdeen coalition, drifted into the war; Martineau, closing her history, presented the declaration of war in March 1854 as “a war accepted on behalf of a good cause” and the natural close of the forty years’ peace. The Russian retreat from the Principalities and the allied landing at Eupatoria opened the campaign in the Crimea.
The war in the Crimea
The allied army, landing in the Crimea, fought the battle of the Alma (20 September 1854), marched round Sebastopol, and invested the fortress. The battles of Balaclava (25 October) — with the celebrated Charge of the Light Brigade and the “thin red line” of the 93rd Highlanders — and of Inkerman (5 November), the “soldiers’ battle” fought in a fog, followed; and then came the terrible winter of 1854–55, in which the hurricane, the breakdown of the commissariat, and the sufferings of the troops before Sebastopol were exposed to the world by the correspondence of W. H. Russell in The Times. The mismanagement revealed by the war — the mortality at the Barrack Hospital at Scutari, relieved by the mission of Florence Nightingale and the organisation of the nursing service — produced a storm of indignation in England. The Roebuck committee of inquiry exposed the failures, the Aberdeen coalition fell, and Palmerston formed his first ministry in February 1855 to carry the war to a conclusion. The renewal of the bombardment, the capture of the Malakoff (8 September 1855), and the Russian evacuation of the south side of Sebastopol broke the fortress, and the Peace of Paris of 30 March 1856 closed the war — the neutralisation of the Black Sea, the independence of the Danubian Principalities, and the containment of Russia.
Significance
The Crimean War was a turning-point of the age. It ended the forty years’ peace and opened the era of the great wars of the second half of the century; it exposed the military and administrative incompetence of the old order and forced the beginnings of army reform; it created the modern war correspondent and the modern military nurse, and made the suffering of the common soldier a matter of national concern. It carried Palmerston to power and to his ascendancy, and it left the balance of power in Europe disturbed and unstable. Within the period 1800–1865 the war closes the story — the event that broke the settled confidence of the Exhibition age and carried England, and Europe, into the new era of the later nineteenth century.
Chronology

1853: The Eastern crisis; Russia occupies the Principalities; Turkey declares war.
1854, March: Britain and France declare war on Russia.
1854, 20 September: Battle of the Alma.
1854, 25 October: Battle of Balaclava; the Charge of the Light Brigade.
1854, 5 November: Battle of Inkerman.
1854–55: The winter; the sufferings of the troops; the Roebuck committee.
1855, February: Fall of Aberdeen; Palmerston forms his ministry.
1855, 8 September: Capture of the Malakoff; the fall of Sebastopol.
1856, 30 March: Peace of Paris.

Sources

Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. IV. The drift to war and the close of the forty years’ peace.

events/crisis-of-1847.title: The Crisis of 1847
events/crisis-of-1847.content:
The Crisis of 1847
The crisis of 1847 was the great commercial and financial catastrophe of the mid-century — a panic of such severity that it brought the country to the verge of a suspension of cash payments and compelled the government to sanction the Bank of England’s infringement of the very law it had enacted three years before. Its causes lay in the railway mania, the bad harvest of 1846, and the Irish famine; its course tested the Bank Charter Act of 1844 to destruction and produced the classic controversy over the currency principle that Tooke and the banking school made the centre of their great indictment. The crisis of 1847 was to the commercial system what the crisis of 1825 had been to the old — the terrible demonstration of the laws of credit, and the standing example for the monetary debates of the rest of the century.
Causes
The crisis had its roots in the over-speculation of the railway mania and the failures of the harvests. The vast capital demands of the railways had absorbed the resources of the country; the bad harvest of 1846 and the terrible famine in Ireland had drained the gold of the Bank of England for the purchase of foreign corn; and the deficient cotton supply added to the general distress. The corn imports, paid for in gold, carried the exchanges against England and drew the bullion from the Bank’s vaults. By 1847 the commercial system, strained by speculation and by the demands of the famine, was on the point of collapse.
The course of the panic
The panic came in the autumn of 1847. The commercial houses, unable to renew their engagements, failed; the discount market was thrown into confusion; and a general run of distrust set in. The Bank of England, whose Banking Department reserve had been exhausted by the drain of gold under the operation of the Bank Charter Act, was unable to relieve the pressure — the Act of 1844, by separating the Issue from the Banking Department, had placed the Bank in a position in which it could not come to the aid of the market without violating the law. The government, on 25 October 1847, sanctioned the Bank to issue notes beyond the statutory limit, an act of suspension in all but name. The announcement at once restored confidence; the panic gradually subsided; and the crisis passed without the complete suspension of cash payments that had been feared.
The controversy
The crisis of 1847 became the pivot of the great currency controversy. Tooke, in his history of prices, subjected the operation of the Bank Act from September 1844 through the close of 1847 to an exhaustive review, and concluded that the Act, far from averting the crisis, had aggravated it — denying the Bank the power to relieve the market when its reserve ran low, and applying the mechanical rule of the currency principle at the moment when discretion was most needed. He compared the crisis of 1847 with that of 1825, tracing the difference to the working of the new law. Peel, defending the Act on 3 December 1847, maintained that its machinery had saved the convertibility of the note and that but for it the panic would have been total; his defenders argued that the Act had averted a complete suspension of cash payments. Gilbart, from the statistical side, traced how the country circulation had behaved through the pressure under the fixed maxima. The controversy was never wholly resolved; but the crisis of 1847 remained the classic test-case of the currency principle, and the suspension of the Act the standing admission that its machinery could not always hold.
Chronology

1845–46: The railway mania reaches its height; the reaction begins.
1846: The bad harvest; the Irish famine begins.
1847, autumn: The drain of gold; the commercial failures; the panic.
1847, 25 October: The government sanctions the Bank to exceed the statutory limit.
1847, 3 December: Peel defends the Act in Parliament.

Sources

Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. IV. The financial panic of 1847 and the suspension of the Bank Act.
Alison, Sir Archibald. History of Europe, Vol. VII. The railway mania and crisis of 1847.
Walpole, Sir Spencer. History of England, Vol. IV. The commercial crisis of 1847.
Gilbart. Laws of the Currency (1854). Country circulation through the pressure of 1847.

events/first-opium-war-1839-42.title: The First Opium War (1839–1842)
events/first-opium-war-1839-42.content:
The First Opium War (1839–1842)
The First Opium War was the war between Britain and China of 1839–1842 — the conflict over the opium trade and the refusal of the Chinese Empire to open its ports, which ended in the British capture of the Chinese coast and the Treaty of Nanking. It was the war that forced China to admit the foreign trade, to cede Hong Kong, and to open the treaty ports, and it was, with the Afghan war and the conquests in India, one of the great acts of the extension of British power in the East in the middle of the century. The war was also, as Martineau acknowledged with evident moral unease, an act of wrong and violence through which free trade was introduced to China — a proceeding whose consequences, she warned, would haunt future generations.
The opium trade and the Chinese prohibition
The war grew out of the British trade with China, and above all the trade in opium. The Chinese Empire, which held the foreign merchants at Canton and confined their commerce, had long prohibited the importation of opium; but the drug was smuggled in on a vast scale, the balance of trade running in favour of the Chinese until the opium reversed it, and the silver of China flowing out in payment. The Chinese government, alarmed at the ruin of its people and the drain of its treasure, resolved to suppress the trade, and in 1839 Commissioner Lin destroyed the opium held by the British merchants at Canton and demanded their submission. The British government, urged by the merchants and by the principle of free trade, resolved upon war.
The course of the war
The war was fought along the Chinese coast, where the superior British forces, with their steamers and their artillery, swept aside the antiquated Chinese defences. The British captured the cities and forts of the coast, blockaded the rivers, and at last, by the capture of the great ports and the threat to the capital, compelled the Chinese to sue for peace. Lord Napier’s earlier failed mission and Commissioner Lin’s crackdown had prepared the ground; the campaigns of the war proper — the capture of Chusan and the other operations of the British fleet and army — brought the Chinese Empire to terms.
The Treaty of Nanking
The Treaty of Nanking, signed in 1842, ended the war and opened China to the foreign trade. It ceded the island of Hong Kong to Britain, opened the treaty ports — Canton, Amoy, Foochow, Ningpo, and Shanghai — to British commerce, and provided for the payment of an indemnity. The treaty was the foundation of the system of the “unequal treaties” by which the Western powers traded with China on their own terms, and it opened the long era of the foreign penetration of China. The First Opium War, and the trade it defended, was the great stain on the record of British free trade in the East.
Significance
The First Opium War was the first of the wars that forced China open to the world, and its significance was immense. It established the British position in China, secured Hong Kong and the treaty ports, and opened the commerce of the Chinese Empire; it was also, in the judgment of the more honest of its contemporaries, a war waged on behalf of a traffic in a destructive drug. Martineau, recording the war with moral ambivalence, acknowledged the wrong and violence through which free trade was introduced to China and warned that the consequences would haunt future generations. Within the period 1800–1865 the war stands, with the extension of British power in India, as one of the great acts of the British empire in the East — at once a triumph of commerce and arms and a standing reproach to the conscience of the age.
Chronology

1834: Lord Napier’s failed mission to China.
1839: Commissioner Lin destroys the opium; the crisis at Canton.
1839–42: The British operations along the Chinese coast.
1842: The Treaty of Nanking; the cession of Hong Kong and the opening of the treaty ports.

Sources

Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. IV. The Opium War with China and the Treaty of Nanking.
Alison, Sir Archibald. History of Europe, Vol. VIII. The First Opium War and the Treaty of Nanking.
Molesworth, William Nassau. History of England from the Year 1830, Vols. I–II. The China war and the fall of Canton.

events/great-exhibition-1851.title: The Great Exhibition (1851)
events/great-exhibition-1851.content:
The Great Exhibition (1851)
The Great Exhibition of 1851 — the Exhibition of the Industry of All Nations — was the great festival of the mid-century: the international exhibition held in the Crystal Palace in Hyde Park, which displayed the manufactures and works of art of all nations and became the emblem of the peace, prosperity, and progress of the age. Opened by the Queen on 1 May 1851, it was the first of the great international exhibitions, the creation of the Prince Consort and of the age’s confidence in industry and peace. Its vast glass palace, its machinery, its crowds, and its profit marked the high noon of the mid-Victorian prosperity, and its memory survived as the “Festival of Peace” that closed the first half of the century.
The Crystal Palace
The Exhibition was housed in the Crystal Palace, the great structure of glass and iron designed by Joseph Paxton and erected in Hyde Park. The building itself was one of the wonders of the age — a vast conservatory of glass, enclosing trees and fountains, which seemed to embody the triumph of the new engineering. Within it were arranged the products of all nations: the machinery, the manufactures, the works of art, the raw materials that each country sent to display its industry. The British section showed the machinery and manufactures in which England led the world; the foreign sections showed the competition and the friendship of the nations. The whole, in the eyes of the age, was a demonstration of the progress of industry and of the possibility of peaceful international rivalry.
The Festival of Peace
The Exhibition was conceived in the spirit of peace. Its patron and moving spirit was the Prince Consort, Albert, who saw in it the means of promoting the arts, manufactures, and commerce of the nations and of binding them together in peace. It was opened by the Queen on 1 May 1851, and during the months of its continuance it was visited by vast crowds — the whole population of England seemed to pour into London, and the railways, the inns, and the streets were filled with the visitors. The Exhibition was a commercial success, yielding a profit that founded the South Kensington museum complex, and it was a moral and political triumph — a proof of the prosperity of England and of the peace of the world. Martineau presented it as the “Festival of Peace” that closed the forty years’ peace and crowned the national advancement of the age.
Significance
The Great Exhibition stands as the emblem of the high noon of the mid-Victorian age. It was the demonstration of the industrial and commercial supremacy of England, the celebration of the peace and prosperity that had followed the reform and free-trade decades, and the beginning of the great international exhibitions that were to be a feature of the later century. It marked, as contemporaries felt, the close of one epoch and the opening of another: the period of the forty years’ peace, of which the Exhibition was the crowning festival, was about to be broken by the Crimean War, and the Exhibition stood as the last great pageant of the peaceful age. Its significance in the period 1800–1865 is that of the supreme expression of the confidence, the industry, and the peace of mid-Victorian England.
Chronology

1850: The project for the Exhibition takes shape under the Prince Consort.
1851, 1 May: Opening of the Great Exhibition by the Queen.
1851, autumn: The Exhibition closes; the profit funds the South Kensington museums.

Sources

events/indian-mutiny-1857.title: The Indian Mutiny (1857)
events/indian-mutiny-1857.content:
The Indian Mutiny (1857)
The Indian Mutiny of 1857 was the great revolt of the Bengal army and of large parts of northern and central India against British rule — the most serious challenge the British empire in India had faced, and the event that brought the East India Company’s rule to an end and transferred India to the Crown. Beginning with the mutiny of the sepoys at Meerut in May 1857, the revolt spread to Delhi, to Oude, and to the plains of central India, and was marked by the seizure of Delhi, the massacre at Cawnpore, and the long sieges of Lucknow before it was at last suppressed. The mutiny convulsed India and horrified England, and its suppression, and the transfer of the government of India to the Crown, closed one epoch of British India and opened another.
The causes and the outbreak
The mutiny had its origins in the grievances of the Bengal army and of the Indian population against the East India Company’s rule — the greased cartridges of the new Enfield rifle, which offended the religious sensibilities of Hindu and Muslim sepoys alike, the annexations and the innovations of the Company’s later years, and the general distrust of its government. In May 1857 the sepoys at Meerut mutinied, murdered their officers, and marched on Delhi, where the aged Mughal emperor was proclaimed. The revolt spread rapidly through the Bengal army and through Oude, whose annexation had been a standing grievance; the British, few in number and caught unprepared, were swept aside in many places, and the mutiny became a general rising against the Company’s rule.
The war in India
The suppression of the mutiny was a desperate struggle. Delhi was besieged and at last recaptured by assault, in which John Nicholson was killed; at Cawnpore the garrison and the women and children surrendered to Nana Sahib, who massacred them — the atrocity that filled England with horror and a cry for vengeance; at Lucknow the garrison under Outram held the Residency through a long siege until relieved by Havelock and finally by Sir Colin Campbell. The news of the mutiny, arriving in England with the slow mails, produced a shock and a demand for retribution that the British public had not felt since the beginnings of the empire. The reconquest of Oude and the relentless suppression of the rising completed the work, and by the end of 1858 the mutiny was crushed.
The end of the East India Company
The mutiny brought the East India Company’s rule to an end. The Government of India Act of 1858 transferred the government of India from the Company to the Crown, abolished the Company’s double government, and created the India Office and the Council of India. The Queen, in the famous proclamation of 1858, promised the Indian princes and peoples the protection of the Crown and the respect of their religions and customs. The mutiny, and the transfer of power, marked the beginning of the imperial system of the later nineteenth century — the rule of India as a dependency of the Crown, the memorial of the Mutiny as the great and terrible event of British India, and the beginning of the closer, more responsible, and more conservative government of the subcontinent.
Significance
The Indian Mutiny was the greatest crisis of the British empire in the nineteenth century, and its significance was immense. It exposed the weakness and the unpopularity of the East India Company’s rule and brought it to an end; it produced the transfer of India to the Crown and the beginning of the modern imperial system; and it left an enduring mark on the British imagination — the memory of the massacres, the sieges, and the heroism that coloured the relations of England and India for the rest of the century. Within the period 1800–1865 it stands as the event that closed the era of the Company and opened the era of the Crown — the great and terrible boundary between the old and the new British India.
Chronology

1857, 10 May: The mutiny at Meerut; the march on Delhi.
1857: The seizure of Delhi; the massacre at Cawnpore; the siege of Lucknow.
1857–58: The recapture of Delhi; the relief of Lucknow; the reconquest of Oude.
1858: The suppression of the mutiny; the Government of India Act; the Queen’s proclamation.

events/irish-famine-1845-49.title: The Irish Famine (1845–1849)
events/irish-famine-1845-49.content:
The Irish Famine (1845–1849)
The Irish famine of 1845–1849 — the Great Famine, or an Gorta Mór — was the terrible catastrophe of the mid-century: the failure of the potato crop, the staple food of the Irish people, and the resulting mortality and emigration on a scale that transformed Ireland and haunted the conscience of the age. The blight first appeared in 1845; the crop failed again in 1846 and 1847, and the famine ran through the end of the decade, carrying off perhaps a million people and driving more than a million more to emigrate. The famine was the great moral and political disaster of the period, the event that made the repeal of the Corn Laws possible, that exposed the inadequacy of the relief measures, and that set in motion the long decline of the Irish population.
The potato and the blight
Ireland in the 1840s was a country of extraordinary poverty and density of population, in which the potato — a crop of great yield on small plots — had become the staple food of the mass of the people. The country, as Walpole and the other observers recorded, was over-populated, without coal or manufactures, and dependent on the potato for its subsistence. In 1845 the potato crop was struck by a blight — a disease that rotted the tubers in the ground — and the failure threatened a terrible famine. The blight was the event that convinced Peel of the necessity of repealing the Corn Laws: the free importation of food was a national necessity, and the repeal of the duties was carried in 1846. But the repeal came too late and was too small to save Ireland.
The failure and the relief
The crop failed again in 1846 and 1847, and the famine settled upon the country. The Russell ministry, which succeeded Peel, struggled with the catastrophe — the introduction of Indian meal, the organisation of relief works and relief committees, the inadequacy of the measures, and the terrible mortality. The relief works proved unable to cope with the scale of the disaster, and were discontinued; the Irish Poor Law, the Encumbered Estates Act, and the other measures of the government proved insufficient. Martineau’s account of the famine records the government’s struggle with the catastrophe and the inadequacy of its relief; the emigration and the mortality ran on through the end of the decade. The famine in western Scotland and the western Highlands paralleled, on a smaller scale, the Irish catastrophe.
The consequences
The famine’s consequences were immense and lasting. A vast number of the Irish people died of starvation and disease; a vast number more emigrated, chiefly to America and to England, in the exodus that transformed the Irish population and created the Irish communities abroad. The land of Ireland was left to fewer people and to a new class of proprietors under the Encumbered Estates Act, which sold the insolvent estates. The famine embittered the relations between Ireland and England, fed the Irish national and repeal movements, and became the central grievance of Irish history. It also produced the permanent Irish immigration into the English towns that Engels and the social observers recorded — the Irish who crowded the poor districts of Manchester, Liverpool, and London, and who formed the great reservoir of unskilled labour of the industrial age.
Significance
The Irish famine was the greatest single disaster of the period, and its significance was moral, political, and social at once. It revealed the depth of Irish poverty and the inadequacy of the English government’s measures; it made the repeal of the Corn Laws; it set in motion the emigration that emptied Ireland; and it fixed the Irish question as the great standing difficulty of the English state. Within the period 1800–1865 it stands as the darkest chapter — the catastrophe that the contemporary writers recorded with horror, that the economists and the statesmen struggled to relieve, and that left its mark on Ireland, on England, and on the relations between them for generations.
Chronology

1845, autumn: The first appearance of the potato blight; Peel’s conversion to repeal.
1846: Repeal of the Corn Laws; the second failure of the crop; the famine deepens.
1846–49: The relief works, the mortality, and the emigration.
1847: The worst year of the famine.
1849: The Encumbered Estates Act; the slow end of the catastrophe.

Sources

events/mayhew-morning-chronicle-survey-1.title: Mayhew's Morning Chronicle Survey of London Labour (1850)
events/mayhew-morning-chronicle-survey-1.content:
Mayhew’s Morning Chronicle Survey of London Labour (1850)
Henry Mayhew’s Morning Chronicle survey of the labour and the poor of the metropolitan districts, published as a series of letters in January–March 1850, was the founding work of the English social survey — the investigation of the condition of the London poor by first-hand inquiry, personal testimony, and statistics that laid open to the public the hidden world of the metropolis. Mayhew, writing as Special Correspondent of the Morning Chronicle, explored the casual wards, the vagrancy, the sweated trades, and the lodging-houses of London; his letters formed the raw material from which he built his greater work, London Labour and the London Poor (1861–62), and they established the method of the Victorian social investigation of poverty.
The letters
The fourteen letters of the survey, published in the Morning Chronicle from January to March 1850, carried Mayhew’s investigation through the chief problems of metropolitan poverty. He began with the casual wards and the vagrancy of the metropolis — the evils of uncertain labour, the system of casual wards in the workhouses, and the class of habitual vagrants that the system created. He traced the geographical history of vagrancy over fourteen years, with the tables of the Asylum for the Houseless Poor showing the numbers by county and country and the effect of the Irish famine. He investigated the causes of depredation, vagrancy, and mendicancy, drawing on the Constabulary Commissioners’ Report of 1839. He examined the boot and shoe trade and the sweated trades, the slop work, the toy-makers and the doll manufacture, the low lodging-houses in which the poor herded together, and the whole condition of the metropolitan labouring poor.
The method
The importance of the survey lay in its method as much as its findings. Mayhew combined the personal interview — the testimony of the poor themselves, recorded in their own words — with exact statements of earnings, expenditure, and cost of living, and with statistical tables. He went among the people, into the lodging-houses and the workshops, and reported what he saw and heard with a fidelity and a detail that no earlier inquiry had attempted. The letters established the model of the social survey — the direct investigation of the condition of the poor, the precise record of their earnings and their miseries — on which the later Victorian inquiries into poverty were built.
Significance
The Morning Chronicle survey was the first great public revelation of the condition of the London poor, and it made Mayhew’s reputation as the leading social investigator of the age. It fed the growing concern with the condition of the people, the reform of the Poor Law, of sanitation, and of the housing and the labour of the poor; and it supplied the raw material for London Labour and the London Poor (1861–62), the four-volume encyclopaedia of the street-folk, the street trades, and the criminal and destitute classes that remains the indispensable record of mid-Victorian London. Within the period 1800–1865 the survey of 1850 stands at the head of the great Victorian social investigation — the moment the condition of the London poor was first laid open to the public in all its detail, and the foundation of the modern social survey.
Chronology

1850, January–March: The fourteen letters published in the Morning Chronicle.
1850s: Mayhew expands the material.
1861–62: London Labour and the London Poor published in four volumes.

Sources

Mayhew, Henry. The Morning Chronicle Survey of Labour and the Poor: The Metropolitan Districts (1850). The fourteen letters.
Mayhew, Henry. London Labour and the London Poor, Vol. I (1861–62). The survey’s expansion into the street-folk.
