events/municipal-reform-1835.title: The Municipal Corporations Act (1835) and the Reform of the City of London
events/municipal-reform-1835.content:
The Municipal Corporations Act (1835) and the Reform of the City of London
The Municipal Corporations Act of 1835 (5 & 6 Will. 4 c. 76) was the great reform of English local government — the measure that swept away the close, self-perpetuating corporations of the old boroughs and established elected town councils throughout England and Wales. It was the second great act of the reform era, following the Reform Act of 1832, and it remade the government of the towns as decisively as the Reform Act had remade Parliament. But the Corporation of the City of London was excepted from the Act — deliberately excluded from its schedules because of the antiquity, the privileges, the revenues, and the peculiar position of the ancient City. The completion of municipal reform in London was thus deferred to the inquiries of 1837 and 1854, and to the long controversy over the government of the metropolis.
The old corporations and the reform
The unreformed municipal corporations of England and Wales were among the worst abuses of the old system. The Municipal Commissioners, in their First Report of 1835, found that “the most common and most striking defect in the constitution of the municipal corporations of England and Wales, is that the corporate bodies exist independently of the communities among which they are found” — separate and exclusive bodies, whose powers and privileges had no identity of interest with the inhabitants of the towns they governed. The reform of these corporations was one of the great demands of the reform era, and after the Reform Act of 1832 the first Reformed Parliament took up the question. The Municipal Corporations Act of 1835 established elected town councils in the boroughs enumerated in its schedules, sweeping away the close corporations and applying the principle of popular election to the government of the towns.
The exception of London
The City of London was not included in the schedules of the Act. The First Report of the Municipal Commissioners had not extended to the Corporation of London, and the Act founded on it did not include the City among the enumerated boroughs. The reason was the peculiar character of the London Corporation, which the Report itself acknowledged: the continued predominance of the popular element in the formation of its governing body distinguished it from the close corporations that the Act was designed to reform, and the Common Council of London had for many years secured an identity of interests between the governing body and the municipal community. The City was therefore left outside the general measure of municipal regulation — a fit subject, as the Commissioners held, for special and separate legislation.
The Second Report of 1837
The Commission reported on London only in its Second Report of 1837, which examined the Corporation of London and Southwark and the London Companies in full — its limits and municipal territory, its wards and wardmote elections, the Lord Mayor, the Court of Aldermen, the Common Council, the Sheriffs, the courts, the freemen and liverymen, the property and revenue, and the Companies. The Report set out the peculiarities of the City: how small a proportion of the metropolis was comprehended within the municipal boundary, and the difficulty of applying to London the reasoning that had justified the extension of the other boroughs. But no legislative measure was founded upon the Second Report; the Municipal Commissioners themselves intimated that many of the defects they pointed out might be remedied by the Common Council itself, without recourse to Parliament. The reform of the Corporation was thus left for the future, and for the Corporation’s own hands.
The Royal Commission of 1854
A generation later the question was taken up again. The Royal Commission of 1854, appointed to inquire into the existing state of the Corporation of the City of London, revisited the whole subject. Its Report reviewed the position of the City as distinguished from the other municipal corporations, examined the constitution and administration of the Corporation, and concluded that, in revising it, the leading provisions of the Municipal Corporations Act should be applied, with due allowance for the peculiar circumstances of London. It set out thirty-two numbered recommendations: a new charter consolidating the preservable charters and customs; the election of the Lord Mayor by the Common Council; the election of the aldermen by the burgesses of the wards for six years; the abolition of the Court of Aldermen and the transfer of its functions to the Common Council; the reduction of the wards to between twelve and sixteen; the £10 occupancy franchise; the abolition of the elections in Common Hall; the consolidation of the Lord Mayor’s and Sheriff’s Courts; the abolition of the freemen’s exclusive trading privileges and the dissolution of the Fellowship of Porters; the incorporation of the City police with the metropolitan police; the transfer of the conservancy of the Thames to a new board; and, for the metropolis as a whole, the division of the rest of London into municipal districts and the creation of a Metropolitan Board of Works. The Commission expressly abstained from recommending an extension of the City boundaries to embrace the whole metropolis, proposing instead that the Corporation form part of a general metropolitan system.
The unfinished reform
The reform of the City of London, unlike the reform of the other boroughs in 1835, was long drawn out and only partially accomplished. The 1854 recommendations — the abolition of the Court of Aldermen, the £10 franchise, the metropolitan system — were not wholly carried into effect as the Commission proposed; the Corporation survived, its ancient forms largely intact, and the Metropolitan Board of Works was established in 1855 in the form the Commission had sketched. Within the period 1800–1865 the story runs from the great reform of 1835, through the exception of London and the fundamental inquiry of 1837, to the reform programme of 1854 — the long attempt to apply the recognized municipal policy of the country to the most ancient and most peculiar of the English corporations.
Chronology

1835, September: The Municipal Corporations Act (5 & 6 Will. 4 c. 76); the City of London excepted from its schedules.
1837, April: The Second Report of the Municipal Corporations Commission on London and Southwark and the London Companies.
1835–1854: No legislative reform of the Corporation; the question deferred.
1853, June: The Royal Commission appointed.
1854: The Royal Commission’s Report with its thirty-two recommendations.

Sources

Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. III. The Municipal Corporations Act of 1835 and the reform era.
Molesworth, William Nassau. History of England from the Year 1830, Vol. I. The Municipal Corporations Act and the first Reformed Parliament.

Royal Commission. Report on the Corporation of London (1854). The reform programme and the thirty-two recommendations.

events/navarino-1827.title: The Battle of Navarino (1827)
events/navarino-1827.content:
The Battle of Navarino (1827)
The Battle of Navarino, fought in the bay of Navarino on the south-west coast of the Morea on 20 October 1827, was the last great fleet action of the age of sail — the destruction of the combined Turkish and Egyptian fleet by the combined British, French, and Russian squadrons, in support of the Greek war of independence. It was an action of extraordinary and unforeseen completeness: without a formal declaration of war, the allied squadrons under the British admiral Sir Edward Codrington entered the bay and, in the ensuing engagement, annihilated the fleet of the Sultan. Navarino secured the independence of Greece, and it was the decisive demonstration of the power of the allied navies in the Eastern Question — though in England it was received with mixed feelings, since it had destroyed a fleet of the power with which Britain was nominally at peace.
The Greek war and the Eastern Question
The background of Navarino was the Greek war of independence — the rising of the Greeks against the Ottoman Empire that had begun in 1821, and the cruel suppression of the revolt by the Sultan and his Egyptian ally, Ibrahim Pasha. The Greek cause roused great sympathy in Europe — in Britain, in France, and in Russia — and the powers, while professing neutrality, pressed for the pacification of Greece. In 1827 Britain, France, and Russia concluded the Treaty of London, by which they agreed to mediate between the Greeks and the Sultan and to enforce an armistice. The allied squadrons, under Codrington, were sent to the Levant to compel the suspension of hostilities, and Ibrahim’s fleet, which was preparing operations against the Greek islands, was blockaded in the bay of Navarino.
The battle
On 20 October 1827 the allied squadrons — British, French, and Russian — entered the bay of Navarino, where the Turkish and Egyptian fleet lay at anchor under the protection of the forts. The entrance was designed to enforce the armistice, but the two fleets came to blows, and in the engagement that followed the combined British, French, and Russian squadrons destroyed the Ottoman fleet — most of the Turkish and Egyptian ships being sunk or burnt, with the loss of thousands of men. The allied losses were comparatively small. The battle was in effect the destruction, at one blow, of the naval power of the Ottoman Empire in the Levant.
The aftermath and the significance
Navarino secured the independence of Greece. The destruction of the Ottoman fleet left the Sultan unable to suppress the Greek revolt, and Greece was established as an independent state by the London Protocol and the subsequent settlement. In England the news of Navarino was received with divided feelings: it was a great naval victory, but it had destroyed the fleet of a power with which Britain was technically at peace, and the government of Wellington, which had sent the squadron to enforce, not to fight, disavowed the action in a formal note. Martineau records the allied destruction of the Turkish-Egyptian fleet at Navarino as a key event in Greek independence. Within the period 1800–1865 Navarino stands as the last great fleet action of the age of sail and the decisive act of the Greek cause — the naval demonstration of the powers that settled the Eastern Question in favour of Greek independence.
Chronology

1821: The Greek war of independence begins.
1827, July: The Treaty of London; Britain, France, and Russia agree to mediate.
1827, 20 October: The Battle of Navarino; the destruction of the Ottoman fleet.
1830: The establishment of the independent Greek state.

Sources

events/new-poor-law-1834.title: The New Poor Law (1834)
events/new-poor-law-1834.content:
The New Poor Law (1834)
The New Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834 was the great reform of the relief of the poor — the measure that swept away the old system of outdoor relief and allowances and substituted the principle that relief should be given only inside the workhouse, on conditions less eligible than those of the independent labourer. Carried by the first Reformed Parliament on the report of the Poor Law Commission, it was the most important and the most fiercely contested social legislation of the reform era. Its supporters saw it as the application of reason and economy to the wasteful and demoralising system of the old Poor Law; its opponents, from the Tory paternalists to the Chartists, denounced it as the “Bastille” that criminalised poverty and crushed the labourer.
The old Poor Law and the abuses
The old Poor Law, resting on the Elizabethan statutes and the system of parish relief, had degenerated by the early nineteenth century into the practice of allowances and outdoor relief. Under the Speenhamland system, wages were supplemented from the rates according to the price of bread and the size of the family, and the result, in the eyes of the reformers, was the demoralisation of the labourer, the encouragement of population, and the burdening of the ratepayers. The reports of the Poor Law Commission exposed the abuses of the old system — the allowances that made the employer reduce wages and the labourer depend on the parish, the corruption and inefficiency of the parish administration — and recommended a radical reconstruction.
The Act of 1834
The New Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834 carried the Commission’s recommendations into law. Its principles were two: the workhouse test, that relief should be given only to those who entered the workhouse; and less eligibility, that the condition of the pauper in the workhouse should be less eligible — less desirable — than that of the lowest independent labourer. The Act established a central Poor Law Commission to administer the system, grouped the parishes into unions, and set about building the workhouses — the “union workhouses” or “Bastilles” of the new system — in which the poor were to be relieved. The old system of outdoor relief and allowances was to give way to the discipline of the workhouse.
The agitation against it
The Act provoked fierce opposition. The Tory paternalists denounced it as cruel and unchristian; the working classes saw it as the criminalisation of poverty, the workhouse as a prison; and the agitation against the “New Poor Law Bastilles” became one of the great popular causes of the 1830s, feeding the Chartist movement. The Andover workhouse scandal, with its revelations of the starvation and misery of the inmates, gave the opponents their most terrible weapon. Engels, writing of the condition of the working class, described the operation of the Poor Law and the workhouse as among the cruellest of the measures that bore down on the poor. Yet the Act was carried, and its principles — less eligibility and the workhouse test — remained the basis of English poor relief for the rest of the century, modified by the later reforms but never wholly abandoned.
Significance
The New Poor Law was the central social legislation of the reform era, and it expressed the economic and moral temper of the age. It was the application to the relief of the poor of the principles of political economy — the belief that the condition of the labourer should depend on his own exertions, and that indiscriminate relief demoralised the people and burdened the state. It was also, in the eyes of its opponents, the emblem of the callousness of the new industrial order. Within the period 1800–1865 it stands with the Factory Act and the abolition of slavery as one of the three great social measures of the reformed Parliament — the measure that determined, for good and ill, the treatment of the poor in Victorian England.
Chronology

1832: The Poor Law Commission appointed.
1834: The Poor Law Commission’s report.
1834, August: The New Poor Law Amendment Act.
1834 onwards: The establishment of the Poor Law Commission and the union workhouses.

events/oxford-movement-1833.title: The Oxford Movement (1833–1845)
events/oxford-movement-1833.content:
The Oxford Movement (1833–1845)
The Oxford Movement was the great religious revival that began at Oxford in 1833 and convulsed the Church of England for a generation — the attempt of a group of High Churchmen, led by John Keble, John Henry Newman, Edward Pusey, and Richard Hurrell Froude, to recall the Church of England to its Catholic and apostolic character. Beginning with Keble’s Assize Sermon of 1833 and the publication of the Tracts for the Times, the Movement taught the apostolic succession, the divine character of the Church, and the reality of the sacraments, and it set the Church of England against the Erastian spirit of the age — the treatment of the Church as a mere department of the state. The Movement reached its crisis with the condemnation of Tract XC and the secession of Newman to Rome in 1845, but it survived to transform the Church.
The origin and the occasion
The immediate occasion of the Movement was the state’s treatment of the Church. The suppression of the Irish bishoprics, the reforms of the establishment carried by the Reformed Parliament, and the general tendency to treat the Church as subject to the state — the Erastianism of the age — alarmed the High Churchmen of Oxford. Keble’s Assize Sermon of 1833, preached at the opening of the assizes, was long regarded as the origin of the Movement: in it Keble protested against the national apostasy, the treatment of the Church as if it were a human institution subject to the state. From that sermon, and from the deliberations of the Oxford High Churchmen, grew the series of Tracts for the Times, published from 1833 onwards, from which the Tractarians took their name.
The teaching of the Movement
The Tractarians taught the Catholic and apostolic character of the Church of England. They asserted the apostolic succession of the bishops and clergy, the divine foundation of the Church, the reality and efficacy of the sacraments, and the continuity of the Church of England with the primitive and medieval Church — a branch of the universal Church, reformed of medieval abuses but not a new creation of the Reformation. They insisted on the beauty and dignity of the worship of the Church, on fasting and the observance of the Church’s seasons, and on the authority of the Church’s doctrine against the secular state. The Movement was, at once, a religious revival and a protest — a claim that the Church of England was something more than a department of the state and that its doctrine and worship must be preserved.
The crisis: Tract XC and the secessions
The Movement roused the most violent controversy. The Tractarians were accused of Romanism; the bishops and the universities condemned their teaching; and Parliament and the courts were drawn into the examination of their doctrine. The crisis came with the publication of Tract XC in 1841, in which Newman sought to reconcile the Thirty-nine Articles with Catholic doctrine — a proceeding that was condemned by the university and that brought the Movement into disrepute. The secession of Newman to Rome in 1845, followed by others of the Tractarians, seemed to break the Movement; Martineau records the Tractarian secessions and the excitement they caused. Under Pusey, however, the Movement continued, and the High Church party that it had created became a permanent and powerful force in the Church.
Significance
The Oxford Movement was the decisive religious event of the age. It revived the Catholic and sacramental life of the Church of England, transformed its worship and its sense of itself, and created the High Church or Anglo-Catholic party that was to run through the later nineteenth century, with its ritual controversies and its conflicts over the Eucharist and the ornamentation of the churches. It divided the Church — the Evangelicals and the Low Churchmen opposed the Tractarians, and the secessions to Rome marked the limits of the Movement — but it gave the Church of England a new energy and a new sense of its character. Within the period 1800–1865 the Oxford Movement is, with the revival of the Evangelicals and the reform of the establishment, one of the great religious subjects of the age — the movement that transformed the Church and the religious life of the country.
Chronology

1833: Keble’s Assize Sermon; the beginning of the Tracts for the Times.
1833–1841: The rise and spread of the Movement; the controversies.
1841: Tract XC; the condemnation; the crisis of the Movement.
1845: Newman’s secession to Rome.
Afterwards: The Movement continues under Pusey as the High Church party.

Sources

Overton. The English Church in the Nineteenth Century (1800–1833). The state of the Church before the Movement.
Wakeman. An Introduction to the History of the Church of England. The High Church revival and the Tractarians.
Martineau. History of England, Vols. III–IV. The beginning of the Tractarian movement and the secessions.
Walpole. History of England, Vol. IV. The Oxford Movement, Tract XC, and the secessions.

events/panic-of-1825.title: The Panic of 1825
events/panic-of-1825.content:
The Panic of 1825
The panic of 1825 was the great financial crisis of the postwar decade — the sudden collapse of a vast speculative boom that had swept the country in 1824–25, and the ensuing run on the banks that prostrated the credit system and taught the age its most terrible lesson in the dangers of paper money. It was the crisis that broke the old joint-stock and country-bank system, brought down some seventy country banks, and drove the government and the Bank of England to the measures — the suppression of the small notes and the reform of the banking law — that were to shape the monetary history of the rest of the century. To the writers on credit and currency, from Martineau to Carey to the later banking school, 1825 was the classic example of the speculation and collapse that followed over-issue and over-trading.
The speculation mania
The years 1824–25 saw one of the greatest outbursts of speculation in English history. The resumption of peace and the revival of trade, with an abundance of capital and credit, produced a mania of company-floating and overtrading. Joint-stock companies were projected for every purpose — Latin American mining, canals, gas-lighting, steam laundries, and even, as Martineau noted with irony, a company for the supply of “milk and eggs from cows and poultry” — and their shares were bid up to absurd prices on the Stock Exchange. The exportation of gold, the eager buying of South American securities, and the reckless extension of credit fed the speculation, and the whole country, from the great merchants to the humblest, was drawn into the vortex.
The collapse
The collapse began in the autumn of 1825. The speculative shares fell rapidly, the South American securities proved worthless, and the credit of the great houses gave way. The panic spread to the banks: a run began, and the country banks, whose issues were largely uncovered, failed in great numbers — some seventy country banks broke in the course of the crisis. The Bank of England, besieged by the demands of the bankers and merchants, took desperate measures to relieve the pressure, and the whole fabric of credit seemed on the point of dissolution. The immense suffering of the time — the bankruptcies, the ruined fortunes, the distress of the manufacturing districts — was followed by the defeat of the government’s financial proposals in the aftermath.
The lessons and the reform
The panic of 1825 taught the age its great lesson in the management of the currency. The speculation was laid at the door of the country banks and the over-issue of paper; the legislative answer, in the years that followed, was the suppression of the small notes — the stamps under £5 were withdrawn, and existing small notes were required to cease by 1829 — and the reform of the banking law, which allowed banks of more than six partners beyond sixty-five miles from London and drew the Bank of England into provincial branches. The crisis also showed the superior stability of the Scotch banks, whose small-note system had survived the panic comparatively well, and it furnished the standing example — for the banking school and the currency school alike — of the dangers and the laws of credit. Carey’s analysis of 1825, set beside the panic of 1836, drew from it the lesson of the cyclical character of English credit; Tooke’s history of prices placed it in the long sequence of crises that the currency controversies of the following decades were meant to prevent.
Chronology

1824–25: The speculation mania; the company-floating and overtrading.
1825, autumn: The collapse of the speculation; the panic and the run on the banks.
1825–26: The suppression of small notes; the reform of the banking law; the aftermath of distress.

Sources

Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. II. The speculation mania and the panic of 1825.
Carey, Henry C. The Credit System (1838). England in 1825 and 1836 — the cyclical crises.
Tooke, Thomas. A History of Prices, Vols. I–II. The panic within the currency history.

events/peoples-charter-1838.title: The People's Charter and Chartism (1838–1848)
events/peoples-charter-1838.content:
The People’s Charter and Chartism (1838–1848)
Chartism was the great working-class political movement of the 1830s and 1840s — the attempt, organised around the six points of the People’s Charter, to secure for the working classes of England the political power that the Reform Act of 1832 had denied them. For a decade, from the publication of the Charter in 1838 through the torchlight meetings and the Newport rising of 1839, the monster meetings of the early 1840s, and the great petition and the Kennington Common meeting of 1848, Chartism was the standing fear of the propertied classes and the great expression of the discontent of the poor. It failed as a political movement — Parliament never enacted the Charter — but it left its mark on the age, and its six points became the programme of later reform.
The six points
The People’s Charter, published in 1838, demanded the reform of the representation on six points: universal suffrage (for men), equal electoral districts, the ballot, annual parliaments, the abolition of the property qualification for members of Parliament, and the payment of members. The programme was the answer of the working classes to the Reform Act of 1832, which had enfranchised the middle-class householder and left the town workman and the agricultural labourer still outside the pale. The Charter united the various strands of working-class radicalism, and its demand for universal suffrage became the rallying cry of the movement.
The phases of the agitation
Chartism rose in the dark times of the late 1830s — the years of distress, bad harvests, and discontent that followed the Reform Act. The movement organised its National Convention, its monster meetings and torchlight processions, and its great National Petition with its millions of signatures. In 1839 came the Newport rising, in which John Frost and the Welsh Chartists marched on the Westgate Hotel and were dispersed by the military, with the leaders transported. The movement revived in the early 1840s under the leadership of Feargus O’Connor and the auspices of his Northern Star, with O’Connor’s Land Scheme promising to settle the poor upon the land. The final and most famous phase came in 1848, in the year of the continental revolutions: the monster petition was prepared, and the great meeting was to be held at Kennington Common on 10 April 1848. The government, alarmed, organised its special constables — the Duke of Wellington is said to have arranged the defence of London — and the meeting passed off quietly; the petition, delivered to Parliament, was found to contain a vast number of forged signatures, and Chartism collapsed as a mass movement.
Chartism and the working class
Martineau’s account of Chartism places it in the economic conditions of the age — the state of the crops, the distress of the working classes, the near-revolutionary atmosphere among them — and she is sharply critical of the men who professed to take no interest in politics while blaming the commotions on the innate wickedness of the lower orders, missing entirely the economic roots of the unrest. Engels, writing of the condition of the working class, treated Chartism as the political expression of the working-class movement, the counterpart of the trade unions in the economic sphere, and the inevitable product of the class antagonism of industrial England. To its supporters the Charter was the means of redress of every grievance; to the government and the propertied classes it was the threat of revolution.
Significance
Chartism failed in its immediate object — the six points were never enacted in its lifetime, and the movement collapsed after 1848. But its significance was lasting. It demonstrated, as nothing else had done, the depth of working-class discontent and the exclusion of the working classes from the reformed constitution; it kept alive the demand for universal suffrage, the ballot, and the reform of Parliament through the decades when those causes were most unfashionable; and its six points were gradually realised in the course of the century — the ballot in 1872, equal districts in 1885, and the suffrage by the successive reform acts. Chartism was the great political apprenticeship of the English working class, and its history belongs to the making of the democratic state.
Chronology

1838: Publication of the People’s Charter.
1839: The Chartist Convention; the monster petition; the Newport rising; the leaders transported.
1840s: O’Connor’s leadership; the Land Scheme; the revival of the agitation.
1848, 10 April: The Kennington Common meeting; the petition delivered; the collapse of the movement.

Sources

Molesworth, William Nassau. History of England from the Year 1830, Vol. II. The People’s Charter, the Chartist movement, and its phases.
Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. IV. Chartism, the dark times of 1839–40, and the crisis of 1848.
Engels, Friedrich. The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845). Chartism and the labour movement.
Alison, Sir Archibald. History of Europe, Vols. III and VII. Chartism and the Chartist agitation.

events/peterloo-1819.title: Peterloo and the Manchester Massacre (1819)
events/peterloo-1819.content:
Peterloo and the Manchester Massacre (1819)
On 16 August 1819 a great open-air meeting assembled on St. Peter’s Field, Manchester, to demand reform of the representation of the people. The gathering — a legal and peaceable meeting of some tens of thousands, with the radicals of the north gathering from the surrounding towns — was charged by the magistrates with having been dispersed with violence by the Manchester and Salford Yeomanry Cavalry and the hussars, who cut down men, women, and children in the crowd. The event, soon known as “Peterloo” in ironic contrast to Waterloo, became the great atrocity of the postwar radical agitation, and the immediate sequel — the thanks of the Prince Regent to the magistrates and yeomanry, and the repressive Six Acts — turned the anger of the reformers into a national crisis of press, politics, and the right of public meeting.
The meeting of 16 August
The meeting at St. Peter’s Field had been convened to demand reform of the representation of the people — the redress of grievances that the radical reformers, in the deep postwar distress, pressed with growing urgency. After Waterloo the country had fallen into a severe depression: falling prices, unemployment, agricultural distress, and the weight of taxation and the national debt bore down on the working classes and the small producers. The radicals, led in the north by such figures as Henry Hunt and sustained by the cheap press of Cobbett and Carlile, demanded a reform of Parliament that would give the people a voice. The Manchester meeting was to be the great demonstration of the demand. The magistrates, fearing disorder, had resolved to prevent it from taking place, and called in the yeomanry — the volunteer cavalry of the county gentry — and the hussars.
When the crowd had assembled, the yeomanry cavalry charged into the field to arrest the speakers and disperse the gathering. The result was a massacre: men, women, and children were ridden down and cut with sabres, and a large number were killed and many hundreds wounded. The reformers insisted that the meeting had been peaceable and legal, and that the violence was wholly the magistrates’ and yeomanry’s. Richard Carlile, who had been present as a spectator, described it in his published letters as a “horrid massacre” — the murder of a peaceable and defenceless people by the holders of the sword of justice.
The Regent’s thanks
The conduct of the authorities in the days that followed inflamed the reformers beyond measure. On 21 August 1819 the Home Secretary, Lord Sidmouth, wrote to the Earl of Derby in the name of the Prince Regent, expressing the Regent’s “great satisfaction” at the magistrates’ “prompt, decisive, and efficient measures” for the preservation of the public tranquillity, and his “high approbation” of Major Trafford and the officers and men under his command. To the reformers this was the crown of the atrocity: the Regent thanked the “murderers” of Manchester for their work. Carlile’s letter of 30 August 1819 to the Prince Regent, printed in The Republican, dwelt upon the public indignation — a satisfaction expressed “to the Magisterial and Yeomanry Assassins of Manchester for Murders committed by them on the 16th of August last” — and argued that only the offenders’ own account had been heard, that hundreds of disinterested spectators had not been sought, and that the whole proceeding was a violation of English jurisprudence and moral decency. He insisted, on the evidence of dates, that the Regent could not have deliberated — the news could not have reached the Home Office before the evening of the 17th, and the Regent was then more than a hundred miles away — so that Sidmouth’s thanks, given in the Regent’s name on the 21st, anticipated and stamped the Regent’s will.
Carlile’s account and the prosecutions
Carlile’s Republican of 3 September 1819 carried the first extended Republican response in this period. It printed, with the letters to the Regent and to Lord Sidmouth, the full text of the Sidmouth–Derby letter, and set the massacre in the context of the tyranny of the day: the expensive monarchy, the standing army, the fundholder against the artisan and agriculturist, the corruption of the Cabinet. Carlile had published an earlier letter of 18 August giving his narrative as a spectator of the meeting, for which the police had acted against him, Morris the police officer swearing the letter an unlawful, inflammatory, and seditious libel before the Lord Mayor, Lord Mayor Atkins; he was held and then bailed. To Carlile and the reformers the Manchester magistracy had shown want of feeling, and the blood spilt at Manchester was not to be washed away by libel-hunting in London. The prosecutions of the press were the counterpart of the massacre: the authorities answered the radical challenge not only with the sabre but with the law of seditious libel, and the trials of the radical publishers in the years that followed became the central battleground of the freedom of the press.
The aftermath and the Six Acts
The massacre and the government’s approval of it produced a wave of horror and anger across the country, and at the same time the government proceeded to legislation. In the months after Peterloo Parliament passed the Six Acts, a body of repressive legislation directed against the radical press and public meeting — measures to prevent seditious meetings, to gag the radical journals, and to extend the powers of the magistrates. To the reformers the Six Acts completed the work of 16 August: the meeting was dispersed by force, and then the very right of meeting and of a free press was curtailed by law. The agitation continued into the 1820s, feeding the broader movement for reform that culminated in the Reform Act of 1832; but Peterloo left its mark as the emblem of the postwar repression — the day the yeomanry rode down a peaceable crowd and the Prince Regent thanked them for it, an episode that the radical press of Carlile, Cobbett, and Hone kept before the country and the courts.
Chronology

1819, 16 August: Meeting on St. Peter’s Field, Manchester; the yeomanry and hussars disperse it with violence; many killed and wounded.
1819, 18 August: Carlile’s letter giving his spectator narrative.
1819, 21 August: Sidmouth writes to Derby with the Regent’s thanks to the magistrates and yeomanry.
1819, 30 August: Carlile’s letter to the Prince Regent on the “Magisterial and Yeomanry Assassins of Manchester.”
1819, 1 September: Carlile’s second letter, to Lord Sidmouth.
1819, 3 September: The Republican, No. 2, Vol. I, printed with the letters.
1819, late: Passage of the Six Acts.

Sources

Carlile, Richard. The Republican, No. 2, Vol. I (3 September 1819), in the Harrison-bound miscellany. The primary Republican account: letters to the Prince Regent (30 August) and Lord Sidmouth (1 September), the Sidmouth–Derby letter in full, and the Atkins and Fitch letters.
Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. II. The postwar distress and radical agitation of 1819.
Alison, Sir Archibald. History of Europe, Vol. I. England from 1815 to 1819 — Peterloo and the Six Acts.

events/queen-caroline-affair-1820.title: The Queen Caroline Affair (1820–1821)
events/queen-caroline-affair-1820.content:
The Queen Caroline Affair (1820–1821)
The Queen Caroline affair was the great scandal and political crisis of the first years of the reign of George IV — the attempt of the new King to divorce his wife, Queen Caroline, and the extraordinary national agitation in her support that followed. From the Queen’s return to England in 1820 to claim her rights, through the proceedings of the Bill of Pains and Penalties before the House of Lords, to her death in 1821, the affair convulsed the country, united the radicals and the mob in defence of the wronged Queen, and made the King the most unpopular man in England. It was at once a royal scandal, a legal drama, and a political battle in which the popular opposition to the government and the crown found a voice.
The unhappy marriage
George IV and Caroline of Brunswick had been married in 1795, in a match of mutual detestation, and had long lived apart. Caroline, excluded from the court and subjected to accusations, had gone abroad, where she lived a wandering and disreputable life, the centre of scandal. On the death of George III and the accession of the Prince Regent as George IV in January 1820, the King resolved to be rid of his wife, and Caroline, learning of his intention and of the proposed exclusion of her name from the liturgy, resolved to return to England and assert her rights as Queen. The country watched her arrival with extraordinary interest, and the mob, which hated the King and loved a victim, took her part.
The Bill of Pains and Penalties
The King sent a message to Parliament demanding a divorce, and in 1820 the government introduced the Bill of Pains and Penalties in the House of Lords — a bill to deprive Caroline of her title and dissolve the marriage on the ground of her alleged adultery with Bartolomeo Bergami, one of her household. The “trial” before the Lords examined the evidence of the Queen’s conduct abroad, and was conducted on her behalf with great skill by Brougham and Denman — Denman’s celebrated speech, “where is the injured husband?” exposing the monstrous spectacle of a King who had himself lived in open adultery calling his wife to account. The enormous public sympathy for the Queen was expressed in the mobs that supported her and in the hissing of the King in the streets. The bill, though it had a majority in the Lords, was so narrow — nine on the third reading — that the government abandoned it, and the attempt to divorce the Queen collapsed.
The death and funeral
The Queen, her position now acknowledged, was not admitted to the coronation in July 1821, when George IV was crowned; Caroline, denied her place, appeared before the doors and was refused. She fell ill shortly afterwards and died in August 1821. Her funeral became the occasion of a final demonstration: the government sought to keep the procession quiet, but it was forced through the City over the objections of the authorities, and two men were killed in the confrontation at Hyde Park. The affair closed with the death of the woman who had been the rallying-point of the popular opposition to the King.
Significance
The Queen Caroline affair was the great domestic crisis of the early 1820s, and its significance was political as well as scandalous. It united the radicals, the reformers, and the London mob in a popular agitation against the King and the government, and it gave the radical press — above all Hone’s illustrated satires, the Queen’s Matrimonial Ladder, Non Mi Ricordo!, the Political House that Jack Built, and the other squibs with Cruikshank’s cuts — its greatest opportunity. The affair exposed the corruption and unpopularity of the monarchy and the court, and it nourished the spirit of reform and opposition that was to find expression in the agitation of the later 1820s and the Reform crisis of 1830–32. The King was left detested, the government humiliated, and the popular movement strengthened — a lasting blow to the prestige of the crown.
Chronology

1820, January: Death of George III; accession of George IV.
1820, spring: The Queen returns to England to assert her rights.
1820: The Bill of Pains and Penalties before the Lords; the “trial”; the bill abandoned.
1821, July: The Queen excluded from the coronation.
1821, August: Death of the Queen; the funeral demonstrations.

Sources

Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. II. The Queen’s return, the Bill of Pains and Penalties, and her death.
Hone, William. Pamphlets and Parodies on Political Subjects (Chidley collection, 1830). The illustrated satires of the Queen Caroline era.
Hone, William. The Three Trials of William Hone (1818). The bound-with Caroline pamphlets.

events/railway-mania-1845-47.title: The Railway Mania (1845–1847)
events/railway-mania-1845-47.content:
The Railway Mania (1845–1847)
The railway mania of 1845–1847 was the great speculative fever of the mid-century — a frenzy of railway promotion and investment that swept the country, bid up the shares of projected lines to fantastic prices, and ended in the commercial crisis of 1847 and the financial ruin of countless investors. The opening of the Liverpool & Manchester Railway in 1830 had inaugurated the railway age; the rapid extension of the system through the 1830s and 1840s had made railways the great new industry of the country. In 1845 the appetite for railway investment, fed by the prospect of enormous profit, exploded into a mania that for a time seemed to absorb the whole speculative energies of the nation, and whose collapse prostrated the credit system and forced the government and the Bank of England to their extremities.
The growth of the railways
The railway system had grown with extraordinary rapidity since the opening of the Liverpool & Manchester line in 1830. George and Robert Stephenson had carried the locomotive from the triumph of the Rainhill trials to the construction of the great trunk lines — the London & Birmingham, the Manchester & Leeds, the Midland — and railways had spread across England and into Europe. The railway was the greatest engineering and commercial phenomenon of the age, and its profits seemed boundless. The Railway Regulation Act of 1844 (Gladstone’s measure) had begun the parliamentary supervision of the new industry, with its compulsory parliamentary train and provisions for third-class passengers; but the appetite for railway investment had outrun all regulation.
The mania of 1845
In 1845 the railway speculation reached its height. A vast number of projected lines were promoted — lines for every part of the country, competing, overlapping, and often absurd — and their shares were bid up on the Stock Exchange to prices that bore no relation to their value. The whole country seemed seized with the railway fever: noblemen, merchants, tradesmen, and clerks invested in the shares, and the extension of the system, in the estimate of the age, would cover the country with a network of iron. Parliament was deluged with railway bills, and the capital demanded for the projected railways was far beyond what the country could supply. The mania, as the railway historians and the economists recorded, was the purest example of the speculative fever — the overtrading, the reckless confidence, the absorption of the nation’s capital in an industry whose possibilities had been exaggerated to the point of madness.
The collapse and the crisis of 1847
The reaction came in 1846–47. The vast capital demands of the railways, the difficulty of raising the enormous sums, the failure of many projected lines, and the general strain on the money market brought the speculation to an end. The commercial crisis of 1847 followed — the financial panic, the failure of great houses, the drain on the Bank of England, and the suspension of the Bank Charter Act to allow the issue of extra notes. Tooke’s history traced the railway mania and its consequences in the long sequence of speculation and collapse, and Martineau described the financial panic of 1847 as the result of the railway speculation, the bad harvest of 1846, and the Irish famine. The crisis prostrated the credit system; the railway mania, which had promised a golden age, ended in ruin for the multitudes who had bought the shares at their inflated prices.
Significance
The railway mania was the great economic catastrophe of the mid-century, and its lesson was the standing example of the dangers of speculation and over-trading. It was also, for all its ruin, the instrument of a lasting transformation: out of the mania and the crash came the completed railway system, the great lines that bound the country together, and the railways that were to be the foundation of Victorian prosperity. The mania and the crisis of 1847 supplied the age with its most terrible demonstration of the laws of credit, and they framed the monetary debates — the currency question, the Bank Charter Act, the management of the Bank of England — that occupied the economists and the statesmen of the following years.
Chronology

1830: Opening of the Liverpool & Manchester Railway.
1844: Gladstone’s Railway Regulation Act.
1845: The railway mania reaches its height.
1846–47: The reaction; the strain on the money market.
1847: The commercial crisis; the suspension of the Bank Charter Act.

Sources

Tooke & Newmarch. A History of Prices, Vols. III–IV. The railway speculation and the crisis of 1847.
Tooke & Newmarch. A History of Prices, Vols. V–VI. The railway construction boom and its effects.
Alison, Sir Archibald. History of Europe, Vol. VII. The railway mania and crisis of 1847.
Molesworth, William Nassau. History of England from the Year 1830, Vol. II. The railway legislation of 1844 and the speculation.
Smiles, Samuel. Lives of the Engineers: The Locomotive. The Railway Mania of 1845–46.

events/reform-act-1832.title: The Reform Act of 1832
events/reform-act-1832.content:
The Reform Act of 1832
The Reform Act of 1832 — “the great Reform Bill” — was the decisive constitutional change of the age, remaking the House of Commons by destroying the rotten boroughs, transferring representation to the new manufacturing towns, and establishing the £10 householder franchise in the boroughs. Carried by Earl Grey’s ministry after a national crisis that brought the country to the verge of revolution, the Act broke the long Tory ascendancy and opened the era of reformed and party government. It transferred power from the landed aristocracy and the closed boroughs to the middle classes of the towns, and left the working classes — as the Chartists were soon to insist — still outside the pale.
The unreformed system and the crisis
The unreformed House of Commons was the creation of an older England, its seat distribution fixed when the agricultural south and the corporate towns carried the population and wealth. Nomination boroughs — seats owned by a patron, such as Old Sarum with no inhabitants and Gatton the classic pocket borough — survived intact, while Manchester, Birmingham, and Leeds returned no member at all. The franchise was an incoherent patchwork of ancient customs. Agitation for reform, suppressed since the 1790s, revived with the distress of 1829–30; Catholic Emancipation (1829) had broken the old alliance against change; the July Revolution in France frightened and encouraged; and the “Captain Swing” machine-breaking and rick-burning spread alarm through the southern counties. When the Duke of Wellington declared in November 1830 that the existing system possessed the full and entire confidence of the country and that he would bring forward no measure of reform, his ministry fell, and Earl Grey — a reformer since the 1790s — was summoned to form a government.
The introduction and the single vote
Grey made reform a Cabinet question, and on 1 March 1831 Lord John Russell rose to introduce the first Reform Bill. Its details — disfranchisement of the rotten boroughs, enfranchisement of the new towns, the £10 householder franchise — were debated through a crisis that convulsed the nation. The Bill passed its second reading by a single vote, 302 to 301, on the famous night when the strangers’ gallery was crowded with the people; it was then defeated in committee on General Gascoigne’s wrecking amendment. The ministry dissolved Parliament, and the general election of April–May 1831 returned a great reform majority. The second Bill passed the Commons by large majorities but was rejected by the Lords in October 1831 by forty-one votes, the bishops voting almost solidly against.
The popular fury and the Days of May
The Lords’ rejection provoked a national explosion. Riots at Derby and Nottingham, the burning of Nottingham Castle, the destruction of the Mansion House and Bishop’s Palace in the Bristol riots, the breaking of the windows of anti-reform peers, and the grim determination of the Political Unions — disciplined organisations spread from Thomas Attwood’s Birmingham Union across the country — to march on London brought the government and the country to the edge of convulsion. The third Reform Bill was introduced; the Lords, under Lyndhurst, carried a motion to postpone the disfranchising clauses. The Grey ministry resigned, and the King sent for Wellington, who failed to form a government — he could not take office on a reform basis, and Peel refused to serve with him. Grey was recalled with the King’s reluctant promise to create enough peers to carry the Bill. The threat was enough: the Tory peers abstained in great numbers, the Bill passed the Lords, and the Reform Act received the royal assent on 7 June 1832.
Provisions and the first Reformed Parliament
The Act disfranchised fifty-six rotten boroughs, reduced thirty more to a single member, enfranchised forty-two new towns, extended the county representation, and established the £10 householder franchise in the boroughs. The electoral map of Britain was redrawn and power shifted decisively to the middle classes of the towns. The first Reformed Parliament assembled in January 1833 with the reformers triumphant — the Conservative party (as the Tories now called themselves) reduced to about 150 members. It went on to carry the great measures of the reform era: the abolition of slavery, the Factory Act of 1833, the New Poor Law of 1834, the renewal of the Bank and India charters, and the Municipal Corporations Act of 1835. The settlement of 1832 was the turning-point of the constitutional history of the century — the moment the old constitution was broken and the long Victorian argument over the franchise began.
Chronology

1829: Catholic Emancipation breaks the old order.
1830, June: Death of George IV; accession of William IV; general election.
1830, July: French Revolution of 1830.
1830, November: Wellington’s anti-reform speech; his ministry falls; Grey forms a government.
1831, 1 March: Russell introduces the first Reform Bill.
1831, 22 March: Second reading carried by a single vote (302–301).
1831, April–May: Defeat in committee; dissolution; general election returns a reform majority.
1831, 8 October: Lords reject the second Bill by 41; riots follow.
1832, May: The Days of May crisis; Wellington’s failure; Grey recalled with the promise to create peers.
1832, 7 June: Royal assent to the Reform Act.
1833, January: The first Reformed Parliament assembles.

Sources

Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. III. The Reform Bill crisis, the first Reformed Parliament, and the consolidation of reform.
Molesworth, William Nassau. History of England from the Year 1830, Vol. I. The unreformed constitution, the introduction and passage of the Bill, and the Days of May, in full parliamentary detail.
Alison, Sir Archibald. History of Europe, Vol. III. Reform and the early Victorian transition.

events/six-acts-1819.title: The Six Acts (1819)
events/six-acts-1819.content:
The Six Acts (1819)
The Six Acts were the body of repressive legislation passed by the Liverpool ministry in the winter of 1819, in the immediate aftermath of the Manchester massacre of 16 August 1819. Directed against the radical press and the right of public meeting, the Six Acts were the most repressive legislation of the postwar period — the government’s answer, by law, to the agitation that the yeomanry had dispersed by force at Peterloo. To the reformers they completed the work of 16 August: the meeting had been broken up by the sabre, and the Six Acts now curtailed, by statute, the very rights of meeting and of a free press that the agitation had used.
The measures
The Six Acts were passed in the months after Peterloo, and comprised a series of measures directed to the suppression of the radical movement:

The Training Prevention Act, forbidding the drilling and arming of the people — the radical practice of military drill on the moors.
The Seizure of Arms Act, empowering the magistrates to search for and seize arms.
The Seditious Meetings Prevention Act, restricting the holding of public meetings for the consideration of grievances and petitions, and giving magistrates power to suppress them.
The Blasphemous and Seditious Libels Act, imposing severe punishments for the publication of blasphemous and seditious libels.
The Newspaper and Stamp Duties Act, extending the stamp duty on newspapers and cheap publications so as to price the radical journals out of the reach of the poor.
The Misdemeanours Act, providing for the more speedy trial and punishment of misdemeanours.

The measures struck at the whole apparatus of the radical movement — its drills, its arms, its meetings, its press — and their effect was to drive the radical agitation, already struck by the sabre at Peterloo, deeper into illegality and to curtail the cheap press through which Cobbett, Carlile, and the other radicals had reached the people.
The repression in context
The Six Acts were the culmination of the government’s response to the postwar radicalism. The agitation had risen to its height in 1819 — the mass reform meetings, the election of “legislatorial attorneys,” the female reform societies, the radical drilling on Tandle Hill, and the great Manchester meeting of 16 August that the yeomanry had dispersed. The government had supported the magistrates, and the Prince Regent had approved their conduct; the prosecution of Burdett for his inflammatory letter and the York trials of the radical leaders followed. The Six Acts carried the repression from the field and the court into the statute book. Martineau presents them as the most repressive legislation of the period, and the reformers of every shade regarded them as a tyrant’s answer to the just demands of the people.
The radical response
To the radicals, the Six Acts were the crown of the government’s tyranny. Carlile and the radical press denounced them, insisting that the blood spilt at Manchester was not to be washed away by libel-hunting and restrictive legislation in London, and that the object of the prosecutions and the Acts was not to protect religion or public order but to crush the press and stifle discussion. The Acts did not end the agitation; they drove it into new forms and prolonged the struggle. The radical movement of the 1820s, the revival of reform agitation, and eventually the great agitation that carried the Reform Act of 1832 all grew out of the repression of 1819, of which the Six Acts were the legislative expression.
Chronology

1819, 16 August: The Manchester massacre (Peterloo).
1819, autumn: Prosecutions of the radical leaders and the press.
1819, winter: Passage of the Six Acts.

Sources

Martineau, Harriet. History of England, Vol. II. The passage of the Six Acts in the aftermath of Peterloo.
Alison, Sir Archibald. History of Europe, Vol. I. England from 1815 to 1819 — Peterloo and the Six Acts.
Carlile, Richard. The Republican, No. 2 (3 September 1819), in the Harrison-bound miscellany. The radical response.

events/trafalgar-1805.title: The Battle of Trafalgar (1805)
events/trafalgar-1805.content:
The Battle of Trafalgar (1805)
The Battle of Trafalgar, fought off Cape Trafalgar on the coast of Spain on 21 October 1805, was the decisive naval engagement of the Napoleonic War. A British fleet of twenty-seven ships of the line under Vice-Admiral Horatio Lord Nelson destroyed a combined Franco-Spanish fleet of thirty-three ships commanded by Admiral Villeneuve, capturing or destroying eighteen of the enemy without the loss of a single British ship. The victory ended Napoleon’s hope of invading England and established British command of the sea for the rest of the war and long after — but it was won at the cost of Nelson’s life, struck down in the moment of triumph. Trafalgar was the climax of the long pursuit that had begun when Villeneuve escaped from Toulon in the spring of 1805.
The pursuit of Villeneuve
The campaign that ended at Trafalgar began as a race across the Atlantic. Napoleon, having assembled a great invasion flotilla at Boulogne and crowned himself Emperor in 1804, conceived a plan to combine the French and Spanish fleets and sweep the Channel clear long enough for the army to cross. In January 1805 Villeneuve’s squadron escaped from Toulon and, joined by a Spanish squadron, sailed to the West Indies, drawing Nelson after him across the Atlantic. The combined fleet plundered the British islands and then, hearing that the invasion was postponed, turned back for Europe. Nelson, having guessed the enemy’s return, set a course for Cadiz by way of the Mediterranean; the French admiral, afraid of being caught, did not enter the Mediterranean but made for Ferrol and finally to Cadiz, where he was blockaded. Calder’s action off Cape Finisterre in July 1805, an indecisive brush that cost two Spanish ships, had already persuaded Napoleon to abandon the invasion of England; but the combined fleet still lay at Cadiz, and the opportunity remained to destroy it.
The fleets and Nelson’s plan
At Cadiz lay thirty-three ships of the line — eighteen French and fifteen Spanish — under Villeneuve. Nelson, who had taken command of the blockading fleet and had hoisted his flag in the Victory, planned to meet the enemy’s force at sea. His celebrated stratagem was to attack in two or three columns, breaking the enemy’s line at right angles rather than engaging in the old parallel fashion, so that the whole force might be concentrated on the centre and rear before the van could turn to help. The order of sailing became the order of battle: each ship was to pass through the enemy’s line, engage closely, and trust that the resolution of his captains and the superiority of British seamanship would win the day. Nelson’s last signal, “England expects every man will do his duty,” was hoisted as the fleets closed.
The battle
On the morning of 21 October 1805 the combined fleet was sighted off Cape Trafalgar. The wind was light, the sea calm, and the British columns took some hours to come up. The weather column under Nelson and the lee column under Vice-Admiral Collingwood broke through the enemy line in the afternoon. The battle resolved itself into a ferocious close engagement. The Victory, leading the weather column, passed under the stern of Villeneuve’s flagship the Bucentaure, raking her, and then became entangled with the Redoutable; in the exchange of musketry a sharpshooter’s ball struck Nelson in the shoulder and spine. He was carried below, and died at half-past four in the afternoon, having learned that the battle was won. The enemy’s centre and rear were overwhelmed; eighteen of the thirty-three Franco-Spanish ships were captured or destroyed, among them the Santissima Trinidad, the largest ship in the world. Villeneuve himself was taken. Not a single British ship was lost.
The storm
The triumph was immediately clouded by a violent storm that blew up after the battle. The heavily damaged prizes, many dismasted and jury-rigged, were scattered; several were driven ashore or had to be sunk or abandoned rather than risk them falling back into the enemy’s hands. James’s account of the action includes the discussion of rival accounts of the battle and its aftermath, and of the storm that followed. The British fleet, commanded after Nelson’s death by Collingwood, brought what prizes it could into Gibraltar and the home ports. Of the eighteen captured or destroyed enemy ships, only a portion survived the storm to be brought in as prizes; the rest were lost on the Spanish coast.
Command of the sea
Trafalgar established British naval supremacy beyond dispute. Napoleon’s combined fleet was destroyed as a fighting force; the invasion of England was never again seriously contemplated; and the sea remained open to British commerce and closed to the enemy’s for the rest of the war. The victory made possible the whole subsequent course of the struggle — the blockade, the Peninsular War, and the eventual defeat of Napoleon — by securing the command of the sea on which Britain’s existence and her continental alliances depended. It also sealed the reputation of Nelson, already the hero of the Nile and Copenhagen, as the greatest of British admirals; his death in the moment of victory gave the triumph a peculiar pathos. In the larger story of sea power, Trafalgar was the decisive proof of the principle Mahan later elaborated — that command of the sea, once established, governs the destiny of nations — and it stood for the remainder of the nineteenth century as the emblem of Britain’s naval greatness.
Chronology

1804: Napoleon crowned Emperor; Spain enters the war on France’s side.
1805, January: Villeneuve escapes from Toulon.
1805, spring–summer: Combined fleet sails to the West Indies and back; Nelson’s pursuit.
1805, 22 July: Calder’s action off Cape Finisterre.
1805, August–September: Combined fleet blockaded at Cadiz; Napoleon abandons invasion.
1805, 21 October: Battle of Trafalgar; Nelson killed; eighteen enemy ships captured or destroyed.
Afterwards: Storm scatters the prizes.

Sources

James, William. Naval History of Great Britain, Vol. III (1800–1805). The detailed account of the pursuit, the battle, Nelson’s death, the rival accounts, and the storm.
Clowes, Sir William Laird. The Royal Navy: A History, Vol. V (1803–1815). The Trafalgar campaign within the naval struggle with Napoleon.
Martineau, Harriet. History of England, 1800–1815 bridge volume. The war narrative.
Alison, Sir Archibald. History of the French Revolution, Vol. II. Trafalgar within the Napoleonic system.
