events/war-of-1812.title: The Naval War of 1812
events/war-of-1812.content:
The Naval War of 1812
The naval war between Great Britain and the United States, fought from the American declaration of war in June 1812 to the peace of early 1815, was a conflict conducted almost wholly at sea and on the North American lakes, in single-ship actions and small-squadron operations rather than in fleet engagements. The United States, with a navy of a few powerful frigates and a host of privateers, could not meet the great British fleet in line of battle; but in a remarkable series of frigate duels in 1812–13 the American ships — the Constitution, the United States, the President — captured or defeated their British opponents, striking a blow at the prestige of the Royal Navy that the British public felt keenly. James’s contemporary account, written while details were still being gathered, set out the comparative force of every action to determine whether the British losses were the result of superior seamanship or of superior armament and size.
Declaration and the early single-ship actions
The United States declared war against Great Britain in June 1812, over impressment, the orders in council, and the rights of neutral commerce. The Royal Navy, which had been in an inactive state since the peace following Trafalgar, was caught unprepared for the quality of the American frigates. The opening campaign was marked by a series of American victories. The Constitution escaped from the British squadron off the American coast, and then on 19 August 1812 captured HMS Guerriere in an engagement that James analysed in detail — comparing the force of the two ships and the effect of the American official account on the public mind. In October the United States captured the Macedonian; in December the Constitution captured the Java after a hard-fought action in which Captain Lambert was killed. These three frigate victories, following so closely, produced a profound impression both in America and in Britain, and raised the question — which James set himself to answer — whether the American ships had really been the stronger.
The comparative force and the British reply
James’s method was to compute the comparative force of the two ships in every action, by tonnage, by the weight of metal in the broadside, and by the number and calibre of the guns. He concluded that the American frigates were not the equals of the British in name alone: they were larger, more heavily armed, and more strongly built than the nominal “frigates” they met, mounting long guns and carronades of heavier metal and carrying larger complements. The British losses were therefore to be ascribed in great part to inferiority of force, not to any failure of British courage or skill. The run of American victories was broken on 1 June 1813, when the Shannon, commanded by Captain Broke, engaged and boarded the Chesapeake off Boston, taking her after fifteen minutes’ fighting and killing her captain, Lawrence. Broke’s victory restored the credit of the British flag and was followed by other successes — the Pelican over the Argus, the Reindeer and later the Avon against the Wasp, and the recapture of the President by a British squadron under Captain Hayes on 15 January 1815.
The lakes and the closing operations
Alongside the ocean duels the war was fought on the Great Lakes and Lake Champlain, where the two sides built rival squadrons. The Battle of Lake Erie (10 September 1813) ended in a British defeat under Captain Barclay, and the British lost command of the lake; James analysed the reasons for the defeat and the relative force of the squadrons. The Essex, which had ravaged British commerce in the Pacific, was at last taken at Valparaiso in March 1814 by the Phoebe and Cherub. In the closing months of the war American privateers ranged widely, and the Chasseur carried her depredations to the British coast; the Peacock captured the Nautilus and the Penguin was taken by the Hornet after the news of peace had arrived — a capture James denounced as an act of piracy.
Summary of losses
James’s closing summary computed the losses on each side. Against British losses of three frigates, seven sloops, and five smaller vessels, he set American losses of five frigates, nineteen sloops, and numerous smaller vessels, including those recaptured; he calculated the comparative tonnage and force lost on each side, and noted the vast amount of American merchant shipping captured by British cruisers. By this accounting the war, though it had opened with a humiliating run of American frigate victories, ended with the British flag restored and with the balance of captures in Britain’s favour. The peace of Ghent (December 1814, ratified early 1815) restored the status quo, and the naval war — a side-show of the great European struggle — passed into history as the conflict in which the young American navy first measured itself against the mistress of the seas.
Chronology

1812, June: United States declares war on Great Britain.
1812, 19 August: Constitution captures Guerriere.
1812, 25 October: United States captures Macedonian.
1812, 18 October: Wasp captures Frolic.
1812, 29 December: Constitution captures Java.
1813, 1 June: Shannon captures Chesapeake; Captain Lawrence killed.
1813, 10 September: Battle of Lake Erie; British defeat.
1814, 28 March: Essex captured at Valparaiso.
1815, 15 January: President captured by British squadron.
1815, 20 February: Constitution takes Cyane and Levant.
1815, March: Peace ratified.

Sources

James, William. A Full and Correct Account of the Chief Naval Occurrences of the Late War Between Great Britain and the United States (1817). The contemporary British account, with comparative force computed for every action, official letters, and the summary of losses.
James, William. Naval History of Great Britain, Vols. V–VI. The war within the general naval history.
Clowes, Sir William Laird. The Royal Navy: A History, Vol. VI. The War of 1812 and the peacetime Navy.

See also: command-of-the-sea, trafalgar-1805, james-william, continental-system

index.title: index
index.content:
United Kingdom 1800–1865 Wiki
A narrative-research knowledge base on British history from the Act of Union through the end of the Napoleonic Wars, the Reform era, and the mid-century transformations.
Total pages: 120
What follows is the map of the wiki — people, events, and concepts — then the source library on which every claim rests.
Entities
Crown, Court, and Party Leaders

victoria — Accession 1837; the young Queen and the making of the modern constitutional crown
peel-robert — The great Conservative minister: police, tariff and currency reform, repeal of the Corn Laws
palmerston — Foreign Secretary and twice Prime Minister; the “Civis Romanus sum” and the Crimean War
disraeli — The rival of Gladstone: Young England, the attack on Peel, and the Reform Act of 1867
melbourne — The Whig premier and the young Queen’s constitutional tutor
liverpool — The long-lived postwar premier of the Tory ascendancy
canning — The liberal Tory who transformed foreign policy and “called the New World into existence”
wellington — The victor of Waterloo, minister, and elder statesman
grey-charles — The minister who carried the Reform Act of 1832
russell — The introducer of the Reform Bill and champion of reform
derby — Three times Prime Minister; the Conservative of the “leap in the dark”

Radicals and the Press

cobbett-william — The great popular journalist of the “twopenny trash”
carlile-richard — The resolute publisher of The Republican, imprisoned for the press
hone-william — The satirist acquitted at the three trials of 1817

Engineers and Scientists

stephenson-george — The father of the railway locomotive
babbage-charles — The critic of English science and inventor of the calculating engines

Events
Reform, Constitution, and Politics

reform-act-1832 — Grey’s great Bill: rotten boroughs, the £10 franchise, the Days of May
peterloo-1819 — The Manchester massacre and the Regent’s thanks
six-acts-1819 — The repressive legislation that followed Peterloo
queen-caroline-affair-1820 — The King’s attempt to divorce his Queen and the popular agitation
catholic-emancipation-1829 — Wellington and Peel concede the Catholic claims
accession-of-victoria-1837 — The opening of the Victorian age
corn-laws-repeal-1846 — Peel’s conversion, free trade, and the split of the Conservative Party
peoples-charter-1838 — The six points of the Charter and the Chartist movement
new-poor-law-1834 — The workhouse test and the reform of the relief of the poor
abolition-of-slavery-1833 — The £20 million compensation and the end of colonial slavery

Financial and Commercial

panic-of-1825 — The great speculative collapse and the run on the banks
railway-mania-1845-47 — The railway fever and the crash
crisis-of-1847 — The panic, the suspension of the Bank Act, and the currency controversy

War and Empire

trafalgar-1805 — Nelson’s victory and death; command of the sea
war-of-1812 — The frigate war with the United States
bombardment-of-algiers-1816 — Exmouth’s blow against Barbary piracy and Christian slavery
navarino-1827 — The destruction of the Ottoman fleet and Greek independence
crimean-war-1853-56 — Sebastopol, the Charge of the Light Brigade, and the end of the forty years’ peace
indian-mutiny-1857 — The great revolt and the end of the East India Company
first-opium-war-1839-42 — The China war and the Treaty of Nanking
american-civil-war-alabama — The cotton famine, the Trent, and the Alabama claims

Society, Culture, and Disaster

irish-famine-1845-49 — The potato blight, the mortality, and the exodus
great-exhibition-1851 — The Crystal Palace and the Festival of Peace
oxford-movement-1833 — The Tractarians and the Catholic revival of the Church
mayhew-morning-chronicle-survey-1850 — The founding of the English social survey
municipal-reform-1835 — The reform of the boroughs and the long reform of the City of London

Concepts
Currency and Banking

bank-charter-act-1844 — Peel’s Act: the currency principle, the fixed maximum, and the crisis of 1847
country-banks — The note-issuing bankers of the provinces and their seasonal “laws”
bank-of-england — The great national reserve of gold and the pivot of the currency
currency-vs-banking-school — The monetary controversy behind the Act of 1844
public-credit-and-national-debt — The funding system, the debt, and the fears of bankruptcy

Economy and Trade

corn-laws — The protective duties and the struggle over them
free-trade — The great doctrine of the Victorian age

Constitution and Empire

parliamentary-reform — The remaking of the Commons from 1832 to the Chartist decades
chartism — The working-class movement for the six points
responsible-government-colonies — Colonial self-government on the Westminster model

Local Government and the City

city-of-london — The Corporation, its wards, Livery, courts, and exclusive privileges (1837 & 1854 inquiries)

Society, Religion, and Industry

london-street-folk — The street-sellers, the casual poor, and the London underworld (Mayhew)
church-of-england-and-oxford-movement — The establishment, the parties, and the Tractarian revival
engineering-and-steam — The canals, roads, bridges, and steam engines of the age (Smiles)
socialist-thought-communist-manifesto — The Communist Manifesto and the class antagonism (Marx/Engels)

Naval Power

command-of-the-sea — The foundation of British power from Trafalgar to the ironclad
ironclad-transition — From wooden walls to armour, steam, and the turret

Source Navigation

sources-map — guided map of the source pages by subject and date range, including a reading path for the period from the end of the Crimean War to 1865.

Sources


Municipal Corporations Commission — Second Report of the Commissioners Appointed to Inquire into the Municipal Corporations in England and Wales — London and Southwark; London Companies (1837). The fundamental inquiry into the Corporation of the City of London: its limits and municipal territory, the wards and wardmote elections, the Lord Mayor, Court of Aldermen, Common Council, Sheriffs, courts, freemen and liverymen, property and revenue, the London Companies, the Southwark connexion, and the evidence and correspondence. Read source page


Royal Commission — Report of the Commissioners Appointed to Inquire into the Existing State of the Corporation of the City of London (1854). The Royal Commission into the Corporation of the City of London: its constitution, order, and government, jurisdictions, prisons and police, elections, freemen and liverymen, property, revenue, and expenditure, with the thirty-two recommendations for reform and the Minutes of Evidence and Appendix. Read source page


Justin McCarthy — A History of Our Own Times: From the Accession of Queen Victoria to the General Election of 1880. One-volume Burt edition covering Victoria’s accession through 1880; chapters I–XLVII cover 1837–1865 and chapters XXX–XLVII are especially useful for the post-Crimean period through Palmerston’s death. Read source page


Justin McCarthy — A History of Our Own Times, Vol. II. Belford, Clarke Vol. II, beginning with chapter XXX, “The Lorcha Arrow,” and carrying the narrative from the post-Crimean settlement through the later Victorian continuation; chapters XXX–XLVII cover 1856–1865. Read source page


Babbage, Charles — Reflections on the Decline of Science in England (1830). A polemic on the state of British science, criticising the Royal Society and calling for reform. Read source page


Buller, Charles — Responsible Government for Colonies (1840). The most sustained contemporary argument for applying the Westminster model of cabinet government to the British colonies, written in support of Lord Durham’s Report by his former secretary. Read source page


Carey, Henry C. — The Credit System in France, Great Britain, and the United States (1838). An economic analysis comparing banking, credit, and confidence across the three nations, drawing on data from the 1810s–1830s. Read source page


Gilbart, J. W. — The Laws of the Currency, as Exemplified in the Circulation of Country Bank Notes in England, since the Passing of the Act of 1844 (Journal of the Statistical Society of London, 1854). Statistical paper on English country-note circulation after Peel’s Bank Charter Act: seasonal “laws” for England, Scotland, and Ireland; extinction of issues; 1847 pressure; recommendations against a single amalgamated issue. Read source page


Imlac — Insecurity of the British Funds / Essay on Public Credit (1817). A post-war tract reprinting Hume’s essay on public credit with commentary on the national debt, the funding system, paper money, and the risk of national bankruptcy. Read source page


Hone, William — The Three Trials of William Hone (1818). Self-published report of the three Guildhall prosecutions (18–20 December 1817) for political parodies on the Catechism, Litany, and Athanasian Creed; ex-officio informations before Abbott and Ellenborough; three Not Guilty verdicts; Address, subscription meeting for liberty of the press and trial by jury, full parody texts, and (in this scan) later Queen Caroline–era bound pamphlets. Read source page


Hone, William — Pamphlets and Parodies on Political Subjects (Chidley collection, 1830). Nine Cruikshank-illustrated political squibs of 1820–22 reissued together: Political House that Jack Built, Queen’s Matrimonial Ladder, Miraculous Host, Caroline Form of Prayer, Non Mi Ricordo!, Political Showman, Man in the Moon, Right Divine of Kings to Govern Wrong!, and Slap at Slop (Bridge-Street Gang). Read source page


Hone, William — The Every-Day Book, Vol. I (1826). Day-by-day everlasting calendar of popular amusements, saints’ days, customs, and seasons (January–December), with 170 engravings; dedicated to Charles Lamb and Miss Lamb; preface and explanatory address; six indexes (subjects, saints, poetry, floral directory, correspondents, engravings). Read source page


Carlile, Richard — The Republican, Volume VIII (11 July–26 December 1823). Weekly freethought and republican journal from Dorchester Gaol; dedicated to Spaniards in Exile; Nos. 1–25 at 6d.; war with the Vice Society, materialism vs Methodism and Swedenborgianism, Dorset addresses, Elizabeth Fry, and Mechanics’ Institutes as temples of science. Read source page


Carlile / Hone / Cobbett — Harrison-bound radical miscellany. Hone’s Political House that Jack Built; Cobbett 1817 Weekly Political Register / Political Pamphlet (Vol. 32); Carlile’s The Republican No. 2, Vol. I (3 September 1819, 2d.) with letters to the Prince Regent and Sidmouth on the 16 August 1819 Manchester killings (the first Republican Peterloo locus in this wiki). Read source page


Engels, Friedrich — The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845). A contemporary investigation of the English working class during the Industrial Revolution, based on Engels’s two-year observation in Manchester and official reports. Covers the factory system, the great towns, Irish immigration, labour movements (Chartism, trade unions), the mining and agricultural proletariats, and the attitude of the bourgeoisie. Read source page


Marx, Karl, and Frederick Engels — Manifesto of the Communist Party (1848; this extract Moore/Engels English lineage with prefaces 1872–1893). Programme of the Communist League: bourgeoisie and proletarians, proletarians and Communists, socialist and communist literature, position of Communists to the various existing opposition parties; closing “Working Men of All Countries, Unite!”; later prefaces on the Paris Commune and international circulation. Read source page


James, William — Naval History of Great Britain, Vol. I: Introduction and the French Revolutionary War (1488–1796). Covers the history of naval architecture and ship classification, then the first four years of the French Revolutionary War: Lord Howe’s campaigns, the Glorious First of June, Hood at Toulon and Corsica, Bridport off Isle-Groix, Hotham off Genoa and Hyères, Cornwallis’s retreat, the capture of the Cape of Good Hope, and the war with Holland and Spain (1796). Read source page


James, William — Naval History of Great Britain, Vol. II: The Crisis Years (1797–1799). The mutinies at Spithead and the Nore, Jervis at Cape St. Vincent, Camperdown, Nelson at Santa Cruz and the Nile, the Bonaparte’s Egyptian expedition, Sir Sidney Smith at Acre, the Anglo-Russian expedition to Holland, and extensive light squadron and single-ship operations. Read source page


James, William — Naval History of Great Britain, Vol. III: From the Armed Neutrality to Trafalgar (1800–1805). The Baltic expedition and Copenhagen, the Peace of Amiens, Napoleon’s invasion preparations, Villeneuve’s chase across the Atlantic, the Battle of Trafalgar and Nelson’s death, the storm and its aftermath. Read source page


James, William — Naval History of Great Britain, Vol. IV: From the Declaration of War in 1793 to the Accession of George IV (1805–1809). A detailed chronological account of British naval operations from the aftermath of Trafalgar through the Basque Roads and Walcheren expeditions: Strachan’s action, Copenhagen, the Dardanelles, the Chesapeake affair, single-ship actions, and colonial campaigns across the Atlantic, Baltic, and East Indies. Read source page


James, William — Naval History of Great Britain, Vol. V: From the Declaration of War in 1793 to the Accession of George IV (1809–1813). A detailed chronological account of British naval operations: single-ship actions, fleet engagements, and colonial expeditions from the Napoleonic wars through the War of 1812, with annual abstracts of the Royal Navy. Read source page


James, William — Naval History of Great Britain, Vol. VI: From the Declaration of War in 1793 to the Accession of George IV (1813–1827). The final volume covering the end of the Napoleonic wars, the War of 1812 (Shannon and Chesapeake, the burning of Washington, Baltimore, Lake Champlain, New Orleans), and the post-war period: the bombardment of Algiers, the Burmese War, and the Battle of Navarino. Read source page


Clowes, Sir William Laird — The Royal Navy: A History, Vol. V (1803–1815). The whole naval struggle with Napoleon: the Trafalgar campaign, the blockade system, and the minor single-ship actions, covering civil administration, major fleet operations, and minor operations with appendices of ships taken and lost by each belligerent. Read source page


Clowes, Sir William Laird — The Royal Navy: A History, Vol. VI (1812–1856). The War of 1812 (by Theodore Roosevelt), the peacetime Navy 1816–1856 (Algiers, Navarino, St. Jean d’Acre, the Crimean War and Sebastopol), the transition from sail to steam, and Arctic and Antarctic voyages of discovery (by Sir Clements Markham). Read source page


Clowes, Sir William Laird — The Royal Navy: A History, Vol. VII (1857–1900). The late Victorian Navy from the Second China War and Indian Mutiny through the bombardment of Alexandria, the Sudan campaigns, and the Boer War; the transition to ironclads; Arctic, Antarctic, and the Challenger expedition (by Sir Clements Markham). Read source page


James, William — A Full and Correct Account of the Chief Naval Occurrences of the Late War Between Great Britain and the United States of America (1817). A contemporary British account of the naval War of 1812, written while details were still being gathered from officers across the United Kingdom. Covers every major naval action (Guerriere, Java, Macedonian, Shannon and Chesapeake, Essex, Lake Erie, President, Constitution vs. Cyane and Levant) with comparative force calculations, British and American official accounts compared, and an appendix of official documents. Read source page


Mayhew, Henry — The Morning Chronicle Survey of Labour and the Poor: The Metropolitan Districts (1850). A compilation of 14 of Mayhew’s Morning Chronicle letters (Letters XXVII–XL, Jan–Mar 1850) investigating vagrancy, casual wards, low lodging-houses, the boot and shoe trade, slop work, toy-makers, and doll manufacture in the London metropolitan districts. Read source page


Mayhew, Henry — London Labour and the London Poor, Vol. I: The London Street-Folk (1861–62). The first volume of Mayhew’s encyclopædic survey, covering the street-folk: wandering tribes, costermongers, street-sellers of fish, fruit, vegetables, game, flowers, green stuff, eatables and drinkables, stationery and literature, manufactured articles, and the women and children street-sellers. Read source page


Mayhew, Henry — London Labour and the London Poor, Vol. II: The London Street-Folk, Book the Second (1861–62). The second volume of the survey, continuing the Street-Folk subject: street-sellers of second-hand articles and live animals, street-buyers, the street Jews, street-finders and collectors, the sanitary condition of London’s streets (dust-yards, sewers, night-soil), chimney-sweepers, and crossing-sweepers. Read source page


Mayhew, Henry — London Labour and the London Poor, Vol. III: The London Street-Folk (1861–62). The third volume of the survey, covering street-folk trades and labour: destroyers of vermin (rat-killers, bug-destroyers), street-exhibitors (Punch, acrobats, conjurors), street-musicians, street-vocalists, street-artists, trained animals, garret-masters (cheap cabinet-makers), coal-heavers, ballast-men, lumpers, dock-labourers, cheap lodging-houses, London watermen, omnibus-drivers, cab-drivers, carmen, vagrants, and ticket-of-leave men. Read source page


Mayhew, Henry — London Labour and the London Poor, Vol. IV: Those That Will Not Work — Prostitutes, Thieves, Swindlers, Beggars and Vagrants (1861–62). The fourth and final volume, covering the criminal and destitute classes with contributions by Bracebridge Hemyng (prostitution), John Binny (thieves and swindlers), Andrew Halliday (beggars), and the Rev. William Tuckniss (introductory essay on London’s charitable and reformatory agencies). Read source page


Martineau, Harriet — History of England, Vol. I: Introduction (1790–1809).


Martineau, Harriet — History of England, Vol. II: From the Congress of Vienna to the End of Lord Liverpool’s Government (1815–1826). Post-war depression, the Corn Laws, radicals and Peterloo, the Queen Caroline affair, Canning’s foreign policy, the panic of 1825, and the Catholic question. Read source page


Martineau, Harriet — History of England, Vol. III: From the Canning Ministry to the Dissolution of the Orange Societies (1827–1836). The Reform Bill crisis, the abolition of slavery, the New Poor Law, municipal reform, the Tractarian movement, and the consolidation of the Reformed Parliament. Read source page


Sir Archibald Alison — History of Europe, Vol. I: From the Fall of Napoleon (1815–1823). The post-war settlement, the Holy Alliance, England from 1815 to 1819 (Peterloo, the Six Acts, the resumption of cash payments), France under the Restoration, the Spanish Revolution of 1820, Russia under Alexander I, and the death of Louis XVIII. Read source page


Sir Archibald Alison — History of Europe, Vol. II: From the Greek Revolution to the Polish Revolution (1823–1831). The state of Turkey and Greece, the Greek War of Independence, Navarino, France under Charles X through the Revolution of 1830, English domestic history from 1822 through the Reform Bill crisis, and the Polish Revolution. Read source page


Sir Archibald Alison — History of Europe, Vol. III: From the Reform Era to the Afghan Disaster (1831–1842). Constitutional history of Germany, the July Monarchy in France, England from the Reform Bill to the early years of Victoria (Peel, Melbourne, Chartists, Corn Law agitation), the Eastern Question and Mehemet Ali, and British India from the Mahratta War to the first Afghan War. Read source page


Sir Archibald Alison — History of Europe, Vol. IV: From Peel’s Ministry to Louis Napoleon (1841–1851). Peel’s ministry and the Bank Charter Act, the Corn Law repeal, Ireland and the famine, the Revolution of 1848 in France, the Italian and German revolutions, Hungary, and the Indian campaigns in Gwalior and the first Sikh War. Read source page


Sir Archibald Alison — History of Europe, Vol. V: Constitutional Germany, France under Louis Philippe, and England after Reform (1831–1837). A constitutional survey of Germany from 1814–1848, German literature, the suppression of republican and royalist insurrections in France, England from the Reform Bill to the fall of Earl Grey, the Eastern Question from the Treaty of Adrianople, and the consolidation of Louis Philippe’s government. Read source page


Sir Archibald Alison — History of Europe, Vol. VI: France under the July Monarchy, England from Peel to Melbourne, and British India (1834–1842). The Eastern crisis and the fall of Thiers, the abortive Peel ministry of 1834–35, the return of Melbourne, the accession of Victoria, Chartism and the Canadian rebellion, the fall of the Whigs in 1841, and a detailed retrospective on British India from the Mahratta War to the Afghan disaster of 1842. Read source page


Sir Archibald Alison — History of Europe, Vol. VII: Peel’s Second Ministry, the Corn Law Repeal, and the Revolutions of 1848 (1841–1848). Peel’s financial reforms and the Bank Charter Act, the railway mania and crisis of 1847, the repeal of the Corn Laws, the Chartist suppression, France from the Eastern crisis of 1841 to the fall of Louis Philippe, the French wars in Algeria, and the diplomatic crisis leading to 1848. Read source page


Sir Archibald Alison — History of the French Revolution, Vol. II: From the Renewal of the War (1799) to the Peace of Tilsit (1807). The campaigns of 1799, Marengo, the Peace of Amiens, Trafalgar, Austerlitz, Jena, Eylau, Friedland, and the reconstruction of French society under the Consulate and Empire. Read source page


Smiles, Samuel — Lives of the Engineers, Vol. I: Early Engineering — Vermuyden, Myddelton, Perry, Brindley. The earliest British engineering works: drainage of the Fens (Vermuyden), the New River water supply (Myddelton), the Dagenham Breach (Perry), and the canal system (Brindley). Read source page


Smiles, Samuel — Lives of the Engineers, Vol. III: History of Roads — Metcalfe and Telford. The development of British roads and road-making: John Metcalf (the blind road-maker) and Thomas Telford (Highland roads, Menai and Conway bridges, the Caledonian Canal, the Holyhead road). Read source page


Smiles, Samuel — Lives of the Engineers, Vol. IV: The Steam-Engine — Boulton and Watt. The partnership of Matthew Boulton and James Watt, the invention of the condensing steam engine, the Soho Manufactory, the Cornish engine trade, and the beginnings of gas-lighting. Read source page


Smiles, Samuel — Lives of the Engineers: The Locomotive — George and Robert Stephenson. The story of the two Stephensons and the railway revolution: from the Killingworth collieries to the “Rocket,” the Stockton & Darlington and Liverpool & Manchester railways, the tubular bridges, and the spread of railways across the globe. Read source page


Smiles, Samuel — Lives of the Engineers, Vol. II: Harbours, Lighthouses, and Bridges — Smeaton and Rennie. The development of British civil engineering through the lives of John Smeaton (Eddystone Lighthouse, steam-engine improvements) and John Rennie (Waterloo and London Bridge, London Docks, fen drainage, the dredging machine). Read source page


Tooke, Thomas — A History of Prices, Vols. I–II: From 1793 to 1837. The foundation of the empirical study of British prices and currency: the effects of seasons, war, and the Bank Restriction on prices, from the outbreak of the French wars through the end of William IV’s reign. Read source page


Tooke, Thomas, and William Newmarch — A History of Prices, Vols. III–IV: From 1838 to 1847. The continuation through the years leading to Corn Law repeal and the railway mania: corn prices, currency debates, the Bank Charter Act of 1844, and the crisis of 1847. Read source page


Tooke, Thomas, and William Newmarch — A History of Prices, Vols. V–VI: From 1848 to 1856. The final volumes covering the free-trade era: corn prices after repeal, the railway construction boom, the Bank of England under Peel’s Act, French finance, and the great gold discoveries in California and Australia. Read source page


Sir Archibald Alison — History of Europe, Vol. VIII: The Chinese War, Indian Conquests, and the Close of the Period (1841–1852). The First Opium War and the Treaty of Nanking, the Afghan War and its recovery, the conquest of Scinde, the Sikh Wars, the Revolutions of 1848 across Europe, and the consolidation of the Second Empire. Read source page


Reed, Edward J. — Our Iron-Clad Ships; Their Qualities, Performances, and Cost (1869). A comprehensive technical survey of the British ironclad navy by the Chief Constructor of the Royal Navy, covering design, armour, armament, steam and sailing performance, turret-ships, rams, and costs — from Warrior (1860) to the Devastation-class monitors under construction. Read source page


Mahan, Alfred Thayer — The Influence of Sea Power upon History, 1660–1783 (1890). The foundational work of naval strategic theory, establishing Mahan’s thesis that command of the sea is the decisive factor in national power. Covers the sailing-ship era from the Restoration through the end of the American Revolution: the Anglo-Dutch wars, the wars of Louis XIV, the War of the Spanish Succession, the Seven Years’ War, and the American Revolutionary War. Included as the essential theoretical and historical foundation for British naval supremacy in the 1800–1865 period. Read source page

sources-map.title: Sources Map
sources-map.content:
Sources Map
This page maps the wiki’s source pages by what they cover. The collection is strongest for parliamentary and political narrative, naval history, industrial and social inquiry, Church history, prices and credit, engineering, and mid-Victorian imperial questions.
For the specific period from the end of the Crimean War to 1865, begin with Walpole, Vol. VI, McCarthy’s A History of Our Own Times, Clowes, Vol. VII, Reed, Mayhew, and Wakeman.

Core Political Narrative
Royal Commission — City of London

second-report-municipal-commission-city-of-london-1837 — The Second Report of the Municipal Corporations Commission (1837) on London and Southwark and the London Companies: limits, wards, governing bodies, courts, freemen and liverymen, property and revenue, the Companies, and the evidence.
royal-commission-city-of-london-1854 — The 1854 Royal Commission into the Corporation of the City of London: constitution, government, courts, police, freemen and liverymen, property and revenue, the thirty-two recommendations, and the Minutes of Evidence.

Harriet Martineau — History of England

martineau-1800-1815 — A compact narrative of Britain from 1800 to the end of the Napoleonic War, useful as the bridge from the war state to the postwar settlement.
martineau-history-of-england-vol1 — Introductory volume covering 1790–1809: war, administration, domestic policy, and the opening phase of the nineteenth-century story.
martineau-history-of-england-vol2 — 1815–1826: postwar distress, the Corn Laws, radical agitation, Peterloo, Queen Caroline, Canning, the 1825 panic, and Catholic emancipation politics.
martineau-history-of-england-vol3 — 1827–1836: Canning, Wellington, the Reform Bill crisis, abolition of slavery, the New Poor Law, municipal reform, and early Victorian party realignment.
martineau-history-of-england-vol4 — 1837 to the Crimean War: Victoria’s early reign, Peel, free trade, Ireland, Chartism, 1848, Palmerston, and the road to war.

Sir Spencer Walpole — History of England from the Conclusion of the Great War in 1815

walpole-history-of-england-vol4 — Reform-era and early Victorian political narrative, useful for the 1830s–1840s transition.
walpole-history-of-england-vol5 — Mid-century narrative overlapping 1850–1878 in the earlier edition; useful for the Crimean War, the Indian crisis, and the move into late Palmerstonian politics.
walpole-history-of-england-vol6 — The main general source for 1853–1880 in the expanded edition. This is the strongest existing single source page for the period from the Crimean War settlement through 1865, especially the end of the Crimean War, India, colonial self-government, and imperial questions.

William Nassau Molesworth — The History of England from the Year 1830

molesworth-history-1830-1874-vols1-2 — Vols. I & II (1873), covering 1830–1854. Vol. I runs from the Reform struggle through the death of William IV (1830–1837); Vol. II covers the reign of Victoria from her accession through the Crimean War preliminaries (1837–1854). Strong on parliamentary politics, the Corn Law struggle, Chartism, and the Great Exhibition era.
molesworth-history-1830-1874-vol3 — Vol. III (1875), covering 1854–1874. The Crimean War, the Indian Mutiny, the Palmerston ministry, the Reform Bill of 1867, and the first Gladstone ministry. Molesworth’s narrative is especially full for the transition from Palmerstonian stability to the Liberal reforming era.

Justin McCarthy — A History of Our Own Times

mccarthy-history-of-our-own-times-complete-burt-1880 — One-volume Burt edition covering Victoria’s accession through the general election of 1880. For this wiki, chapters I–XLVII cover 1837–1865; chapters XXX–XLVII are the key post-Crimean sequence.
mccarthy-history-of-our-own-times-vol2-belford-1884 — Belford, Clarke Vol. II, beginning with chapter XXX, “The Lorcha Arrow,” and running through chapter LXVII. Its opening half covers 1856–1865: China, transportation, the Indian Mutiny, the end of Company rule, the Orsini crisis, Derby and Disraeli, the Ionian Islands, the French treaty, the American Civil War, the Alabama, Palmerston’s last victory, and Palmerston’s death.

Sir Archibald Alison — History of Europe

alison-history-of-europe-vol1 — 1815–1823: the post-Napoleonic settlement, Holy Alliance, Peterloo, France under the Restoration, Spain, Russia, and Louis XVIII.
alison-history-of-europe-vol2 — 1823–1831: Greek Revolution, Navarino, France under Charles X, English domestic politics through the Reform crisis, and Poland.
alison-history-of-europe-vol3 — 1831–1842: Reform, Germany, July Monarchy France, Chartism, Corn Law agitation, the Eastern Question, and British India to the Afghan disaster.
alison-history-of-europe-vol4 — 1841–1851: Peel, the Bank Charter Act, Corn Law repeal, famine, 1848 in Europe, and the first Sikh War.
alison-history-of-europe-vol5 — 1831–1837: constitutional Germany, France under Louis Philippe, England after Reform, and the Eastern Question.
alison-history-of-europe-vol6 — 1806–1842: French, English, and Indian chapters reaching into the Melbourne and Peel period.
alison-history-of-europe-vol7 — 1841–1848: Peel, finance, railway mania, Corn Law repeal, Chartist suppression, and the road to 1848.
alison-history-of-europe-vol8 — 1841–1852: China, India, the Afghan recovery, Scinde, Sikh wars, 1848 Europe, and the Second Empire.
alison-history-of-french-revolution-vol2 — 1799–1807: background for the Napoleonic system against which the early nineteenth-century British state was formed.


Naval War, Sea Power, and Maritime Strategy

james-naval-history-vol1 — Introduction and the French Revolutionary War to 1796; useful background on naval architecture and the early war at sea.
james-naval-history-vol2 — 1797–1799: Spithead and Nore, St. Vincent, Camperdown, the Nile, Acre, and the Anglo-Russian expedition to Holland.
james-naval-history-vol3 — 1800–1805: Copenhagen, Amiens, invasion preparations, Villeneuve’s chase, Trafalgar, and Nelson’s death.
james-naval-history-vol4 — 1805–1809: the aftermath of Trafalgar, Copenhagen, the Dardanelles, the Chesapeake affair, Basque Roads, and Walcheren.
james-naval-history-vol5 — 1809–1813: naval operations from the late Napoleonic war through the War of 1812.
james-naval-history-vol6 — 1813–1827: the end of the Napoleonic wars, War of 1812 episodes, Algiers, Burma, and Navarino.
james-naval-occurrences-war-1812 — A contemporary British account of the naval War of 1812 with comparative force calculations and official documents.
clowes-royal-navy-vol5 — 1803–1815: the Royal Navy in the struggle with Napoleon, including Trafalgar, blockade, administration, and minor operations.
clowes-royal-navy-vol6 — 1812–1856: War of 1812, peacetime navy, Algiers, Navarino, St. Jean d’Acre, Crimean War, steam transition, and polar voyages.
clowes-royal-navy-vol7 — 1857–1900: the essential post-Crimean naval source, covering the Second China War, Indian Mutiny naval dimensions, ironclads, later expeditions, and late Victorian naval transition.
mahan-sea-power-history — A strategic and theoretical source on sea power from 1660 to 1783, useful for interpreting the foundations of British maritime supremacy.
reed-our-iron-clad-ships — Edward J. Reed’s technical survey of British ironclads. Essential for the 1860s naval-technology transition from wooden walls to armour, steam, turrets, rams, and monitor-style ships.


Press, Libel, and Radical Politics

hone-three-trials — William Hone’s self-published report of the three Guildhall trials (18–20 December 1817) for political parodies on the Catechism, Litany, and Athanasian Creed. Primary source for ex-officio informations, special-jury practice, Abbott and Ellenborough charges, uncounselled defence by historical parody, three Not Guilty verdicts, and the 29 December 1817 liberty-of-the-press subscription meeting. This scan also binds later Queen Caroline–era Hone squibs (Non Mi Ricordo!, Political House that Jack Built, Queen’s Matrimonial Ladder).
hone-pamphlets-and-parodies — 1830 Chidley collection of nine Hone political pamphlets (1820–22 Ludgate Hill originals) with Cruikshank cuts: Political House that Jack Built, Queen’s Matrimonial Ladder, Miraculous Host, Caroline Form of Prayer, Non Mi Ricordo!, Political Showman, Man in the Moon, Right Divine of Kings to Govern Wrong!, and Slap at Slop (Bridge-Street Gang). Primary illustrated radical satire of the Queen Caroline and reform years.
hone-every-day-book — Hone’s 1826 Every-Day Book Vol. I: day-by-day calendar of popular amusements, customs, saints’ days, and seasons (full year), dedicated to Charles Lamb; 170 engravings; six indexes. Non-political antiquarian sequel to the trial and pamphlet years.
carlile-republican-harrison-bound — Composite IA dump: Hone Political House that Jack Built; Cobbett 1817 cheap weekly run; Carlile The Republican No. 2, Vol. I (3 Sept. 1819). Primary Republican source for the 16 August 1819 Manchester killings — Carlile’s letters to the Prince Regent (30 Aug.) and Sidmouth (1 Sept.), with the Sidmouth–Derby thanks of 21 Aug. printed in full; Atkins and Fitch letters. First Republican Peterloo locus in this wiki.
carlile-republican-vol8 — The Republican Vol. VIII (11 July–26 Dec. 1823), Carlile from Dorchester Gaol. Dedication to Spaniards in Exile; weekly freethought (Vice Society, materialism, Methodism, Swedenborgians, Quakers); Dorset prison addresses; Mechanics’ Institutes as temples of science. Not a Peterloo reportage volume.


Economy, Prices, Credit, and Public Finance

imlac-insecurity-of-british-funds — A postwar public-credit tract using Hume and contemporary commentary to discuss debt, funding, paper money, and bankruptcy anxieties.
carey-credit-system — Henry C. Carey’s comparative analysis of banking, credit, and confidence in France, Great Britain, and the United States.
gilbart-laws-of-the-currency-country-notes-1844 — J. W. Gilbart’s 1854 statistical paper on English country bank notes after the Bank Charter Act of 1844: seasonal “laws of the currency” for England, Scotland, and Ireland; lapsed issues; comparison with 1845 Scottish/Irish rules; recommendations against amalgamation into a single issue.
tooke-history-of-prices-vol1-2 — 1793–1837: prices, currency, seasons, war, and Bank Restriction from the French wars through the end of William IV’s reign.
tooke-history-of-prices-vol3-4 — 1838–1847: Corn Law repeal, Bank Charter Act, railway mania, currency debates, and the crisis of 1847.
tooke-history-of-prices-vol5-6 — 1848–1856: free trade, corn prices, railway construction, Bank of England practice under Peel’s Act, French finance, and gold discoveries. This reaches the end of the Crimean War but does not carry the story to 1865.


Industrial Society, Labour, London, and Social Inquiry

engels-condition-of-the-working-class — Engels’s 1845 account of industrial England, especially Manchester, factory work, urban conditions, Irish immigration, mining, agriculture, Chartism, and class relations.
marx-engels-communist-manifesto — Marx and Engels, Manifesto of the Communist Party (1848 programme of the Communist League; this extract Moore/Engels English lineage with prefaces 1872–1893). Bourgeoisie and proletarians, Communists and the proletariat, critique of contemporary socialist literature, position toward opposition parties; later notes on the Paris Commune and international circulation. Pair with Engels’s Condition for English industrial context.
mayhew-morning-chronicle-survey — Mayhew’s 1850 Morning Chronicle letters on London labour, vagrancy, lodging houses, trades, slop work, toy-makers, and doll manufacture.
mayhew-london-labour-london-poor-vol1 — London street-folk: costermongers, street-sellers, food, flowers, literature, manufactured articles, women, and children.
mayhew-london-labour-london-poor-vol2 — Further street-folk: second-hand articles, live animals, street-buyers, Jewish street traders, finders, sewer and night-soil work, chimney-sweeps, and crossing-sweepers.
mayhew-london-labour-london-poor-vol3 — Street trades and labour: rat-killers, performers, musicians, garret-masters, coal-heavers, dock labour, cheap lodging houses, watermen, cab-drivers, vagrants, and ticket-of-leave men.
mayhew-london-labour-london-poor-vol4 — Those who will not work: prostitution, thieves, swindlers, beggars, vagrants, and charitable/reformatory agencies. The Mayhew volumes are the key social sources for London in the early 1860s.


Engineering, Science, and Technology

babbage-decline-of-science — Babbage’s 1830 polemic on the Royal Society, British science, scientific institutions, and reform.
smiles-engineers-vol1-vermyden-brindley — Early engineering: drainage, water supply, and canals through Vermuyden, Myddelton, Perry, and Brindley.
smiles-engineers-smeaton-rennie — Harbours, lighthouses, bridges, docks, dredging, and civil engineering through Smeaton and Rennie.
smiles-engineers-vol3-metcalfe-telford — Roads, bridges, canals, Highland works, the Menai and Conway bridges, and Telford’s civil engineering.
smiles-engineers-vol4-boulton-watt — Boulton, Watt, Soho, the condensing steam engine, Cornish engines, and gas-lighting.
smiles-locomotive-stephenson — George and Robert Stephenson, colliery railways, the Rocket, Stockton & Darlington, Liverpool & Manchester, tubular bridges, and railway expansion.


Church and Religion

overton-english-church-1800-1833 — Church of England history from 1800 to 1833, before the Oxford Movement.
overton-church-19th — Another Overton source page focused on the English Church in the early nineteenth century, including institutional condition and church reform.
wakeman-church-of-england — Broad Church of England history into the late nineteenth century. For the post-Crimean period it is useful for the High Church revival, Eucharistic controversy, ritual questions, and the widening of religious conflict through the 1850s–1860s.


Best Reading Paths
From the end of the Crimean War to 1865
Read walpole-history-of-england-vol6, mccarthy-history-of-our-own-times-vol2-belford-1884, and molesworth-history-1830-1874-vol3 together. Walpole supplies a broad historical structure; McCarthy gives a continuous Victorian political narrative from the Congress of Paris through Palmerston’s death. Molesworth Vol. III provides a detailed parliamentary and political narrative for the same period with strong coverage of the Palmerston and first Gladstone ministries. Add clowes-royal-navy-vol7 for naval and imperial dimensions, reed-our-iron-clad-ships for naval technology, mayhew-london-labour-london-poor-vol1 through mayhew-london-labour-london-poor-vol4 for London social life in the early 1860s, and wakeman-church-of-england for Church controversies.
For the Napoleonic and postwar transition
Use Martineau, James, Clowes Vol. V–VI, Tooke Vols. I–II, Alison Vols. I–II, Imlac, and Hone (three trials, 1817) for press, libel, and radical political culture.
For industrial and social transformation
Use Engels, Mayhew, Smiles, Babbage, Tooke, Carey, and Reed.
For empire and overseas crises
Use Alison Vols. III–VIII, Walpole Vols. V–VI, McCarthy, Clowes Vols. VI–VII, and James where naval detail is needed.

sources/alison-history-of-europe-vol1.title: Alison — History of Europe, Vol. I: From the Fall of Napoleon (1815–1823)
sources/alison-history-of-europe-vol1.content:
Alison — History of Europe, Vol. I: From the Fall of Napoleon (1815–1823)
Sir Archibald Alison (1792–1867) — History of Europe from the Fall of Napoleon in MDCCCXV to the Accession of Louis Napoleon in MDCCCLII. Vol. I. — Harper & Brothers, New York, 1859.
The first volume of Alison’s multi-volume history of the post-Napoleonic period. It opens with a general sketch of the whole period from 1815 to 1852, then proceeds to a detailed narrative of European affairs from the Peace of Paris in 1815 through the early 1820s. The author explains in his preface that the work was undertaken to trace the consequences of the long Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars, and that he has arranged it by subject — each chapter treating a single nation’s affairs through a sequence of years — to avoid the confusion of keeping every European state “abreast” year by year.
The text is 476 pages, extracted from the University of California library copy.
Content Summary

Preface — explanation of the work’s scope and method: each subject is treated in a single chapter throughout several consecutive years; the first volume is chiefly occupied with the Parliamentary history of England and the policy of France after the Restoration
Chapter I — General Sketch of the Whole Period from the Fall of Napoleon to the Accession of Louis Napoleon — a panoramic view of the thirty-seven years: the reaction after the wars, the rise of democratic ambition in peacetime, the Revolution of 1830 in France and its effects on England, the Reform Bill, free-trade policy, the expansion of the United States and Russia, the Revolutions of 1848, and the discovery of the gold mines of California and Australia
Chapter II — History of England from the Peace of Paris, 1815, to the End of the Year 1816 — the commanding position of Great Britain at the close of the war, the consolidation of the English and Irish Exchequers, the detention of Napoleon, the marriage of the Princess Charlotte, votes for public monuments, the new coinage, the Spa Fields Riots, the expedition to Algiers under Lord Exmouth, and efforts of the factious to stir up sedition
Chapter III — The Holy Alliance and the Affairs of Spain and Portugal — the Holy Alliance described, its principles and signatories; the state of Spain under Ferdinand VII, the revolt of Riego and the Spanish Constitution of 1812, the Neapolitan and Piedmontese revolutions; British neutrality, Canning’s foreign policy, the recognition of the South American republics
Chapter IV — Domestic History of England from the Commencement of 1817 to the Repeal of the Bank Restriction Act in 1819 — continued distress and disaffection, the suspension of Habeas Corpus, the Gagging Acts, the Manchester meeting (Peterloo) and its dispersion, the Six Acts, the resumption of cash payments, the Bullion Committee and the Bill of 1819
Chapter V — (not confirmed in the text)
Chapter VI — History of France from the Coup d’État of September 5, 1816, to the Creation of Peers in 1819 — the democratic basis of the elective franchise after the coup, the elections of 1815 and 1816, the Law of Elections of February 1817, the state of parties in the Chamber of Deputies, the laws on personal freedom and the liberty of the press, the great distress in France in the winter of 1816–17
Chapter VII — Affairs of Spain from the Revolution of 1820 to the French Invasion of 1823 — the revolution at Madrid, the King accepts the Constitution, the establishment of clubs and revolutionary measures, the meeting of the Cortes, the counter-revolution, the French expedition of 1823 under the Duc d’Angoulême, the restoration of Ferdinand’s absolute authority
Chapter VIII — Russia under Alexander I (1820–1825) — the conspiracy against the Emperor, the death of Alexander, the contest between Constantine and Nicholas, Nicholas mounts the throne in 1825, the Decembrist revolt and its suppression
Chapter IX — The Resumption of Cash Payments and the Currency Question — the dangers of an inconvertible paper currency, the standard of value, the effects of the Bill of 1819, the great prosperity of England in 1818–19, the disastrous contraction of the currency, its effects on prices and disaffection in the country
Chapter X — Affairs of France (1820–1822) — the Law of Septenniality, the law for the reduction of interest on the national debt, the rise and fall of M. de Chateaubriand, the death of Louis XVIII, his character, the state of France after the Spanish expedition
Chapter XI — Affairs of France (1822–1824) — the Carbonari conspiracy, the abortive conspiracy at Béfort, Berton’s conspiracy at Thouars, the conspiracy at La Rochelle and the execution of the four sergeants, the budget of 1822, the elections and the state of public opinion

Note on the text: The OCR is at times garbled, especially on the title page and running headers. The chapter numbers in the main text are drawn from the original’s running heads and Contents.

sources/alison-history-of-europe-vol2.title: Alison — History of Europe, Vol. II: From the Fall of Napoleon (1823–1831)
sources/alison-history-of-europe-vol2.content:
Alison — History of Europe, Vol. II: From the Fall of Napoleon (1823–1831)
Sir Archibald Alison (1792–1867) — History of Europe from the Fall of Napoleon in MDCCCXV to the Accession of Louis Napoleon in MDCCCLII. Vol. II. — Harper & Brothers, New York, 1859.
The second volume of Alison’s multi-volume history, covering European affairs from the Greek Revolution through the Polish Revolution of 1830–31. The volume opens with an extended survey of Asia Minor, Greece, and Turkey under Ottoman rule before turning to the Greek War of Independence, the Battle of Navarino, and the establishment of the Greek kingdom. It then treats France under Charles X through the Revolution of 1830, English domestic history from the death of Lord Londonderry (1822) through the Reform Bill crisis of 1831–32, and closes with the Polish Revolution and its suppression by Russia.
The text is approximately 500 pages, extracted from the University of Chicago library copy.
Content Summary

Chapter XIII — Asia Minor and Greece: Their Social, Political, and Statistical State — Turkey — a comprehensive survey of the Turkish Empire at the close of the Napoleonic wars: the variety of races under Ottoman dominion, the Turkish system of government, the condition of the Christian subjects, statistics of population and revenue, the military forces of Turkey, the Janizaries, the Caucasus as a defensive barrier, Constantinople and its strategic position, and the long contest between Russia and Turkey for influence in the East
Chapter XIV — Greek Revolution — Battle of Navarino — Establishment of Greek Independence — the elements of Greek national feeling, the Hetairist conspiracy, the insurrection in Wallachia under Ipsilanti, the outbreak in Greece proper and the islands, the Turkish reprisals and massacre of the Patriarch, the naval successes of the Greeks, the struggle in the Morea, the siege of Tripolitza and its storm, the intervention of the European powers, the destruction of the Turkish-Egyptian fleet at Navarino, and the establishment of an independent Greek kingdom
Chapter XV — Russia and Turkey, from the Accession of Nicholas in 1825, to the Peace of Adrianople in 1830 — the accession of the Emperor Nicholas and the Decembrist revolt, the rupture with Persia and the Russian victories, the renewed war with Turkey, the campaign of 1828 and the siege of Varna, the campaign of 1829 and the Russian advance to Adrianople, the Treaty of Adrianople and its terms
Chapter XVI — France from the Death of Louis XVIII to the Accession of the Polignac Administration — the character of Charles X on his accession, the abolition of the press censorship, the election of 1824 and the growing liberal opposition, the fall of Villele, the ministry of Martignac and its reforms, the formation of the Polignac ministry
Chapter XVII — France from the Accession of the Polignac Ministry to the Fall of Charles X — the character and policies of Prince Polignac, the extreme liberal opposition and Lafayette’s journey, the conflict over the Charter, the Royal Ordinances of July 1830, the outbreak of revolution in Paris, the three days (27–29 July), the abdication of Charles X, and the accession of Louis Philippe
Chapter XVIII — Literature of France During and After the Restoration — the effect of the Revolution on French literature, the romantic school and its pernicious tendencies, Chateaubriand, Madame de Staël, the historians (Thierry, Barante, Thiers, Guizot, Mignet), the poets (Lamartine, Hugo, Béranger), and the general character of French intellectual life under the Restoration
Chapter XIX — Domestic History of England, from the Death of Lord Londonderry in 1822 to the Monetary Crisis in December, 1825 — the state of English currency and trade after the resumption of cash payments, the effects of the South American revolution on British commerce, the speculative mania of 1824–25, the expansion of the currency through country banks, the crash of December 1825 and the run on the Bank of England
Chapter XX — Ireland from 1822 to the Monetary Crisis of December, 1825 — the condition of the Irish peasantry, statistics of Irish poverty, the ruinous effects of landlord power, the redundant population, the Catholic Association, the rise of O’Connell and the demand for Catholic emancipation
Chapter XXI — British Empire from the Monetary Crisis of December, 1825, to the Emancipation of the Catholics in March, 1829 — the depression and rioting of 1826, the relief bill for the poor, the crisis in agriculture, the question of the currency, the progress of the Catholic claims, the formation of the Wellington ministry, the Clare election and the crisis of 1828–29, the final passage of the Catholic Relief Bill
Chapter XXII — Domestic History of England from the Passing of the Catholic Relief Bill in 1829, to the Fall of the Wellington Administration in 1830 — the interval between emancipation and the Reform Bill, the want of representation for the commercial towns, the progress of the reform agitation, the death of George IV and the accession of William IV, the general election of 1830, the fall of Wellington
Chapter XXIII — Domestic History of England from the Fall of the Wellington Administration in 1829, to the Passing of the Reform Bill in 1832 — the formation of Earl Grey’s ministry, the introduction of the Reform Bill, the long parliamentary struggle, the rejection of the bill by the House of Lords, the agitation in the country, the creation of peers, the final passage of the Reform Bill
Chapter XXIV — France and Europe from the Accession of Louis Philippe in 1830, to the Overthrow of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the Same Year — the new French monarchy and the European powers, the Belgian revolution, the breach with Holland, the London Conference, the establishment of Belgian independence
Chapter XXV — France from the Overthrow of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in October, 1830, to the Abolition of the Hereditary Peerage in September, 1831 — the trial of the late ministers, the riots in Paris, the disturbances at the funeral of the Prince of Condé, the abolition of the hereditary peerage, the elections and the consolidation of the July Monarchy
Chapter XXVI — Polish Revolution and War, from its Commencement in November, 1830, to its Termination in September, 1831 — the causes of the Polish insurrection, the outbreak in Warsaw, the dictatorship of Chlopicki, the campaign against the Russians, the battle of Ostrolenka, the storming of Warsaw by Paskevich, the suppression of the revolution and the end of Polish autonomy

Note on the text: The OCR is at times garbled, particularly on the title page and running headers. Chapter numbering runs XIII–XXVI, continuing from Vol. I.

sources/alison-history-of-europe-vol3.title: Alison — History of Europe, Vol. III: From the Fall of Napoleon (1831–1842)
sources/alison-history-of-europe-vol3.content:
Alison — History of Europe, Vol. III: From the Fall of Napoleon (1831–1842)
Sir Archibald Alison (1792–1867) — History of Europe from the Fall of Napoleon in MDCCCXV to the Accession of Louis Napoleon in MDCCCLII. Vol. III. — Harper & Brothers, New York, 1871.
The third volume of Alison’s history, covering European affairs from the early 1830s through the opening of the 1840s. It opens with a detailed constitutional history of Germany from the end of the War of Liberation, then treats France under the July Monarchy, the domestic history of England from the Reform Bill through the early years of Queen Victoria, the Eastern Question (Mehemet Ali and the Treaty of 1841), and closes with the history of British India from the Mahratta War to the Afghan disaster of 1842.
The text is approximately 480 pages, extracted from the Rutgers University library copy. Chapters XXVII–XL continue the numbering from Vols. I and II.
Content Summary

Chapter XXVII — Constitutional History of Germany, from the Termination of the War of Liberation in 1814 to the Great Convulsions of — the German Confederacy after the Peace, its military forces and material prosperity, the promise of constitutional government and its delay, the influence of the Spanish and Italian revolutions, the assassination of Kotzebue and the repressive measures of Metternich, the Final Act of Confederation, the Zollverein, the religious movement of 1845, and the convocation of the general Diet in 1847
Chapter XXVIII — Literature of Germany in the First Half of the Nineteenth Century — the romantic character of German literature, Lessing and Winckelmann, Wieland, Goethe and Faust, Schiller, the philosophical writers (Kant, Fichte, Hegel, Schelling), the historians (Niebuhr, Müller, Schlosser, Heeren), and the influence of German literature on European thought
Chapter XXIX — France from the Extinction of the Hereditary Peerage in December, 1831, to the Establishment of Military Government by the Suppression of the Revolt in the Cloister of St. Meri in June, 1832, and the Treaty with Holland in May, 1833 — the increase of the crown’s power, the social dangers of the government, the republican insurrection in Paris, the suppression of the revolt in the Cloister of St. Meri, the cholera epidemic, the treaty with Holland and the settlement of Belgian affairs
Chapter XXX — France from the Suppression of the Insurrection in the Cloister of St. Meri, in June, 1832, to the Final Establishment of the Government of Louis Philippe by the Elections of June, 1834 — the victory of Louis Philippe over the Royalists and Republicans, force and corruption as the principles of government, the conspiracy of the Rue des Prouvaires, the trial of the republicans, the elections of 1834
Chapter XXXI — Internal History of Great Britain, from the Passing of the Reform Bill in 1832, to the Fall of Earl Grey’s Ministry in the End of 1834 — the dangers of the country after the Reform Bill, the assault on the Duke of Wellington and the king, the immense power of ministers, the question of the Irish Church, the tithe war in Ireland, the fall of Grey and the formation of Melbourne’s ministry
Chapter XXXII — Turkey, Greece, Egypt, and the East, from the Treaty of Adrianople in 1828, to the Treaty of 13th March, 1841 — the revolt of distant provinces and the decay of Eastern states, the weakness of Turkey after Adrianople, Mehemet Ali of Egypt and his policy, the war in Syria, the intervention of the European powers, the Treaty of 1841 and the settlement of the Eastern Question
Chapter XXXIII — France from the Social Establishment of Louis Philippe’s Government in 1834, to the Fall of Count Mole’s Administration in the End of 1837 — the repeated defeats of the Republicans, the opening of the chamber, ministerial changes, the trial of Marshal Ney again, the Fieschi conspiracy and the assassination attempt on the king, the September laws, the fall of Mole
Chapter XXXIV — France from the Capture of Constantine in October, 1837, to the Treaty Regulating the Affairs of the East in July, 1841 — the universal joy at the storming of Constantine in Algeria, the fresh creation of peers, the coalition against the ministry, the elections, the Eastern crisis of 1840, the Treaty of London, the fall of Thiers, the formation of the Guizot-Soult ministry
Chapter XXXV — Internal History of England from the Accession of Sir R. Peel in the End of 1834, to the Fall of his Ministry in April, 1835 — the effect of changes in the currency laws, the leading evils of the currency system, Peel’s accession to power, the Tamworth Manifesto, the financial measures of Peel’s short ministry, the fall of Peel and the return of the Whigs
Chapter XXXVI — Domestic History of England, from the Return of the Whigs to Power in April, 1835, to the Accession of Queen Victoria in June, 1837 — Lord Melbourne’s principles of government, the defeat of ministers at the new elections, the Scotch Burgh Reform Bill, the Government Reform Bill, the Irish Church question, the Tithe Commutation Act, the registration of births and marriages, the decline of the Whig majority, the death of William IV
Chapter XXXVII — England from the Accession of Queen Victoria in June, 1837, to the Resignation of Lord Melbourne in May, 1839 — the extent and prosperity of the British Empire, the Canadian rebellions, Lord Durham’s mission, the question of the paper currency in America and its effects, the commercial crisis of 1837, the Bedchamber question, the resignation of Melbourne and his immediate return
Chapter XXXVIII — England from the Restoration of the Whig Ministry in May, 1839, to their Fall in August, 1841 — the queen’s popularity after her accession, her coronation, her marriage to Prince Albert, the Penny Post, the Chartist movement, the Anti-Corn Law League, the budget and the financial crisis, the general election of 1841, the fall of Melbourne
Chapter XXXIX — India from the Termination of the Mahratta War in 1806, to the Fall of Bhurtpore in 1826 — the universal feeling against foreign aggression and the apparent exception of British India, the advantages and evils of English government in India, the administration of Lord Hastings, the Pindari war, the conquest of the Mahratta states, the Burmese war, the first siege of Bhurtpore
Chapter XL — India from the Fall of Bhurtpore in 1826, to the Afghanistan Disaster in 1842 — the consequences of British triumphs and the reduction of forces, the finances of India under Lord W. Bentinck, the abolition of suttee, the suppression of the Thugs, Lord Auckland’s policy, the Russian advance in Central Asia, the first Afghan war, the occupation of Kabul, the disaster of the retreat, and the British recovery

Note on the text: The OCR is at times garbled, particularly on the title page and running headers. Chapter numbering runs XXVII–XL, continuing from Vols. I and II.

sources/alison-history-of-europe-vol4.title: Alison — History of Europe, Vol. IV: From Peel's Ministry to Louis Napoleon (1841–1851)
sources/alison-history-of-europe-vol4.content:
Alison — History of Europe, Vol. IV: From Peel’s Ministry to Louis Napoleon (1841–1851)
Sir Archibald Alison (1792–1867) — History of Europe from the Fall of Napoleon in MDCCCXV to the Accession of Louis Napoleon in MDCCCLII. Vol. IV. — Harper & Brothers, New York, 1878.
The fourth volume of Alison’s post-Napoleonic history, covering the years from Sir Robert Peel’s accession to power in 1841 through the Revolutions of 1848 and the rise of Louis Napoleon in the early 1850s. The volume treats in parallel the domestic history of England (the Peel administration, the Bank Charter Act, the Corn Law debates, the Repeal of the Navigation Laws), the Revolution of 1848 in France and the rise of the Second Republic, the Italian and German revolutions, the Hungarian war of independence, and the extension of British power in India through the Afghan, Scinde, and Sikh wars.
The text is 716 pages, extracted from the University of Illinois library copy.
Content Summary

Chapter XLI — England from the Accession of Sir R. Peel to Power in November 1841, to the Passing of the Bank Charter Act in June 1844 — the character of Sir Robert Peel, variously represented by his contemporaries; his administrative powers and style of oratory; his views on the currency; the immense difficulties of the country in foreign and domestic affairs; statistical details proving the distress; Peel’s measures for financial and commercial reform; the Bank Charter Act of 1844
Chapter XLII — England from the Bank Charter Act to the Fall of Sir R. Peel’s Government (1844–1846) — (continues the narrative of Peel’s ministry, leading to the free trade crisis)
Chapter XLIII — The Repeal of the Corn Laws — the resignation of Sir R. Peel; the failure of Lord John Russell to form a government; Peel’s restoration; the announcement of the Corn Law repeal in the Times; Peel’s argument in favour of free trade; Mr. Disraeli’s caustic remarks; the passage of the bill; the Duke of Wellington’s speech
Chapter XLIV — The Effects of Free Trade — the consequences of the repeal; the effects of free trade on prices of food, national progress and independence; the necessity of maritime superiority to the existence of Britain
Chapter XLV — Ireland and the Repeal Movement — the state of Ireland after the Union; O’Connell’s agitation; the Repeal Association; the prosecution of O’Connell; the famine of 1845–46; the Encumbered Estates Act
Chapter XLVI — Affairs of France from the Spanish Marriages to the Banquet Campaign (1846–1847) — the Spanish marriages question; the state of parties in France under Louis Philippe; the Reform Banquet agitation; the growing unpopularity of the Guizot ministry
Chapter XLVII — The Revolution of 1848 in France — the revolt in Sicily and the publication of a constitution at Naples; the convulsions in Italy; Lord Palmerston and the Liberal Italian agents; the affairs of Switzerland and the Sonderbund; the progress of democracy in the Swiss cities; in France: the reform banquets, the King’s indecision, the abdication of Louis Philippe, the flight of the royal family, the Duchess of Orleans, the treachery of Lamartine, the proclamation of the Republic
Chapter XLVIII — The Provisional Government and the June Days (1848) — the Provisional Government installed; the national workshops; the insurrection of June; Cavaignac as dictator; the three days of street fighting; the storming of the Pantheon; the murder of General Bréa; the suppression of the rising
Chapter XLIX — From the Fall of Louis Philippe to the Election of Louis Napoleon — the National Assembly; the constitution of the Second Republic; the state of the finances; the increasing conservatism of the electors; agitation in favour of Louis Napoleon; the Presidential election of December 1848
Chapter XLX — India under Lord Ellenborough and Sir H. Hardinge — the Gwalior campaign and the Battle of Maharajpore; the brilliant results of Lord Ellenborough’s administration; his recall; Sir Henry Hardinge as Governor-General; the first Sikh War and the Battles of Moodkee, Ferozeshah, Aliwal, and Sobraon; the Treaty of Lahore
Chapter LI — France from the Election of Louis Napoleon to the Coup d’État (1849–1851) — the Presidency of Louis Napoleon; the expedition to Rome; the fall of the Roman Republic; the conservative reaction; the revision of the constitution; the coup d’état of 2 December 1851
Chapter LII — Italy from the Breaking Out of the Insurrection in January 1848 to the Pacification — the Five Days of Milan; Radetzky’s retreat; Charles Albert’s campaign; the Battle of Novara; the abdication of Charles Albert; the restoration of Austrian authority; the French intervention at Rome; the defeat of the Roman Republic; the fall of Venice
Chapter LIII — Germany, Belgium, and Denmark from the French Revolution of 1848 to the Treaty of Olmütz (1850) — the convulsions in Central Europe; the races of Austria; the Frankfurt Parliament; the Prussian Constitution; the Danish war for the duchies; the Battle of Idstedt; the final settlement of the Danish question
Chapter LIV — Austria and Hungary: the Hungarian War of Independence (1848–1849) — the revolution in Vienna; the Emperor’s flight to Innspruck; the Hungarian Diet; Kossuth and the Hungarian army; the intervention of Russia; the surrender at Világos; the execution of the Hungarian generals
Chapter LV — The Repeal of the Navigation Laws and the State of England (1849–1851) — the arguments for and against repeal; the passage of the bill; its results; the great improvements in agriculture; the completion of the railway system; Mr. Disraeli’s motion for relief to the agriculturists
Chapter LVI — (events of 1850–1851: the Don Pacifico affair, the Ecclesiastical Titles Act, the Great Exhibition)
Chapter LVII — (the consolidation of the Second Empire and the close of the period)

Alison, History of Europe Vol. V (Ch. XXVII–XXXIII, 1831–1837)
Title: History of Europe from the Fall of Napoleon in MDCCCXV to the Accession of Louis Napoleon in MDCCCLII
Author: Sir Archibald Alison, Bart., D.C.L.
Volume: V (chapters XXVII–XXXIII)
Edition: Harper & Brothers, New York, 1874 (printed by William Blackwood and Sons, Edinburgh)
Source: University of Illinois copy (OCLC 310355400)
Overview
This volume covers the period 1831–1837 across Germany, France, Great Britain, and the Eastern Question. It opens with a long constitutional survey of Germany spanning the entire period from 1814 to 1848, includes a chapter on German literature, then moves to France under Louis Philippe (from the abolition of the hereditary peerage through the suppression of the republican and royalist insurrections), the domestic history of Great Britain after the Reform Bill, the Eastern question from the Treaty of Adrianople, and closes with France from 1834 to the fall of Count Molé’s ministry in 1837.
Chapters
Ch. XXVII: Constitutional History of Germany, from the Termination of the War of Liberation in 1814 to the Great Convulsions of 1848
A broad retrospective survey of the German Confederation: the Federal Act, the military forces of the Confederation, the material prosperity and education of the German states, the promise of constitutional government, the delay in fulfilling it, the influence of the Spanish and Italian revolutions of 1819–20, the Carlsbad Decrees, the Supreme Austregal Court, the assassination of Kotzebue, and the progress of constitutional struggles through 1847 up to the eve of the 1848 revolutions.
Ch. XXVIII: Literature of Germany in the First Half of the Nineteenth Century
A survey of German intellectual life: philosophy (Kant, Fichte, Schelling, Hegel), theology (rationalism, Strauss’s Life of Jesus), poetry and drama (Goethe, Schiller, the Romantic school), historiography (Niebuhr, Müller), and the fine arts (Thorwaldsen, Danneker, the Romantic school of painting, German architecture).
Ch. XXIX: France from the Extinction of the Hereditary Peerage in December 1831, to the Establishment of Military Government by the Suppression of the Revolt in the Cloister of St Méri in June 1832, and the Treaty with Holland in May 1833
Covers the struggle between Louis Philippe’s government and the Republican and Royalist (Legitimist) opposition: the abolition of the hereditary peerage, the Lyon insurrections of 1831–32 (the Canuts), the Royalist rising in the Vendée under the Duchesse de Berry, the republican insurrection in the Cloister of St Méri in Paris (June 1832), the death of General Lamarque, the establishment of a state of siege, and the treaty with Holland regarding Belgium.
Ch. XXX: France from the Suppression of the Insurrection in the Cloister of St Méri, in June 1832, to the Final Establishment of the Government of Louis Philippe by the Elections of June 1834
The consolidation of the July Monarchy: the trial and imprisonment of the Duchesse de Berry, the law against secret societies, the formation of the Société des Droits de l’Homme, the April 1834 insurrections in Lyon and Paris (the Rue Transnonain massacre), the subsequent elections that gave Louis Philippe a decisive majority, and the strengthening of the conservative party.
Ch. XXXI: Internal History of Great Britain, from the Passing of the Reform Bill in 1832, to the Fall of Earl Grey’s Ministry in the end of 1834
The political consequences of the Reform Act: the Reformed Parliament, the Irish Coercion Bill and the Church Temporalities Bill, the abolition of colonial slavery (the Emancipation Act of 1833), the Factory Act of 1833, the struggle over the renewal of the Bank Charter, the Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834, the rise of the Conservative party under Peel (the Tamworth Manifesto), and the fall of Grey’s ministry.
Ch. XXXII: Turkey, Greece, Egypt, and the East, from the Treaty of Adrianople in 1828
The Eastern Question: the Treaty of Adrianople (1829), the independence of Greece, the revolt of Mehemet Ali of Egypt against the Porte, the Russian intervention, the Treaty of Unkiar Skelessi (1833), the weakening of the Ottoman Empire, the rivalry of the European powers in the Levant, and the state of the Turkish dominions.
Ch. XXXIII: France from the Social Establishment of Louis Philippe’s Government in 1834, to the Fall of Count Molé’s Administration in the end of 1837
The middle period of the July Monarchy: the Fieschi assassination attempt (1835), the September laws restricting the press, the founding of the Revue des Deux Mondes and the growth of literary opposition, the Spanish civil war (the Carlist War) and French policy toward Spain, the rising of the secret societies, the financial difficulties of the government, the Ministry of Count Molé and its fall in 1837.
