Alison, History of Europe Vol. VI (Ch. XXXIV–XL, 1806–1842)
Title: History of Europe from the Fall of Napoleon in MDCCCXV to the Accession of Louis Napoleon in MDCCCLII
Author: Sir Archibald Alison, Bart., D.C.L.
Volume: VI (chapters XXXIV–XL)
Edition: William Blackwood and Sons, Edinburgh and London, 1857
Source: University of Illinois copy (940.9 A14 v.6)
Overview
This volume covers the period 1834–1842 in England and France, with two retrospective chapters on India reaching back to 1806. Its main focus is the final crisis of the Whig ascendancy in England and the consolidation of Louis Philippe’s government in France, set against the background of the Eastern Question, Canada, and the Chartist movement at home. Chapters XXXIV and XXXV follow the Eastern crisis and the fall of the Thiers ministry in France; Chapters XXXV–XXXVIII trace the abortive Peel ministry of 1834–35, the return of the Whigs under Melbourne, the accession of Queen Victoria, and the eventual fall of the Whig ministry in 1841; Chapters XXXIX and XL give a detailed retrospective of British India from the Mahratta War to the Afghanistan disaster of 1842.
Chapters
Ch. XXXIV (§1–93): France from the Capture of Constantine in October 1837, to the Treaty Regulating the Affairs of the East in July 1841
France under the second Molé ministry and the crisis of the Eastern Question: the universal joy at the storming of Constantine, the creation of peers, the rise of M. Arago as a political leader, the rapid growth of railway companies and the accompanying speculation mania, the scandalous corruption in public life, the death and character of Talleyrand, Hubert’s conspiracy, Louis Napoleon’s departure from Switzerland for England, the evacuation of Ancona, the Belgian question and the failure of the Bank of Brussels, differences with Mexico, the coalition against Molé and dissolution of the Chambers, the ministerial crisis and attempt to form a Liberal administration, the Société des Familles and its transformation into the Société des Saisons, the insurrection of 12 May 1839, the second ministry of Marshal Soult, the character of M. Villemain, the trial and conviction of Barbès and the conspirators, the progress of the Napoleon party, the debate on the affairs of the East, Marshal Soult’s measures in the Levant, the insurrection in Africa, the agitation for lowering the suffrage, the marriage and dotation of the Duc de Nemours, M. Thiers’ second ministry, the project for removing Napoleon’s remains to Paris, Louis Napoleon’s expedition to Boulogne, his trial and imprisonment, and the Treaty of London (July 1841) regulating the Eastern question.
Ch. XXXV (§94–end): Internal History of England from the Accession of Sir R. Peel in the End of 1834, to the Fall of His Ministry in April 1835
The brief first Peel administration: the indignation in France on hearing of the Eastern treaty, the fortifications of Paris, M. Thiers’ downfall, the new ministry under Soult and Guizot, the King’s speech at the opening of the Chamber, the continuation of the fortifications, Marshal Soult’s military view, the alarming state of the French finances, the Treaty of 13 February 1841 regarding the East, and reflections on the Eastern question. Then back to England: Peel’s accession, the divisions on the Address, the King’s reception of the Address as amended, the exasperation of the Whigs at Peel not resigning, the motion for repeal of the malt-tax, the great diminution in beer consumption, the debate on Lord Londonderry’s appointment as ambassador to St Petersburg, Lord Londonderry’s declinature, Peel’s remedial measures, the attack on Government on the Irish Church question, Lord John Russell’s motion regarding the Irish Church, the division and resignation of Sir R. Peel, the return of Lord Melbourne, the importance of Peel’s short administration in averting the danger of revolution, its pernicious effects on Ireland, the rise of Peel in general estimation, and the merits of Russell’s proposal on the Irish Church.
Ch. XXXVI (§1–93): Domestic History of England, from the Return of the Whigs to Power in April 1835, to the Accession of Queen Victoria in June 1837
The second Melbourne ministry: the great though gradual creation of Whig peers, the state of the West Indies, the commencement of the troubles in Canada, the opening of Parliament and the King’s speech, the state of the Irish corporations, the Government’s plan for Irish reform, the Irish Church Bill passed in the Commons and thrown out in the Lords, the increased agitation against the House of Lords, the re-establishment of the Catholic Association, the report recommending a Poor Law in Ireland and Mr Nicholls’ Report with its awful revelations, the English Tithe Bill and the registration of births, marriages, and deaths, the Agricultural Distress Committee, the Budget, the deplorable weakness of the navy and army, Lord Dudley Stuart’s speech on Russian power, the increasing discontents of Canada and the settlement of the upper province, the violent proceedings of the Assembly in Lower Canada, the public meetings and banquets in London and Leeds, the Glasgow banquet to Sir R. Peel, the opening of Parliament, the Irish Corporations Bill, the Poor Law Bill, and the statistics of Irish destitution.
Ch. XXXVII (§1–116): England from the Accession of Queen Victoria in June 1837, to the Resignation of Lord Melbourne in May 1839
The beginning of the Victorian era: the death of William IV, the accession of Queen Victoria, the separation of Hanover and Great Britain, the death of Mrs Fitzherbert, the character of William IV, the effect of the change of ministry and dissolution, the commercial distress of the period, the excess of imports over exports, the calamitous harvests of 1838 and 1839, the immense distress in the country, the contraction of the currency, the rise of interest, the stoppage of credit, the general terror in Great Britain and America at the export of gold, the panic in Belgium and France, the decline of prices, the effect of these disasters on the new Poor Law Act, the great cotton-spinners’ strike of 1837 and its break-up, the rise of trades-unions and strikes, the origins of Chartism and the six points of the Charter, the Chartist riot in the Bull Ring in Birmingham, the Duke of Wellington’s declaration on the subject. Then the Canadian rebellion: the commencement of the insurrection, Colonel Wetherell at St Charles, Sir John Colborne at St Eustache, the rebellion in Upper Canada, the burning of the Caroline by Colonel M’Nab, Lord Durham’s mission and his valuable report, the fresh breaking-out of the rebellion, the defeat of the American sympathisers, the state trials, the execution of the leading American sympathisers, and the vast growth of Canada after 1841.
Ch. XXXVIII (§1–end): England from the Restoration of the Whig Ministry in May 1839 to Their Fall in August 1841
The final phase of the Melbourne government: the Bedchamber Question, Sir R. Peel being sent for and forming the programme of a government, the difficulty about the household appointments causing the negotiation to be broken off, the observations of Peel, Melbourne, and the Duke of Wellington, the election of a Speaker, the second Jamaica Bill, Lord Palmerston’s reply, the vote of want of confidence, the dissolution of Parliament, the immense excitement in the country, the result of the elections decidedly in favour of the Tories, the defeat of Ministers in both Houses and their resignation, reflections on the fall of the Whigs, the argument that the Reform Bill had destroyed the supremacy of England, and the role of Catholic ascendancy in Ireland and the passion for self-government.
Ch. XXXIX (§1–73): India from the Termination of the Mahratta War in 1806, to the Fall of Bhurtpore in 1826
A retrospective on British India: the discreditable terms of the treaty to the English Government, the death of Lord Cornwallis and the accession of Sir George Barlow, the mutiny at Vellore, Lord Minto’s administration, Lord Moira’s administration, the Ghoorka War, early disasters of the campaign, General Ochterlony’s successes, the conclusion of peace with the Ghoorkas, the causes of the Pindarree War, Lord Hastings’ great preparations and the battle of Kirkee, the second check of the Peishwa, the ravages of the cholera in Lord Hastings’ army, the victory of Hastings and termination of the war, reflections on Lord Hastings’ government of India, the Amherst administration and the war with Burmah, the irruption of the Mughs, the difficulties of the war, the taking of Rangoon, the slow progress and sickness of the British, the reverses sustained, the sufferings of the British in Rangoon, the decisive victories, the storming of Arracan, the advance towards the Burmese capital and the submission of the Burmese, the renewal of hostilities and final defeat, the conclusion of peace, and reflections on the Burmese and Pindarree wars.
Ch. XL (§1–131): India from the Fall of Bhurtpore in 1826, to the Afghanistan Disaster in 1842
The Afghan war: the siege of Herat by the Persians, the raising of the siege by English interference, the great effects of the raising of the siege in Asia and the defeat of Russia, the preparations for the Afghanistan expedition, the treaty for the restoration of Shah Soojah, the magnificent displays in the Punjab, the commencement of the march, the passage of the Indus and the Bolan Pass, the reception of Shah Soojah in Candahar, the passage of the Kyber by Colonel Wade’s force, the movement towards Cabul, the description of Ghuznee and plans of Dost Mahommed, the assault and capture of Ghuznee, the flight of Dost Mahommed, the entry of the British into Cabul, the plans of Lord Auckland for the future, the attack on Khelat, the pleasant quarters of the troops in Cabul, the growing difficulties of the British position, the progress of the Douranee insurrection, the state of affairs at Cabul, the infatuation of the defensive arrangements, the breaking out of the insurrection and the death of Burnes, the loss of the Commissariat Fort, the actions on the heights, the call for troops from Jellalabad and Candahar, the destruction of the Ghoorka regiment in the Kohistan, the action of 23 November and the total defeat of the British, the negotiations and the arrival of Akbar Khan, the capitulation, Sir W. Macnaghten’s secret negotiation with Akbar Khan and his murder, the conclusion of the treaty, the commencement of the retreat, the increasing horrors of the march, the passage of the Coord Cabul defile, the ascent of the Coord Cabul plateau, and the surrender of the ladies.

Notes

This is a Blackwood 1857 edition, not the Harper edition of the other volumes in the set. The volume numbering (VI) and chapter numbering (XXXIV–XL) are consistent with the Harper edition, but the page layout, pagination, and type-setting differ.
Chapter XXXIX is a retrospective on Indian affairs reaching back to 1806, before the nominal starting point of the work (1815).
The volume overlaps chronologically with Vol. VII (Ch. XLI–XLVII, 1841–1848) at the 1841–42 boundary, and with Vol. V (Ch. XXVII–XXXIII, 1831–1837) at the 1834–37 boundary.

Alison, History of Europe Vol. VII (Ch. XLI–XLVII, 1841–1848)
Title: History of Europe from the Fall of Napoleon in MDCCCXV to the Accession of Louis Napoleon in MDCCCLII
Author: Sir Archibald Alison, Bart.
Volume: VII (chapters XLI–XLVII)
Edition: William Blackwood and Sons, Edinburgh and London, MDCCCLVIII (1858)
Source: University of Illinois copy (OCLC 310355400)
Overview
This volume covers the period 1841–1848, focusing primarily on the second Peel ministry and the crisis of the 1840s in England — the Bank Charter Act, the Corn Law repeal, the railway mania, the Chartist crisis — alongside France from the Eastern crisis of 1841 through the fall of Louis Philippe in the February Revolution of 1848. Also includes a detailed account of French Algeria from the revolt of Abd-el-Kader, and a survey of European external affairs in the final years of the July Monarchy.
Chapters
Ch. XLI: England from the Accession of Sir R. Peel to Power in November 1841, to the Passing of the Bank Charter Act in June 1844
Peel’s character as a statesman and orator, his administrative abilities, the formation of the new ministry, the immense difficulties of the country in foreign and internal affairs (Chartist agitation, manufacturing distress, the riots of 1842 in England and Scotland, the Anti-Corn-Law League), Peel’s plan for financial reform, the opening of Parliament in 1842, the Income Tax, the Bank Charter Act of 1844.
Ch. XLII: England, from the Passing of the Bank Charter Act in 1844, to the Fall of Sir R. Peel’s Ministry in June 1846
The currency and banking controversies following the 1844 Act, the railway speculation mania of 1845, the Irish potato famine of 1845–46, the split in the Conservative party over the Corn Laws, Peel’s conversion to Free Trade, the repeal of the Corn Laws in June 1846, and Peel’s resignation.
Ch. XLIII: England, from the Introduction of Free Trade and Fall of Sir R. Peel in June 1846, to the Suppression of the Chartist Insurrection in April 1848
The financial crisis of 1847 (the railway collapse and commercial panic), the rise in cotton prices from the American crash of 1839, the distress in Ireland and the Poor Law extension, the Chartist revival, the great Kennington Common demonstration and its suppression, the weakness of Britain’s military preparations, and the resilience of representative institutions during the Continental revolutions.
Ch. XLIV: France from the Treaty of February 13, 1841, to the Death of the Duke of Orleans in July 1843
France under the Guizot ministry: the prosperous condition of France in 1841, the Treaty of London (the Straits Convention), the debates on the fortification of Paris, the first Free Trade proposals in France (Loi des Douanes), the Spanish marriages question, the trial of the Legitimist conspiracy, the progress of commercial and colonial interests (Algeria, the right of search controversy, the Pritchard affair in Tahiti), and the sudden death of the Duke of Orleans in 1842, which removed the most popular figure of the Orleanist dynasty.
Ch. XLV: Wars of the French in Algeria from the Revolt under Abd-el-Kader in 1840 to the Fall of Louis Philippe in 1848
The geography of Algeria (the Tel, the mountains, the desert), the early French occupation under General Bugeaud, the struggle with the Emir Abd-el-Kader, his guerrilla tactics, the French campaigns of scorched earth (razzias), the construction of forts and the bureaux arabes, the treaty of Tafna (1837) and its rupture, the submission of the Arab tribes, Abd-el-Kader’s flight to Morocco, and the final pacification of Algeria.
Ch. XLVI: External Affairs of France and Europe, from the Death of the Duke of Orleans in 1843, to the Revolution of 1848
French foreign policy under Guizot: the entente cordiale with England and its gradual deterioration, the Spanish marriages crisis (1846), the Swiss Sonderbund war and the federalist struggle in the Swiss Confederation, the abortive Polish rising in Gallicia (1846), the Prussian reform of agrarian law in Posen, the French expeditions in the Pacific (Tahiti, the Marquesas), and the formation of a conservative European league against the revolutionary movement.
Ch. XLVII: France from the Middle of 1847 to the Fall of Louis Philippe in February 1848
The alarming state of France in 1847: corruption scandals (Teste-Cubières affair), the disintegration of the Guizot ministry, the Reform Banquet campaign, the paralysis of the National Guard, the death of the Duchess of Orleans, the riots of 22–24 February 1848, the abdication of Louis Philippe, the flight of the royal family, the Duchess of Orleans’s attempt to secure the regency, the formation of the Provisional Government, and the establishment of the Second Republic.

sources/alison-history-of-europe-vol8.title: Alison — History of Europe, Vol. VIII: The Chinese War, Indian Conquests, and the Close of the Period (1841–1852)
sources/alison-history-of-europe-vol8.content:
Alison — History of Europe, Vol. VIII: The Chinese War, Indian Conquests, and the Close of the Period (1841–1852)
Sir Archibald Alison (1792–1867) — History of Europe from the Fall of Napoleon in MDCCCXV to the Accession of Louis Napoleon in MDCCCLII. Vol. VIII. — William Blackwood and Sons, Edinburgh and London, 1859.
The eighth volume of Alison’s post-Napoleonic history, covering the later years of the period from the First Opium War with China (1841–1842) through the great Indian campaigns of the 1840s — the Afghan disaster and its avenging, the conquest of Scinde under Sir Charles Napier, the first and second Sikh wars, and the annexation of the Punjab — and then turning to Europe for the Revolutions of 1848 and their aftermath in France, Italy, Germany, Austria, and Hungary. The volume closes with the consolidation of the Second French Empire under Louis Napoleon.
The text is 950 pages, extracted from a copy of the Edinburgh edition by Blackwood.
Content Summary

Chapter XLVIII — The Chinese War and Indian History, from the Afghanistan Disaster in 1841 to the General Pacification of the East in 1842 — a description of China: its extent, population, government, and military forces; the origins of the First Opium War; the British operations on the coast; the storming of the forts; the captures of Amoy, Chusan, Chinghae, Ningpo, and Chapoo; the forcing of the Yang-tze-Kiang river; the storming of Chin-Kiang-foo; the British arrival before Nankin; the Treaty of Nanking
Chapter XLIX — Afghanistan, Scinde, and the Sikh Wars (1842–1846) — the murder of Shah Soojah; the advance of Pollock and Nott to Cabul; the victory at Jugdulluck; the spectacle of the bones of the former army; the operations of Nott’s troops against Ghuznee; the Battle of Meanee and Napier’s conquest of Scinde; the Battle of Hyderabad; the annexation of Scinde; the first Sikh War: Mudkee, Ferozeshah, Aliwal, Sobraon; the Treaty of Lahore
Chapter L — India under Lord Hardinge and Lord Dalhousie (1845–1852) — the great works undertaken by Lord Dalhousie; the second Burmese War and the capture of Rangoon; the annexation of Oude; the fall of the East India Company; the picture of the Indian empire at this period; the danger of direct government of India by Britain
Chapter LI — France from the Election of Louis Napoleon to the Coup d’État (1849–1851) — the Presidency of Louis Napoleon; the expedition to Rome; the fall of the Roman Republic; the Law of 31 May 1850 restricting the suffrage; the revision of the constitution; the coup d’état of 2 December 1851; the consolidation of power
Chapter LII — Italy from the Breaking Out of the Insurrection in January 1848 to the Pacification — the Five Days of Milan; Radetzky’s retreat behind the Adige; the campaign of Charles Albert; the Battle of Custozza; the armistice; the murder of Rossi; the flight of the Pope; the Roman Republic; the renewal of the war; the Battle of Novara; the abdication of Charles Albert; the French attack on Rome; the fall of the Roman Republic; the submission of Sicily; the restoration of the old governments
Chapter LIII — Germany, Belgium, and Denmark from the French Revolution of 1848 to the Treaty of Olmütz in 1850 — the agitated state of Central Europe; the races of Austria; the state of Prussia; the great prosperity of Germany during the peace; the Frankfurt Parliament; the election of the Grand-Duke John as Regent; the Polish revolt; the new Constitution of Prussia; the dissolution of the Assembly; the Danish war for the Duchies; the Battle of Idstedt; the Treaty of Olmütz
Chapter LIV — Austria and Hungary from the Revolution to the Pacification (1848–1849) — the revolution in Vienna; the flight of the Emperor to Innspruck; the Hungarian Diet; Kossuth and the Hungarian army; the fidelity of the Croatians under Jellachich; the conquest of Vienna by Windischgrätz; the intervention of Russia; the capitulation at Világos; the execution of the Hungarian generals; the restoration of order
Chapter LV — The Repeal of the Navigation Laws and the English Reaction (1849–1850) — the arguments for and against the repeal; the passage of the bill; its results; the state of English agriculture; the effects of free trade; the railway system; the political consequences
Chapter LVI — Events of 1850–1851: Don Pacifico, the Ecclesiastical Titles Act, and the Great Exhibition — the Don Pacifico affair and Lord Palmerston’s foreign policy; the debate on Greece; the Ecclesiastical Titles Act and the “papal aggression”; the Great Exhibition of 1851 in Hyde Park; the state of parties
Chapter LVII — The Coup d’État of 1851 and the Consolidation of the Second Empire — the events of 2 December 1851; the dissolution of the Assembly; the arrest of the deputies; the resistance of the barricades; the plebiscite; the establishment of the Second Empire; the character and prospects of the new régime

sources/alison-history-of-french-revolut.title: Alison — History of the French Revolution, Vol. II: From the Renewal of the War (1799) to the Peace of Tilsit (1807)
sources/alison-history-of-french-revolut.content:
Alison — History of the French Revolution, Vol. II: From the Renewal of the War (1799) to the Peace of Tilsit (1807)
Sir Archibald Alison (1792–1867) — History of Europe from the Commencement of the French Revolution in 1789 to the Restoration of the Bourbons in 1815. Vol. II. — Harper & Brothers, New York, 1875.
The second volume of Alison’s earlier work on the Revolutionary and Napoleonic period. This volume covers the second coalition against France, the campaigns of 1799 in Italy and Switzerland, the rise of Napoleon as First Consul, the Peace of Amiens, the renewal of war with England, and the great campaigns of the Third and Fourth Coalitions — Ulm, Austerlitz, Jena, Eylau, and Friedland. The volume ends with the Peace of Tilsit and the reconstruction of society in France under the Consulate and Empire.
The text is 616 pages, extracted from an American edition published by Harper & Brothers.
Note: Though this volume covers events before 1815, it is included in the United Kingdom 1800–1865 wiki because it provides the necessary military and diplomatic background for Alison’s later History of Europe from the Fall of Napoleon, whose subsequent volumes treat British affairs after 1815.
Content Summary

Chapter XXVIII — From the Renewal of the War to the Battle of the Trebbia (1799) — the alliance of England, Austria, and Russia against France; the internal state and measures of England; the forces of the opposing parties on the Continent; the Battle of Stockach; the dissolution of the Congress of Rastadt; operations in Italy; Suwarrow’s campaign and the Battle of the Trebbia
Chapter XXIX — From the Battle of the Trebbia to the Landing of Bonaparte at Fréjus (1799) — Massena’s operations in Switzerland; the Battle of Zurich; the Russian disaster in the Grisons; the English expedition to the Helder; the Battle of Bergen; the capitulation of the Russian army; Bonaparte’s return from Egypt
Chapter XXX — The Consulate: from the 18th Brumaire to the Battle of Marengo (1799–1800) — the Revolution of the 18th Brumaire; the Constitution of the Year VIII; Bonaparte as First Consul; the campaign of 1800; the crossing of the Alps; the Battle of Marengo; Moreau’s campaign and the Battle of Hohenlinden; the Peace of Lunéville
Chapter XXXI — England and the Armed Neutrality (1800–1801) — the rupture of the Peace of Amiens preliminaries; the Armed Neutrality of the North; the Battle of Copenhagen under Nelson; the death of Paul I; the dissolution of the Northern Confederacy
Chapter XXXII — The Peace of Amiens and the Internal Government of France (1801–1802) — the negotiations; the Treaty of Amiens; the state of Europe after the peace; Bonaparte’s internal reforms; the Code Napoléon; the Concordat with the Papacy; the Legion of Honour
Chapter XXXIII — The Renewal of War (1803) — the rupture of the Peace of Amiens; the causes of the quarrel; the seizure of Hanover by the French; the preparations for the invasion of England; the Boulogne flotilla; Pitt’s return to power
Chapter XXXIV — The Third Coalition and the Campaign of Ulm (1805) — the formation of the Third Coalition between England, Austria, Russia, and Sweden; the campaign in Bavaria; the capitulation of Ulm; Nelson’s pursuit of Villeneuve; the Battle of Trafalgar and the death of Nelson; the Battle of Austerlitz; the Treaty of Pressburg; the death of Pitt
Chapter XXXV — Reconstruction of Society in France by Napoleon (1802–1805) — measures of the First Consul to restore order; the Infernal Machine and the severity against the Jacobins; the establishment of religion; the consulship for life; the creation of the Empire; the civil and military institutions of the new reign
Chapter XXXVI — (the internal condition of England during the war)
Chapter XXXVII — The Fourth Coalition and the Campaign of Jena (1806) — the formation of the Fourth Coalition; Prussia’s entry into the war; the campaign in Saxony; the Battle of Jena; the destruction of the Prussian army; Napoleon’s entry into Berlin; the Berlin Decrees
Chapter XXXVIII — The Polish Campaign and the Battle of Eylau (1806–1807) — the war in Poland; the Battle of Eylau; the winter campaign; the siege of Danzig
Chapter XXXIX — The Campaign of Friedland and the Peace of Tilsit (1807) — the summer campaign of 1807; the Battle of Friedland; the meeting of Napoleon and Alexander at Tilsit; the Treaty of Tilsit; the division of Europe
Chapters XL–XLVIII — (continuation covering the Continental System, the Peninsular War, Austria 1809, the Russian campaign of 1812, the War of Liberation, the fall of Napoleon, and the Restoration of the Bourbons in 1815)

sources/babbage-decline-of-science.title: Babbage — Reflections on the Decline of Science in England
sources/babbage-decline-of-science.content:
Babbage — Reflections on the Decline of Science in England
Charles Babbage (1791–1871) — Reflections on the Decline of Science in England, and on Some of Its Causes. — London, 1830. Project Gutenberg eBook #1216.
Charles Babbage, the mathematician and inventor of the Difference Engine, argues that British science is in decline relative to continental Europe. He criticises the Royal Society, attacks its management, and calls for government support of scientific research.
The text is 5,727 lines, extracted from the Project Gutenberg EPUB.
Content Summary

Introduction — the state of English science compared to France, Germany, and Italy
The Royal Society — criticism of its administration, the abuse of fellowship elections, the neglect of science
The learned societies — the state of the Astronomical Society, the Geological Society, etc.
The universities — Oxford and Cambridge’s neglect of science
Government support — the lack of public patronage for science compared to the Continent
The Board of Longitude and the reform of the Greenwich Observatory
The Congress of Philosophers at Berlin (1828) — a contrast with the English system
Appendices — statistical tables of scientific publications, lists of foreign members of the Royal Society

sources/buller-responsible-government-co.title: Buller — Responsible Government for Colonies (1840)
sources/buller-responsible-government-co.content:
Buller — Responsible Government for Colonies (1840)
Charles Buller (1806–1848) — Responsible Government for Colonies. — James Ridgway, Piccadilly, London, 1840.
Charles Buller, a British MP and reformer who had served as secretary to Lord Durham during his 1838 mission to Canada, expounds and defends the doctrine of responsible government for the British colonies — the principle that colonial executive councils should command the confidence of the elected assembly, in the same manner as the British cabinet is responsible to the House of Commons. The work first appeared as a series of articles in the Colonial Gazette in December 1839–February 1840, and is here collected, revised, and published in book form. It is the most sustained contemporary argument for applying the Westminster model of cabinet government to the colonies, and was written in direct support of Lord Durham’s recommendations in his famous Report on the Affairs of British North America (1839).
The text is 3,910 lines (132 KB), extracted from the McGill University Library copy via Internet Archive _djvu.txt OCR.
Content Summary


Advertisement — explains the origins of the work in a series of newspaper articles written week by week for the Colonial Gazette (December 1839–February 1840) to elucidate and apply a doctrine of Lord Durham’s Report that had been misunderstood in party politics; received with favour in British America and the West Indies.


Chapter I — Introductory — the paradox that while the British public recognise the value of colonies, Parliament and Government treat them as subjects of difficulty and annoyance; colonial discontent is constant whether colonies are under arbitrary rule or representative institutions; representative bodies appear to become only more efficient organs of discontent; the prevailing notion that representative government is a privilege to be granted only when a colony is “ripe” for it, and the scepticism bred by the fact that representative institutions seem to increase disorder.


Chapter II — What “Responsible Government” Is, and What It Is Not — the term has been wilfully misrepresented by those whose emoluments depend on the existing system; it is falsely equated with an elective executive on the American model; Buller defines it as requiring that the colonial executive should be composed of persons enjoying the confidence of the majority in the representative assembly, with the governor selecting his advisers accordingly; it is the English constitution transplanted, not republicanism.


Chapter III — Colonial Dependence Consistent with Responsible Administration — responsible government is not incompatible with imperial supremacy; there are certain affairs — foreign relations, war and peace, the regulation of trade, disposal of public lands — on which the Imperial Government must have the final voice; but these reserved powers are compatible with full local responsibility in internal affairs; the American Revolution is adduced as proof that attempting to govern colonies without local responsibility leads to separation.


Chapter IV — Chronic Anarchy of Irresponsible Colonial Government — the existing system produces incessant conflict between the legislative and executive branches; the local parties vie for power while the real authority resides in an irresponsible governor and his clique; the assemblies use the power of supply to wrest control, but this only produces paralysis; the pernicious influence of patronage in maintaining executive power without responsibility; the system works nothing but evil to the colony while giving the Mother Country no real advantage.


Chapter V — Ordinary Objections to Responsible Government — the main objections answered: that it would lead to republicanism (it is merely the English system); that it would weaken the Governor’s authority (it would strengthen it by placing him above party); that it would subject imperial officers to local persecution (they would be protected by imperial reservation of key powers); that the colonies are not fit for it (the North American colonies already possess the intelligence and education for self-government).


Chapter VI — Mr. Mothercountry, of the Colonial Office — a satirical personification of the permanent officials of the Colonial Office in Downing Street, whose steady but irresponsible rule is contrasted with the fleeting tenures of Secretaries and Under-Secretaries of State; the real power in colonial administration lies not with ministers but with the permanent clerks who make decisions in obscurity; the impossibility of forming any real public opinion in England on colonial questions; the apathy of Parliament.


Chapter VII — Mr. Mothercountry’s Faults: The Sighing-Rooms at the Colonial Office — the vices of permanent official rule: arbitrary power exercised at a distance without local knowledge; the reliance on second-hand and one-sided information; the characteristic delays, evasions, and timid conservatism of the office; the “sighing-rooms” as a metaphor for the hopelessness of obtaining redress from Downing Street; the personal cost to colonists who must travel to London and wait endlessly on officials who have no real interest in their affairs.


Chapter VIII — Conclusion — the evils described are those of the system, not of individuals; the permanent officers of the Colonial Department must be men of no ordinary ability to have worked such a system at all; but the only remedy is to bring the influence of public opinion to bear on the Colonial Department; the union of the two Canadas and Lord John Russell’s recent despatches suggest that responsible government is on the eve of being established; Parliament should now reform the constitution and practice of the Colonial Office itself.

sources/carey-credit-system.title: Carey — The Credit System in France, Great Britain, and the United States
sources/carey-credit-system.content:
Carey — The Credit System in France, Great Britain, and the United States
Henry Charles Carey (1793–1879) — The Credit System in France, Great Britain, and the United States. — Carey, Lea, & Blanchard, Philadelphia, 1838.
An economic treatise comparing the credit and banking systems of France, Britain, and the United States, by the leading American economist of his generation. The work analyses the relationship between confidence, credit, capital, and productivity across the three nations, drawing on banking data from the 1810s–1830s.
The text is 8,637 lines, extracted from the Harvard College Library copy.
Content Summary

Chapter I — Rise and Progress of Credit — the theoretical foundations: security of person and property, the role of capital, the function of banks and credit instruments
Chapter II — Of Credit in France — the low level of confidence in France, high interest rates, the scarcity of banks, the consequences for economic development
Chapter III — Of Credit in England — the high level of confidence, the joint-stock banks, the Bank of England, the bankruptcy rates in Manchester and elsewhere, the crisis of 1825
Chapter IV — Of Credit in the United States — the development of banking from 1811 to 1836, the failure rates by state, the contrast between New England and the South/West
Chapter V — Insecurity of Property and its Effects — a comparative analysis
Chapter VI — Friction — England, France, Scotland, United States
Chapter VII — The United States in 1836–7 — the panic of 1837
Chapter VIII — England in 1825 and 1836 — the cyclical crises
Chapter IX — Conclusion

sources/carlile-republican-harrison-boun.title: Carlile / Hone / Cobbett — Harrison-bound Radical Miscellany (Political House, Cobbett 1817, Republican No. 2)
sources/carlile-republican-harrison-boun.content:
Carlile / Hone / Cobbett — Harrison-bound Radical Miscellany
Composite bound volume (library miscellany / binder’s gathering) whose Internet Archive plain-text dump runs Hone’s Political House that Jack Built, a long run of Cobbett’s Weekly Political Register / Weekly Political Pamphlet (1817, chiefly Vol. 32), and Carlile’s The Republican No. 2, Vol. I (3 September 1819) with the immediate post–16 August 1819 letters on Manchester—then unrelated later tracts. The dump is the working extract for the 1819 Carlile Peterloo-week Republican and the co-bound Hone and Cobbett pieces; it is not a clean single-title edition of The Republican Vol. I.
IA / Google-style OCR plain text; 38,093 lines / 239,051 words. Binder and shelfmarks in the scan tradition associated with Harrison-type radical gatherings (treat provenance as the IA text dump + internal imprints below). After Carlile’s No. 2 matter the file continues into non-series tracts (e.g. Rev. James Ashley letter to George Maxwell, 1797 Spalding/Fleet drainage controversy; later society/subscription and moral-essay leaves)—out of scope for this source page except as trailing bound-with noise.
Content Summary
1. Hone — The Political House that Jack Built (opening of extract)

Title block — The Political House that Jack Built. “A straw—thrown up to show which way the wind blows.” With Thirteen Cuts. Motto block from Cowper’s Task. London: Printed by and for William Hone, Ludgate Hill. Price one shilling. (OCR title year 1810 in this dump—treat as digitization/print error relative to the well-known 1819 Ludgate Hill political-house campaign; cuts and Doctor Slop dedication match the post-Peterloo / Queen Caroline-era squib.)
Dedication — To Doctor Slop, “in acknowledgment of many public testimonials of his filial gratitude,” and to “the Nursery of Children six feet high, his readers”; signed as the Doctor’s political godfather, the author. Note: the name “Doctor Slop” was conferred in Hone’s Buonaparte-phobia, or Cursing made easy… (reprinted, one shilling).
Form — Nursery-rhyme parody stanzas with Cruikshank (or associated) cuts: “This is the House that Jack built,” placemen, privilege, and public-office ladder in the usual Hone manner.
Relation — Same title as item 1 in the 1830 Chidley collection hone-pamphlets-and-parodies; this opening is an earlier separate printing bound at the head of the miscellany, not the full nine-pamphlet Chidley volume.

2. Life of William Cobbett (biographical insert)

Caption Life of William Cobbett. Autobiographical narrative first framed as written in America, 1797: no illustrious ancestry; grandfather a day-labourer (scythe, reap-hook, flail); father a farmer who drove plough for twopence a day and learned land-surveying; Cobbett born 9 March 1766; three brothers; earliest work scaring birds from turnips and rooks from pease. Contrast with Franklin’s etymological family pretensions. Serves as preface/companion matter before the Register run in this binding.

3. Cobbett — Weekly Political Register / Weekly Political Pamphlet, 1817 (Vol. 32 region)
Long middle of the extract: successive two-penny numbers under titles Cobbett’s Weekly Political Register and Cobbett’s Weekly Political Pamphlet (title shifts with the cheap pamphlet form). Recoverable dated openings include:

















































Region (extract)Masthead cues~L3341 ff.Vol. 31/32 border; Price Two Pence~L6710February 8, 1817~L8823February 22, 1817 — Weekly Political Pamphlet~L10931March 8, 1817~L12700March 15, 1817~L14662March 22, 1817~L16586March 29, 1817~L18442August 23, 1817~L21581September 6, 1817furtherVol. 32 Nos. into the 20s (two pence)
Substance (as used in this wiki): postwar distress, parliamentary and funding-system politics, and Cobbett’s cheap weekly voice in the year of Habeas Corpus suspension and the Hone trials—not a substitute for a full bibliographic Cobbett edition. Use for colour and parallel radical cheap print beside hone-three-trials and imlac-insecurity-of-british-funds.
4. Carlile — The Republican, No. 2, Vol. I (3 September 1819) — Peterloo letters
Masthead (extract ~L27442): The Republican. No. 2. Vol. 1.] London, Friday, Sept. 3, 1819. [Price 2d. Printer line: R. Carlile, 55, Fleet Street, London.
This is the first Republican publication in the wiki set that carries Carlile’s direct response to the 16 August 1819 Manchester meeting and killings (the “Peterloo” events—contemporary text says Manchester, yeomanry, magistrates; does not use the later nickname as title).
A. Letter to H.R.H. the Prince Regent
On his thanking the Magisterial and Yeomanry Assassins of Manchester for Murders committed by them on the 16th of August last.
London, 30 August 1819. Signed Richard Carlile.

Opens on public indignation at murders by Yeomanry Cavalry at the instigation of Manchester magistrates upon inhabitants in a legal and peaceable meeting for redress of grievances and radical reform of representation—exceeded only by the Chief Magistrate’s thanks to the “murderers.”
Inserts full Sidmouth / Whitehall letter, 21 August 1819, to the Earl of Derby: Prince Regent’s “great satisfaction” at magistrates’ “prompt, decisive, and efficient measures” for public tranquillity; “high approbation” of Major Trafford and the officers and men under him.
Argues that only the offenders’ own account was heard; hundreds of disinterested spectators not sought; violation of English jurisprudence and “moral decency.”
“Prompt, decisive, and efficient measures” glossed as cutting down a peaceable defenceless people; future historian to rank the Regent with the most ferocious Deys of Algiers; black border on the page that records an English prince’s sanction of the deed.
Blood of murdered countrymen cries for vengeance; people exposed themselves under the “fatally supposed mildness” of the regime; wipe the stain or face an insulted people; frenzy of a starving people.
Alternative: restore Justice and sweep corrupt influence, or the people recal delegated power and acknowledge no sovereign but their own authority; denial risks the fate of Charles or James.
Timing proof that the Regent could not have deliberated: news could not reach the Home Office before evening of the 17th; Regent then ≥100 miles from the metropolis (or at sea); yet Sidmouth thanks the “murderers” in the Regent’s name on the 21st—proof that Sidmouth anticipates and stamps the Regent’s will.
Expensive monarchy, standing army, fundholder vs. artisan and agriculturist, open-day murders by holders of the sword of Justice receiving sanction of constituted authorities—stage at which liberal writers have argued the justice of a people’s dernier resort force and beginning de novo.
High treason charge against meeting leaders softened to conspiracy and misdemeanor—pitiful before a jury; traitors in the Cabinet.

B. Second Letter to Lord Sidmouth
On the conduct of the Magisterial and Yeomanry Assassins of Manchester, on the 16th August, 1819; and on his Lordship’s conduct as subsequently connected with that Assassination.
London, 1 September 1819.

Refers to Carlile’s public letter of 18 August giving a narrative as spectator of the “horrid massacre”; thanks Sidmouth for the notice that produced police action—Morris the police officer swearing the letter an unlawful, inflammatory, seditious libel before Lord Mayor Atkins; Attorney-General prudence and bail after four days’ “conclave.”
Sidmouth (Home Secretary; Society for the Suppression of Vice; High Steward associations listed in invective) accused of preparing yeomanry minds, then approving murder without enquiry; hope of future impeachment when the state of things changes.
Metropolitan police farce: placard-holders seized while authors speak freely (Crown and Anchor meeting on the Manchester massacre; Kennington Common “Order” board / postponed meeting / Smithfield appeal to the Regent—man imprisoned, bill found, jury acquits).
Manchester magistracy and police: want of feeling; blood spilt at Manchester not washed away by libel-hunting in London.

C. Letter to John Atkins, Esq., Lord Mayor of the City of London
(continues the No. 2 sequence; satire on mayoral warrant process and choice of bail if Sidmouth orders another warrant). Closes toward R. CARLILE.
D. Supporting letter in the same number
Joseph Fitch, Old Road Academy, Stepney, 31 August 1819 — “To Mr. Carlile”: thanks for firmness against exactions; contest between government and people, Vice Society and liberal public, boroughmongering despotism and universal liberty; confidence London juries will not rear an Inquisition on the ruins of Magna Charta; Reformation memory and the press; “prove all things.” Printer line again Carlile, 55 Fleet Street.
5. Trailing bound-withs (out of core scope)
After the Republican leaves (~after L28253 printer line): Letter to Mr. George Maxwell from the Rev. James Ashley, Rector of Fleet (second edition; printed by John White; gratis from printer / rectory / King’s Head Spalding; internal date frame 1797)—South Holland Drainage and Fleet Inclosure commissioner disputes. Further leaves include subscription/donation tables, American imprint notes, and moral/religious essay extracts (war, peace societies, Erasmus, &c.). Not treated as part of the Carlile–Hone–Cobbett radical core for indexing.
Key Data Points









































FieldValueNatureBinder’s miscellany / composite OCR dump — not a single publisher’s uniform editionCore piece AHone, Political House that Jack Built, Ludgate Hill, 1s., 13 cuts; Doctor Slop dedicationCore piece BCobbett autobiographical Life + 1817 Register / Political Pamphlet run (Vol. 32, 2d.)Core piece CCarlile, The Republican No. 2, Vol. I, 3 Sept. 1819, 2d.; R. Carlile, 55 Fleet StreetPeterloo contentYes — Regent letter 30 Aug. 1819; Sidmouth letter 1 Sept. 1819; spectator claim for 16 Aug.; full Sidmouth–Derby thanks of 21 Aug. printed; Atkins letter; Fitch letter 31 Aug.Raw extractwiki/raw/carlile-republican-harrison-bound.txt — 38,093 lines, 239,051 words, 1,323,487 bytesProvenanceInternet Archive plain-text dump of the bound gathering; Google-OCR noise throughoutDoes not replaceFull Republican Vol. I; full Cobbett Register; Chidley Pamphlets and Parodies hone-pamphlets-and-parodies
Scan completeness audit

Hone Political House: title, dedication, and opening stanzas present at head; not audited here as a complete standalone pamphlet transcription (prefer hone-pamphlets-and-parodies for the nine-title set).
Cobbett 1817: long continuous cheap-weekly prose; mastheads and February–September 1817 dates recoverable; OCR long-s and broken words heavy.
Republican No. 2: title, three Carlile political letters, Sidmouth Whitehall insert, and Fitch letter recoverable as continuous argument; page folios “THE REPUBLICAN” / “SEPTEMBER 3, 1819” visible in OCR.
Tail: Ashley–Maxwell 1797 and later leaves are foreign to 1817–19 radical core—ignore for entity work unless a separate source is opened.
Quality: adequate for quotation of Carlile’s Regent/Sidmouth argument and for identifying Hone/Cobbett co-binds; not clean library typeset.

Relationship to Other Sources

Peterloo / 16 August 1819: this page is the wiki’s first Republican locus containing Carlile’s published letters on the Manchester killings and the Regent’s thanks. Pair with narrative sources (martineau-history-of-england-vol2, Alison peers) for chronological frame; do not read later “Peterloo” label back into Carlile’s own titles.
carlile-republican-vol8 — 1823 Dorchester half-year; freethought, Vice Society, Spanish dedication, Mechanics’ Institutes; not a substitute for these 1819 letters.
hone-three-trials, hone-pamphlets-and-parodies (incl. Slap at Slop / Bridge-Street Gang), hone-every-day-book — Hone press world; Political House here overlaps the Chidley item 1 title.
imlac-insecurity-of-british-funds (1817) — same distressed postwar credit year as the Cobbett pamphlet run.

Raw Text
wiki/raw/carlile-republican-harrison-bound.txt (38,093 lines; 239,051 words) — IA OCR dump of the Harrison-type bound miscellany containing Hone Political House, Cobbett 1817 weekly matter, and Carlile Republican No. 2 (3 Sept. 1819).

sources/carlile-republican-vol8.title: Carlile — The Republican, Volume VIII
sources/carlile-republican-vol8.content:
Carlile — The Republican, Volume VIII
Richard Carlile (1790–1843) — The Republican, Volume VIII, from 11 July to 26 December 1823. London: Printed and Published by R. Carlile, 84, Fleet Street, 1823. Weekly numbers (price 6d.); imprint footers also give 5, Water Lane, Fleet Street, with correspondence directed to 84 Fleet Street or Dorchester Gaol. Epigraph (title-page): restraint of writing and speaking makes men “less than men, less than any kind of animals; for all other animals have the liberty of speech.”
Bound half-year of Carlile’s weekly freethought and republican journal, written principally from Dorchester Gaol in the fourth–fifth year of his imprisonment for publishing Paine’s theological works and related deist/atheist tracts. The volume is dedicated “To Spaniards in Exile” after the collapse of the Spanish constitutional regime (1823 French intervention; death of Riego). Carlile urges Spanish patriots to examine Christian foundations, break priestly influence, and aim at an avowed republic rather than constitutional monarchy. He presents the volume’s leading feature as morality uncontaminated with religion, and recommends all eight volumes of The Republican to the exiles once they can read English.
The extract is 45,123 lines / 366,587 words from a Harvard College Library Google Books digitization (Wendell Fund; IA identifier republican08carl; Google/IA OCR plain text). Continuous weekly issue structure is recoverable; long-s / broken-word OCR noise is frequent; Google watermark and digitization prelims precede the title.
Content Summary
Front matter

Google / Harvard prelims — public-domain usage guidelines; Harvard College Library bookplate; Evert Jansen Wendell Fund.
Volume title — The Republican, Volume VIII, 11 July–26 December 1823; Carlile, 84 Fleet Street, 1823; liberty-of-speech epigraph.
Dedication — To Spaniards in Exile — Defeat blamed above all on absence of free discussion and on religious orders as enemies of the constitution; priests fomented insurrection and called in French aid with Ferdinand; church-property applied to national wants made reformers “heretics”; next Spanish revolution must end in republic; monarchy and freedom incompatible; constitutional monarchy contains the germ of civil war. Theological part of the volume denies supernatural designing power beyond the animal world and equates religion with idolatry (“not so much atheism as idolism”). Riego’s fate used against truce with Ferdinand. Attention directed especially to No. 1 (Cartwright / constitution). Signed Richard Carlile.
Contents of Volume VIII — issue-by-issue list opening with No. 1 review of Major Cartwright’s English Constitution produced and illustrated.

Issue map (Nos. 1–25, July–December 1823)
Digests follow the weekly numbers as recovered from headers and openings in the extract (not a publisher’s chapter scheme). Intermediate numbers without a distinctive lead letter are noted briefly.
No. 1 — Friday 11 July 1823

To the Republicans of the Island of Albion — review of Major Cartwright’s English Constitution produced and illustrated against Paine’s challenge to Burke (“no such thing as a Constitution exists in England”).
Fielding and Acts mottoes; constitution treated as fact, not name.

No. 2 — early August region

Subscriptions / acknowledgements block; ongoing prison correspondence.

Nos. 3–4 — No. 4 Friday 1 August 1823

To the Vice Society — defiance of the Society for the Suppression of Vice begging for prosecution money.
Near four years a prisoner for Paine’s Theological Works and Palmer’s Principles of Nature, both still sold in London; sister twenty-one months a prisoner.
Challenge that he can raise defendants as fast as they raise funds.

Nos. 5–10 — August to mid-September

Continued gaol letters, theological and political essays, subscription notices (imprints Water Lane / Fleet Street).

No. 11 — Friday 19 September 1823

Materialism versus Methodism — to Joseph Butterworth, Fleet Street bookseller, Methodist, and MP.
Methodism has neither moralized nor mollified him; clash with Hume on toleration of sects.

No. 12 — Friday 26 September 1823

To the Rev. William Wait, A.B., King’s Square, Bristol — insolent letters since imprisonment.
Still “Christianity’s Prisoner” after nearly four years; Wait’s 1820 insinuation that publications bring men to the gallows; Christians cast as the criminals who rob and cut throats.

No. 13 — early October

Intermediate number (gaol / theological series).

No. 14 — Friday 10 October 1823

To the Inhabitants of the County of Dorset — first address.
Mock loyal replies (King’s Arms waiter, Vicar of Cerne, magistrates, gaoler, postmaster Pitt); locked up as blasphemer and seditionist so that none may be “corrupted” by seeing him.

No. 15 — mid-October

Continuation of Dorset / prison series.

No. 16 — Friday 24 October 1823

To Mrs. Elizabeth Fry, St. Mildred’s Court — addresses Quakers as Society of Friends.
Free of the reproach he levels at persecuting sects; moral instruction characteristic; questions the foundation of the society while praising non-persecution.

Nos. 17–18 — late October to 7 November

No. 18 dated Friday 7 November 1823 (header); prison and freethought continuations.

No. 19 — Friday 14 November 1823

To the Inhabitants of Dorset again — nature of the conduct that made him prisoner four years.
No kindness from gaol management; simple natural opinions vs. spiritual catalogue (God, Christ, Holy Ghost, angels, devil, heaven, hell).

No. 20 — Friday 21 November 1823

To the Rev. Robert Hindmarsh, Swedenborgian priest, New Jerusalem Temple, Salford, Manchester.
Materiality infinite and eternal vs. Spirituality; Swedenborg and Clowes On the Two Worlds; German metaphysics and “diseased imaginations.”

No. 21 — late November

Intermediate number.

No. 22 — Friday 5 December 1823 (header OCR “1833”)

To the Inhabitants of Dorset — exposures driving county “high bloods” mad; bark then bite.
Prepared for destruction since Republican of November 1819; unpublished documents on gaol treatment; James Dare death / inquest correspondence with Visiting Magistrate Wollaston (cross-ref. No. 12 documents).

Nos. 23–24 — mid–late December

Closing prison and political numbers.

No. 25 — Friday 26 December 1823

Philosophical Institutions for the Improvement of Mechanics — Mechanics’ Institutes in London, Edinburgh, Glasgow (Glasgow: 1,000+ subscribers, 700 volumes purchased, 400 donated).
Substitute for public worship: halls or temples of science; as institutes increase, places of worship deserted as idolatry; Leeds Mercury lecturer obstacle dismissed—experiments and printed lectures preferred.

Recurring themes across the half-year

Prison testimony — Dorchester conditions; visiting magistrates; local clerical and loyal hostility; sister’s imprisonment; open sale of prosecuted titles in London despite confinement.
Vice Society war — prosecutions for irreligious publication as contest of stamina and subscriptions, not of argument.
Constitution and republican theory — Cartwright answered with Paine; Spanish lesson against monarchical compromise; laws and elective magistrates as sufficient government.
Sectarian addresses — Methodism (Butterworth), Church clergy (Wait), Quakers (Fry), Swedenborgians (Hindmarsh)—each used as a named medium to the public.
Materialism — denial of spiritual entities; morality without religion; idolatry as the genus of worship.
Popular instruction — Mechanics’ Institutes as the constructive alternative to chapel and church.

Key Data Points





















































FieldValueAuthor / publisherRichard Carlile; printed and published by R. sources/clowes-royal-navy-vol5.title: Clowes — The Royal Navy, Vol. V (1803–1815)
sources/clowes-royal-navy-vol5.content:
Clowes — The Royal Navy, Vol. V (1803–1815)
Sir William Laird Clowes (1856–1905) — The Royal Navy: A History from the Earliest Times to the Present. Vol. V. — Sampson Low, Marston & Co., London, 1900. 696 pages.
The fifth volume of Clowes’s seven-volume history covers the whole of the great naval struggle with Napoleon from the renewal of war in 1803 to the summer of 1815. The central episode is the Trafalgar campaign and the long struggle for command of the sea. The volume is in three main chapters: a civil/administrative history of the Navy during the war, the major fleet operations (Trafalgar and the blockade system), and the minor operations (single-ship actions, cutting-out expeditions, colonial captures). The war with the United States (1812–1815) was deferred to Vol. VI by Roosevelt.
The OCR text is at times garbled, especially on running headers and tables. Year-headings within the military chapters provide a chronological structure.
Content Summary


Introduction to Volume V — scope: the entire naval war with Napoleon from 1803 to 1815. The war with America (1812-1815) is deferred to Vol. VI as it is sufficiently independent in origin and character


Chapter XXXVIII — Civil History of the Royal Navy, 1803-1815 — naval administration, finance, dockyards, shipbuilding, manning, the carronade, lists of flag-officers promoted during the war

Appendix to Chapter XXXVIII: List of Flag-Officers Promoted, 1803-1815



Chapter XXXIX — Military History of the Royal Navy, 1803-1815: Major Operations — the renewal of war in 1803, the blockade of Brest, Nelson in the Mediterranean, the Trafalgar campaign (Villeneuve’s escape to the West Indies and back, the battle of Trafalgar), subsequent major operations in 1806-1815, the command of the sea

Subsections by year: 1803 (blockade, invasion flotilla actions, Nelson in Mediterranean), 1804 (Toulon affairs, the catamaran expedition, first Trafalgar campaign plans), 1805 (secret convention with Spain, Villeneuve’s sally, Trafalgar), 1806-1815 (continuing major operations)



Chapter XL — Military History of the Royal Navy, 1803-1815: Minor Operations — single-ship actions, cutting-out expeditions, colonial operations, the defence of convoys, operations in the East Indies, the West Indies, the Mediterranean, and home waters. Year-by-year arrangement.

Subsections by year with dozens of named actions (Capture of the Affronteur, Dance and Linois, cutting-out of the Curieux, defence of the Arrow and Acheron, the San Fiorenzo and the Psyché, Yeo at Muros, the capture of the Marengo, action off Lissa, capture of the Java, etc.)
Appendix to Chapters XXXIX, XL, and XLI: (a) List of H.M. Ships Taken, Lost, etc., 1803-1815; (b) French Losses, 1803-1815; (c) Spanish Losses, 1804-1808; (d) Dutch Losses, 1803-1810; (e) Danish Losses, 1807-1813; (f) Russian Losses, 1808-1809; (g) Turkish Losses, 1807-1808; (h) United States’ Losses, 1812-1815

sources/clowes-royal-navy-vol6.title: Clowes — The Royal Navy, Vol. VI (1812–1856)
sources/clowes-royal-navy-vol6.content:
Clowes — The Royal Navy, Vol. VI (1812–1856)
Sir William Laird Clowes (1856–1905) — The Royal Navy: A History from the Earliest Times to the Present. Vol. VI. — S. Low, Marston & Co., London, 1901. 644 pages.
The sixth volume of Clowes’s seven-volume history. It begins with the War of 1812 (contributed by then-President Theodore Roosevelt), and continues with the peacetime Navy of 1816–1856 — the major expeditions (Algiers, Navarino, St. Jean d’Acre, the Baltic and Crimean operations, Sebastopol), the civil and administrative history of the Navy during a period of technological transition from sail to steam, and voyages of discovery and Arctic exploration. The period is described in the introduction as one “of small wars with uncivilised peoples” and of “comparatively quiet” routine, punctuated by the great naval actions of Algiers, Navarin, St. Jean d’Acre, and Sebastopol.
The OCR text is at times garbled, especially on running headers and tabular material.
Content Summary


Introduction to Volume VI — explains the extension of the work from 5 to 6 (and ultimately 7) volumes; the volume covers the War of 1812, the period 1816–1856 of small wars, the Crimean campaign, and shows the Navy adapting to steam. Theodore Roosevelt contributed the War of 1812 chapter. Sir Clements Markham contributed the voyages chapters.


Chapter XLI — The War with the United States, 1812-1815 — by Colonel Theodore Roosevelt, President of the United States. Full narrative of the naval war: the causes of the war, impressment and British seamen in American service, the frigate actions (Constitution vs. Guerrière, United States vs. Macedonian, Constitution vs. Java), the actions on the Lakes (Lake Erie, Lake Champlain), the blockade of the American coast, single-ship duels (Shannon vs. Chesapeake, etc.), the operations against Washington and Baltimore, the battle of New Orleans


Chapter XLII — Voyages and Discoveries, 1803-1815 — by Sir Clements R. Markham, K.C.B. The exploratory voyages undertaken during the Napoleonic period, including hydrographic surveys and early Arctic exploration


Chapter XLIII — Civil History of the Royal Navy, 1816-1856 — by W. Laird Clowes. Naval administration in peacetime: the Board of Admiralty, dockyard extensions, the introduction of steam propulsion, the screw propeller, changes in ship design from sail to steam and from wooden walls to ironclads, naval estimates, manning, discipline, the abolition of impressment, conditions of service


Chapter XLIV — Military History of the Royal Navy, 1816-1856 — by W. Laird Clowes. The active operations of the Navy in a period of peace punctuated by punitive expeditions and one great war:

The bombardment of Algiers (1816) under Lord Exmouth
Operations against the Barbary pirates
The battle of Navarino (1827) and the Greek War of Independence
The Portuguese civil war and the action off Cape St. Vincent (1833)
The Syrian operations and the bombardment of St. Jean d’Acre (1840)
The Opium War with China (1839–1842)
The suppression of the slave trade
Anti-piracy operations in the West Indies, Mediterranean, and Chinese waters
The First Sikh War and naval co-operation on the Indus
The Russian War (Crimean War) 1854–1856: the Baltic campaign, the Black Sea operations, the bombardment of Sebastopol, the expedition to the Sea of Azof, the siege of Petropavlovsk
Commanders-in-Chief at home and abroad
Appendix to Chapter XLIV: List of H.M. Ships Wrecked, Foundered, Burnt, Taken, or Destroyed, 1816-1856



Chapter XLV — Voyages and Discoveries, 1816-1856 — by Sir Clements R. Markham, K.C.B. The great exploratory voyages of the period: Arctic expeditions in search of the North-West Passage (Parry, Franklin, Ross), the Antarctic voyages (Ross’s expedition to the Southern Ocean), hydrographic surveys around the world (Beechey, FitzRoy, Belcher, Owen), the development of scientific naval exploration

sources/clowes-royal-navy-vol7.title: Clowes — The Royal Navy, Vol. VII (1857–1900)
sources/clowes-royal-navy-vol7.content:
Clowes — The Royal Navy, Vol. VII (1857–1900)
Sir William Laird Clowes (1856–1905) — The Royal Navy: A History from the Earliest Times to the Present. Vol. VII. — Sampson Low, Marston & Co., London, 1903. 722 pages.
The seventh and final volume of Clowes’s seven-volume history, completing the narrative from the earliest times down to the death of Queen Victoria in 1901. This volume covers the late Victorian Navy (1857–1900), a period of rapid technological transformation from wooden sailing ships to ironclad steam warships. It chronicles the Second China War, the Indian Mutiny, the Abyssinian Expedition, the bombardment of Alexandria (1882), the Sudan campaigns, colonial wars in Africa and Asia, and the great Arctic and Antarctic expeditions. For the UK 1800–1865 period, only the first few years (1857–circa 1865) fall within range.
The OCR text is at times garbled, especially on running headers and tabular material.
Content Summary


Introduction to Volume VII — the volume completes the History down to the end of the Victorian era in 1901. It describes the transition from sail to steam and from wood to iron, the rise of the ironclad, the expansion of the Empire, and the Navy’s role in the Second China War, Indian Mutiny, and the Sudan campaigns


Chapter XLVI — Civil History of the Royal Navy, 1857-1900 — by Sir Wm. Laird Clowes. Naval administration during the later Victorian period: the transition from sail to steam, the introduction of the ironclad (Warrior, Monitor, turret ships), developments in naval ordnance and armour, dockyard expansion, manning and continuous service, naval education and training, the Naval Defence Act of 1889 and the Two-Power Standard

Appendix to Chapter XLVI: Flag-Officers holding the Principal Commands, 1857-1900



Chapter XLVII — Military History of the Royal Navy, 1857-1900 — by Sir Wm. Laird Clowes. The active operations: the Second China War (1857–1860, capture of the Canton forts, capture of the Taku forts, the Peiho River operations), the Indian Mutiny (1857–1858, naval brigades at Cawnpore and Lucknow), the Abyssinian Expedition (1868), the Ashanti War (1873–1874), the bombardment of Alexandria (1882) and the Egyptian campaign, the Sudan campaigns and the Nile expeditions, the Benin Expedition (1897), the Boer War (1899–1902, naval brigades at Ladysmith and elsewhere), Chinese piracy suppression, the Boxer Rebellion (1900)


Chapter XLVIII — Voyages and Discoveries, 1857-1900 — by Sir Clements R. Markham, K.C.B., P.R.G.S. The great exploratory voyages: the later Arctic expeditions (Nares, the Alert and Discovery), the Challenger expedition (the first great oceanographic voyage), the Antarctic explorations, hydrographic surveys and the development of naval science, the rescue expeditions for Franklin and later Arctic explorers

Appendix A to Chapters XLVI–XLVIII: List of Flag-Officers Promoted, 1857-1900
Appendix B to Chapters XLVI–XLVIII: List of H.M. Ships Lost, etc., 1857-1900

sources/engels-condition-of-the-working-.title: Engels — The Condition of the Working Class in England
sources/engels-condition-of-the-working-.content:
Engels — The Condition of the Working Class in England
Friedrich Engels (1820–1895) — The Condition of the Working Class in England. — Translated by Florence Wischnewetzky (American edition, 1886); republished in Penguin Classics, 1987, with a Foreword by Victor Kiernan, and the text checked against the German first edition (1845) for accuracy.
Engels wrote this book in late 1844 and early 1845, after a two-year stay in Manchester (1842–1844) where he was sent by his father to learn the family textile business. The book is a contemporary investigation of the English working class during the Industrial Revolution, based on Engels’s own observations in Manchester and other industrial towns, official reports (Factory Reports, Parliamentary Papers, reports of the Children’s Employment Commission), and contemporary writings. It was written in German for a German audience but describes conditions in England — then the most advanced industrial nation — both as a record and as a warning.
The text is 3,479 lines, extracted from the 1987 Penguin Classics EPUB (translation based on the Florence Wischnewetzky American edition of 1886, with stylistic revision by Victor Kiernan).
Content Summary
This Penguin edition includes a modern scholarly apparatus:


Foreword by Victor Kiernan (1987) — a biographical and historiographical introduction setting Engels’s book in its context: Engels’s background in the Rhineland, his arrival in Manchester, the sources he drew on, the strengths and limitations of his analysis, and the book’s enduring significance


To the Working Classes of Great Britain (1845) — Engels’s original dedication, addressed directly to the English working men, explaining his purpose in writing the book


Preface to the First German Edition (1845) — Engels’s original preface, explaining that he wrote the book for a German audience but based on English conditions, and noting his use of “Mittelklasse” (middle class) to mean the capitalist class


Preface to the English Edition (1892) — Engels’s retrospective preface, written nearly fifty years later, surveying how much had changed: the repeal of the Corn Laws, the passing of the Ten Hours’ Bill, the growth of the labour movement, the rise of trade unions, and the industrial monopoly of England now threatened by foreign competition


Introduction

The Industrial Proletariat

The Great Towns

Competition

Irish Immigration

Results

Single Branches of Industry. Factory-hands
The influence of machinery — Hand-loom weavers — The work of men being superseded by machinery — Female labour, the dissolution of the family — The reversal of all relations within the family — The moral consequences of the mass employment of women in factories — Jus primae noctis — The work of children — The apprentice system — Subsequent measures — The facts related by the Factory Report — Long working-day — Night-work — Cripples — Other deformities — The nature of factory work — Relaxation of the whole organism — Special diseases — Testimony of the Commissioners — Premature old age — The specific influence of factory work upon the female physique — Some especially injurious branches — Accidents — The bourgeoisie’s opinion of the factory system — Factory laws and agitation for the Ten Hours’ Bill — The stupefying and demoralizing nature of factory work — Slavery — Factory regulations — The truck system — The cottage system — The comparison of the serf of 1145 with the free working man of 1845
The Remaining Branches of Industry

Labour Movements
Preliminary remarks — Crimes — Revolts against machinery — Associations, strikes — The objects of the unions and strikes — Excesses connected with them — The general character of the struggle waged by the English proletariat against the bourgeoisie — The battle in Manchester in May 1843 — Respect for the law is alien to the proletariat — Chartism — The history of the Chartist movement — Insurrection of 1842 — The decisive separation of proletarian Chartism from bourgeois radicalism — the social nature of Chartism — Socialism — The working men’s views
