sources/gilbart-laws-of-the-currency-cou.title: Gilbart — The Laws of the Currency (Country Bank Notes since 1844)
sources/gilbart-laws-of-the-currency-cou.content:
Gilbart — The Laws of the Currency (Country Bank Notes since 1844)
James William Gilbart, F.R.S. (1794–1863) — The Laws of the Currency, as Exemplified in the Circulation of Country Bank Notes in England, since the Passing of the Act of 1844. — Journal of the Statistical Society of London, vol. 17 (1854), pp. 289–321.
Paper read before the Statistical Section of the British Association for the Advancement of Science at Liverpool, 22 September 1854; printed in the Society’s journal for December 1854. Gilbart, general manager of the London and Westminster Bank and author of The History and Principles of Banking, treats currency as a subject for statistical investigation rather than party politics. The inquiry is limited to country bank notes in England and to the fluctuations in their circulation after the Bank Charter Act of 1844 (7 & 8 Vict. c. 32). An appendix of statistical tables (licenses and bankruptcies, stamp duties, stamp issues, Gazette returns, authorized vs. actual issues, deposits, comparative monthly series, &c.) supports the narrative.
Raw extract: Internet Archive item jstor-2338289 (2338289_djvu.txt, JSTOR Early Journal Content); about 99 KB OCR text, pages 289–321 of the journal.
What the paper is and how it opens
Gilbart opens by welcoming the detachment of currency debate from faction and its transfer to statistics. He then walks the reader through the genealogy of English note issue before turning to the Act of 1844 and to what monthly returns show about “laws” of circulation—uniform seasonal patterns that differ for the Bank of England, English country banks, Scotland, and Ireland.
Origins of country notes and the growth of country banking
Country bank notes, he reminds the section, began as goldsmiths’ notes. After Charles I seized merchants’ deposits in the Tower mint (1640), and after apprentices proved unsafe custodians in the Civil War, merchants lodged money with goldsmiths who both borrowed and lent, took rents, advanced on the taxes to the Crown, and issued receipts that passed from hand to hand. Statutes long spoke of “bankers’ or goldsmiths’ notes”; Irish acts of 1709 and 1729 treated such notes like inland bills and punished forgery. After the Bank of England’s foundation (1694), its notes gradually superseded the goldsmiths’; banking separated from the goldsmith’s craft, though many London bankers still belonged to the Goldsmiths’ Company mid-century.
Authentic continuous statistics of country banking are scarce for the early period. Few country banks existed before the American war; they multiplied after that war, suffered in 1793 (twenty-two bankruptcies), and expanded rapidly after the Bank Restriction Act. From 1808 note-issuing banks took annual licenses; stamp duty on notes dates from 1804 and was raised in 1808 and 1815. Parliament barred notes under 20s. in 1775 and under £5 in 1777; Restriction (1797) reopened £1 and £2 issues, continued toward the 1833 charter expiry, until after the panic of 1825 government stopped stamps under £5 and required existing small notes to cease by 1829. Speculations before 1825 were blamed on country banks; the legislative answer abolished small notes, allowed banks of more than six partners beyond sixty-five miles from London, and drew the Bank of England into provincial branches.
Lancashire, bills of exchange, and Bank of England branches
Lancaster—especially Manchester and Liverpool—formed a special case: little country paper and few Bank of England notes; circulation ran mainly on bills of exchange endorsed from hand to hand. Large notes for customs duties and small notes for wages came from London; manufacturers and dealers settled among themselves on London-payable bills. After 1826, Bank of England branches at Manchester and Liverpool, and joint-stock banks that took Bank of England paper at a preferential discount rather than issuing their own, displaced much of the bill circulation. With weak private banks gone or merged, and notes under £5 abolished, a “secure” country circulation seemed achieved—until later panics shifted the indictment.
Accusations against country issues, 1836–1841, and bankers’ replies
In late 1836 another panic produced a charge not of unsafety but of excess, aimed especially at joint-stock banks. Unlike 1825, when circulation could only be guessed from stamps, Lord Althorp’s Act of 1833 (3 & 4 Will. IV c. 83) forced quarterly averages of weekly circulation into the Stamp Office and the London Gazette. Those returns showed country circulation up by early 1836; contemporaneous speculation and year-end panic were then blamed on the notes. In 1839 the complaint changed again: country circulation was ill-regulated—it did not move with Bank of England gold (nor even with Bank of England notes) as some political economists required. A Commons committee on banks of issue sat in 1840–41; the practical fruit was weekly returns (4 & 5 Vict. c. 50).
Gilbart sets out the country bankers’ earlier answers (including their 1833 memorial to Earl Grey): London failures were relatively worse; great fluctuations began with influential merchants in great cities and with Bank of England issues, not in country channels (Liverpool failures of a few houses ran to seven or eight millions where country notes never circulated); country issues promoted domestic production and had less power to throw the exchanges; forcing miners and manufacturers into direct contact with exchange-regulating operations without the cushion of local circulation would be hazardous.
The Act of 1844 and the choice of maximum
When Peel returned to office and the Bank charter came up in 1844, the statute “to regulate the issue of bank notes” answered mainly the charge of excess. No new bank of issue might be created in the United Kingdom. Each existing English bank’s maximum average over four weeks was fixed at its average for the twelve weeks ending 27 April 1844; weekly averages were returned, and four-week excess brought a penalty equal to the excess. Increasing partners beyond six (for a small bank), certain unions, bankruptcy, or ceasing to issue extinguished the right forever. The Act did not compel country issues to track Bank gold: October 1844 gold about £12.15m, October 1847 about £6.75m, July 1852 about £21.85m, without corresponding legal contraction or expansion of country maxima.
The April 1844 twelve-week base was a compromise. Peel first proposed a two-year average; private bankers asked five years; joint-stock banks preferred the maximum of two years lest an average-turned-ceiling shrink issues further. Certified totals settled near £5.15m private and £3.50m joint-stock (205 private, 72 joint-stock banks). Country circulation had already fallen sharply 1839–1843 (from about £11.7m to about £7.7m). Bankers blamed dull trade and low corn prices; Gilbart also lists lasting causes: banks swapping own notes for Bank of England paper under advantageous contracts; railways returning notes faster; penny post (1840) and letter registration speeding inter-bank remittance of rivals’ notes to London; the spread of deposit accounts and cheques instead of pocket notes. Even without 1844, he thinks actual issues would not have recovered former peaks. A hard maximum on a seasonal series forces the average below the ceiling; the maximum was sliced among many banks each keeping a safety margin; the penalty equal to the whole excess made prudence keep issues well under the line.
How restriction was felt—and how deposits softened it
Restriction showed in attempted evasions (a circular under Sir Charles Wood; note-like cheques on penny stamps later stopped by stamp law); in fourth-week dips when banks pulled in their own paper and fetched £5 and £10 Bank notes from London to hold four-week averages; and in joint-stock banks that issued only at some branches and used Bank of England notes elsewhere. Branch Bank of England circulation rose as country issues fell (country about £11.7m with branches £3.5m in 1836; country about £7.7m with branches £6.5m in 1846). Yet the deposit system offset much pressure: once notes lodge with bankers and payments move by cheque and clearing, transfers replace note circulation. London joint-stock deposits had already passed £22m while Bank of England private deposits rose from about £5m to £12m; Gilbart believes similar deposit growth was general in the provinces without extinguishing private banks. Joint-stock admission to the clearing house and settlement by Bank of England cheques would economize notes still further.
“Laws of the currency”: seasonal circuits before and after 1844
From Commons monthly averages (Bank of England, English country, Scotland, Ireland), Gilbart had earlier derived “laws of the currency,” by analogy with laws of mortality—uniform recurrences in chronological figures.

Bank of England: four tides a year with the public dividends—January higher than February–March, April than May–June, July than August–September, October than November–December—because the Bank alone pays the dividends.
English country notes: one annual circuit—lowest about end of August, rising through November (slight December reaction) to a peak in April, then down again to August; governed by agricultural and local trade seasons, not by dividend dates.
Scotland: lowest in March, high in May and especially November (mortgage interest, annuities, deposit interest, servants’ wages, mortgage transfers); Scottish habit settles large and small payments in notes rather than London-style cheques; monthly pattern highly regular year to year.
Ireland: agricultural rhythm—rise with harvest and cattle and bacon trade, peak around January, then decline; expansion strongest in rural joint-stock districts and in the smallest denominations; annual level set by harvest and produce prices; Bank of Ireland in Dublin expands less than branches in towns, which expand less than agricultural issuers.

Before the 1841 banks-of-issue committee he drew the general moral: each of these circulations obeys laws peculiar to itself; they cannot be forced into one amalgamated system without wrecking the “beautiful system of country banking” that receives surplus capital in one district and releases it for trade and industry where wanted, expanding and contracting locally as trade requires.
After 1844, tables in the appendix show the same seasonal laws still governing English country issues. The Act capped the height of the wave; it did not rewrite the calendar of the tide.
Extinction of issues, topography, and actual vs. authorized circulation
Because lapsed issues cannot be revived, the ceiling itself erodes. Since 1844, thirty-seven private country banks had ceased to issue (eleven inside the sixty-five-mile circle, twenty-six outside; combined fixed issue about £536,793) and seven joint-stock banks (about £169,589)—among them houses at Devonport, Ipswich, Stockton, Leeds, Sheffield, Newcastle—cutting original certified issue from about £8.65m to about £7.94m. Topographically: inside the sixty-five-mile London circle there is no joint-stock bank of issue and no Bank of England branch of the provincial type under discussion; forty-seven private banks there hold about £1.30m authorized issue; outside, 120 private banks about £3.31m and sixty-five joint-stock banks about £3.33m. Average authorized size of private banks is nearly the same inside and outside the circle (about £27,700).
For actual circulation in 1853 (April, August, December), private banks run further below authorization than joint-stock banks, and private banks inside the circle further below than those outside—joint-stock actuals often in the high 80s–low 90s percent of authorization in peak months, private banks inside the circle nearer the mid-70s. Causes are assigned cautiously (competition, Bank branches, deposit banking, the penalty cushion). Gilbart notes that if the long policy is gradual extinction of country issues toward a single issuer, non-revival of lapsed rights serves that end; he doubts that London expansion of Bank of England notes can replace notes extinguished in a remote district, and he rehearses older evidence that depriving country bankers of note profit would raise charges on accommodation and close marginal rural offices.
Crisis of 1847, Scotland and Ireland under 1845, and small notes
He reviews how country circulation behaved through commercial pressure (including 1847) under the fixed maxima, and contrasts English rules with the 1845 arrangements for Scotland and Ireland. There a bank may exceed its authorized issue if it holds gold equal to the excess; in England excess is a full-value penalty with no gold (or Bank-note) offset. Bank of England notes are not legal tender in Scotland or Ireland (hence coin reserves there), yet English banks cannot lawfully expand against Bank of England notes the way Scottish and Irish banks expand against sovereigns. Unions of issuing banks may carry combined circulation in Scotland and Ireland; in England unions that push partners above six can destroy issue rights—though English banks are often small and would gain by union. When issues lapse, the Bank of England may take up to two-thirds of the extinguished amount; the Bank of Ireland may take the whole—another disparity Gilbart flags without defending.
The sharpest institutional difference remains power to issue notes under £5. In England that band is gold and silver coin. Amid the Russian war he notes the Russian silver ruble versus a heavily depreciated paper ruble as a caution against careless state paper, yet also treats English small-note prohibition as a reserve magazine: if foreign drain and war needs required it, reopening small country issues could release gold from domestic pockets—matter for statesmen, not for bankers alone, while Australian gold still meets foreign and domestic needs.
Closing recommendations
Gilbart’s practical programme, grounded in the statistical “laws” and in the comparative statutes, includes among other points: measuring the English maximum on a twelve-month average rather than four weeks; restoring issue rights, when Bank of England agency agreements expire (1856), to banks that had circulated Bank notes under those agreements; keeping aggregate country circulation from falling below the 1844 quantum by redistributing the roughly £706,000 already lost among issuing or non-issuing banks in the districts of the deficiency; allowing English banks, on the Scottish and Irish model, to exceed fixed issue against gold—and, gold being demandable for them, against Bank of England notes held as equivalent; letting banks of not more than six partners keep fixed issue in the same locality even if partners later exceed six, retrospectively covering unions since 1844; and allowing two or more issuing banks, whatever their partnership numbers, to unite and retain the sum of their issues. Notes under £5 he leaves to political judgment, with the war-reserve thought attached.
The appendix then prints the supporting tables—licenses and commissions of bankruptcy against country banks year by year, stamp duties on country notes, stamp quantities, Gazette and weekly circulation series, authorized and actual issues, deposit figures, and comparative monthly circulations that exhibit the seasonal laws for England, Scotland, and Ireland.

sources/hone-every-day-book.content:
Hone — The Every-Day Book (Vol. I)
William Hone (1780–1842) — The Every-Day Book; or, Everlasting Calendar of Popular Amusements, Sports, Pastimes, Ceremonies, Manners, Customs, and Events, incident to each of the Three Hundred and Sixty-Five Days, in Past and Present Times; forming a complete History of the Year, Months, & Seasons, and a Perpetual Key to the Almanack; including Accounts of the Weather, Rules for Health and Conduct, Remarkable and Important Anecdotes, Facts, and Notices, in Chronology, Antiquities, Topography, Biography, Natural History, Art, Science, and General Literature; derived from the most authentic sources, and valuable original communications, with poetical elucidations, for daily use and diversion. — Volume I. With one hundred and seventy engravings. London: Published for William Hone, by Hunt and Clarke, Tavistock-Street, Covent-Garden, 1826. Printer’s line: A. Applegath, Stamford-Street. Epigraph from Herrick on festivals, fairs, mummings, May-poles, wassails, and fairy lore.
Self-described specimen of a day-by-day miscellany of manners and customs: each of the 365 days distinguished by occurrences and by methods of celebrating every holyday; framed as everlasting calendar, history of the year/months/seasons, and perpetual key to the almanack. Dedication (5 May 1826) to Charles Lamb and Miss Lamb, acknowledging Lamb’s early approval of the notice of St. Chad’s Well, public friendship, sympathy in glooms, and spontaneous sparkling of Lamb’s pen in the book. Preface avows aims beyond the prospectus: communicate important and diverting facts without exciting uneasy sensation; cultivate high moral feeling and the best affections of the heart by not seeming to teach; promote social and benevolent feelings. Explanatory Address lists national and domestic festivities still kept (New Year, Twelfth-day, Valentine, Shrovetide, May day, Gunpowder Plot, Christmas-tide, &c.) and popular merriments (fairs, wakes, morris, harvest homes, mummings, Eton Montem, Hogmanay, Yule, &c.).
The extract is 95,364 lines / 585,249 words (3,334,261 bytes) from an Anna’s Archive / Hathi-style page-OCR zip of a University of California Santa Barbara library copy (bookplate and Houghton / D.N. Coll. marks); 882 page markers. This scan is Volume I only (January–December day entries through printed p. ~1656, then six indexes). The zip filename also styles the work with the later “Table Book” pairing common in collected Hone editions; imprint on the title page of this volume is the 1826 Hunt and Clarke Every-Day Book Vol. I.

Title page — full style as above; Vol. I; 170 engravings; Hunt and Clarke for Hone, 1826.
Dedication to Charles Lamb, Esq. (and Miss Lamb), 5 May 1826 — St. Chad’s Well approval; public naming as friend; sympathy; Lamb’s contributions when Hone’s mind was “in clouds and darkness.”
Preface — specimen collection of ancient and modern manners and customs with seasons of popular pastime; definitions of everlasting calendar / history of year, months, seasons / perpetual key to the almanack; labour of reducing facts into order; avowed moral and social aims; appeal to readers for “something that will do for the Every-Day Book.”
Explanatory Address to the Readers — ancestors appropriated each day to remarkable persons or events; programme of feast-days and popular merriments; sample topics (Hand of Glory, Glastonbury thorn, Dunmow flitch, Robin Hood, Highgate oath, barber’s pole, &c.).

Running heads of the form The Every-Day Book.—[Month] [Day]. Typical entry furniture: saint or feast of the day; antiquarian and historical notices; popular customs and amusements; natural-history and weather notes; Floral Directory plant dedicated to the day; verse (original and selected); occasional correspondence and anecdotes of London life.

sources/hone-pamphlets-and-parodies.title: Hone — Pamphlets and Parodies on Political Subjects
sources/hone-pamphlets-and-parodies.content:
Hone — Pamphlets and Parodies on Political Subjects
William Hone (1780–1842) — Pamphlets and Parodies on Political Subjects. Containing: 1. The House that Jack Built. 2. Queen’s Matrimonial Ladder. 3. The Miraculous Host. 4. Form of Prayer. 5. Non Mi Ricordo. 6. Political Showman. 7. Man in the Moon. 8. Rights Divine for Kings, &c. 9. Slap at Slop. — By William Hone. With numerous wood cuts by Cruikshank. London: P. Chidley, 151, Goswell Street, 1830.
1830 collected reissue binding together Hone’s best-known post-trial political squibs of the Queen Caroline and reform years (individual title-pages inside retain original Ludgate Hill imprints and high edition counts from 1820–1822). Wood-engraved cuts throughout (Cruikshank). The volume is a primary dossier of radical illustrated satire: Regent and ministry caricature, Caroline defence, bank-restriction and ex-officio jibes, Peterloo allusion, Bridge-Street Constitutional Association (“Bridge-Street Gang”), and a verse polemic against divine right dedicated to the Holy Alliance.
The extract is 12,188 lines / 93,046 words (534,438 bytes) from an Anna’s Archive page-OCR zip; 348 page markers. Spine/library styling in the scan includes “Hone’s Political Pamphlets”; ownership marks (e.g. John Farrar Buttrick; later Fairmont Hotel / San Francisco bookplate leaf near end). After the nine listed works the dump continues with a Political Christmas Carol, publisher advertisements, a second pass of Miraculous Host matter, and trailing Catholic hagiographic/“Hell opened” leaves that appear as bound-with or filler at the end of this physical volume—not part of the 1830 contents list.
Content Summary
Collection title and contents (extract ~pp. 13–17)

Binder’s / half titles: “Hone’s Political Pamphlets”; Pamphlets and Parodies on Political Subjects.
Contents (1830 Chidley title) — nine works as numbered above; Cruikshank cuts; London, P. Chidley, 151 Goswell Street, 1830.

1. The Political House that Jack Built (~pp. 19–38)

Separate title: The Political House that Jack Built. “A straw—thrown up to show which way the wind blows.” With thirteen cuts. Fifty-first edition. London: Printed by and for William Hone, Ludgate Hill, 1821. One shilling.
Author’s dedication to his “political godchild” Doctor slop, and to the “nursery of children six feet high” (readers); note that the name Slop was conferred in the earlier Buonapartephobia, or Cursing made Easy.
Illustrated cumulative rhyme on the “House” of the constitution (Magna Charta, Bill of Rights, Habeas Corpus) versus bank restriction, bills of indemnity, ex-officio process, public informers, “reasons of lawless power,” the Man all shaven and shorn / Dandy of Sixty (Regent figure), yeomanry who sabred peaceable reformers (Peterloo sequence), the Doctor, Derry-Down Triangle, and the Spouter of Froth; closing hopes in Norfolk, Bedford, Fitzwilliam, Grosvenor, Albemarle, &c.

2. The Queen’s Matrimonial Ladder (~pp. 39–62 region)

The Queen’s Matrimonial Ladder, a National Toy, with Fourteen Step Scenes; and Illustrations in Verse, with Eighteen other Cuts. By the author of The Political House that Jack Built. Epigraph from Her Majesty’s Answer to the Norwich Address on rights of the individual. Step labels in the cut sequence include Qualification, Declaration, Coronation, Separation, Indignation, Emigration, Remigration, Accusation, Publication, &c.
Advertisement leaf in-scan also pushes Nero Vindicated and Non Mi Ricordo! editions.

3. The Miraculous Host (~pp. 65–98 region; reprise ~307 ff.)

The Miraculous Host Tortured by the Jew, under the Reign of Philip the Fair in 1290; being one of the Legends which converted the Daughters and Niece of Douglas Loveday… Preface on the Loveday conversions and the editor’s use of the legend; narrative of the Paris Host of 1290 (stabbing, boiling, fire, blood); additions citing Fleury and episcopal process. Anti-superstition / anti-bigotry pamphlet framed through a medieval Eucharistic legend rather than direct parliamentary satire.

4. Form of Prayer (~pp. 99–114)

The Form of Prayer, with Thanksgiving to Almighty God, to be used daily by all devout People throughout the Realm, for the Happy Deliverance of Her Majesty Queen Caroline from the late most Traitorous Conspiracy. Eighth edition. London: Printed for William Hone, 45, Ludgate Hill, 1820. Sixpence. Motto cuts: Populus / Knowledge is Power / Libertas.
Full liturgical parody structure: hymn/versicles, psalm-like thanksgivings for overthrow of “traitorous, heady, and high-minded men,” collects, and epistle/gospel-style marital texts turned to Caroline’s deliverance.

5. “Non Mi Ricordo!” (~pp. 115–130)

“Non Mi Ricordo!” &c. &c. &c. Thirty-first edition. London: Printed by and for William Hone, Ludgate Hill, 1820. Sixpence. Motto from Cymbeline.
Cross-examination squib: witness answers only “Non mi ricordo” (and variants); “old yellow chariot”; lost-memory / government-victualling jokes; court cries of Withdraw. Public-office parody notice (1 September 1820) that the free house called the Political House that Jack Built has been feloniously entered—bridge into the next pamphlet.

6. The Political Showman—At Home! (~pp. 131–162)

The Political Showman—At Home! Exhibiting his Cabinet of Curiosities and Creatures—All Alive! By the author of The Political House that Jack Built. With twenty-four cuts. Twentieth edition. London: Printed for William Hone, 45, Ludgate-Hill, 1821. One shilling. Epigraphs on a Den (Bunyan) and “the putrid and mouldering carcase of exploded Legitimacy.”
Cabinet-of-curiosities satire: constitutional monsters and political animals “all alive,” with Cruikshank exhibition cuts (promised constitution, &c.).

7. The Man in the Moon (~pp. 163–178)

The Man in the Moon, &c. &c. &c. With fifteen cuts. Twenty-seventh edition. London: Printed by and for William Hone, 45, Ludgate-Hill, 1821. One shilling. Motto from Cymbeline on Caesar hiding the sun.
Dream-journey to the moon; Speech from the Throne to the Senate of Lunataria; reform iconography in the cuts.

8. The Right Divine of Kings to Govern Wrong! (~pp. 179–238)

The Right Divine of Kings to Govern Wrong! Dedicated to the Holy Alliance. By the author of The Political House that Jack Built. London: Printed for William Hone, 45, Ludgate-Hill, 1821. Eighteenpence.
Extended verse treatise in three books: invention of kings; law above magistrate; nations pulling down oppressors; English succession and usurpation examples; possession vs. right; people’s right of choosing; despots in heart under limited forms; Providence dooming tyrants by the people’s hand. Epigraphs from Shakespeare and satirical “Discord of Steel.”

9. A Slap at slop and the Bridge-Street Gang (~pp. 239–296)

A Slap at slop and the Bridge-Street Gang. By the author of The Political House that Jack Built. With twenty-seven cuts. London: Printed by and for William Hone, 45, Ludgate Hill, 1822. Half-a-crown.
Opens in newspaper-imitation layout (New Times printing-office spoof). “To the Reader”: the Slap first arranged in imitation of a newspaper. Extended assault on Doctor slop (loyalist press persona) and the Constitutional Association of Bridge-Street, Blackfriars (“Bridge-Street Gang”): life of Slop, rejection of virulent copy, official paper sneers, “New Devil upon Two Sticks,” “New Lock Hospital for the Reception of Incapables,” visionary set-pieces, &c.

Additional matter in this scan (not on 1830 contents list)

A Political Christmas Carol, set to music (~p. 297 ff.) — to be chaunted throughout the United Kingdom and dominions; “Go draw your quills, and draw six Bills…”
Publisher notices / edition pushers for the Political House (e.g. fifty-second edition entered at Stationers’ Hall) and related cuts.
Repeated or extended Miraculous Host block toward the rear.
Trailing leaves of Hell Opened to Christians / Description of Hell / St. Catharine of Siena / St. Martin-type devotional matter and empty/bookplate pages (Fairmont Hotel, San Francisco)—bound-with or volume endpapers in this copy, outside the Chidley political contents.

Key Data Points

Empty / near-empty leaves: extract pp. 1–5, 7–8, 10–15, 18, 42, 136, 240, 285–286, 305, 341–344, 346–348 (library spine, plates, and end matter).
Plate-heavy pages: Cruikshank cuts often yield thin or broken OCR; verse captions usually recoverable on facing text pages.

sources/hone-three-trials.title: Hone — The Three Trials of William Hone
sources/hone-three-trials.content:
Hone — The Three Trials of William Hone
William Hone (1780–1842) — The Three Trials of William Hone, for publishing three parodies; viz. The Late John Wilkes’s Catechism, The Political Litany, and The Sinecurist’s Creed; on three ex-officio informations, at Guildhall, London, during three successive days, December 18, 19, & 20, 1817; before three special juries, and Mr. Justice Abbott, on the first day, and Lord Chief Justice Ellenborough, on the last two days. — London: Printed by & for William Hone, 67, Old Bailey, 1818. Epigraph: “Thrice the brindled cat hath mew’d!” (Shakespeare). Sold with the proceedings of the public meeting; price four shillings in boards (title-page imprint). Third-trial section separately marked “Tenth Edition,” price one shilling.
Self-published report of Hone’s three successive Guildhall prosecutions for political parodies on forms of Church of England worship. The Crown proceeded by ex-officio information (Attorney-General Sir Samuel Shepherd). Hone defended himself without counsel. Each jury returned Not Guilty. The Address is dated 23 January 1818; the third-trial “To the Reader” is dated 22 January 1818. Hone states that he intends a later enlarged royal-octavo report with full shorthand of the third day’s defence, Attorney-General’s reply, and Chief Justice’s charge, fac-simile coloured prints shown at trial, Notes and Appendix, subscriber list, and portrait—this 1818 volume is the shorter contemporary report “with the proceedings of the public meeting.”
The extract is 10,136 lines / 90,886 words from a University of Minnesota Library bound volume (call 942.07 H75a; AA/Hathi page-OCR dump, 248 page images; OCLC 785874045; AA hash 5b0ddd2b3c9563f1d02f66a849f53843). After the three-trial matter the same physical volume continues with later Hone political pamphlets of the Queen Caroline period (Non Mi Ricordo!, matter related to The Political House that Jack Built, The Queen’s Matrimonial Ladder, &c.), treated below as bound-with material in this scan.
Content Summary
Front matter (extract pages 1–10)

Library prelims — University of Minnesota bookplate and empty leaves; OCR noise leaf.
Title page — full style as above; three special juries; Abbott day 1; Ellenborough days 2–3; Old Bailey imprint; four shillings in boards with public-meeting proceedings.
Address (William Hone, 23 Jan. 1818) — Hone says he had meant to exhort fellow-citizens against parodying Scripture or forms of worship established by law, and is glad the intimation had effect. Ministers are “laughed out of Court.” He jibes at the Home Secretary and at the President of the Board of Control as “my brother parodist.” He announces intention to commence bookselling “upon a more respectable footing,” and to prepare at leisure an enlarged permanent report (shorthand of third-day defence, AG reply, CJ charge; narrative from stopping the sale through the public subscription; subscriber list; Notes/Appendix; correct copies of parodies read in court; reduced coloured fac-similes of prints exhibited; portrait by subscription; royal octavo).

Subscription for Mr. Hone (extract p. 12; meeting 29 Dec. 1817)
Meeting of the Friends of the Liberty of the Press and Trial by Jury, City of London Tavern, Monday 29 December 1817, Mr. Waithman in the chair. Unanimous resolutions: liberty of the press inseparable from purity of trial by jury; Hone’s acquittals as demonstration of that right; scriptural parody long practised (Luther, church dignitaries, &c.), so exception taken by present Ministers was for political purposes against the press; hypocritical use of religion as a mask for political persecution; object of the prosecutions was not to protect religion but to crush an individual who had exposed ministerial delinquencies, stifle discussion, destroy liberty of the press, and uphold abuse; praise of Hone’s knowledge, talents, intrepidity, and perseverance. (Hone’s third-trial “To the Reader” states that a report of the speeches at this meeting, with a list of subscribers, is added to that account.)
The First Trial — The Late John Wilkes’s Catechism (18 Dec. 1817)

Caption — The King against William Hone, ex-officio information for publishing the late John Wilkes’s Catechism; Guildhall, Thursday 18 December 1817, London Sittings after Michaelmas Term; before Mr. Justice Abbott and a special jury.
Court opening — Crowds from early morning; Hone enters with parcels of books covering the table; special jury sworn (foreman later John Godwin Bowring of Leadenhall Street; panel includes Godwin Bowring, Gardiner, Hilton, Brook, Hunter, Thompson, Lewis, Edwards, Syme, Woollett, O’Brien, Noakes).
Pleadings (Mr. Shepherd) — Information for an impious, profane, and scandalous libel on the Catechism, intent to excite impiety and irreligion and bring the Catechism into contempt.
Attorney-General (Sir Samuel Shepherd) — Christianity “parcel of the Common Law” (Hale); Book of Common Prayer annexed to statute under Charles II; the parody is a “Cutechism… to be learned of every person before he be brought to be confirmed a Placeman or Pensioner by the Minister”; Creed and Commandments parodied as courtier’s faith and Minister’s Ten Commandments (loyalty to place, hostility to Cochrane and Friends of the People, &c.). Cheap circulation among the “lower classes” stressed; even if meant as a political squib, tendency to contempt of religion remains.
Parody substance (as read/quoted) — Political catechism of placemen and pensioners; articles of belief including Jacobite/legitimist jibes and faith in Finance and Secresy committees and the “Pitt System”; Commandments addressed to “I the Minister… who brought thee out of Want and Beggary, into the House of Commons.”
Defence (Hone) — Long uncounselled speech. Narrative of arrest on Lord Ellenborough’s warrant, lock-up in Shire-lane, ignorance of the charge, pressure to plead; complaint of injustice by Ellenborough and of public misrepresentation; historical parade of scriptural and liturgical parodies (Luther and others) as evidence of custom and of non-prosecution; argument that intention was political, not to ridicule religion; family distress; assertion he would deny to his dying moment any design against the religion of the country. Court applause noted in the report.
AG reply — Prior parodies (even by venerable names) if they profaned Scripture were libels; a parody becomes libel when it excites ludicrous ideas about the thing parodied and brings sacred offices into contempt; intention gathered from acts; secondary effect still grounds guilt if tendency proved; cheap form accelerates mischief.
Abbott’s charge — Offence is publication with design/intent to promote impiety; if tendency is obvious on the face, law presumes contemplation of it; discontinuance of sale does not erase publication; Christian religion part of the law of the land; political application does not purge profaneness; quotes the commandment against taking the Lord’s name in vain; reads/comments early part of the libel, declines to shock the jury with the Lord’s Prayer parody; states his opinion that the production is highly scandalous, irreligious, and libellous, while leaving the verdict to the jury’s conscience; hands jury the publication, an official copy of the information, and a Prayer-book.
Verdict — Jury withdraws; returns in less than a quarter of an hour; Bowring as foreman: NOT GUILTY. Loud acclamations in court; Abbott asks rejoicing to be reserved for a fitter place.

The Second Trial — The Political Litany (19 Dec. 1817)

Caption — Second trial; ex-officio information for publishing “The Political Litany”; Guildhall, Friday 19 December 1817; before Lord Ellenborough and a special jury.
Scene — After the first acquittal, public expectation that the AG would drop remaining informations; instead he perseveres. Avenues blocked; court cannot hold a twentieth of the crowd. Hone arrives with large bundles of books. Ellenborough (unexpected after Abbott the day before) takes the bench; sends for the Sheriffs.
Jury — Only six special jurymen answer; Crown prays a tales; six common jurymen added after one challenge (John Austen, shoemaker, Aldgate, challenged by the Crown). Special jurors named (Wilson, Lindsay, Thornton, Gillman, Mackie, Black); talesmen (Jones, Smith, Thorne, Donaldson, Hale, Green).
Pleadings — Two counts: (1) impious and profane libel on the Litany or General Supplication; (2) wicked and seditious libel of and concerning the Prince Regent and the Houses of Lords and Commons. Plea: Not Guilty.
AG opening — Stresses the solemnity of the Litany; quotes parody openings: “O Prince, ruler of the people, have mercy upon us, miserable subjects”; “O House of Lords, hereditary legislators…”; “O House of Commons, proceeding from corrupt borough-mongers…”; “Son of George, we beseech thee to hear us” for “Son of God…”. Auditory laughter noted in the report.
Full text insert — The Political Litany (extract ~pp. 66–67 ff.) — “diligently revised; to be said or sung, until the appointed Change come, throughout the Dominion of England and Wales, and the Town of Berwick-upon-Tweed… 1817. Price Two-pence.” Supplications against unnational debt, unmerited pensions and sinecures, extravagant civil list, starvation, warlike establishments in peace, corrupt elections, pensioned hirelings of the press, distress for taxes, crowded jails, overflowing poor-houses, Parliament chosen by one-tenth of tax-payers; petitions for constitutional rule, economy of the Royal Family, equal representation, rights of citizens regardless of creed, &c.
Defence and reply — Hone again piles historical parodies; AG answers that historical profanation is no justification, that Hone was selected as leader of recent parodies, that stopping sale (stated as 27 February) goes only to mitigation, that the Litany is among the most beautiful compositions in the ritual and stands in the statute-book, and that Christianity is part of the common law (Hale).
Ellenborough’s charge — Delivers “solemn opinion” under the Act that the piece is a most impious and profane libel; hopes the jury as Christians will agree. Report notes his lordship much oppressed with indisposition; charge almost inaudible beyond the bench.
Verdict — Jury retires quarter past six; returns at eight; foreman NOT GUILTY. Reiterated shouts; Sheriffs cannot keep order; acclamations through Guildhall and King-street. Ellenborough asks AG what case next; AG: the Sinecurists’ Creed. Hone nearly crushed by greetings on leaving.

The Third Trial — The Sinecurist’s Creed (20 Dec. 1817)

Separate title (extract p. 105) — The Third Trial of William Hone… for publishing a parody on the Athanasian Creed, entitled “The Sinecurist’s Creed.” Tenth Edition. Printed by & for William Hone, 67, Old Bailey; price one shilling.
To the Reader (22 Jan. 1818) — Delay from constant callers from all parts of the country; thanks for unacknowledged marks of attention; adds proceedings of the City of London Tavern meeting and subscriber list as suggested.
Jury and preliminaries — Hone exhausted from prior days but elects to proceed. Special jury and talesmen sworn (Morewood, Elwall, Edgar, Eckenstein, Barry, Brockbank, Clerk; talesmen Lewis, Coles, Pearce, Sansum, Newman). Ellenborough warns objections to Crown challenges must be taken now; Hone waves objection—“The Jury are all strangers to me.”
Pleadings — Information for irreligious and profane libel on the Creed of St. Athanasius, intent to scandalize and bring it into contempt.
AG — Established form of prayer defended by law; doctrinal differences do not license scoffing; tendency is the question; deliberation in writing/publishing bars plea of impulse; similar works by others are no excuse.
Proof and reading — Purchase proved (Swanson, Treasury Solicitor’s office) at Hone’s late Fleet-street shop, 17 February. Hone insists St. Athanasius’s Creed be read before the parody. Full Sinecurist’s Creed (Quicunque vult; “From Hone’s Weekly Commentary, No. II”; two-pence): sinecurist’s faith as holding a place of profit; Trinity of ministry burlesqued as Old Bags, Derry Down Triangle, and the Doctor—coeternal folly, mountebanks, quacks, and fools; mystification of Derry Down Triangle as Minister and Manager; majority-with-ministry as the thing “to be worshipped.”
Defence (Hone) — Multi-hour speech (report: precisely eight hours and five minutes on this day, after long efforts on prior days). Political ground of the prosecution; Canning as ministerial parodist (Pitt as Elijah, mantle dropping); Fox lampooned in old prints; Sidmouth and Ellenborough as persecutors who would “crush the insect”; defiance—“They could only immortalize him”; Scott editing Somers’s parody without prosecution; Southey’s path from Wat Tyler to pension; taxes on children’s bread funding secret-service pursuers; solemn denial of intent to ridicule the Athanasian Creed; Gibbon/Warburton/Waterland/Tillotson and clergy petitions to Bishop Porteus on the Creed; jury not bound to the judge’s opinion; Fox’s libel act; liberty of the press attacked through him; two prior acquittals; hopes to dine Sunday with his family. Declines re-calling stoppage witnesses; Ellenborough reads his notes of that evidence; Thomas Cleary proves Hone’s stated intention (near Charing-cross, 21 February) to stop the parodies after the Lords’ Report called them profane and seditious.
AG reply — Duty to persevere; stoppage vs. claim of right; danger of republication if right admitted; judge’s right to state opinion on law of libel; distinguishes Hone’s citations (Reeves, Toplady, Scott’s zealots) from the present paper.
Ellenborough’s charge — Defendant’s grievance narrative groundless; AG’s discretion to separate charges; scriptural libel not a privileged class (Woolston, Paine); Fox’s Act did not strip the judge of stating the law; intent concluded from the act; reads the parody (Old Bags / Derry Down Triangle / the Doctor as Father / Son / Holy Ghost associations); question is whether ludicrous images attach to the Creed itself.
Verdict and aftermath — NOT GUILTY; spontaneous burst in court and hall. Crowd estimated in the report at not less than 20,000 in the Hall and avenues during the jury’s absence. Hone slips out alone and unnoticed after a decoy group is cheered. Side episode: Mr. Thomas Wetherell (King’s College, Cambridge; lately from the West Indies) brought up for riotous conduct on the steps after asserting right of entry to an open court; scuffle with City marshals.

Bound-with pamphlets in this scan (extract ~pp. 149–242)
Not part of the 1817–18 three-trials title proper; later Hone (and associated) political squibs bound in the Minnesota volume and present in the page-OCR dump:

Non Mi Ricordo!(~pp. 149–162) — Queen Caroline-era cross-examination squib (“Non mi ricordo” refrain; “old yellow chariot,” &c.).
Political-house / placemen matter (~pp. 163–196 region) — including “Strayed and Missing,” “Political House” public-office parody dated 1 September 1820, sinecure/place lists (Hastings, Hertford, Liverpool, Vansittart, bishops, &c.).
The Political House that Jack Built title region (~p. 197 ff.) — with “The Doctor” and “Derry-Down Triangle” character pages.
The Queen’s Matrimonial Ladder (~p. 221 ff.) — “A National Toy, with Fourteen Step Scenes; and Illustrations in Verse.”
Closing squibs (~pp. 234–242) — Sheridan epigraph on liberty of the press; “Publication” verse; “The Joss and His Folly,” &c.

Key Data Points

























































FieldValueAuthor / publisherWilliam Hone (1780–1842); printed by & for himself, 67 Old BaileyImprint year1818 (Address 23 Jan.; third-trial note 22 Jan.)Trial dates18, 19, 20 December 1817, Guildhall, LondonJudgesMr Justice Abbott (1st); Lord Chief Justice Ellenborough (2nd & 3rd)ProsecutorAttorney-General Sir Samuel Shepherd (pleadings opened by Mr Shepherd)Form of processThree ex-officio informations; special juries (with tales on days 2–3)Parodies charged(1) Late John Wilkes’s Catechism; (2) Political Litany; (3) Sinecurist’s Creed (Athanasian Creed)VerdictsNot Guilty / Not Guilty / Not GuiltyPublic meeting29 Dec. 1817, City of London Tavern; Waithman chair; liberty of the press & trial by juryRaw extractwiki/raw/hone-three-trials.txt — 10,136 lines, 90,886 words, 248 pages, 513,292 bytesProvenanceAnna’s Archive / Hathi-style page-per-file OCR; zip members 319510023101563/00000001.txt–00000248.txt; OCLC 785874045; AA hash 5b0ddd2b3c9563f1d02f66a849f53843Library marksUniversity of Minnesota 942.07 H75a; bindery stamps OCT 16 1913 / U of M NOV ’63; accession 3 1951 002 310 156 3
Scan completeness audit

Empty leaves: extract pages 1, 3–6, 106, 243–247.
Near-empty / OCR junk: pp. 8, 60 (stray CJK/zero-width garbage).
Non-text library leaves: p. 2 (bookplate); p. 248 (accession stamp).

Relationship to Other Sources

Pair with imlac-insecurity-of-british-funds (1817) for the immediate postwar climate of debt, funding-system anxiety, and public contention in the year of these trials.
Use beside martineau-history-of-england-vol2 and alison-history-of-europe-vol1 for narrative framing of Liverpool-ministry repression, radical press culture, Habeas Corpus suspension (alluded to in Hone’s Address), and the road toward Peterloo and the Six Acts—without treating those later events as content of this volume.
The bound-with Caroline pamphlets connect forward to Martineau’s Queen Caroline chapters in the same postwar volume sequence.
Methodologically a primary law-and-press source: full AG theory of religious libel, judicial charges under Fox’s Libel Act practice, special-jury process, and an uncounselled defendant’s multi-day historical-parody defence.

sources/imlac-insecurity-of-british-fund.title: Imlac — Insecurity of the British Funds / Essay on Public Credit
sources/imlac-insecurity-of-british-fund.content:
Imlac — Insecurity of the British Funds / Essay on Public Credit
“Imlac” (pseudonym) — Insecurity of the British Funds. An Essay on Public Credit: By David Hume. (Reprinted from the Edition of 1752.) With Observations on the Sound and Prophetic Nature of Its Principles; Shewing from Indisputable Facts, that a Perseverance in the Pitt and Paper System must Eventually Produce a National Bankruptcy; and Pointing Out the Only Mode of Averting so Fatal a Calamity. — Printed for T. Keys, London, 1817.
A post-Napoleonic war tract that reprints David Hume’s essay “Of Public Credit” (1752) and argues that Britain’s massive national debt and paper money system are heading towards inevitable bankruptcy. Written under the pseudonym “Imlac” (taken from Johnson’s Rasselas), dedicated to Princess Charlotte.
The text is 12,192 lines, OCR’d from the Columbia University Libraries copy.
Content Summary

Hume’s “Of Public Credit” (1752) — the full original essay arguing that national debts, if they grow too large, must eventually cause national bankruptcy
Preface and commentary — the author’s analysis applying Hume’s principles to the post-1815 situation
The funding system — criticism of Pitt’s policy of borrowing rather than taxing
The Bank Restriction Act (1797) — the suspension of cash payments, the bullion controversy
The National Debt — its growth through the 18th century and the Napoleonic Wars
The paper money system — the dangers of inconvertible paper currency
Parliamentary reform — argued as necessary to avert financial disaster
Bentham’s plan — analysis of Jeremy Bentham’s proposals
Statistical tables — data on the national debt, taxes, and public expenditure

sources/james-naval-history-vol1.content:
William James — Naval History of Great Britain, Vol. I (1488–1796)
Author: William James (d. 1827)
Title: The Naval History of Great Britain, from the Declaration of War by France in 1793, to the Accession of George IV
Edition: A New Edition, with Additions and Notes, Bringing the Work Down to 1827 (London: Richard Bentley & Son, 1886)
OCLC: 1219703
Volume: Vol. I (of 6)
Period covered: Introduction (1488–1792) and 1793–1796
Raw text: wiki/raw/james-naval-history-vol1.txt (28,038 lines)
Description
Volume I opens with an extensive Introduction tracing the history of naval architecture, ship classification, and armament from the earliest English warships (c. 1488) through the invention of the carronade and the classification systems of the late 18th century. The narrative proper begins with the outbreak of the French Revolutionary War in February 1793 and covers the first four years of the conflict at sea: Lord Howe’s campaigns, the Glorious First of June, the Mediterranean campaigns under Hood and Hotham, the war with Holland and Spain, and colonial expeditions across the Atlantic, West Indies, and East Indies.
Chapter Breakdown
Introduction (1488 to 1792)

First ship of war; cannon; portholes; improvements in ships of war
Origin of ships’ rates; the unrated classes; calibers of guns
Ancient and modern shot; improved classification of ships
Decks of a ship of war; origin of the term gangway; flush-decked ships
Line-of-battle ships; frigates; British frigates modelled from the French
Constant-Warwick, the first British frigate
English and foreign 18-pounder frigates; the post-ship classes
Invention of the carronade; establishment of carronades for each class
Dispute between the Ordnance and Navy Boards; advantages of the carronade
Calibers of English and foreign guns; tonnage of ships of war

1792–1793

First French Revolutionary War — War declared against England
British and French Fleets — State of the British navy; captains and commanders; Dutch, Spanish, Russian, and other navies; comparative state of the French navy; French seamen; armament of French ships
First republican fleet at sea; Lord Howe’s first cruise; Lord Howe and M. Morard-de-Galles; description of Brest; Lord Howe and M. Vanstabel; description of Toulon
Lord Hood at Toulon (p. 73) — Commodore Linzee at Forneilli; French frigates at Genoa and Spezzia
Light Squadrons and Single Ships (p. 97) — Scourge and Sans-Culotte; Bedford and Leopard; Re-capture of the San Iago; Iris and Citoyenne-Française; Venus and Semillante; Hyæna and Concorde; Nymphe and Cléopâtre (p. 106); Boston and Embuscade (p. 110); Crescent and Réunion (p. 115); Agamemnon and French frigates; Thames and Uranie; Capture of the Inconstante
Colonial Expeditions (p. 124) — North America: Surrender of St. Pierre and Miquelon; West Indies: capture of Tobago, success at Martinique, dreadful hurricane, surrender of Cape-Nicolas-Mole; East Indies: attack upon the Résolue, capture of Pondicherry

1794

British and French Fleets (p. 134) — Violent proceedings at Brest; re-organization of the Brest fleet; sailing of Lord Howe; Rear-admirals Montagu and Nielly; sailing of M. Villaret-Joyeuse; Chase of the Audacieux (p. 144); Lord Howe on the 28th of May; Audacious and Révolutionnaire; Lord Howe on the 29th of May; same on 31st of May; M. Villaret joined by M. Nielly; Lord Howe on the 1st of June (Battle of the Glorious First of June, p. 162); Capture of the Alexander (p. 203); Mutiny on board the Culloden; Lord Hood at Corsica; Lord Hood and M. Martin in Gourjean bay; Mutiny on board the Windsor Castle
Light Squadrons and Single Ships (p. 216) — Extraordinary escape of the Juno; English Indiamen and French privateers; Capture of the Pomone; Capture of the Duguay-Trouin; Capture of the Atalante; Carysfort and Castor (p. 229); Crescent and French squadron; Romney and Sibylle; Destruction of the Volontaire; Capture of the Révolutionnaire; Captains Osborne and Renaud off Isle-Ronde
Colonial Expeditions, West Indies (p. 239) — Capture of Martinique; Capture of Sainte-Lucie; Capture and re-capture of Guadaloupe; Commodore Ford at St. Domingo; Capture of Tiburon
Coast of Africa (p. 253) — French spoliations at Sierra Leone

1795

British and French Fleets (p. 255) — State of the British navy; projected expedition from Brest; Sir Sidney Smith’s peep into Brest; casualties to the Brest fleet; chase of M. Vence into Belle-Isle; junction of Admirals Villaret and Vence; Cornwallis’s retreat (p. 269); Lord Bridport in command of the Channel fleet; Lord Bridport off Isle-Groix (p. 273); Expedition to Quiberon; dreadful gale in the Channel; Capture of the Berwick; Vice-admiral Hotham off Genoa (p. 285); Loss of the Illustrious; Admiral Hotham off Hyères (p. 296); Re-capture of the Censeur; Cruise of M. Ganteaume
British and Dutch Fleets (p. 307) — War between England and Holland
Light Squadrons and Single Ships (p. 308) — Blanche and Pique (p. 309); Lively and Tourterelle; Astræa and Gloire; Burning of the Boyne; Sir Richard Strachan and French convoys; Captain Cochrane and French store-ships; Thorn and Courier-National; Capture of the Minerve; Southampton and Vestale; Rose and French privateers; Mermaid and two corvettes; Capture of the Eveillé
Colonial Expeditions, West Indies (p. 331) — Captain Wilson and a French squadron; Victor Hugues and his successors
East Indies (p. 334) — Capture of the Cape of Good Hope; Capture of Trincomalee and Oostenburg

1796

British and French Fleets (p. 339) — State of the British navy; new constitution in France; force in Toulon; Recapture of the Nemesis; Nelson at Laöna; Evacuation of Leghorn; War between England and Spain
British and Spanish Fleets (p. 346) — Admiral Langara at Toulon; Evacuation of Corsica
British and Franco-Spanish Fleets (p. 349) — Recapture of Corsica by France; Sir John Jervis’s retreat from the Mediterranean
British and French Fleets (p. 350) — Loss of the Courageux; Accident to the Gibraltar
Light Squadrons and Single Ships (p. 354) — Sir Sidney Smith at Herqui; Capture of the Etoile, Unite, Virginie; Boats of Niger near the Penmarcks; Spencer and Volcan; Capture of the Argo; Suffisante and Revanche; Santa-Margarita and Tamise; Unicorn and Tribune; Dryad and Proserpine; Southampton and Utile; Glatton and French frigates; Aimable and Pensée; Mermaid and Vengeance; Quebec and two French frigates; Destruction of the Andromaque; Raison and Vengeance; Capture of the Elizabet and Bonne-Citoyenne; Rear-admiral Sercey in the Indian seas; M. Sercey and two British 74s; Loss of the Amphion; Pelican and Médée; Terpsichore and Mahonesa (p. 399); Minerve and Sabina; Blanche and Ceres
Colonial Expeditions, North America (p. 408) — Rear-admiral Richery at Newfoundland
West Indies (p. 410) — Capture of Demerara; Recapture of Sainte-Lucie; Capture of St. Vincent and Grenada; British at Léogane and Bombarde, St. Domingo
East Indies (p. 413) — Capture of Colombo, Amboyna, and Banda; Capture of Dutch squadron in Simon’s bay; Destruction of French settlement at Foul point, Madagascar

Appendix

Appendix (p. 419) — Supplementary notes and documents
Annual Abstracts — Annual Abstract No. 1 (1793), No. 2 (1794), No. 3 (1795), No. 4 (1796)
Notes to Annual Abstracts (p. 449)

Diagrams

Action of the Nymphe and Cléopâtre
Lord Howe cutting the French line on the 29th of May, 1794
Lord Howe cutting the French line on the 1st of June, 1794
Cornwallis’s retreat; wearing of the Royal Sovereign to cover the Mars
Action of the Blanche and Pique

Key Events

1793: Outbreak of war with France; Lord Hood occupies Toulon; Nymphe captures Cléopâtre (first frigate action of the war); Boston captures Embuscade
1794: Battle of the Glorious First of June (Lord Howe defeats Villaret-Joyeuse, captures six French ships); capture of Martinique, Sainte-Lucie, and Guadaloupe; sinking of the Vengeur du Peuple
1795: Cornwallis’s famous retreat from a superior French fleet; Bridport’s action off Isle-Groix; Hotham’s actions off Genoa and Hyères; capture of the Cape of Good Hope from the Dutch; war with Holland
1796: Spain joins France (Treaty of San Ildefonso); British evacuation of the Mediterranean; Jervis’s retreat; Nelson’s actions with the Minerve; capture of Colombo and Dutch possessions in Ceylon and the East Indies

sources/james-naval-history-vol2.title: james-naval-history-vol2
sources/james-naval-history-vol2.content:
William James — Naval History of Great Britain, Vol. II (1797–1799)
Author: William James (d. 1827)
Title: The Naval History of Great Britain, from the Declaration of War by France in 1793, to the Accession of George IV
Edition: A New Edition, with Additions and Notes, Bringing the Work Down to 1827 (London: Richard Bentley & Son, 1837)
OCLC: 1924562
Volume: Vol. II (of 6)
Period covered: 1797–1799
Raw text: wiki/raw/james-naval-history-vol2.txt (22,890 lines)
Description
Volume II opens with the crisis year of 1797 — the mutinies at Spithead and the Nore, Sir John Jervis’s victory off Cape St. Vincent, Nelson’s assault on Santa Cruz, and Duncan’s victory at Camperdown. The volume traces the naval war through 1798, the year of Bonaparte’s Egyptian expedition and Nelson’s triumph at the Nile, and concludes with the campaigns of 1799: the expulsion of the French from Italy and the Mediterranean, Sir Sidney Smith’s defence of Acre, and the abortive Anglo-Russian expedition to Holland. A section on the American navy (Constellation vs Insurgente) and extensive coverage of light squadrons and single-ship actions appear throughout.
Chapter Breakdown
1797

British and French Fleets — State of the British navy; single British and French fleets; expedition to Ireland; Lord Malmesbury’s peace mission; mutiny at Spithead; mutiny at the Nore; Sir John Jervis and the Spanish fleet; Sir John Jervis off Cape St. Vincent; bombardment of Cadiz; cutting out the Mutine; Nelson at Santa-Cruz; Admiral Duncan off Camperdown (Battle of Camperdown, 11 October 1797); light squadrons and single ships — capture of the Ninfa and Sta-Elena; destruction of the Calliope; Arethusa and Gaieté; gallantry of Mr. Middleton; loss of the Tribune; colonial expeditions — West Indies operations; squadron off Congrejos Point; British and French at Cape Roxo; East Indies operations

1798

British and French Fleets — State of the British navy; Mars and Hercule; Buonaparte’s plan for invading England; invasion-flotilla — its origin; Captain Popham at Ostende; destruction of the Confiante; capture of General Humbert; expeditions to Ireland; capture of the Hoche and consorts; Melampus and Résolue; Kangaroo and Loire; Mermaid and Loire; the Anson and Loire; Fisgard and Immortalité; expedition to Ireland
Buonaparte’s Egyptian Expedition — Buonaparte’s seizure of Malta; Nelson’s chase of Buonaparte; Buonaparte at Alexandria; Battle of the Nile (1 August 1798); capture of Goza; Turks at Corfu; massacre of French soldiers; capture of Minorca
Light Squadrons and Single Ships — Lieutenant Pym and Désirée; chase of the Charente; capture of the Couleuvre; Princess-Royal and Aventurier; Seahorse and Sensible; Sibylle and Fox at Manilla; Sibylle and Fox at Samboangon; loss of the Resistance; capture of the Seine; Flora and Mondovi; action with the Lodi; Espoir and Liguria; capture of the Vaillante; Leander and Généreux; capture of the Leander; Herald and French privateers; Ambuscade and Baionnaise; evacuation of Port au Prince; Spanish attack on Honduras

1799

British and French Fleets — British squadron off Brest; British fleet off Cadiz; Admiral Bruix in the Mediterranean; pursuit of the French fleet; action in Basque Roads; surrender of Corfu
Mediterranean Operations — Captain Foote at Naples; Lord Nelson at Naples; Lord Nelson and Caraccioli; Captain Troubridge at Capua; Buonaparte at Suez; bombardment of Alexandria; Sir Sidney Smith at Acre; siege of Acre; battle of Aboukir
Expedition to Holland — Anglo-Russian expedition; action with the Dutch fleet; surrender of the Dutch squadron
Light Squadrons and Single Ships — Wolverine and two French luggers; loss of the Proserpine; Dædalus and Prudente; American navy — Constellation and Insurgente; Sibylle and Forte; Fortune and Salamine; capture of Spanish vessels; Clyde and Vestale; capture of the Draak and Gier; Rattlesnake and Camel with Preneuse; Jupiter and Preneuse; Speedy and Spanish coasters; Ferret and Spanish privateer; Trincomalee and Iphigenie; Cerberus and five Spanish frigates; cutting out the Hermione; Racoon and Intrepide; Glenmore and Aimable — Sirène and Bergère; the Viper and Furet

Key Events

1797: Jervis defeats Spanish fleet off Cape St. Vincent (14 February); Nelson loses his arm at Santa Cruz (24 July); Duncan defeats the Dutch at Camperdown (11 October); Spithead and Nore mutinies threaten the fleet
1798: Nelson destroys the French fleet at the Battle of the Nile (1 August); Bonaparte lands in Egypt and seizes Malta; Minorca captured; Irish expeditions fail
1799: Sir Sidney Smith defends Acre against Bonaparte (March–May); Nelson restores the Kingdom of Naples and sanctions the execution of Caraccioli; capture of Corfu; Bruix’s Mediterranean cruise; Anglo-Russian expedition to Holland fails; Battle of Aboukir (land battle, 25 July)

sources/james-naval-history-vol3.title: james-naval-history-vol3
sources/james-naval-history-vol3.content:
William James — Naval History of Great Britain, Vol. III (1800–1805)
Author: William James (d. 1827)
Title: The Naval History of Great Britain, from the Declaration of War by France in 1793, to the Accession of George IV
Edition: A New Edition, with Additions and Notes, Bringing the Work Down to 1827 (London: Richard Bentley & Son, 1886)
OCLC: 1219703
Volume: Vol. III (of 6)
Period covered: 1800–1805
Raw text: wiki/raw/james-naval-history-vol3.txt (25,947 lines)
Description
Volume III covers the final years of the French Revolutionary War (1800–1801), the short-lived Peace of Amiens (1802), and the opening campaigns of the Napoleonic War (1803–1805), culminating in the Battle of Trafalgar. The volume includes the British expedition to the Baltic and Nelson’s victory at Copenhagen (1801), the collapse of the Armed Neutrality, the resumption of war with France, Napoleon’s invasion preparations, the pursuit of Villeneuve’s fleet across the Atlantic and back, and the climactic battle off Cape Trafalgar (21 October 1805) with Nelson’s death. Detailed appendices and annual abstracts are included.
Chapter Breakdown
1800

Light Squadrons and Single Ships — Extensive coverage of single-ship actions and small squadron engagements in the Channel, Mediterranean, West Indies, and East Indies
Colonial Expeditions — West Indies — Operations in the Caribbean theatre

1801

British and Danish Fleets — The Northern Confederacy; attack on the Freya; the Copenhagen expedition; the battle of Copenhagen (2 April 1801); armistice with the Danes; British, Swedish, and Russian fleets
British and French Fleets — Channel — Invasion-flotilla operations; Channel blockade
British and French Fleets — Mediterranean — Egyptian campaign; operations off the coast of Egypt; surrender of the French in Egypt
British and Franco-Spanish Fleets — Operations off Algeciras and Gibraltar; the battle of Algeciras Bay (6–12 July 1801); the action in the Gut of Gibraltar; Saumarez’s pursuit
Light Squadrons and Single Ships — Extensive single-ship engagements across all theatres

1802

State of the British Navy — Annual review; peace establishment after the Treaty of Amiens
America and the Barbary States — The George Washington at Algiers; war with Tripoli
France and St. Domingo — The Leclerc expedition to Saint-Domingue

1803

British and French Fleets — Resumption of war; the King’s message to Parliament; Napoleon’s warlike preparations
British and French Fleets — Channel — Blockade of Brest; Admiral Cornwallis off Ushant; invasion preparations on both sides

Description
Volume IV of William James’s Naval History of Great Britain opens in the immediate aftermath of Trafalgar (October 1805) and covers the years through 1809. It follows Sir Richard Strachan’s pursuit and capture of Dumanoir’s escaped Franco-Spanish squadron, then proceeds year by year through fleet dispositions, frigate and single-ship actions, boat expeditions, and colonial campaigns across the Atlantic, Mediterranean, Baltic, and East Indies. The volume includes the Danish expedition to Copenhagen (1807), the Dardanelles operation (1807), the Basque Roads attack (1809), and the Walcheren / Scheldt expedition (1809), concluding with an appendix of annual abstracts of the Royal Navy’s ships.

It opens in continuation of 1809 with a lengthy account of light squadrons and single-ship actions, then proceeds year by year through the remainder of the Napoleonic naval war and the opening of the War of 1812. The volume includes a final section on the state of the British and American navies in 1813, followed by an appendix containing annual abstracts of the Royal Navy’s ships and vessels with explanatory notes.

Description
Volume VI is the final volume of James’s Naval History, covering the closing years of the Napoleonic wars, the end of the War of 1812, and the post-war period. The 1886 edition extends well beyond James’s original terminal point (the accession of George IV in 1820), adding chapters on the Battle of Algiers (1816), the Burmese War (1824), and the Battle of Navarino (1827). The volume includes the great frigate duels of the War of 1812 — Shannon and Chesapeake, President and Little Belt, Constitution and Java — the burning of Washington, the attack on Baltimore, the Battle of Lake Champlain, the New Orleans expedition, the bombardment of Algiers, and the destruction of the Turco-Egyptian fleet at Navarino.
