State of the British Navy (p. 292) — New classification of the ships; British and American 74s; Sir Robert Sepping’s improvements; New plan of ship-building by Captain Hayes

1824

The Burmese War (p. 302) — The causes of the war; the British expedition to Rangoon; the capture of the great pagoda; operations in the Irrawaddy delta; the siege of Donabew; the march to Prome and the Treaty of Yandabo; Appendix to the Burmese War

1827

The Battle of Navarino (p. 358) — The Greek War of Independence; the Treaty of London; the allied fleet under Codrington; the destruction of the Turco-Egyptian fleet in Navarino Bay; the political consequences

Appendix

Appendix (p. 381) — Supplementary notes and documents
Annual Abstracts — Abstracts of ships and vessels belonging to the British Navy at the commencement of 1810, 1811, 1812, 1813, 1814, 1815
Notes to Annual Abstracts (p. 403)

Diagram

Action of the Shannon and Chesapeake

Key Events

1813: Shannon captures Chesapeake (50-minute action); Pelican takes Argus; Boxer vs Enterprise; Perry’s victory on Lake Erie; Amelia vs Aréthuse; British raids on Chesapeake Bay; Cockburn’s operations
1814: Fall of Napoleon; British burn Washington (Bladensburg); attack on Baltimore (“Star-Spangled Banner”); defeat on Lake Champlain (Macdonough); Essex captured off Valparaiso; Wasp’s cruise (sinks Reindeer, Avon); capture of Cattaro, Ragusa, and Genoa; end of the Napoleonic wars
1815: New Orleans expedition (Pakenham’s defeat); Endymion vs President; Constitution’s escapes and captures; Penguin vs Hornet; Napoleon’s surrender to HMS Bellerophon
1816: Lord Exmouth’s bombardment of Algiers; liberation of Christian slaves
1817–20: Post-war naval reductions; new ship classifications; Sepping’s design improvements
1824: The Burmese War — British expedition to Rangoon; campaigns in the Irrawaddy delta; Treaty of Yandabo
1827: Battle of Navarino — Codrington destroys the Turco-Egyptian fleet; Greek independence secured

sources/james-naval-occurrences-war-1812.title: james-naval-occurrences-war-1812
sources/james-naval-occurrences-war-1812.content:
William James — A Full and Correct Account of the Chief Naval Occurrences of the Late War Between Great Britain and the United States of America (1817)
Metadata

Author: William James (d. 1827)
Full title: A Full and Correct Account of the Chief Naval Occurrences of the Late War Between Great Britain and the United States of America; Preceded by a Cursory Examination of the American Accounts of Their Naval Actions Fought Previous to That Period: to Which Is Added an Appendix; with Plates
Publisher: T. Egerton, Whitehall, London
Year: 1817
Pages: xv + 530 + appendix + plates
OCLC: 754221
Source copy: Yale University Library
Raw text: james-naval-occurrences-war-1812.txt

Description
A contemporary British account of the naval War of 1812, written by William James while some details were still being gathered from officers dispersed across the United Kingdom. The work opens with a critical examination of American naval histories (particularly Clarke’s “Naval History”) before proceeding through the principal naval actions of the war in roughly chronological order. Each major engagement is presented with:

The meeting of the ships and circumstances leading to action
British and American accounts compared together
Each ship’s damages, losses, armament, and complement
Dimensions of each ship
Comparative force computed and exhibited in a statement
Remarks arising from that comparison

The work includes a retrospective on the naval actions of the War of 1776 and the quasi-war between the United States and France (1798–1800), providing context for the character of American naval armament. James was a prisoner in the United States at the outbreak of the war; his earlier pamphlet An Inquiry into the Merits of the Principal Naval Actions between Great Britain and the United States (published at Halifax) was expanded into the present work.
Chapters
Preface (pp. v–xv)
Explains the origin of the work: James, captured and imprisoned in the United States at the war’s outbreak, compiled a series of letters signed “Boxer” for the Naval Chronicle, followed by a Halifax pamphlet. This “entirely new work” expands those materials with fuller details, comparative force calculations, and a retrospective reaching back to the American Revolution. James acknowledges his inability to obtain certain British official letters that were suppressed from publication in the Gazette.
Chapter I — American Naval Histories, Armaments, and Ship Design (pp. 1–24)
Examines American accounts of their naval actions, the nature of ship armament (long guns vs. carronades), the history of the carronade, comparative advantages of large cannon, differences between British and American top-timber designs, tonnage measurement methods, and the standard composition of broadside metal.
Chapter II — Retrospective: The War of 1776 (pp. 25–36)
Naval actions between Britain and the American colonies during the Revolutionary War: H. M. S. Glasgow vs. an American squadron; the Nimrod vs. an American armed vessel; the action between the Serapis and the Bon Homme Richard.
Chapter III — The United States and France, 1798–1800 (pp. 37–54)
The quasi-war between the United States and revolutionary France: the Constellation vs. L’Insurgent; the Constellation vs. La Vengeance; comparative statements of force and official accounts.
Chapter IV — Declaration of War and Early Naval Operations, 1812 (pp. 55–78)
The United States declares war against Great Britain (June 1812). The Jamaica convoy is chased by an American squadron. Actions: the Constitution vs. Hornet (friendly); the President vs. Little Belt (the 1811 affair re-examined); the Constitution’s escape from the Belvidera squadron; the Essex’s early cruise.
Chapter V — The Guerriere Action and the State of the British Navy (pp. 79–98)
The inactive state of the British navy since Trafalgar and its effects. HMS Guerriere is captured by USS Constitution (August 19, 1812). James analyzes the comparative force, the American official account, and the impression created in the public mind.
Chapter VI — Frolic, Macedonian, and Wasp Actions (pp. 99–140)
The Frolic sails from Jamaica with convoy, hears of the war, and is captured by the Wasp. The Macedonian falls in with and engages USS United States (October 25, 1812). The Wasp vs. Frolic action (October 18, 1812). Each action includes comparative force statements and official letters.
Chapter VII — The Java Action (pp. 141–164)
The Java is commissioned and fitted for an East India voyage, departs Spithead, captures an American vessel, and is engaged and captured by the Constitution (December 29, 1812). Detailed comparative force analysis and official accounts, including the death of Captain Lambert.
Chapter VIII — Peacock and Hornet Action (pp. 165–184)
The British official account of the Peacock vs. Hornet action was never published in the Gazette. James provides American details alongside his own investigation, comparative force, and discussion of the Hornet’s subsequent escape from the Spitfire.
Chapter IX — Shannon and Chesapeake Action (pp. 185–212)
The Shannon and Tenedos reconnoitre Boston. The Chesapeake gets in unperceived. The Shannon (Captain Broke) challenges the Chesapeake (Captain Lawrence) to single-ship action (June 1, 1813). The engagement, boarding, and capture of the Chesapeake after fifteen minutes. Death of Captain Lawrence. Official letters, damages, comparative force, and Broke’s wound.
Chapter X — Commodore Rodgers’s North Cape Cruise (pp. 213–226)
Commodore Rodgers’s account of his chase off the North Cape. James identifies the chasing ships and compares the American commodore’s statements with the facts.
Chapter XI — Argus and Pelican Action (pp. 227–244)
The Pelican arrives at and departs from Cork in quest of the Argus, discovers, engages, and captures the American brig (August 14, 1813). The Argus had been焚烧 the British coast. Official letters, comparative force, and the trial of the Argus officers.
Chapter XII — Lake Erie Campaign (pp. 245–268)
Description of Lake Erie. Captain Barclay appointed to the command of the British squadron, list of his vessels. The Battle of Lake Erie (September 10, 1813). Barclay’s official letter, American accounts, comparative force, and the reasons for the British defeat.
Chapter XIII — The Essex in the Pacific (pp. 269–290)
The Phoebe leaves England, joined at Rio Janeiro by the Cherub and Racoon. The ships proceed to the Pacific in search of USS Essex (Captain Porter). The battle at Valparaiso (March 28, 1814). James critiques Porter’s account and presents the comparative force.
Chapter XIV — The President and the Blockading Squadron (pp. 291–322)
Operations of the blockading squadron off New York. The President (Commodore Rodgers) and Loire. The United States and Macedonian blockaded in New London. Boat expeditions, the capture of the Plantagenet’s boat, and the challenge between the Hornet and Loup-Cervier.
Chapter XV — Epervier and Reindeer Actions (pp. 323–342)
The Epervier captures the Alfred. Mutinous state of her crew. The Epervier is captured by the Peacock (April 29, 1814). The Reindeer vs. Wasp action (June 28, 1814), including the death of Captain Manners.
Chapter XVI — Boat Attacks on the Chesapeake (pp. 343–368)
Gallant boat-attack at the mouth of the Rappahannock: capture of four armed American schooners. The Avon vs. Wasp action (September 1, 1814). The Dispatch vs. the American privateer Syren. The British squadron on the coast of Africa.
Chapter XVII — Lake Huron and Lake Ontario (pp. 369–390)
Lake Erie continued: British capture of the Somers and Ohio; also the Scorpion and Tigress. Launching of British vessels on Lake Huron. Operations on Lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence: the Princess Charlotte, the Sir Sydney Smith, and the Netley.
Chapter XVIII — The President’s Last Cruise and Capture (pp. 391–418)
The President, accompanied by the store-ship Macedonian, leaves New York for the Bay of Bengal. Strikes on a mud-bar, springs a leak, and is chased by the British blockading squadron under Captain Hayes. The President is captured by the Endymion, Pomone, and Tenedos (January 15, 1815). James presents a detailed comparison of the American and British accounts.
Chapter XIX — Cyane and Levant vs. Constitution (pp. 419–458)
The Levant and Cyane sail from Gibraltar, fall in with the Constitution and determine to engage her (February 20, 1815). The action and its consequences. The Levant is recaptured. Courts-martial of the surviving officers and crews, who are honourably acquitted.
Chapter XX — Closing Naval Operations (pp. 459–500)
The St. Lawrence schooner bearing despatches. The American privateer Chasseur and her depredations. The Nautilus (East India Company ship) is attacked and captured by the Peacock after the knowledge of peace. James argues that this capture was an act of piracy. The Penguin is captured by the Hornet (March 23, 1815). Comparative statements.
Chapter XXI — Summary of Naval Losses (pp. 501–512)
Tabular summary: British losses (3 frigates, 7 sloops, 5 smaller vessels) against American losses (5 frigates, 19 sloops, and numerous smaller vessels, including those recaptured). James calculates the comparative tonnage and force lost on each side. He also notes the vast American merchant shipping captured by British cruisers.
Appendix (pp. 513–530+)
Contains the official letters and documents referenced throughout the work, numbered as appendices. Includes British and American official accounts, comparative force tables, and supplementary materials.
Plates
Four engraved plates depicting naval actions and profile-views of ships.
Index
Comprehensive alphabetical index to the entire work, including ship names, officers, engagements, and subjects.

sources/mahan-sea-power-history.title: Mahan — The Influence of Sea Power upon History, 1660–1783 (1890)
sources/mahan-sea-power-history.content:
Captain Alfred Thayer Mahan, The Influence of Sea Power upon History, 1660–1783. Published 1890; the text runs to approximately 2,300 lines across a preface, an introductory chapter, and fourteen chapters covering the era of sailing-ship naval warfare from the Restoration to the end of the American Revolution. This is Mahan’s foundational work — the book that established his thesis that control of the sea is the decisive factor in the rise and fall of nations, and that shaped naval strategic thinking worldwide for a generation.
The book’s period (1660–1783) ends before the 1800–1865 range of this wiki, but it is included as the essential theoretical and historical foundation for understanding British naval supremacy in the nineteenth century. Mahan’s analytical categories — the elements of sea power, the strategic role of commerce protection and destruction, the relationship between naval and military operations, and the institutional conditions that produce effective navies — were developed here and applied by him in his subsequent works covering the Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars (the companion volume The Influence of Sea Power upon the French Revolution and Empire, 1793–1812).
Contents at a Glance
Mahan’s argument proceeds on two levels. The first chapter states his general theory: that national power rests on six elements — geographical position, physical conformation, extent of territory, size of population, national character, and character of government — each of which bears upon a nation’s capacity to develop and maintain maritime strength. The remaining thirteen chapters apply this framework to the history of European naval warfare from the Restoration of Charles II in 1660 through the Peace of Versailles in 1783, with particular attention to the Anglo-Dutch wars, the wars of Louis XIV, the War of the Spanish Succession, the mid-century conflicts, and the American Revolutionary War.
Full Contents Map
Preface
Mahan states his object: “an examination of the general history of Europe and America with particular reference to the effect of sea power upon the course of that history.” He notes that historians have generally been unfamiliar with maritime conditions, and that naval historians have equally failed to connect their subject to general history. He dates the period from 1660 (when the sailing-ship era had fairly begun) to 1783 (the end of the American Revolution). ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-history.txt]
Introductory
Opens with the argument that the history of sea power is “largely, though by no means solely, a narrative of contests between nations.” Mahan discusses the methodology of studying naval history under changed technological conditions, arguing that the principles of naval warfare remain constant even as the means change — the sailing-ship era yields lessons of permanent value for the steam era. He distinguishes between precedent (which may be obsolete) and principle (which endures). ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-history.txt]
Chapter I — Discussion of the Elements of Sea Power
Mahan’s theoretical core. He identifies the six fundamental conditions affecting a nation’s sea power: geographical position (insular vs. continental nations), physical conformation (coastline, harbours, rivers), extent of territory (length of coastline relative to land borders), size of population (numbers available for maritime service and naval recruitment), national character (commercial instinct, adventurousness, aptitude for colonisation and seafaring), and character of government (whether the state’s institutions encourage or hamper maritime enterprise). Britain’s insular position, its deep harbours, and the commercial character of its people are presented as structural advantages; France’s continental commitments and its bifurcated Atlantic/Mediterranean coastline are presented as structural limitations. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-history.txt]
Chapter II — State of Europe in 1660. Second Anglo-Dutch War, 1665–1667. Sea Battles of Lowestoft and of the Four Days
Opens with the political situation in 1660: the restored Stuart monarchy in England, the Dutch Republic at its commercial zenith under the Grand Pensionary De Witt, France under the young Louis XIV with Colbert building a navy, and Spain in decline. The chapter centres on the Second Anglo-Dutch War (1665–1667), with detailed tactical accounts of the Battle of Lowestoft (1665) and the Four Days’ Battle (1666). Mahan analyses the Dutch raid on the Medway (1667) as a demonstration of the vulnerability of an unprepared naval power when its guard is down. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-history.txt]
Chapter III — War of England and France in Alliance against the Provinces, 1672–1674. Finally, of France against Combined Europe, 1674–1678. Sea Battles of Solebay, the Texel, and Stromboli
The Third Anglo-Dutch War (1672–1674), fought under the Treaty of Dover with France, marks England’s brief alliance with Louis XIV against the Dutch. Mahan examines the Battle of Solebay (1672) and the Battle of the Texel (1673), the latter in which De Ruyter prevented the Anglo-French combined fleet from landing troops in Holland. The chapter then follows the broader European war (1674–1678) after England’s withdrawal from the conflict, with de Ruyter’s final campaign in the Mediterranean and his death at the Battle of Stromboli. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-history.txt]
Chapter IV — English Revolution. War of the League of Augsburg, 1688–1697. Sea Battles of Beachy Head and La Hogue
The Glorious Revolution (1688) brought William III to the English throne and placed England in the Grand Alliance against Louis XIV. The naval war turns on the Battle of Beachy Head (1690), a French victory that gave Tourville temporary control of the Channel, and the Battle of La Hogue/Barfleur (1692), where the Anglo-Dutch fleet decisively defeated the French. Mahan reads La Hogue as the defining moment of the war: France lost its battle fleet and never seriously contested the Channel again, a strategic decision to abandon fleet action for commerce raiding that Mahan argues fatally weakened France’s position in the eighteenth-century wars. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-history.txt]
Chapter V — War of the Spanish Succession, 1702–1713. Sea Battle of Malaga
The War of the Spanish Succession saw Britain and the Dutch fighting France and Spain over the inheritance of the Spanish throne. Mahan’s focus is on the strategic use of sea power: British control of the Mediterranean (Gibraltar captured 1704, Minorca taken 1708), the supply of land armies in Spain and Portugal by sea, and the Battle of Malaga (1704) — the last fleet action of the war, tactically indecisive but strategically significant because the French fleet never again put to sea in force. The war’s outcome gave Britain Gibraltar and Minorca, commercial concessions in the Spanish Americas, and the Asiento slave-trading monopoly — the foundations of eighteenth-century British commercial supremacy. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-history.txt]
Chapter VI — The Regency in France. Alberoni in Spain. Policies of Walpole and Fleuri. War of the Polish Succession. English Contraband Trade in Spanish America. Great Britain Declares War against Spain. 1715–1739
A period of relative peace covering a quarter-century, through which Mahan traces the underlying commercial rivalry that made war inevitable. In France, the Regency and Cardinal Fleuri avoided naval competition; Britain under Walpole pursued peace and commercial expansion. The Spanish efforts under Alberoni to recover lost territories failed. British contraband trade with Spanish America grew massively, producing the frictions that led to the War of Jenkins’ Ear (1739). Mahan treats this period as a demonstration that peace is not the absence of conflict but the continuation of commercial competition by other means. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-history.txt]
Chapter VII — War between Great Britain and Spain, 1739. War of the Austrian Succession, 1740. France Joins Spain against Great Britain, 1744. Sea Battles of Matthews, Anson, and Hawke. Peace of Aix-la-Chapelle, 1748
The War of the Austrian Succession (1740–1748) merged the Anglo-Spanish conflict into a European war. Mahan covers the Mediterranean campaign of Admiral Matthews (Battle of Toulon, 1744), Anson’s circumnavigation and capture of the Manila galleon, and Hawke’s Atlantic operations. Anson’s reforms of the British navy after the war — improved dockyards, better supply systems, professionalised officer training — are treated as the institutional foundation of Britain’s naval dominance in the subsequent Seven Years’ War. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-history.txt]
Chapter VIII — Seven Years’ War, 1756–1763. England’s Overwhelming Power and Conquests on the Seas, in North America, Europe, and East and West Indies. Sea Battles: Byng off Minorca; Hawke and Conflans; Pocock and D’Aché in East Indies
The chapter that most fully demonstrates Mahan’s thesis in action. The Seven Years’ War is presented as Britain’s master-class in the application of sea power. Byng’s failure to relieve Minorca (1756) and his subsequent execution illustrate the cost of losing command of the sea. Hawke’s victory at Quiberon Bay (1759) destroyed the French invasion fleet in a winter gale and ended the last serious threat of French invasion of Britain. Mahan traces the British war on three global axes simultaneously: North America (the conquest of Canada through naval control of the St. Lawrence), India (Pocock’s defeat of D’Aché giving the British command of the Indian Ocean, allowing Clive’s victories on land), and the West Indies (the capture of French sugar islands). Pitt’s strategic direction — using the navy to transport and supply armies while blockading French ports — is held up as the model of how to conduct a maritime war. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-history.txt]
Chapter IX — Course of Events from the Peace of Paris to 1778. Maritime War Consequent upon the American Revolution. Sea Battle off Ushant
The period 1763–1778, between the end of the Seven Years’ War and the French entry into the American Revolution. Mahan traces the rebuilding of the French navy under Choiseul and Sartine — the only period in the eighteenth century when France made a sustained effort to match Britain at sea — and the political deterioration of the American colonies. The Battle of Ushant (1778), an indecisive action between Keppel and d’Orvilliers, marks the opening of the naval phase of the American war and reveals the persistent tactical conservatism of the British fleet, which Mahan contrasts with the more aggressive spirit that would develop later under Hood, Rodney, and Nelson. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-history.txt]
Chapter X — Maritime War in North America and West Indies, 1778–1781. Its Influence upon the Course of the American Revolution. Fleet Actions off Grenada, Dominica, and Chesapeake Bay
America’s war for independence, complicated by the entry of France (1778) and Spain (1779) and the League of Armed Neutrality (1780). Mahan analyses the naval campaigns in the West Indies and North America: the indecisive action off Grenada (1779), Rodney’s relief of Gibraltar and action off Cape St. Vincent (1780), and the critical Battle of the Chesapeake (1781) — the encounter de Grasse vs. Graves that Mahan makes the analytical centrepiece of the chapter. The Chesapeake is presented as the single clearest demonstration of sea power’s decisive influence: Graves’s failure to control the bay allowed de Grasse to land French troops and keep Washington and Rochambeau supplied, which made Cornwallis’s surrender at Yorktown inevitable. Britain lost an empire because it lost local command of the sea at the decisive moment. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-history.txt]
Chapter XI — Maritime War in Europe, 1779–1782
Operations in European waters: the Channel crisis of 1779 (the combined Franco-Spanish fleet threatening invasion), Rodney’s relief of Gibraltar in 1780, the Second Relief of Gibraltar by Howe in 1782, and the siege of the Rock. Mahan emphasises that Britain, now fighting France, Spain, and the American colonies simultaneously without an ally, was saved from invasion and defeat by the navy’s ability to maintain its squadrons at sea against numerically superior combined fleets — the decisive superiority being qualitative rather than quantitative. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-history.txt]
Chapter XII — Events in the East Indies, 1778–1781. Suffren Sails from Brest
The Indian Ocean theatre, where the brilliant French admiral Suffren fought five campaigns against the British under Hughes. Mahan’s treatment of Suffren — whom he clearly admires as the finest French sea commander of the century — examines his aggressive tactics, his strategic vision (the attempt to coordinate with Hyder Ali against the British in India), and the institutional failures that prevented his victories from being decisive: inadequate resources, lack of support from the French government, and the decaying condition of the French navy after the Revolution. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-history.txt]
Chapter XIII — Events in the West Indies after the Surrender of Yorktown. Encounters of De Grasse with Hood. The Sea Battle of the Saints. 1781, 1782
After Yorktown, the naval war in the West Indies continued. De Grasse prepared a combined Franco-Spanish expedition against Jamaica; Rodney met him at the Battle of the Saints (April 1782). Mahan analyses Rodney’s breaking of the French line — the tactical innovation that allowed the British fleet to defeat a numerically superior French force — and its consequences: Jamaica saved, peace negotiations (Treaty of Paris, 1783) salvaging some British possessions, and the lesson that the French navy, however well-built and officered under the old regime, could not maintain its position against British pressure when the British fought aggressively. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-history.txt]
Chapter XIV — Critical Discussion of the Maritime War of 1778
The concluding chapter is a retrospective analysis of the American Revolutionary War as a naval war. Mahan’s key argument: Britain lost the war not because of the weakness of its navy but because of the dispersion of its force across too many theatres, the indecisive tactics of its commanders (Graves in particular), and the failure to recognise that the American theatre was the decisive theatre. The chapter draws the strategic lessons of the war for British naval policy: concentration of force, destruction of the enemy fleet as the primary objective, and the critical importance of a unified command structure that could coordinate global operations. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-history.txt]
Coverage Guide

Elements of Sea Power theory — Chapter I. The foundational statement of Mahan’s thesis, applicable to understanding British naval supremacy throughout the 1800–1865 period.
Anglo-Dutch Wars — Chapters II–III. The origins of British commercial and naval dominance in the seventeenth century.
War of the Spanish Succession and Mediterranean bases — Chapter V. The acquisition of Gibraltar and Minorca.
Seven Years’ War as a model of amphibious strategy — Chapter VIII. Pitt’s global strategy, the conquest of Canada and India.
War of the American Revolution — Chapters IX–XIV. The loss of the American colonies analysed in naval terms; the Battle of the Chesapeake as the decisive moment.
Suffren’s Indian Ocean campaign — Chapter XII. French naval operations in the East Indies. Cross-reference with clowes-royal-navy for the British view.
Institutional reforms — Chapters VII–VIII. Anson’s and Pitt’s administrative reforms, providing context for the 1800–1865 period.

Quality
Blackmask Online edition, scanned and proofread. Clean text with minimal OCR degradation. The work is classic American naval strategic writing: dense, argument-driven, and clearly structured. Mahan writes as a serving naval officer (later rear-admiral) with a didactic purpose — to demonstrate the permanent importance of sea power to his own nation. His account of eighteenth-century wars is based on extensive use of British and French secondary sources and published documents, and his strategic judgments, though sometimes controversial, rest on clearly stated reasoning.
See Also

british-navy

sources/martineau-1800-1815.title: Martineau — History of England, A.D. 1800-1815 (Introduction to the Peace)
sources/martineau-1800-1815.content:
Martineau — History of England, A.D. 1800-1815 (Introduction to the Peace)
Harriet Martineau (1802–1876) — History of England, A.D. 1800-1815: being an introduction to The history of the peace. — London: George Bell & Sons, 1878 edition.
[A separate single-volume work from Martineau’s larger History of England from the Commencement of the XIXth Century to the Crimean War (4 vols.). This volume was written as an introduction to her History of the Peace and covers the period from the opening of the 19th century through the Battle of Waterloo and the Second Treaty of Paris. It fills the 1807–1815 gap left by the larger work’s first volume, which only reaches 1809.]
The text is 33,563 lines, OCR’d from an Archive.org scan of the Harvard College Library copy (ARL: kat: T1431375).
Relationship to Martineau’s Larger Work
The existing source page martineau-history-of-england-vol1.md covers Vol. I of Martineau’s 4-volume work (1790–1809), with Book I (1800–1807) and Book II (1807–1809). That volume’s Book II ends with the Portland Administration’s collapse, Moore’s death at Corunna, and the cultural survey of ~1809. This separate volume carries the story forward to 1815:

Vol. I (4-vol. set) → ends ~1809 (Portland, Moore, Walcheren, Duke of York scandal)
This volume → covers ALL of 1800–1815, with Book II (Ch I–X) covering 1807–1815 in far greater detail than Vol. I, including the full Peninsular War (through to Toulouse), the War of 1812, Luddism, Perceval’s assassination, and Waterloo.

There is some overlap in Book I (1800–1807), where both volumes cover the same ground from Pitt’s resignation through the Ministry of All the Talents. Book II of this volume is where the principal new material lies.
Content Summary
BOOK I — 1800–1807 (pp. 1–248)
Chapter I: Balancing System [1800]
State of Europe at the close of the 18th century. Martineau opens with the European Balance of Power and the great powers — Russia, Austria, Prussia, England, France. The French Revolution shatters the old equilibrium. Napoleon Bonaparte’s rise to First Consul is presented as both symptom and cause of the new era. The narrative pivots to England’s condition under Pitt: sedition at home, financial strain from the war, naval mutinies, and the smouldering Irish crisis. A detailed portrait of the middle and industrial classes, the harshness of the criminal law, and the subsistence of the poor closes the chapter.
Chapter II: Pitt, Catholic Question, Copenhagen, Aboukir, Peace of Amiens [1801–1802]
Pitt’s resignation, Nelson at Copenhagen, Abercromby in Egypt, the Peace of Amiens. Martineau offers a damning assessment of British statesmanship, calling it a wonder the nation survived the intrigues about the throne. The Catholic Question fractures Pitt’s Cabinet; the King’s first serious illness throws government into crisis. The Northern Confederacy (Russia, Prussia, Sweden, Denmark) is formed; Nelson forces the Battle of Copenhagen (2 April 1801). Meanwhile Abercromby’s expedition defeats the French at Aboukir, though Abercromby falls on the field. Pitt resigns over the King’s refusal to concede Catholic Emancipation. Addington succeeds him and negotiates the Treaty of Amiens (March 1802). A fragile peace, widely mistrusted, is achieved.
Chapter III: Irish Union, Emmett Rebellion, Coercion [1801–1806]
Ireland under the Union, Robert Emmett’s rising. As the Union flag was hoisted on 1 January 1801, the Catholic Question remained unresolved. The Union ended the domination of the great Irish families but the religious quarrel grew more formidable. A mysterious paper, purportedly from Pitt, inflamed Catholic expectations of emancipation that were never fulfilled. The Emmett conspiracy: Robert Emmett’s plot, the outbreak in Dublin, the murder of Lord Kilwarden, and the rebellion’s swift collapse. Martineau dwells on the savage repression that followed. The Duke of Bedford’s viceroyalty and Irish currency troubles compound the distress.
Chapter IV: Precarious Peace, War Declared, Despard’s Plot [1800–1804]
The collapse of the Peace of Amiens, renewal of war, Colonel Despard’s conspiracy. The rejoicing at peace gave way to misgivings before the treaty was concluded. The Bantry Bay mutiny, Addington’s weakness, French provocations (the Peltier affair), and a spectacular Stock Exchange hoax precede the declaration of war. English travellers caught in France by the rupture, the first naval captures, the loss of Hanover, and Colonel Despard’s revolutionary conspiracy in London (he is executed with his accomplices). Governor Wall is also executed for past cruelties. The fragile Addington ministry is exposed.
Chapter V: Grenville Letter, King’s Illness, Addington Falls [1801–1804]
The intercepted Grenville letter, the King’s madness, Pitt’s return. A captured East Indiaman yields Lord Grenville’s frank correspondence revealing the state of parties and the conviction that Addington must go. The King’s anxieties and recurring illness are described with sympathy. Debates on the defence of the country expose the ministry’s paralysis. Addington resigns and Pitt returns as Prime Minister. The loss of West India ships to Admiral Linois and solemn war ceremonials in London mark the chapter’s close.
Chapter VI: Napoleon Emperor, Trafalgar, Austerlitz, Pitt’s Death [1804–1806]
Napoleon’s coronation, the great battles, the death of Pitt. Napoleon’s elevation to Emperor (May 1804, coronation 1 December). The Additional Force Bill, the Catamaran expedition against Boulogne, the seizure of Spanish treasure ships, war with Spain. Lord Melville’s impeachment over naval administration (the Tenth Report scandal). Then the great battles: Nelson’s pursuit of the combined fleet, Trafalgar (21 October 1805), Nelson’s death and character. On land: Mack’s surrender at Ulm, the French in Vienna, Austerlitz (2 December 1805) shatters the Third Coalition. Pitt, broken by the news, falls ill and dies on 23 January 1806.
Chapter VII: Wellesley in India, Mahratta War, Assaye [1801–1806]
Arthur Wellesley’s Indian campaigns. The Mahratta confederacy and its five great chiefs (Scindia, Holkar, the Peshwa, the Gaikwar, the Bhonsla). The Mahratta War: Wellesley in the Deckan, the astonishing victory at Assaye (1803) against overwhelming odds, Argaum, the destruction of the Mahratta infantry. General Lake’s campaign in Hindustan: the battle of Delhi, restoration of the blind Mughal Emperor, the battle of Laswarree. The war’s results — the break-up of the Mahratta empire, new treaties establishing British supremacy. Lord Cornwallis returns as Governor-General but dies soon after.
Chapter VIII: Ministry of All the Talents, Fox, Slave Trade [1806–1807]
The Grenville-Fox coalition, the abolition of the slave trade. With Pitt dead, the King reluctantly accepts a ministry under Lord Grenville with Charles James Fox as Foreign Secretary. Fox’s ill-fated peace negotiations with France fail. The reprobation of the slave trade in Parliament, Wilberforce’s campaign, the colonial slave trade prohibition. Fox’s illness and death (September 1806). The war in Europe: Maida in Calabria, the recapture of the Cape of Good Hope, the disastrous Buenos Ayres expedition. Prussia lies humiliated by Napoleon. The Slave Trade Abolition Act is passed (March 1807) — a moral triumph — but the ministry collapses under the Catholic Question.
Chapter IX: Fall of the Talents, Abolition, “No Popery” [1806–1807]
The dismissal of the Talents and Tory reaction. The King demands pledges against further Catholic relief; the ministry refuses and is dismissed. The Duke of Portland forms a nominal administration. The “No Popery” cry sweeps the general election of 1807, returning an anti-Catholic majority. The short-lived Grenville ministry — the “Ministry of All the Talents” — ends, having achieved the abolition of the slave trade. The country returns to Tory rule with the long war still unresolved. Book I closes.

BOOK II — 1807–1815 (pp. 249–537)
Chapter I: Portland Administration, Copenhagen, Tilsit, Peninsular Opening [1807]
A feeble ministry thrust into a European crisis. Martineau opens with a blistering indictment: the Portland Administration’s imbecility was admitted even by its friends. The Duke of Portland himself sat for hours drugged with laudanum; the Cabinet contained Hawkesbury and Castlereagh, “two of the weakest men in public life.” Into this vacuum came Napoleon’s Berlin Decree and the Continental System. After Tilsit (July 1807), Napoleon and Alexander divide Europe. England responds by seizing the Danish fleet at Copenhagen — a bombardment and surrender Martineau examines with moral ambivalence. The Dardanelles and Egyptian expeditions are followed by the Russian declaration of war and the loss of the Swedish alliance. Napoleon invades Portugal; the Portuguese royal family flees to Brazil. The Spanish Bourbons are enticed to Bayonne. The Peninsular War opens.
Chapter II: Peninsular War, Moore’s Campaign, Corunna, Walcheren, Duke of York Scandal, Castlereagh-Canning Duel [1807–1809]
The disasters of 1808–1809. Moore’s heroic death, Walcheren catastrophe, the Cabinet tears itself apart. Napoleon’s entanglement with the Spanish Bourbons: Godoy’s intrigues, Ferdinand at Bayonne, the Madrid tumult, the Bourbon renunciation. Wellesley’s initial victories and the controversial Convention of Cintra. Sir John Moore’s daring advance into Spain, the terrible winter retreat to Corunna, Moore’s death on the field and burial. The Walcheren expedition — the largest British amphibious operation of the war, a catastrophe of mismanagement and fever that decimated the army. Naval successes under Collingwood and his death. At home: the Duke of York’s mistress Mary Anne Clarke sells commissions; a parliamentary inquiry forces his resignation. The rivalry between Castlereagh and Canning culminates in their duel on Putney Heath. Perceval becomes Prime Minister amid national gloom.
Chapter III: O.P. Question, Bullion Committee, Burdett in Tower, Regency Crisis [1810–1812]
Theatre riots, currency debates, a radical sent to the Tower, and the King’s final madness. The O.P. (Old Prices) riots at Covent Garden — theatregoers rioting for months against raised prices — illustrate the quarrelsome temper of a war-weary nation. The commercial crash, the Bullion Committee’s report on currency and the paper pound, early reform efforts under Romilly and Mackintosh. Sir Francis Burdett’s privilege dispute with the Commons: he defends the right to publish parliamentary debates and is committed to the Tower — a constitutional crisis that grips London. The Princess Amelia’s death (November 1810) triggers George III’s final descent into incurable madness. Parliament adjourns repeatedly; the Regency question dominates politics.
Chapter IV: Restrictions on the Regent, Perceval’s Assassination [1811–1812]
The restricted regency, negotiations fail, Perceval shot dead in the Commons. The ministers hope for the King’s recovery and limit the Prince Regent’s powers; the Whigs expect to return to office. The Prince grows estranged from his old Whig allies. When the restriction expires, he invites Lords Grenville and Grey to form a government — then reneges after their refusal to accept patronage limitations. Perceval continues as Prime Minister. On 11 May 1812, a deranged bankrupt named John Bellingham shoots Spencer Perceval dead in the lobby of the House of Commons. The shock and confusion are profound. Parliament provides for Perceval’s family. The country is adrift, the Peninsular War floundering, with no clear successor.
Chapter V: Luddism, Frame-Breaking, Luddite Acts [1811–1814]
The machine-breaking crisis. Commercial distress, Luddite risings, Lord Sidmouth’s repression. Nothing in living memory compared to the distress of 1811–12. The collapse of foreign commerce, the failure of manufacturing credit, wheat at 112s. a quarter. The factor system broke the relationship between employer and operative. Into this misery came Luddism: frame-breaking in Nottinghamshire, the destruction of machinery by stocking-weavers. The Luddite Acts made frame-breaking capital. Lord Sidmouth as Home Secretary deployed spies, troops, and mass prosecutions. The movement spread to Yorkshire and Lancashire. A plentiful harvest in 1813 and renewed continental trade brought a temporary lull, but by 1814 Luddism resumed as the agricultural crash brought down 240 of 700 country banks.
Chapter VI: Full Peninsular War — Talavera, Torres Vedras, Badajoz, Salamanca, Vittoria, Toulouse [1809–1814]
Wellington’s six-year campaign from Lisbon to Toulouse. Parliament resolves to persevere after Moore’s catastrophe. Wellesley lands at Lisbon on 22 April 1809 — he would not need his ships again until the pacification of Europe. Talavera (1809, after which Wellesley becomes Wellington), the grim defensive Lines of Torres Vedras, Busaco, the expulsion of the French from Portugal. Albuera, the sieges of Ciudad Rodrigo and Badajoz (stormed with terrible loss), Salamanca, the occupation of Madrid, the failure at Burgos, and the harrowing retreat. Napoleon’s Russian campaign shifts the balance. Wellington is made Commander-in-Chief of the allied armies in Spain. Vittoria (1813) breaks French power; Wellington invades France. The campaign of 1814 ends with the storming of Toulouse — fought after Napoleon had already abdicated, costing 8,000 lives from delayed news. Wellington enters Paris as ambassador.
Chapter VII: War of 1812, Treaty of Ghent [1812–1815]
The “bootless war” with America. Martineau is scathing: “as purposeless, as foolish, as unnecessary, as it was ill-managed, useless, and discreditable.” The Orders in Council and the Right of Search were the ostensible causes. The war ends without settling either. The burning of Washington (1814) is the most dramatic British success. The Mississippi expedition, the Battle of New Orleans (fought after peace was signed), and the capture of Fort Mobile. The Treaty of Ghent leaves everything as before the war — no better terms than those rejected in 1808. Martineau closes with the verdict that history should tear out “that page which must contain the narrative of the bootless war of 1812–15.”
Chapter VIII: Princess Charlotte, Press (Cobbett/Hunt), East India Charter, Finance [1812–1814]
The Regent’s unhappy family, the radical press, India, finance. As the King’s recovery becomes hopeless, attention fixes on the Princess Charlotte, heir to the throne, and her troubled relationship with her father the Regent. Charlotte’s suitors (the Prince of Orange), her flight to her mother, and her eventual marriage to Prince Leopold of Saxe-Coburg. A survey of the press: the Morning Chronicle under Perry, William Cobbett’s Political Register, the Hunts (Leigh and John) of the Examiner. The Printers’ Name Bill and prosecutions for seditious libel. The renewal of the East India Company’s Charter (1813) opens India to missionaries and establishes church establishment there. Bible societies, the prophetess Joanna Southcote, a Stock Exchange fraud, and the burning of the Custom House (1814).
Chapter IX: Napoleon’s Fall, Hundred Days, Waterloo [1813–1815]
Leipzig, the abdication, Elba, the Hundred Days, Waterloo. A month after Napoleon’s return from Russia, the remnants of the Grande Armée drift back to Paris. The renewed Allied compact, the spring campaign, the armistice, Austria’s declaration of war, Dresden, Leipzig (the Battle of the Nations) shatters Napoleon’s German Empire. The Allies cross the Rhine; Paris capitulates. Napoleon abdicates at Fontainebleau, attempts suicide, departs for Elba. The Bourbons return; the Treaty of Paris is signed. Then the Hundred Days: Napoleon’s escape, his march to Paris, the renewal of war. Quatre-Bras, Ligny, and Waterloo (18 June 1815). Martineau describes Wellington’s victory and Napoleon’s final exile to St. Helena. The Second Treaty of Paris (November 1815). Wellington’s farewell: “England is still at Peace.”
Chapter X: Cultural Survey, Steam Navigation, Necrology [1801–1815]
Steam, the arts, the reviews, science, and the dead of the period. Martineau traces the early development of steam navigation — Fulton’s Hudson River success (1807), Symington, Henry Bell’s Comet (1811) — and Boulton and Watt’s innovations. Chain cables, steam carriages, Trevithick. The Edinburgh Review (1802) and the Quarterly Review (1809) are discussed with ambivalence. The Edinburgh Review’s tyranny of literary opinion is contrasted with its service to liberal causes. Bentham, Herschel, Davy, Dalton, Wollaston, Leslie, Cavendish, Maskelyne represent science. The artists (Boydell, Morland, Barry, Opie, Hoppner, De Loutherbourg), the authors (Home, Cumberland, Percy, Porson, Dibdin, Dr. Burney), the clergymen (Horsley, Hurd), philologists (Horne Tooke), philosophers (Paley, condemned for shallowness), philanthropists (Granville Sharp), diplomats (Lord Macartney), and explorers (Mungo Park). The book closes with Park’s mysterious death on the Niger.
Necrology (1800–1815)
Key deaths noted in Chapter X: Nelson (1805, Trafalgar), Pitt (1806), Fox (1806), Sir Ralph Abercromby (1801, Aboukir), Sir John Moore (1809, Corunna), Spencer Perceval (1812, assassinated), the Duke of Portland (1809), Lord Collingwood (1810), Lord Melville (acquitted 1805 but politically ruined, his actual death not in this period), Princess Amelia (1810), George III (living at close of volume — he would die in 1820).
All Chapters Present
All 19 chapters are present in the raw text (Book I: Ch I–IX; Book II: Ch I–X). OCR renders “CHAPTER V” as “CHAPTER Y” in some headers but the text is complete. The volume runs to about 33,563 lines of OCR text.

sources/martineau-history-of-england-vol.title: Martineau — History of England, Vol. I: Introduction (1790–1809)
sources/martineau-history-of-england-vol.content:
Martineau — History of England, Vol. I: Introduction (1790–1809)
Harriet Martineau (1802–1876) — History of England from the Commencement of the XIXth Century to the Crimean War. Vol. I. — Porter & Coates, Philadelphia, 1887 (American Edition).
The first volume of Martineau’s comprehensive history serves as an introductory prelude covering the state of Europe before the 19th century, the Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars (1793–1815), the Peace of Amiens, the rise of Napoleon, Pitt’s second ministry and the Third Coalition, Trafalgar and Austerlitz, Wellesley’s Indian campaigns, the Ministry of All the Talents and the abolition of the slave trade, and the troubled Portland administration (1807–1809) with the Copenhagen expedition, the Peninsular War beginning at Vimeiro and Corunna, the Duke of York scandal, and the Regency crisis. The volume closes with an extensive survey of cultural and intellectual life in the first decade of the century.
The text is 25,719 lines, OCR’d from the University of California library copy (ark:/13960/t83j85f5s).
All chapters reported in the Table of Contents are present in the raw text. (Chapters V of Book I and Book II are present — the OCR renders the Roman numeral “V” as the letter “Y” in running headers, which can cause false reports of missing text.)
Content Summary

Preface to the American Edition — a note on the republication, explaining that the original work ended in 1846 and has been extended to the Crimean War; also an editorial note on the division of labour between the original authors

BOOK I — Background to the 19th Century (to 1806)


Chapter I — The Balancing System — the state of Europe before the 19th century: the balance-of-power system and its history in the 18th century, Russia under Paul I, Austria, Prussia, England’s supremacy at sea, France after the Revolution, the rise of Bonaparte as First Consul. England’s proposal of peace to France and the rejection by Bonaparte, French successes in Italy and Egypt, the rupture between England and France, and the challenges of a new kind of warfare and politics


Chapter II — The New Century Opens (1801) — the state of England at the opening of the 19th century: Pitt’s ministry, the Catholic question dividing the Cabinet, the King’s first serious illness, the Northern Confederacy (Russia, Prussia, Sweden, Denmark), Nelson at Copenhagen (April 2, 1801), the Egyptian expedition and the Battle of Aboukir, the death of Sir Ralph Abercromby. Pitt’s resignation over the Catholic question, Addington’s ministry formed, peace negotiations with France, the Treaty of Amiens (March 1802), and the general sense of relief and hope at the arrival of peace


Chapter III — Ireland and Domestic Affairs — the Irish Union (1801) and its aftermath, continuing discontents in Ireland, French tampering with Irish malcontents, Robert Emmett’s conspiracy (1803), the murder of Lord Kilwarden during Emmett’s rising, coercion acts passed, currency troubles and the state of the Irish economy. During the precarious peace: the Bantry Bay mutiny, English travellers flocking to the Continent, the prosecution of Peltier for libel against Bonaparte, French aggressions in Italy and Switzerland, the renewal of war (May 1803), and the seizure of Hanover by the French


Chapter IV — The Addington Ministry — the Prince of Wales’s financial affairs and his disputes with the King, English detained in France at the rupture of the peace, first naval captures of French and Spanish ships, Colonel Despard’s plot for insurrection (hanged 1803), the execution of Governor Wall for murder, the state of party politics, the Grenville letter exposing the weakness of the ministry, the King’s second illness, the defence debates, the volunteer movement, and the fall of Addington’s ministry under accumulating criticism. Pitt returns as War Minister (May 1804)


Chapter V — The New Parliament and Pitt’s Second Ministry — the general election of 1804, Pitt’s second administration formed, the rupture with Spain (the seizure of the treasure fleet), the reconciliation of Pitt and Addington, the additional force bill for raising troops, Lord Melville’s impeachment for mismanagement of the navy (the Tenth Report scandal — Melville acquitted 1805, but politically ruined), Napoleon crowned Emperor, the formation of the Third Coalition with Austria and Russia, Nelson in the Mediterranean


Chapter VI — Napoleon and the War — Napoleon’s Imperial coronation, the additional force bill, the continental alliances against France, the catamaran expedition against Boulogne (failed attempt to destroy the invasion flotilla), relations with Spain and the seizure of Spanish treasure ships, Mack’s surrender at Ulm (October 1805), the French army in Vienna, Nelson’s pursuit of the combined fleet, the Battle of Trafalgar (October 21, 1805) and Nelson’s death, the Battle of Austerlitz (December 2, 1805) and the destruction of the Third Coalition, the Austrian treaty of Pressburg, Pitt’s illness and death (January 1806)


Chapter VII — Wellesley in India — Arthur Wellesley’s administration and military campaigns in India under his brother the Governor-General Marquess Wellesley, the subsidiary system described, the Mahratta confederacy and its five chiefs (Scindia, Holkar, the Peshwa, the Gaikwar, the Bhonsla), the Mahratta War, the Battle of Assye (September 1803) with the 74th and 78th Highlanders, the Battle of Argaum, General Lake’s campaign in Hindustan, the assault on Delhi, the restoration of the blind Mogul Emperor Shah Alam, the Battle of Laswarree and the destruction of the Mahratta artillery, the results of the campaigns consolidating British power, Cornwallis as Governor-General and his death, the recall of Marquess Wellesley


Chapter VIII — The Ministry of All the Talents (1806–1807) — the meeting of Parliament after Pitt’s death, the King’s well-known dislike of Fox, Lord Grenville and Charles James Fox forming the coalition ministry, the negotiations for peace with France (failed), the reprobation of the slave trade by the Commons on Fox’s motion, Wilberforce’s continuing parliamentary campaign, the colonial slave trade prohibition in 1806, the acquittal of Lord Melville on his impeachment, Fox’s illness and death (September 1806), the Battle of Maida (July 1806) in Calabria, the recovery of the Cape of Good Hope from the Dutch, Sir Home Popham’s unauthorised expedition to Buenos Ayres (captured and lost), the humiliation of Prussia after Jena and Auerstädt


Chapter IX — The Fall of the Talents — the dissolution of parties after Pitt’s death, the dissolution of parliament and the general election of 1806, the state of the army and navy and the country’s resources, the financial scheme of Lord Henry Petty (later Lord Lansdowne), the abolition of the slave trade (Act of March 1807, effective May 1), the re-emergence of the Catholic question — the proposal to admit Catholics to the higher ranks of the army and navy, the Irish Act of 1793 limiting Catholic eligibility, the King’s demand that the Cabinet pledge never to concede further Catholic emancipation, the King’s retractation of his promise and the dismissal of the Talents, the “No Popery” cry in the general election of 1807, and the return of an anti-Catholic majority


BOOK II — The Portland Administration (1807–1809)


Chapter I — The Portland Administration — the formation of the Duke of Portland’s nominal administration (the real power with Perceval, Canning, Castlereagh, Eldon, and Liverpool), the dissolution of Parliament and the general election of 1807, the King’s deep prejudices against Catholic relief, the character and influence of Lord Eldon Lord Chancellor and Lord Malmesbury, the changing tone of political discourse with Cobbett and Burdett emerging as tribunes of popular opinion, the weakness and internal disunity of the Cabinet


Chapter II — Copenhagen and the Peninsular Beginnings — Napoleon in northern Europe after Tilsit, the secret Treaty of Tilsit between France and Russia, the Copenhagen expedition (August–September 1807): the British demand that Denmark surrender its fleet, the refusal, the bombardment of Copenhagen, the surrender of the Danish fleet (18 ships of the line, 15 frigates), the moral controversy in England over attacking a neutral power, Napoleon’s Berlin and Milan Decrees establishing the Continental System, the Peninsular War begins with the French invasion of Portugal and Spain, Sir Arthur Wellesley sent to Portugal, the Battle of Vimeiro (August 1808), the controversial Convention of Cintra (allowing the defeated French to evacuate Portugal with their arms and plunder), the recall of Wellesley and the Board of Inquiry


Chapter III — The Duke of York and the War — the Duke of York as Commander-in-Chief, the scandal of his mistress Mary Anne Clarke selling army commissions through her influence, Colonel Wardle’s investigation in the House of Commons, Mrs. Clarke’s sensational revelations before the parliamentary committee, the Duke of York’s resignation as Commander-in-Chief, the trial of the Duke of York, the close of 1809 — a year that had exhausted the nation’s confidence in its military leadership


Chapter IV — The State of the Nation — the opposing views of the ministerial and opposition parties on the condition of the country, parliamentary debates on the conduct of the war and its cost, the financial strain of the war with falling revenue and rising deficits, the state of agriculture, manufactures, and commerce under the weight of war taxation, the condition of the working classes, the debates on the budget and the raising of supplies


Chapter V — The Walcheren Expedition — the disastrous Walcheren expedition of 1809: the largest British amphibious operation of the war conceived to destroy the French fleet at Antwerp, the landing on Walcheren island, the capture of Flushing, the failure to push on to Antwerp, the outbreak of Walcheren fever (malaria) that devastated the army, the evacuation and the loss of 4,000 men to disease, the parliamentary inquiry and the political damage to the ministry, Canning and Castlereagh’s mutual recriminations over responsibility


Chapter VI — The National Consultations — the general election after the scandals and disasters of 1809, the attempt to form a broader administration, Perceval’s ministry formed (October 1809) — a weak government without the leading figures of either party, the debates on the state of the nation, the parliamentary opposition led by Lord Grey and Lord Grenville, attempts to criticise the conduct of the war


Chapter VII — Governing the Country — the immense difficulty of government in 1810 with a hated ministry and a failing King, the Regency question emerges as the King’s health deteriorates, detailed account of George III’s final descent into mental illness (his last period of sanity ending October 1810), the medical and political crisis over the King’s incapacity, the Prince of Wales’s position (not yet formally Regent), the debates on restrictions on the Regent’s powers


Chapter VIII — The King’s Illness — the steady and final decline of George III into incurable mental illness, the growing hopelessness of his recovery (the King would never again resume government), the Regency Bill of 1811 debated at length — restrictions on the Prince Regent’s powers for a period of one year (including the power to create peers and grant offices), the Prince Regent’s attitude and his abandonment of his Whig friends, Spencer Perceval continues as Prime Minister with the Regency


Chapter IX — Napoleon’s Return and the Peninsular War — Napoleon’s return to Paris from Spain after the Austrian war, the Peninsular campaign renewed, Sir John Moore’s advance into Spain and the strategic situation, the French pursuit under Soult and Napoleon, the terrible retreat to Corunna in deep winter, the discipline and suffering of the army, the Battle of Corunna (January 16, 1809), Moore’s death and burial, the evacuation of the British army by sea, the national mourning for Moore and the recognition of his achievement in saving the army


Chapter X — Explorations and the Wider World — the history of a people in wartime — a cultural survey of the first decade of the century: Mungo Park’s second African expedition (his death on the Niger, 1806), Lord Macartney’s embassy to China, the state of scientific and geographical knowledge in 1809, the Royal Institution and the advancement of science, the Edinburgh Review and the Quarterly Review, the Lake poets (Wordsworth, Coleridge, Southey), the essayists (Hazlitt, Lamb, Sydney Smith), the state of the arts and literature at the close of the decade, the condition of the people after ten years of war

sources/martineau-history-of-england-vol.title: Martineau — History of England, Vol. II: From the Congress of Vienna to the End of Lord Liverpool's Government (1815–1826)
sources/martineau-history-of-england-vol.content:
Martineau — History of England, Vol. II: From the Congress of Vienna to the End of Lord Liverpool’s Government (1815–1826)
Harriet Martineau (1802–1876) — History of England from the Commencement of the XIXth Century to the Crimean War. Vol. II. — 1864 Edition.
The second volume covers the decade of peace and unrest that followed the Napoleonic Wars, from the Congress of Vienna (1815) through the Liverpool administration down to the commercial crisis of 1825–26. Martineau traces the great political, economic, and social struggles of the period: the post-war depression, the Corn Laws, the radical agitation culminating in Peterloo, the Queen Caroline affair, the emergence of Canning, the Catholic question, and the speculation mania of 1825.
The text is 25,422 lines, OCR’d from the University of California library copy (ark:/13960/t0wp9wh71).
Note on Chapter XIV: This chapter was previously marked as “[Not present in text]” but is in fact present in the raw text at line 10785. The volume contains 17 chapters in Book I and 12 chapters in Book II — all 29 chapters are present.
Content Summary
BOOK I — From the Settlement of Europe to the Accession of George IV (1815–1820)


Chapter I — The Congress of Vienna and the Peace — the settlement of Europe after Waterloo: the Congress of Vienna’s territorial rearrangements, the second Treaty of Paris, the Holy Alliance and the principles of the allies, the return of the Bourbons, Castlereagh’s navigation of the competing interests of Russia, Austria, and Prussia, Britain’s enormous war debt and the challenge of demobilisation, the state of parties at home — Eldon and Liverpool, the opposition led by Lord Grey, Lord Grenville, and Henry Brougham, the abolitionist movement, Paris in the autumn of 1815, commerce and territorial limits settled by peace, the general results of the peace settlement


Chapter II — The Prince Regent’s Speech and the New Parliament (1816) — Castlereagh’s triumphal reception in the Commons after Vienna, the Prince Regent’s speech praising the establishment of peace, the House of Commons of 1816 and the presumption of the government, the Property Tax debate — Brougham and Lord John Russell demanding rigid economy, Castlereagh’s infamous remark about the people’s “ignorant impatience” to be relieved of taxation, the defeat of the income tax, the civil list and the expenses of the royal family, the character and expenditure of the Prince Regent


Chapter III — Agriculture, Corn Laws, and Currency — post-war agricultural distress from the collapse of wartime prices, the Corn Law of 1815 (prohibiting import of foreign wheat until domestic price reached 80s.), the effects of the Corn Laws on the price of provisions, the burden of tithes and poor rates on the land, the state of manufactures and commerce in the depression, the currency question and the controversy over resuming cash payments, Mr. Horner on currency and the Bullion Committee’s recommendations, petitions from the agricultural counties, Ricardo’s monetary theories


Chapter IV — Poverty, Discontent, and Sedition — the collapse of the wartime economy, high food prices, demobilisation of soldiers and sailors and the failure of employment, post-war poverty and its manifestations, frame-breaking in the Midlands, private benevolence and charitable efforts, the legacy of Luddism, early reform meetings and the government’s growing fear that all popular political organisation was seditious


Chapter V — The Rise of the Radical Movement — the emergence of mass radicalism in 1816–17, the development of a politically conscious middle class, parliamentary reform debates revived, William Cobbett’s writings in the “twopenny trash” Political Register, the Hampden Clubs and Major Cartwright’s provincial tours, the Spencean Philanthropists (followers of Thomas Spence who advocated the common ownership of land), the Spa Fields meeting of December 1816, Orator Hunt’s rise, the riot subdued, the real dangers facing the government, novelty of female reform societies


Chapter VI — The Barbary States and the Algerine Expedition — Lord Exmouth’s 1816 naval expedition against Algiers to suppress Barbary piracy and end Christian slavery, the bombardment of Algiers, the second Algerine expedition, the treaties with Algiers, Tunis, and Tripoli, the release of Christian captives, Britain’s Mediterranean naval power projection and the international effort to suppress piracy, a diversion from domestic affairs


Chapter VII — Social Improvement and Reform — the progress of social improvement in the darkest years of the post-war depression, Sir Samuel Romilly and the reform of the criminal law (his campaign to reduce the number of capital offences), the new police system emerging, gas-lighting in London’s streets, mendicity and vagrancy, Poor Law administration and the system of allowances (Speenhamland system), the workhouse, elementary education and the Education Commission, the founding of savings-banks, the Elgin Marbles purchased for the nation, Elizabeth Fry’s prison work, the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge, Sunday Schools, Robert Owen’s New Lanark experiment, the Bible Society and missionary organisations


Chapter VIII — The Spanish American Colonies — the revolutions in Spanish America (Bolívar, San Martín, O’Higgins), British policy toward the independence movements, the debates over recognising the new republics, English merchants financing the revolutionaries, the strategic interest in breaking Spain’s colonial monopoly, parties in Mexico, New Granada, Venezuela, the drought and earthquakes, Paraguay under Francia, the independence of Chili and Brazil, Castlereagh’s cautious neutrality contrasted with Canning’s later assertiveness


Chapter IX — The Conspiracies of 1817 — the wave of alarms in 1817, the outrage on the Prince Regent (the “popgun plot”), the reports of secret committees on the state of the country, the suspension of Habeas Corpus (February 1817), the March of the Blanketeers (Manchester weavers marching to London with blankets to petition), the Derby Insurrection (Pentridge Rising), Oliver the Spy — government agent provocateur, Jeremiah Brandreth’s rising and execution, the evidence of Samuel Bamford, the results of the trials, parliamentary protests by Romilly against the suppression of civil liberties


Chapter X — The Government’s Repression — systematic repression after 1817: Lord Sidmouth’s circular authorising magistrates to seize and detain persons suspected of publishing seditious or blasphemous libels, the flight of William Cobbett to America, the trial of William Hone for blasphemous parodies (his brilliant three-day self-defence before Lord Ellenborough, resulting in acquittal — three juries in three successive days acquitted Hone), the second and third trials of Hone, the Seditious Meetings Act, the general atmosphere of political repression


Chapter XI — Death of the Princess Charlotte — the death of Princess Charlotte (only legitimate child of the Prince Regent) in November 1817 after giving birth to a stillborn son, the nationwide grief and mourning, the dynastic crisis — no direct heir to the throne, the scramble among the royal dukes to marry and produce an heir, the abolition of sinecures, Charlotte’s significance as a symbol of hope for a happier monarchy


Chapter XII — India: The Pindarree and Mahratta Wars — British campaigns under the Marquess of Hastings, the Pindarrees (bands of freebooters ravaging central India), their leader Cheetoo, the ravages of the Pindarrees, the Pindarree War and extirpation of the robbers, the third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–1818), the Battle of Kirkee, the siege of Nagpur, the Battle of Mehidpore, the ravages of cholera-morbus, the Battle of Corregaum, the defeat and submission of the Peshwa Bajee Rao, the attack on Fort Talnair, the surrender of Bajee Rao, the restoration of peace, the happy effects of British rule as Martineau presents them, rapid improvements in administration and revenue, accessions of territory


Chapter XIII — The Session of 1818 — the general election of 1818 preceded by this session, the Prince Regent’s speech and the debates on the address, the state of the country — which side should be believed about the condition of the people, the reports of secret committees concerning seditious practices, the renewal of the Alien Act, the debates on resumption of cash payments, agricultural distress, the Bank Charter Act, the fall of the income tax (forced by overwhelming opposition), Peel’s first Factory Act (limiting hours of child labour in cotton mills — the beginning of factory legislation), the renewed discussion of the Poor Laws


Chapter XIV — The General Election of 1818, the Manchester Strike, and the Congress of Aix-la-Chapelle — This chapter is present in the text (line 10785). The general election of 1818: the Westminster contest (Romilly at the head of the poll with 5,339 votes, Burdett 5,238, Sir Murray Maxwell 4,808 after a riotous fifteen-day election — Maxwell severely injured by the mob, the Riot Act read and the military called out), the London city election, Brougham’s contest in Westmoreland against the Lowther family, 115 contested seats out of 380 constituencies, the Whig resurgence under Tierney’s leadership. The strike of Manchester cotton spinners (about 15,000) over wages from June 1818, the confrontation at a factory in Ancoat’s Lane on September 2 — soldiers fired, one killed, a coroner’s verdict of justifiable homicide, the strike breaks up. The Congress of Aix-la-Chapelle (September–November 1818): the evacuation of the allied army of occupation from France, the Duke of Wellington’s crucial role in smoothing the negotiations and his appointment as Master-General of the Ordnance with a seat in the cabinet, Robert Owen of New Lanark presenting his schemes to the Emperor Alexander, Clarkson sent by Wilberforce to lobby for abolition (unsuccessful). Deaths: Queen Charlotte (November 17), Sir Samuel Romilly (suicide November 2, four days after losing his wife, aged 61 — Lord Eldon wept openly in court at the sight of Romilly’s empty seat), Lord Ellenborough (December 13), Warren Hastings (August 20), Sir Philip Francis (December). The economic state of the country at the close of 1818: better harvest, but prices still at scarcity levels, growing bankruptcies. The revival of reform agitation: Samuel Bamford introducing women’s voting at radical meetings in Lydgate (Saddleworth), the Birch meeting where Benbow urged marching to London “at the point of the sword and pike” before fleeing to America, Cobbett’s letter from America ridiculing Jeremy Bentham


Chapter XV — The Close of the Session — the opening of the new parliament in January 1819, the Regent’s speech read by commission (mentioning the Queen’s death, the Aix-la-Chapelle treaty, and the commercial convention with the US), Sir James Mackintosh’s successful motion for a select committee on criminal law reform (reducing capital offences), debates on Catholic emancipation (a thin government majority), Scotch burgh reform, cabinet divisions over currency policy, Lord Liverpool’s letter to Eldon threatening resignation if financial measures failed, the state of parties — an administration increasingly divided within itself


Chapter XVI — The Reform Agitation and Peterloo (1819) — the pivotal chapter of the volume. The summer 1819 agitation: mass reform meetings, the election of “legislatorial attorneys,” female reform societies, radical drilling on Tandle Hill. Detailed account of the Manchester meeting of August 16, 1819: orderly processions from the manufacturing towns (Bamford’s Middleton contingent with laurel branches and a banner of “Unity and Strength”), the assembling of perhaps 60,000 people in St. Peter’s Field, Orator Hunt’s arrival in an open carriage, the magistrates’ decision to arrest the leaders, the disastrous charge of the Manchester and Salford Yeomanry (untrained special constables on horseback, many drunk), the intervention of the 15th Hussars, the resulting massacre with 11–15 killed and 400–700 wounded, the panicked flight of the crowd. Draws on Bamford’s memoir, Sir William Jolliffe’s account, and the parliamentary evidence


Chapter XVII — Aftermath of Peterloo — the conduct of the magistrates — the government immediately supporting their actions, the Prince Regent’s letter of approval, nationwide protest meetings, Sir Francis Burdett’s inflammatory letter to his constituents (prosecuted for libel, convicted and fined), the York trials of the radical leaders, the deep division in the cabinet over whether to charge with treason (Eldon arguing for it, the rest opposed — Eldon prevailed in some cases but not in the mass), Hunt’s trial (sentenced to 2½ years in Ilchester Gaol), the passage of the Six Acts (1819): the Training Prevention Act, the Seizure of Arms Act, the Seditious Meetings Prevention Act, the Blasphemous and Seditious Libels Act, the Newspaper and Stamp Duties Act, the Misdemeanours Act — the most repressive legislation of the post-war period


BOOK II — From the Cato Street Conspiracy to the End of Liverpool’s Ministry (1819–1826)


Chapter I — The Revival of Sedition and the Cato Street Conspiracy — the revival of sedition after Peterloo, the Cato Street plot (February 1820): Arthur Thistlewood and a small group of radicals plotting to murder the entire cabinet at a dinner at Lord Harrowby’s house, the government’s knowledge through spies, the dramatic arrest in the Cato Street stable (Thistlewood killed a police officer, Richard Smithers), the trial and execution of five conspirators (Thistlewood, Ings, Brunt, Tidd, Davidson — beheaded after hanging), Edwards the spy controversy (accusations of agent provocateur), the true character of Hunt revealed, the lessons learned by experience, public sentiment that the conspirators were as much victims of government provocation as genuine revolutionaries


Chapter II — The Queen Caroline Affair (1820–1821) — the unhappy marriage of George IV and Caroline of Brunswick, Queen Caroline’s return from her Continental exile to assert her rights, the King’s message to Parliament demanding a divorce, the introduction of the Bill of Pains and Penalties in the House of Lords (depriving Caroline of her title and dissolving the marriage), the “trial” with evidence of Caroline’s alleged adultery with Bartolomeo Bergami, Brougham and Denman’s brilliant defence (Denman’s famous “where is the injured husband?” speech), the enormous public sympathy for the Queen (mobs supporting Caroline, the King hissed in the streets), the abandonment of the bill after a narrow majority of nine in the Lords on the third reading, the Queen’s death (August 1821) and funeral (the procession forced through the City over the government’s objections, two men killed in the Hyde Park confrontation)


Chapter III — Domestic Events (1821) — the dissolution of parliament after George IV’s accession, the King’s visit to Ireland (the first by a reigning monarch since the Union — a success that temporarily quieted Irish discontent), the death of Henry Grattan, popular education, agricultural distress, continuing but reduced reform agitation, the Constitutional Association (the “Bridge Street Gang” for prosecuting libel), the death of Napoleon at St. Helena (May 5, 1821), the cautious steps toward trade recovery and liberalising economic policy


Chapter IV — The Liverpool Ministry in Transition — the weakening of Liverpool’s ministry in 1821–22: unpopular with the King, internally divided by the Catholic question, facing growing pressure for liberal reform — the strength and fragility of the ministry assessed, the retirement of Lord Sidmouth from the Home Office, Mr. Canning’s position (refusing to serve under Liverpool, out of office). The condition of Ireland, the Peterborough Church questions, the new Marriage Act, the death of Lord Londonderry (Castlereagh, August 1822 — suicide by cutting his throat in a paroxysm of overwork and paranoid delusions). Canning becomes Foreign Secretary, Huskisson at the Board of Trade, Peel at the Home Office — the transition from old Tory repression to liberal conservatism


Chapter V — Foreign Affairs Under Canning — the transformation of foreign policy from 1822: the princes of Europe and the Congress of Verona, Canning breaking from the Holy Alliance, his “system” of recognising de facto governments, the French invasion of Spain (1823) to restore the Bourbon monarchy, Canning’s opposition and the British refusal to participate, his great speech on the Spanish question, the recognition of the South American republics (Argentina, Colombia, Mexico — “I called the New World into existence to redress the balance of the Old”), British naval demonstration preventing European intervention in the Americas, the protection of Portugal from Spanish invasion, the death of John VI of Portugal, the death of Alexander I of Russia (1825), the last war with Algiers, the Burmese War, the Oregon question, the renewal of the Alien Act, the influence of foreigners in British political discourse


Chapter VI — Domestic Reform Under Liverpool — a new period opening after the accession of the liberal Tories to key posts, the Cabinet of 1823, Canning and Huskisson’s influence and the opposition of Eldon, Lord Chancellor Eldon and his resistance to change, the debt and the burden of taxation, commercial policy reform: Huskisson’s reduction of the Navigation Acts and the Reciprocity Bill (allowing reciprocal tariff arrangements with other maritime nations), the reform of the Combination Acts (allowing workmen to combine for wage negotiations), the Gaols Act, the sliding scale for corn duties. The Catholic claims: renewed debates and the growth of the Catholic Association. Negro slavery: the government’s resolutions on amelioration, Barbadoes and Demerara, the Smith the Missionary case (a missionary executed for not suppressing a slave rebellion), the close of the session


Chapter VII — Trade, Manufactures, and Labour — economic expansion and its problems: the evils of the smuggling system (along the Kentish and Sussex coasts — a massive illicit industry fuelled by high protective duties), the reform of the Combination Acts and its effects on labour organisation, the silk duties debate and the discontent of the Coventry ribbon-weavers, the reduction of silk duties, tariff reform on wool and other raw materials, the debates on free trade principles, the close of the session


Chapter VIII — The Speculation Mania and the Panic of 1825 — a classic financial bubble and crash: speculation and overtrading in 1824–25, the exportation of gold, the joint-stock company mania (companies floated for every purpose — Latin American mining, steam laundries, canals, gas-lighting, even a company for “milk and eggs from cows and poultry”) — shares bid to absurd prices, the collapse beginning in the autumn of 1825, the panic and the crash of the Stock Exchange, the run on the banks (70 country banks failed), the Bank of England’s desperate measures — the suppression of small notes (under £5), the Scotch banks and their superior stability during the crisis, the position of the ministers, the immense suffering of the time, the defeat of the government’s financial proposals in the aftermath


Chapter IX — Riots, Scarcity, and Emigration — the social consequences of the 1825 panic: riots in manufacturing towns (the Sunderland seamen’s riot — troops firing on strikers, killing five), the Isle of Man potato tithe riots (the poor successfully resisting collection, forcing the bishop to yield), other outbreaks of popular violence, the alarm of scarcity, the opening of bonded corn to relieve distress, the Colonial Office and the beginnings of a systematic emigration policy, the Emigration Committee and the first experiments in assisted emigration to Canada, the reform of the poor laws urged
