Chapter X — The Catholic Question — a comprehensive historical review of the Catholic question from the Reformation to the 1820s: the Treaty of Limerick and its violated guarantees, the penal laws under Henry VIII, Elizabeth, and the Stuarts, the 18th-century relaxations, Irish interest and Mr. Grattan, the coronation oath and the argument that it forbade Catholic emancipation, the disabilities of Catholics (excluded from Parliament, the higher offices of state, the universities), the state of opinion in 1824, the Catholic deputation to London, Mr. Canning’s speech in favour of relief, Mr. O’Connell and the New Catholic Association (the “Catholic rent” of a penny a month), the Duke of York’s speech against emancipation (declaring his unalterable opposition to the last hour of his life), Mr. Plunket’s measured advocacy, Catholics and Dissenters compared


Chapter XI — Parliamentary and Legal Reform — Chancery reform and the campaign against the “insufferable” delays of the Court of Chancery, John Williams leading the inquiry against the obstruction of Lord Chancellor Eldon, reports of the Chancery Commissioners, the reform of the criminal code continued by Peel (reduction of capital offences — the consolidation of the criminal law), jurors in India, the state of the national finances, Lord John Russell’s motion on the state of the country, the disenfranchisement of Grampound (a notoriously corrupt Cornish borough, its seats transferred to Yorkshire), the general election of 1823, the drought and harvest of that year, the irresistible spirit of reform


Chapter XII — Society and Culture (1820s) — the concluding chapter, a social and cultural survey. Capital punishment and banditti: the shocking frequency of executions (boys hanged alongside hardened criminals), the discovery of a Gloucestershire banditti gang living in a subterranean cavern, popular ignorance and the efforts of the education societies (British and Foreign School Society, National Society, the Church of England’s National schools), prosecutions for blasphemy (Richard Carlile and the republican publishers), the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge and the Penny Magazine, the encouragement of emigration. Public works: the Menai Suspension Bridge (Telford’s great work, opened 1826), gas-lighting spreading through the country, the Thames Tunnel under construction (Brunel’s project), the Stockton and Darlington Railway (1825) — the dawn of the railway age. North Polar expeditions and the search for the North-West Passage. Literature and the arts: the Edinburgh and Quarterly Reviews, the rise of the literary magazines, the death of the poets (Byron at Missolonghi 1824, Shelley drowned 1822, Keats at Rome 1821), the progress of science (Herschel, Davy, Jenner — their deaths noted), the Royal Society of Literature, artists lost (Fuseli), patrons of art (Sir George Beaumont), the death of Byron producing a reaction in English opinion. The transformation of English society since 1815

sources/martineau-history-of-england-vol.title: Martineau — History of England, Vol. III: From Canning to the Consolidation of Reform (1827–1836)
sources/martineau-history-of-england-vol.content:
Martineau — History of England, Vol. III: From Canning to the Consolidation of Reform (1827–1836)
Harriet Martineau (1802–1876) — History of England from the Commencement of the XIXth Century to the Crimean War. Vol. III. — 1864 Edition.
The third volume covers the turbulent decade from the collapse of the Liverpool ministry to the consolidation of the reform settlement. Martineau narrates Canning’s brief premiership, the Duke of Wellington’s ministry, Catholic Emancipation, the French Revolution of 1830, the Reform Bill crisis of 1830–32, the first Reformed Parliament, the abolition of slavery, the New Poor Law, municipal reform, Lord Melbourne’s administration, and the dismantling of the Orange societies. The volume presents a philosophic Radical perspective on a period that saw the death of the old Tory order and the birth of the reform era.
The text is 30,461 lines. Note: Book IV has no Chapter XI — the chapter numbering jumps from Chapter X (line 20540) to Chapter XII (line 22293). This appears to be an original feature of the text, not an OCR omission.
Content Summary
BOOK III — From the Close of Lord Liverpool’s Administration to the French Revolution of 1830 (1827–1830)


Chapter I — Opening of Parliament and Death of the Duke of York; Canning becomes Premier — Martineau reflects on 1826–1829 as years of apparent legislative stagnation masking deep political change. The King opens Parliament with Canning’s speech on Portugal. The Duke of York dies in January 1827 — Martineau provides a detailed character assessment and describes his funeral. Lord Liverpool suffers a stroke and resigns. A Corn Bill debate ensues with Canning proposing resolutions and Wellington opposing. The King summons Canning to form a ministry on March 27, 1827. Peel resigns over Catholic relief, Lord Eldon departs. The formation of Canning’s administration amid great political uncertainty — Huskisson, Lord Lansdowne, and Lord Carlisle join


Chapter II — Canning’s Administration, His Death, Goderich, Wellington — Parliament reassembles May 1, 1827. The session is dominated by vicious personal attacks on Canning by the Tories (Eldon’s friends). The Whigs offer support; Lord Grey delivers a notable speech. Canning’s declining health under the strain of office, his death in August 1827. Lord Goderich briefly heads the ministry but proves incapable — “the incapacity of Lord Goderich was the greatest that could exist in a man of honour.” The Duke of Wellington becomes Prime Minister in January 1828, ushering in a new political alignment. The formation of Wellington’s Cabinet with Peel at the Home Office


Chapter III — Wellington, Ireland, Catholic Relief Bill 1829 — The Battle of Navarino (October 1827) — the allied destruction of the Turkish-Egyptian fleet at Navarino Bay, a key event in Greek independence. Lord Anglesey as Lord Lieutenant of Ireland. Wellington’s administration and the growing crisis over Catholic emancipation in Ireland — the Clare election (Daniel O’Connell elected in defiance of the law), Peel’s conversion to the cause of Catholic relief. The passage of the Catholic Relief Act of 1829: Catholics admitted to Parliament and most civil offices, the suppression of the Catholic Association. The Protestant backlash and the Brunswick clubs. The Duke of Wellington deserted by half his friends


Chapter IV — Wellington’s Last Years, the Birmingham Political Union, Death of George IV — Wellington’s final years in power. Rising economic distress and popular agitation for reform. Thomas Attwood founds the Birmingham Political Union in January 1830 — a new phase of extra-parliamentary organisation coordinating the middle and working classes. The agricultural interest and the currency debates. The King’s health deteriorates; George IV dies in June 1830 after a reign of ten years. The coronation of William IV. This triggers a general election. Wellington’s stubborn opposition to reform alienates moderate Tories


Chapter V — Social and Political Conditions — Economic distress gripping the country: agricultural depression, trade union activity, the Swing Riots (rural machine-breaking and rick-burning in southern England — 387 Swing prosecutions in Berkshire, Surrey, Kent, Sussex, and Hampshire). The anxieties of landowners and manufacturers. The collapse of Wellington’s ministry in November 1830 after his famous anti-reform speech (“I am not only not prepared to bring forward any measure of this nature, but I will at once declare that… the existing system possesses the full and entire confidence of the country”). Lord Grey is summoned to form his ministry


Chapter VI — Law of the Press and Reform Agitation — Press prosecutions and the campaign for a freer press: notable libel cases, the growing influence of the Times and other newspapers. The efforts of reformers to secure a freer press and the government’s countervailing efforts. The aftermath of Catholic emancipation, the continuing political ferment in Ireland, Lord Anglesey’s role as Lord Lieutenant


Chapter VII — Foreign Affairs: Russia, Turkey, and Greece — Foreign policy: the Russo-Turkish War (1828–1829), the London Conference on Greek independence, the establishment of the Greek state under the London Protocol, the Treaty of Adrianople (1829), the diplomatic maneuvering between Britain, Russia, France, and the Ottoman Empire. Lord Anglesey’s administration in Ireland and intensifying Irish grievances


Chapter VIII — The Collapse of the Bourbon Monarchy in France — The final years of Charles X’s reign: the resignation of the Villelle ministry, the formation of the Polignac ministry (the “Prince of the Jesuits”), the summoning of the Chambers, the growing opposition to Polignac’s ultra-royalist policies, the dissolution of the Chamber of Deputies, and the July Ordinances (the ordonnances de Saint-Cloud) that triggered the revolution


Chapter IX — The French Revolution of 1830 — The Trois Glorieuses — the Three Days of July (27–29 July 1830) in Paris: the barricades, the defection of the troops, the flight of Charles X, the provisional government. Louis Philippe, Duke of Orleans, accepting the throne as “King of the French” — the revision of the Charter, the abolition of the hereditary peerage, the new electoral law. The impact of the French Revolution on British politics — intensifying the demand for reform, frightening conservatives


Chapter X — Domestic Life and Industrial Unrest — Working-class conditions, notable crimes (Burke and Hare murders — 16 murders for anatomical dissection, Hare turning King’s evidence, the Anatomy Act 1832 subsequently passed). The new General Post Office and postal reform. The spread of Political Unions from Birmingham across the country. The condition of the poor, early Factory Act agitation, the intellectual ferment of the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge (penny magazines, The Penny Magazine, The Library of Useful Knowledge)


Chapter XI — Necrology and the Death of the Old Order — The longest chapter in the volume, a book-length necrology. Martineau catalogues “Political Deaths” (George IV, Canning, Huskisson, Tierney), “Men of Business,” “Artists” (Sir Thomas Lawrence), “Men of Letters,” “Philosophers” (Sir Humphry Davy), and “Philanthropists.” Extensive biographical sketches arguing that the old order of Pittites and anti-reformers was literally dying off, making way for a new generation of reformers. The chapter serves as Martineau’s pivot between the age of reaction and the age of reform


BOOK IV — The Reform Era (1830–1834/35)


Chapter I — The Accession of William IV and the July Revolution — William IV’s accession in June 1830, the Regency question (what if the King died before Princess Victoria came of age). The new King’s popular manners, the dissolution of Parliament, the general election of 1830. The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opening and Huskisson’s death (September 15, 1830 — struck down by Rocket at Parkside). Intensifying O’Connell agitation in Ireland. Sympathy in Britain for the French Revolution of 1830. Agricultural distress, rick-burning. The fall of Wellington’s ministry and Lord Grey being called to form a government


Chapter II — Lord Grey and the Reform Bill — The formation of the Grey Ministry in November 1830 with Reform of Parliament made a Cabinet question. Retrospective on Grey’s long advocacy of parliamentary reform since the 1790s. The composition of the Cabinet: Brougham Lord Chancellor (his “singular character,” possessing more influence than any other single member of the ministry), Lord Althorp Chancellor of the Exchequer (acting leader of the Commons), Lord John Russell Paymaster of the Forces (the sharp-tempered, fearless advocate of reform). The King’s initial support. The presentation of the first Reform Bill by Lord John Russell on March 1, 1831


Chapter III — The Reform Bill Crisis — 1831 opens with machine-breaking, rick-burning. A Manchester manufacturer murdered by trade unionists. The prospect of civil conflict between anti-reformers and the discontented lower classes. The middle classes organise through Political Unions. The first Reform Bill passes its second reading by a single vote (302–301) on March 22, 1831. Defeated in committee on General Gascoigne’s motion. Parliament prorogued and dissolved, the general election of April–May 1831 producing a massive pro-reform majority. The second Reform Bill passes the Commons with large majorities but is rejected by the Lords (41 majority against) in October 1831. Riots at Derby and Nottingham — the burning of Nottingham Castle. The crisis of May 1832: ministers resign after the Lords refuse to yield, the King attempts to get Wellington to form a government (fails), Lord Grey recalled with the King’s reluctant promise to create enough peers. The Reform Act receives royal assent on June 7, 1832


Chapter IV — The Reformed Parliament — The general election of 1831 in detail — the role of non-electors in pressuring voters. The emergence of Political Unions as disciplined reform organisations. The “Waverers” and the threat of creating peers. The King’s appeals to the Lords to yield. The Reform Act’s provisions: disenfranchisement of 56 rotten boroughs, 30 reduced to one MP, enfranchisement of 42 new towns, county representation extended, £10 householder franchise in boroughs. The new constituency map of Britain. The first Reformed Parliament assembles (January 1833)


Chapter V — The New Poor Law and Other Reforms — After the Reform Act’s passage, Martineau turns to the great social questions. The cholera epidemic of 1832 (from Sunderland through the country — panic, the spread of cholera as a social and political event). The New Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834: the principles (the workhouse test, less eligibility, central Poor Law Commission), its machinery, its reception and opposition. The 1833 Factory Act limiting hours for children. The Bank Charter renewal (1833). The India Company’s Charter renewal (1833 — the Company’s trading monopoly ended, India opened to free trade). The Slavery Abolition Act (1833, effective August 1, 1834) — £20 million compensation to slave-owners


Chapter VI — Irish Church and Tithe Reform — The Irish Church question paramount in the post-Reform Parliament. Statistics: an Established Church of 853,000 members with four archbishops and eighteen bishops, supported by tithes from a population of 6.5 million Catholics. The Tithe War — Irish Catholics refusing to pay tithes, seizures of property by armed police and soldiers. The Coercion Bill (1833). The Irish Church Temporalities Bill (reducing bishoprics from 18 to 12, creating the Ecclesiastical Commission). The prosecution of O’Connell. The Appropriation controversy — whether surplus Church revenues should be applied to secular purposes (especially education)


Chapter VII — Municipal Reform — The reform of the Civil List under William IV: the King surrendering hereditary revenues for a fixed parliamentary grant. The reform of the pension list. The Municipal Corporations Commission (appointed 1833). The history of English municipal institutions. The Commission’s report exposing widespread corruption and self-perpetuating oligarchies in the old borough corporations. The Municipal Corporations Act (1835) — elected town councils established for 178 boroughs


Chapter VIII — Ecclesiastical Affairs and the Great Charters — The Bank of England Charter renewed (1833) — the secret parliamentary committee on banking, the recommendation to limit paper money to a single London issuing bank and require periodic publication of accounts. The East India Company Charter renewed (1833) — the Company’s trading monopoly abolished, India opened to free trade and Christian missionaries. The Ecclesiastical Commission (1835), the Non-residence Act (abolishing absentee clergy), the abolition of sinecures, the preliminaries of the Tithe Commutation Act


Chapter IX — Irish Church and Affairs of France — Criticism of the Whig Ministry’s failures in Ireland: “Catholic emancipation would not tranquillize Ireland while she suffered under the burden of ‘too much Church.‘” The tithe collection system backed by armed police, the 1832 Tithe Act, the proposed 1834 Act (lost), the Irish Ecclesiastical Commission, the Irish census, reductions in bishoprics, the Appropriation controversy. Affairs of France under the July Monarchy: Louis Philippe’s acceptance of the crown, the revision of the Charter, abolition of the hereditary peerage, the electoral law, the characteristics of the July Monarchy. The Belgian Revolution (separation from Holland, Prince Leopold becoming King of the Belgians). Disturbances across Europe: Brunswick, Saxony, Hesse, Baden, Switzerland, Italy. Spain (death of Ferdinand VII, the Carlist claim). Portugal (death of Don Pedro, the Queen’s marriage). Egypt and Turkey (Mehemet Ali). The Polish Revolution of 1830–31 (the revolt, the struggle, the defeat)


Chapter X — Religious Life and Controversy — A comprehensive survey of Britain’s religious crisis. Three parties in the Church of England: the Evangelical Party, the High Church/Tractarian movement (just beginning with the Tracts for the Times, 1833–41), and the Moderate Church Party. The death of William Wilberforce (1833) and Hannah More (1833). The opening of the universities to Dissenters (debated 1834–35). The admission of Quakers to Parliament (Mr. Pease, 1833). The continued exclusion of Jews from Parliament. Deaths of prominent religious figures: Robert Hall (the great Baptist preacher), Rowland Hill, Charles Wesley, Adam Clarke, Rammohun Roy (the Hindu reformer), Dr. Doyle (the Catholic Archbishop of Dublin). The schism in the Scotch Church (the beginnings of the Disruption leading to the Free Church in 1843). Edward Irving and the Catholic Apostolic Church. St. Simonism and the spread of socialist ideas. Budgets from 1831–34: the assessed taxes movement, the house-tax, the malt-tax, the surplus of 1834, the corn-laws debated. Poor Law for Ireland. The ballot question. Military flogging and the impressment of seamen


[No Chapter XI in Book IV — the numbering jumps from X to XII. This is a feature of the original text, not an OCR omission.]


Chapter XII — The Progress of the Country and the Fall of the Grey Ministry — Popular discontents and the power of Trades’ Unions in 1834: the murder of a Manchester manufacturer, the tyranny of union leaders, the new combination system where trades supported each other’s strikes, the collapse of these efforts. The Dorsetshire labourers (the Tolpuddle Martyrs — transported for administering unlawful oaths under the Unlawful Oaths Act of 1797). The disintegration of the Grey Ministry: Lord Althorp’s resignation (over the Irish Tithe question raised by Mr. Ward’s motion), Lord Grey’s resignation in July 1834, Lord Brougham’s removal from the Chancellorship (Lord Lyndhurst succeeds), Lord Durham’s discontent, the Grey Banquet. Lord Melbourne’s first short-lived ministry


Chapter XIII — Affairs of France (continued) — A detailed study of the July Monarchy from 1830–1834. Louis Philippe’s personal history: his barefoot exile across the Alps, teaching mathematics in Switzerland, living in Philadelphia, his modest courtship. His acceptance of the crown, the revision of the Charter (especially the controversial Article 14 allowing emergency royal decrees). Disquiet in France, the suicide of the Duke de Bourbon (the last of the Condés). Disturbances in Paris, the abolition of the hereditary peerage, the new electoral law, the emergence of parties (Legitimists, Orleanists, Republicans). Press prosecutions. Insurrections: the Lyons silk-weavers’ uprising, the Paris rising of 1832 (the funeral of General Lamarque). The fortifications of Paris. The death of Lafayette (1834). The characteristics of the reign: Louis Philippe’s bourgeois monarchy, the consolidation of the new order


Chapter XIV — The Accession of William IV and the Progress of the Country — William IV’s genuine popularity: the King walking in the streets, visiting the theatre, greeted with “Reform” and “Glorious King” placards. The coronation on September 8, 1831 — quiet and economical (no banquet). Princess Victoria (aged 12) beginning tours of the country. An assault on the King. Popular ignorance and riots. The Anatomy Bill (1832, allowing doctors to dissect unclaimed bodies). Medical education reform. Notable criminal trials. “The Progress of the Country”: an eclectic catalogue covering the introduction of steam navigation in the East, mail conveyance improvements, the Drummond Light (limelight for surveying), polar discoveries, the Islington Cattle Market, the rebuilding of London Bridge (opened August 1, 1831), education reform, the British Association for the Advancement of Science, statistics of suicide, duelling, the loss of the steamship Rothesay Castle, the fire at the Dublin Custom House, the burning of the Houses of Parliament (October 16, 1834 — the two Houses of Parliament completely destroyed). A substantial necrology of the period’s deaths: political figures, men of science (Sir Humphry Davy covered more fully here), seamen, travellers, actors, musicians, architects, antiquarians, artists, authors, and philanthropists


BOOK V — The Consolidation of Reform (1834–1836)


Chapter I — The Three Parties — After the Reform Act, the parties adopt new titles: Tories become “Conservatives,” Whigs become “Reformers,” Radicals become “Radical Reformers” (or “Destructives” by opponents). A sophisticated analysis of party dynamics: the representatives of those with much to lose, those with much to gain, and the “umpire party” that interposes in crises. The Duke of Wellington’s continuing role though out of office. Sir Robert Peel’s position. The formation of Peel’s first ministry (December 1834), the dissolution of Parliament. Peel’s Tamworth Manifesto (December 1834) — accepting the Reform Act as final and promising moderate reform. The new Parliament assembles, Mr. Abercromby elected Speaker. Peel’s minority government weak from the start


Chapter II — Lord Melbourne’s Ministry — Peel’s “Hundred Days” ministry (December 1834–April 1835): the King’s Speech, angry debates, the malt-tax debate, Lord Londonderry’s diplomatic appointment controversy, ministers defeated on ecclesiastical questions. The Dissenters’ Marriages Bill, the Ecclesiastical Commission, the London University Charter, the decisive struggle over the Appropriation question. Peel’s government defeated and resigns in April 1835. Lord Melbourne forms his second ministry: Lord John Russell Home Secretary, Mr. Charles Grant Colonial Office. The new government’s Irish administration and its reform agenda


Chapter III — Irish Church and Municipal Reform — The two great questions of the Melbourne ministry. First, the Irish Church: the Appropriation question — whether to appropriate surplus Church revenues to non-religious purposes — Church-rates, the eventual surrender of the Appropriation principle by the ministry. Second, Municipal Reform: the Corporation Commission, a detailed history of English municipal institutions, the Commissioners’ report exposing the corrupt self-perpetuating nature of old borough corporations (closed governing bodies, misuse of funds, no accountability), the principle of the case, the passage of the Municipal Corporations Act (1835) after bitter Lords opposition


Chapter IV — Ecclesiastical Commission and Tithe Commutation — The Ecclesiastical Commission (established 1835): its composition, its work in redistributing Church revenues, the Non-residence Act (clergy required to live in their parishes), the abolition of sinecures. The Tithe Commutation Act (1836) — commuting tithes in kind into a money rent-charge. Popular education: Lord Brougham’s education scheme and the ministerial scheme of 1834. Attacks on the House of Lords and the growing demand for Peerage Reform. O’Connell’s tour of Scotland and England (1835). The emergence of Chartism: its various factions (Radical, Tory, Hungering, Factious Chartists), the growing working-class disenchantment with the results of the Reform Act


Chapter V — The Dissolution of the Orange Societies — The final chapter, a detailed investigation of Orangeism in Britain. The Orange Lodges: secret Protestant societies headed by the Duke of Cumberland (the King’s brother and Grand Master), Colonel Fairman as the key organiser. The extent of Orange infiltration into the army, the Church, and the peerage. The lodges organising political intimidation against Catholics and reformers. A suspected plot involving a military coup or replacement of Melbourne with Wellington. Detection through parliamentary inquiry: Mr. Hume’s resolutions leading to a Committee of Inquiry exposing the scale of the conspiracy. The Duke of Cumberland compelled to resign his grand mastership. Colonel Fairman flees or refuses to testify. The Orange Society dissolved, addresses to the King adopted. The book closes with the end of organised Orangeism in England and the consolidation of the reform settlement

sources/martineau-history-of-england-vol.title: The History of England from the Commencement of the XIXth Century to the Crimean War, Vol. IV
sources/martineau-history-of-england-vol.content:
The History of England, Vol. IV — by Harriet Martineau
Vol. IV covers 1835–1854, beginning with the later years of the second Melbourne Ministry through Queen Victoria’s accession, the Peel ministry and the Repeal of the Corn Laws, and concluding with the outbreak of the Crimean War. The volume is divided into three Books:

Book V — “1835–1840” — Ireland, Church affairs, agricultural distress, death of William IV, accession of Victoria, Canada (Lord Durham), Jamaica, Chartism, the Bedchamber Question, the Queen’s marriage
Book VI — “1841” — Peel’s ministry, the Opium War, the Afghan disaster, the Corn Laws, the Anti-Corn-Law League, the Disruption of the Scottish Church, the Irish Famine, Peel’s fall
Book VII — “Last Years of the Peace” — the Irish Famine (continued), the financial panic of 1847, the Revolutions of 1848, the Papal Aggression, Palmerston’s foreign policy, the Great Exhibition, and the declaration of war against Russia


Book V — “1835–1840”
Book V covers the latter half of the 1830s, dominated by the second Melbourne Ministry, the accession of Queen Victoria, and gathering social and political storms — Irish agitation, Church crises in Scotland and England, the Canadian rebellions, Chartism, agricultural distress, and the first stirrings of the free-trade movement.
Chapter VI — Ireland under Lord Mulgrave’s Administration
Martineau opens with a reflection on the hopes and heartbreaks of Irish governance during the 1835–40 period. She describes the administration of Lord Mulgrave (later Lord Normanby) as an experiment in conciliation — an attempt to govern Ireland through justice and mercy rather than coercion. The chapter captures the high expectations of the time but also carries the weight of subsequent disappointment, as the hopes for Irish redemption proved premature. The chapter concludes that even the most strenuous administration of justice was ultimately too small an instrument for Ireland’s redemption.
Chapter VII — Church and State
This chapter examines the parallel ecclesiastical disturbances shaking England, Ireland, and Scotland — viewing them as another aspect of the same transitional struggle that produced the Reform Bill. Martineau is sharply critical of successive governments’ inability to comprehend or apply principles in ecclesiastical affairs. She focuses particularly on the Church of Scotland, where the Melbourne government’s mishandling of patronage and church accommodation questions set the stage for the Disruption. The English Tractarian movement and the Dissenters’ cry for separation of Church and State are presented as parallel symptoms of the same crisis.
Chapter VIII — Agricultural Distress & Parliamentary Business
With the great constitutional questions dominating Parliament, ordinary legislative business was crowded out. The chapter opens with the Marquis of Chandos’s motion in 1835 for repeal of taxes burdening agriculture — the first of many insistent demands that would grow into the great Corn Law struggle. The session of 1835 was declared “ingloriously remarkable” for how little was transacted. This chapter covers the routine yet consequential legislative skirmishes of 1835–37 against a backdrop of deepening rural hardship.
Chapter IX — Whig Struggles & Death of William IV
Martineau paints a vivid picture of the Whig ministry’s desperation in the spring of 1837 — blocked in the Lords, abandoned by Radicals in the Commons, unable to carry their Irish measures, and unable to secure a dissolution from the King. The ministers were believed to desire resignation, the King was believed to desire their removal, yet neither acted. The chapter captures the paralysis at the heart of government before the death of William IV on June 20, 1837, which unexpectedly broke the deadlock and opened a new era.
Chapter X — The Melbourne Ministry & Queen Victoria’s Accession
Lord Lyndhurst’s single “ray of comfort” — the character of the new young Queen — proved prophetic. The chapter details the remarkable collapse of Whig power: from a majority of 300 after the Reform Bill to a precarious 26. Yet the Melbourne Ministry was allowed another trial, a decision that proved fateful. Martineau traces how the young Queen’s popularity temporarily shored up a failing administration, and how the nation’s affections turned to the girl sovereign as the one bright spot in a dispiriting political landscape. Includes the general election on the demise of the crown and the continuance of the Melbourne ministry.
Chapter XII — Canada: Lord Durham’s Mission
Martineau treats the Canadian crisis with unusual severity, declaring that “all parties might be too happy to pass over” this chapter of history if possible, and that the disgrace of the Whig ministers and opposition members over Canada is inescapable. She details Lord Durham’s mission, his famous Report, the Rebellion of 1837–38, and the constitutional crisis that forced a fundamental rethinking of colonial governance. The retribution for incapacity, presumption, and disregard of constitutional principle — on all sides — was, she insists, not yet exhausted. Covers Lord Sydenham’s governance and Lord Durham’s legacy.
Chapter XIII — Jamaica & Colonial Constitution
Canada was not the only colony in crisis. The affairs of Jamaica reached a climax in the spring of 1839 with the question of whether its constitution should be suspended. Martineau reflects with admiration on the quiet conduct of the former slaves after emancipation, contrasting it with the behavior of their former masters. The chapter examines the hostility between the Jamaican Legislature and the Executive, the Melbourne government’s attempt to suspend the constitution, and the broader implications for colonial self-government and the post-slavery order.
Chapter XIV — Dark Times: Chartism, Distress & Torchlight Meetings
The gloom of 1839–40 was the deepest since the peace. Martineau traces the causes — as usual — to the state of the crops, but devotes deeper analysis to the social convulsions that followed: Chartist torchlight meetings, the Newport Rising, machine-breaking, and the near-revolutionary atmosphere among the working classes. She observes that the men who professed to “take no interest in politics” were the same who blamed the commotions on the innate wickedness of the lower orders, missing entirely the economic roots of the unrest. This chapter forms the hinge of Book V, connecting the political failures of the Melbourne years to the social explosion that was to reshape British politics.
Chapter XV — Beneficent Legislation
Amid the darkness, Martineau finds light in three great legislative achievements: the consolidation and reform of the criminal law (making it accessible to the people who lived under it), prison reform, and the establishment of penny postage. The Penny Post, associated with Rowland Hill, receives special attention as a democratizing force that drew the nation closer together.
Chapter XVI — Privilege of Parliament
One of the last major questions debated before the Melbourne Ministry fell was the privilege of Parliament — a seemingly arcane constitutional issue that had become a deadlock between the Court of Queen’s Bench and the House of Commons. Martineau treats it with appropriate gravity even as she notes the levity with which the public and press regarded it. The chapter examines the apparent incompatibility between the privileges of the Commons and the rights of the subject, concluding with the dissolution of the 13th Parliament and the approach of the general election of 1841.
Chapter XVII — The Coronation & the Young Queen
The closing chapter of Book V returns to the figure of the young Queen Victoria — the strongest and most genial interest of the period. After the “feeble old man” William IV, Victoria’s youth and gaiety were exhilarating. Martineau captures the Queen’s early popularity: her delight in being seen, her drives through thronged parks, her Guildhall dinner, her command “Let my people see me.” The chapter covers the coronation, the Queen’s marriage to Prince Albert (February 1840), and the birth of the Princess Royal (November 1840), closing Book V on a note of cautious hope.

Book VI — “1841”
Book VI is the longest and most dramatic book of the volume, covering Peel’s great ministry (1841–1846). It traces the growing free-trade movement, the Opium War, the disastrous First Afghan War, the Disruption of the Scottish Church, O’Connell’s Repeal agitation, and the climactic struggle over the Corn Laws that ended in Peel’s conversion to free trade and the splitting of the Conservative Party. It closes with a lengthy necrology.
Chapter I — General Election of 1841
The general election of 1841 was of extraordinary importance — not because one great question was to be settled as in 1831, but because something yet more important was at stake. The Whig ministers had staked their tenure on the free-trade question, proposing a fixed duty on corn, but they were three times mistaken: the people were not ready for the struggle, the Reform Bill’s provisions still favored the landed interest, and no one trusted the Melbourne government to handle the matter. The chapter sets up the central drama of Book VI: the rise of Peel and the gathering forces that would ultimately compel him to split his party.
Chapter II — New Administration
The country watched the distribution of offices with great eagerness. The first great hope was that Peel would unite the Treasury and the Exchequer, for the pressing evil was the state of the finances — annual deficits, deepening distress, working-class hopelessness. There was regret when Goulburn was made Chancellor instead, but confidence that Peel’s mind would preside over the department. The chapter outlines the formation of Peel’s cabinet — a united, able government — and the nation’s guarded optimism.
Chapter III — Policy of China: The Opium War
Martineau provides a sweeping geographical and historical meditation on why the interior of Asia had been peaceful for a century, before turning to the crisis that shattered that peace: the Opium War with China. She traces British ignorance of China, the opium question, Lord Napier’s failed mission, Commissioner Lin’s crackdown, and the military campaigns that followed — the capture of Chusan, the Treaty of Nanking, and the opening of treaty ports. The chapter is notable for its moral ambivalence: Martineau acknowledges the wrong and violence through which free trade was introduced to China, and warns that the consequences will haunt future generations.
Chapter IV — India: Afghanistan & Lord Ellenborough
Among the difficulties Peel inherited, none was more conspicuous than the state of Indian affairs. Under Lord Auckland, the Melbourne Administration had embarked on the disastrous Afghan policy — the invasion of Afghanistan, the installation of Shah Soojah, and the catastrophic British retreat from Cabool. Martineau recounts the First Anglo-Afghan War in harrowing detail: the rising at Cabool, the murder of the Envoy (Sir William Macnaghten), the retreat and annihilation of the British force, and the rescue of the prisoners. The chapter closes with Lord Ellenborough’s controversial proclamation and subsequent recall, followed by Sir Henry Hardinge’s appointment. Includes the Gwalior campaign and the exploits of James Brooke in Borneo.
Chapter V — Condition & Fate of Parties
When Peel met Parliament at the beginning of 1842, his party strength appeared greater than any administration in years. Yet something stronger than party support was at work: an inward change in the minister’s own mind, and outward changes in the elements that create human food. The chapter surveys the political landscape — the Conservative party, the weakened Whig opposition, and the growing influence of the “Young England” movement. But the real story is the undercurrent of economic distress that was forcing a fundamental re-examination of protective tariffs.
Chapter VI — Opinion of the Session: The Corn Bill of 1842
Peel’s government took the recess to prepare their financial measures thoroughly, maintaining profound secrecy about their intentions. The chapter details the Queen’s Speech, the introduction of the new Corn Bill with its revised sliding scale, and the financial scheme that included the reimposition of the income tax — a measure that aroused fierce opposition. Includes the Poor Law Renewal Act and the Copyright Law of 1842 (Lord Mahon’s bill).
Chapter VII — Central Subject of Debate: Social Reform
Parliament reassembled in February 1843 with no increased hopefulness — distress had deepened, revenue had fallen, and agricultural interests were as alarmed as the manufacturing classes. The central subject of debate was Lord Howick’s motion on the corn laws, but the chapter ranges widely over social reform: Lord Ashley’s Mines and Collieries Act (prohibiting women and children from underground work), the Government Factory Bill with its controversial education clauses, the early closing movement, and improvements in working-class dwellings.
Chapter VIII — Movement in Ireland: O’Connell & Repeal
The chapter opens with O’Connell’s declaration in January 1841 that the Whigs had lost the hearts of the Irish people. Martineau traces the monster meetings — Tara, Clontarf — the government’s ban on the Clontarf meeting, O’Connell’s arrest, the trials, the packed jury, the conviction, and the subsequent reversal by the House of Lords. She examines O’Connell’s decline, his death (1847), and the broader Irish reform efforts: agricultural schools, the Charitable Bequests Act, the Devon Commission, the Maynooth Grant, and the new Colleges. Peel’s efforts to “kill Home Rule by kindness” are given their due, even as the potato blight loomed.
Chapter IX — Church Patronage in Scotland: The Disruption
The ecclesiastical disturbances in Scotland had by now become of the gravest import. Martineau traces the problem back to the Act of 1711, which subjected the power of the presbytery to the control of the civil courts. She recounts the Auchterarder Case, the Strathbogie Case, Lord Aberdeen’s Bill, and the Great Disruption of 1843, when over 400 ministers walked out of the General Assembly to form the Free Church of Scotland. The chapter closes with a parallel examination of the Oxford Movement — Pusey, Hampden, Ward, Oakeley, and the Tractarian secessions to Rome.
Chapter X — Canada Corn Question & the League
The harvest of 1842 was abundant. But a more significant event was Lord Stanley’s letter granting favorable terms for Canadian corn — a step that acknowledged the principle of free trade between colony and mother country. The chapter traces the confused state of parties over the Canada Corn Bill, and the growing power of the Anti-Corn-Law League under Richard Cobden’s leadership. The League’s methods — registration, the freehold land scheme, the campaign against the game laws — are examined in detail as the movement gathered force for the climactic struggle of 1846.
Chapter XII — Antagonism in Europe
The mere rumor that the Sardinian government was jealous of Mazzini’s residence in England pointed to approaching troubles in Italy and across the despotisms of Europe. Martineau surveys the European landscape: Russia’s ambitions (the Caucasus, Servia, Cracow), the turmoil in Portugal and Spain, Switzerland, Hanover, Sweden, Turkey and Egypt (the Eastern Question), and the route to India. She pays particular attention to France — the war spirit over the right of search, the Tahiti affair, the Spanish marriages, the death of the Duc d’Orléans, the return of Napoleon’s remains, and Guizot’s ministry. Concludes with American relations: the frontier dispute, the Creole affair, the Ashburton Treaty, the Oregon question.
Chapter XIII — India & Colonial Affairs
The records of Indian affairs during this period show curious minglings of progress and conflict: railway companies alongside hints that the British might soon be compelled to interfere in the Punjab. The chapter covers the Sikh invasion of 1845, the battles of the First Anglo-Sikh War, and the settlement under Sir Henry Hardinge. It then surveys colonial and international affairs: the Sandwich Islands, Van Diemen’s Land, South Australia, New Zealand, and Canadian governance under Sir Charles Bagot and Sir Charles Metcalfe.
Chapter XIV — The Corn Question: 1845
At the opening of the 1845 session, the harvest of 1844 had been good, trade was brisk, and even Ireland was quieter than usual. Then came the portents — the bad weather, the potato rot in Ireland. Martineau traces the mounting crisis: the League’s intensified agitation, Lord John Russell’s famous letter declaring his conversion to free trade, the Cabinet councils, the announcement in the Times, Peel’s resignation, Lord Grey’s obstruction, and the climactic return of Peel to power, now committed to repeal.
Chapter XV — Further Remission of Duties: 1846
The Queen’s speech of January 19, 1846, expressed satisfaction in tariff reform and recommended further remissions. Martineau details the final legislative battles: the reduction of duties on raw materials, the corn duties, relief to farmers, and the passage of the great measure through both Houses. The chapter captures the agony of the Conservative Party splitting under Peel’s leadership, the dissolution of the League, the Irish Life Bill, and finally Peel’s resignation after the defeat on the Irish Coercion Bill. The closing passage is a magnificent tribute to Peel’s last position in the British Legislature — “the noblest that, in our period of time, could be held by any man.”
Chapter XVI — Deaths: Necrology
With the charm of a youthful Sovereign and a fresh royal generation came the mournfulness of seeing the old drop off. The chapter forms a lengthy necrology covering the deaths of the period: the Duke of Sussex, the Princess Sophia of Gloucester, Lord Ashburton, Lord Wharncliffe, Lord Denman, Lord Lyndhurst, Thomas Arnold, Sydney Smith, Thomas Campbell, James Montgomery, the painter Haydon’s suicide, Turner, Wilkie, George Stephenson, Sir John Herschel’s father, Brunel, and many more. It is both a memorial and a reckoning with the passing of the generation that had shaped the post-Napoleonic world.

Book VII — “Last Years of the Peace”
Book VII carries the narrative from Peel’s retirement in 1846 to the declaration of war against Russia in 1854. It covers the Irish Famine, the financial panic of 1847, the European Revolutions of 1848, the Great Exhibition of 1851, the Papal Aggression controversy, Palmerston’s foreign policy, and the drift toward war.
Chapter I — Ireland: The Famine
This opening chapter was written when the history appeared to be closing at 1846, before the final four years of peace could be foreseen. The chapter surveys the period from Peel’s retirement (June 29, 1846) to the outbreak of the Crimean War (March 1854). The first great national interest was the famine in Ireland — the failure of the potato crop, the government’s introduction of Indian meal, the inadequacy of relief measures, the emigration, and the terrible mortality. Martineau traces the Russell ministry’s struggle with the catastrophe.
Chapter III — Financial Panic of 1847
The prosperity acknowledged in 1852 had a special significance given the trials through which other countries — and Ireland — had passed. In 1847 came severe commercial distress and a financial panic such as it had been hoped the Bank Act of 1844 would never permit again. Martineau traces the causes: the railway speculation mania of 1845, the bad harvest of 1846, the Irish famine, and the deficient cotton supply. The Bank Act was suspended to allow the issue of extra notes, and the panic gradually subsided.
Chapter IV — Continental Agitations: Revolutions of 1848
Before the commercial embarrassment was over, the political trouble of the impending revolutions had begun. Martineau surveys the revolutionary wave of 1848: the fall of Louis-Philippe in France, the upheavals in Germany, Austria, Italy, Hungary, and the impact on British politics. She examines how the Chartist movement suddenly collapsed in the face of continental events — the Kennington Common meeting, the monster petition, and the government’s firm response that revealed Chartism’s hollow core.
Chapter V — Greek Controversy, Papal Aggression & Political Changes
During the brief remnant of the years of peace, the most stirring events received their impulse from abroad. The chapter opens with the Greek Controversy of 1850 — the Don Pacifico affair, Palmerston’s gunboat diplomacy, and the great debate in which Palmerston defended his policy with the famous “Civis Romanus sum” speech. It then traces the death of Sir Robert Peel (July 1850), and the explosion of the “Papal Aggression” controversy when Pius IX restored the Roman Catholic hierarchy in England. The chapter examines the resulting Ecclesiastical Titles Bill, the wave of anti-Catholic sentiment, and the fall of the Russell ministry.
Chapter VI — Political Disturbances: Palmerston’s Fall & the Derby Ministry
The chapter traces the condition of France after the coup d’état of Louis Napoleon, the recognition of the Second Empire, and the effect on English opinion. Lord Palmerston’s retirement (after his unauthorized endorsement of the coup), the formation of the short-lived Derby Ministry (February–December 1852), the general election, the fall of Derby, and the formation of Lord Aberdeen’s coalition ministry (Christmas 1852) — all lead toward the approaching war. The chapter closes with the “delusions of the Czar” and the beginning of the Eastern crisis.
Chapter VII — The United States
While political troubles perplexed Europe, deeply interesting events were happening in the United States — the spirit of the Southern slave-power ruling at Washington. The chapter examines the Mexican War (1846–48), which Martineau presents as an unprovoked aggression driven by slavery’s lust for fresh territory. She covers the Lopez filibustering expeditions to Cuba, the gold discoveries in California, the Oregon boundary settlement, and the Compromise of 1850. The closing of the book’s main narrative reaches its climax with the declaration of war against Russia in March 1854 — “a war accepted on behalf of a good cause, and there could scarcely have been a better or more natural close to the forty years’ peace.”
Chapter VIII — Arctic Expedition, Discoveries & National Advancement
This final chapter serves as a panoramic review of national advancement during the forty years’ peace. It opens with the Arctic Expedition of 1846 — Sir John Franklin and his comrades sailing in the Erebus and Terror, never to return. The chapter then surveys the great achievements of the age: the electric telegraph, photography (“sun-painting”), Lord Rosse’s telescope, the electric discoveries of Faraday, the steam revolution and railways, the Thames Tunnel, gun-cotton, chloroform and ether, the Nineveh marbles and Layard’s discoveries, the Great Exhibition of 1851 (the “Festival of Peace”), the Portland Breakwater, the Britannia Bridge, university reform, church dissensions, royal births and deaths, and a final necrology of the notable dead (the Duke of Wellington, 1852; Napier; Bentinck; George Stephenson; Wordsworth; Moore; Southey; Coleridge; James Watt’s legacy; Brunel). The volume closes with a reflective meditation on the meaning of progress — the slow, grand advance of the human race.

sources/marx-engels-communist-manifesto.title: Marx and Engels — Manifesto of the Communist Party
sources/marx-engels-communist-manifesto.content:
Marx and Engels — Manifesto of the Communist Party
Karl Marx (1818–1883) and Frederick Engels (1820–1895) — Manifesto of the Communist Party (German original 1848; this extract is an English text with the authorized Moore translation lineage and later prefaces). Commissioned at the November 1847 London Congress of the Communist League; manuscript sent to London for printing a few weeks before the February Revolution of 1848. First published in German; English first in Helen Macfarlane’s version in Harney’s Red Republican (1850); the authorized English translation by Samuel Moore, revised with Engels, London 1888 (William Reeves, 185 Fleet Street).
The extract is 2,270 lines / 18,899 words (121,106 bytes) from an Anna’s Archive plain-text dump (hash a07b587392459167b8c7d152b0c1a22a). It comprises successive prefaces (1872–1893), then the four chapters of the Manifesto proper with Engels’s notes from the 1888 English and related German editions. No separate modern scholarly foreword is present beyond the historical prefaces and notes in the file.
Content Summary
Prefaces


1872 German Edition (Marx & Engels, London, 24 June 1872) — Origin of the Manifesto as programme of the Communist League (secret international workers’ association under pre-1848 conditions); commission at the November 1847 London Congress; manuscript to London shortly before the February French Revolution. Publication history: many German editions in Germany, England, and America; English first 1850 (Red Republican, Helen Macfarlane) and American translations 1871; French before the June 1848 insurrection and again in Le Socialiste (New York); Polish (London); Russian (Geneva, 1860s); Danish. General principles still correct; practical application depends on historical conditions; revolutionary measures at the end of Section II would be worded differently after modern industry’s strides and especially the Paris Commune (proletariat holding power two months)—“the working class cannot simply lay hold of the ready-made state machinery, and wield it for its own purposes” (Civil War in France, 1871). Criticism of socialist literature stops at 1847; Section IV on opposition parties is principle-correct but practice-antiquated. The Manifesto is a historical document they have no right to alter.


1882 Russian Edition (Marx & Engels, London, 21 January 1882) — First Russian edition (Bakunin) early 1860s via the Kolokol printing office was a “literary curiosity”; no longer so. In 1847 Russia and the United States were missing from Section IV: Russia as reserve of European reaction, the United States absorbing surplus European proletarian forces; both as raw-material suppliers and markets for European industry. Now American agriculture shakes European landed property; American industry threatens Western European (especially English) industrial monopoly; a mass industrial proletariat and concentration of capital appear in the United States. The Tsar, once chief of European reaction, is “prisoner of war of the revolution in Gatchina”; Russia forms the vanguard of revolutionary action in Europe. Question of the Russian obshchina: if the Russian Revolution becomes the signal for a proletarian revolution in the West so that both complement each other, present Russian common ownership of land may serve as starting-point for communist development.


1883 German Edition (Engels alone, London, 28 June 1883) — Signed alone after Marx’s death (14 March 1883; Highgate Cemetery). Basic thought of the Manifesto—economic production and the social structure arising from it as foundation of political and intellectual history; history (since dissolution of primeval communal land ownership) as history of class struggles; the proletariat can emancipate itself only by freeing the whole of society—belongs solely to Marx.


1888 English Edition (Engels, London, 30 January 1888) — League history: German then international secret society; November 1847 commission; January 1848 German draft to London printer before 24 February; French before June 1848; Macfarlane English 1850; Danish and Polish. Defeat of the June 1848 Parisian insurrection drove proletarian aspirations into the background; propertied-class struggle resumed; Cologne Communist Trial (4 October–12 November 1852), fortress sentences, formal dissolution of the League; Manifesto seemed doomed to oblivion. International Working Men’s Association (1864) needed a broad programme acceptable to English trade unions, Proudhonists, and Lassalleans; Marx drew it; by the International’s break-up (1874) Proudhonism and Lassalleanism were dying and even English trade unions had advanced (Swansea president: “Continental socialism has lost its terror for us”). German text reprinted; 1872 New York English; authorized Moore translation revised jointly; Engels adds explanatory notes. Quotes 1872 preface on principles, Commune, and the Manifesto as unalterable historical document. Note equating the Manifesto’s basic thought, for history, with Darwin’s theory for biology; Engels’s independent approach shown in Condition of the Working Class in England; Marx had it worked out by spring 1845 Brussels.


1890 German Edition (Engels) — Records further translations: second Russian (Vera Zasulich, Geneva 1882) with the Marx–Engels preface; Polish (Manifest Kommunistyczny, Geneva); Danish (Socialdemokratisk Bibliothek, Copenhagen 1885, incomplete/careless in places); French 1886 in Le Socialiste (Paris), best to date; Spanish from that French text in El Socialista (Madrid) and pamphlet form; Armenian manuscript offered at Constantinople but publisher refused Marx’s name. Authentic English 1888 (Moore). History of the Manifesto: early enthusiasm of scientific-socialism’s vanguard; background after June 1848; “excommunicated by law” after Cologne 1852; return with the workers’ movement and the International; May Day 1890 mass demonstrations for the eight-hour day as international proletarian solidarity (Paris Congress of the Second International, July 1889).


1892 Polish Edition (Engels, London, 10 February 1892) — Demand for the Manifesto as index of large-scale industry’s development on the Continent. New Polish edition marks progress of Polish industry; Congress Poland as big industrial region of the Russian Empire, concentrated and hence both advantaged and a seedbed of socialist ideas. Polish independence necessary for harmonious collaboration of European nations; can be gained only by the young Polish proletariat; workers of the rest of Europe need Polish independence as much as Polish workers.


1893 Italian Edition (Engels, London, 1 February 1893) — Manifesto’s publication coincided with 18 March 1848 (Milan and Berlin). Revolution of 1848 the work of the working class on the barricades; only Paris workers aimed at overthrowing the bourgeois regime, but conditions not yet ripe for social reconstruction; fruits reaped by the capitalist class. Bourgeois rule requires national independence; 1848 brought unity and autonomy to Italy, Germany, Hungary; Poland will follow. 1848 not socialist but paved the way by creating a numerous concentrated proletariat—“its own grave-diggers.” Without national autonomy and unity, international union of the proletariat is impossible. Italy as first capitalist nation; Dante as last poet of the Middle Ages and first of modern times; will Italy give the new Dante of the proletarian era?


Manifesto of the Communist Party
Opening: A spectre is haunting Europe—the spectre of Communism. All the powers of old Europe have entered into a holy alliance to exorcise it. It is high time that Communists should openly publish their views, aims, and tendencies, and meet the nursery tale of the Spectre with a manifesto of the party itself. Communists of various nationalities have assembled in London and sketched the following manifesto, to be published in English, French, German, Italian, Flemish, and Danish.
Chapter I. Bourgeois and Proletarians
The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles (Engels note: written history; since 1847, research on primeval communal forms—Haxthausen, Maurer, Morgan). Freeman and slave, patrician and plebeian, lord and serf, guild-master and journeyman; modern epoch simplifies antagonisms into two great hostile camps—bourgeoisie and proletariat (definitions in Engels’s 1888 note: owners of the means of social production employing wage labour; wage labourers reduced to selling labour power).
From the serfs of the Middle Ages sprang the chartered burghers; from these the first elements of the bourgeoisie. Discovery of America, rounding of the Cape, East Indian and Chinese markets, colonisation of America, trade with the colonies, increase of means of exchange and commodities, revolutionary impetus to feudal society. The feudal or guild system of industry no longer sufficed; manufacturing system took its place; markets kept growing; steam and machinery revolutionised industrial production; modern industry and the world market. The bourgeoisie has played a most revolutionary part: ended feudal, patriarchal, idyllic relations; left no other nexus than naked self-interest and callous “cash payment”; drowned religious fervour, chivalrous enthusiasm, philistine sentimentalism in the icy water of egotistical calculation; resolved personal worth into exchange value; set up free trade in place of chartered freedoms; stripped occupations of their haloes; converted the physician, the lawyer, the priest, the poet, the man of science into paid wage labourers; tore away the veil from the family and reduced it to a mere money relation.
Constant revolutionising of production; uninterrupted disturbance of all social conditions; everlasting uncertainty—“All that is solid melts into air, all that is holy is profaned.” Need of a constantly expanding market chases the bourgeoisie over the whole surface of the globe. Exploitation of the world market gives a cosmopolitan character to production and consumption; national industries destroyed or daily destroyed; raw material drawn from remotest zones; new wants requiring products of distant lands; intellectual creations become common property; national one-sidedness becomes more impossible. Country subjected to the towns; barbarian and semi-barbarian countries dependent on the civilised, the East on the West. Agglomeration of population, centralisation of means of production, concentration of property, political centralisation. In scarce one hundred years the bourgeoisie has created more massive productive forces than all preceding generations together: subjection of Nature’s forces, machinery, chemistry in industry and agriculture, steam-navigation, railways, electric telegraphs, clearing of continents, canalisation of rivers, whole populations conjured out of the ground.
Feudal relations of property became fetters and were burst asunder; free competition and bourgeois sway stepped into their place. A similar movement now: modern bourgeois society is like the sorcerer no longer able to control the powers of the nether world he has called up. Commercial crises periodically destroy products and productive forces; epidemic of over-production. The weapons with which the bourgeoisie felled feudalism are turned against the bourgeoisie itself. But it has also called into existence the men who are to wield those weapons—the modern working class, the proletarians.
In proportion as the bourgeoisie is developed, the proletariat is developed—a class of labourers who live only so long as they find work, and who find work only so long as their labour increases capital. These labourers, who must sell themselves piecemeal, are a commodity. Owing to the extensive use of machinery and to division of labour, the work of the proletarians has lost all individual character; the cost of production of a workman is restricted almost entirely to the means of subsistence; wages equal to that cost; mass of labourers crowded into the factory organised like soldiers. Distinctions of age and sex have no longer any distinctive social validity; all are instruments of labour. No sooner is the exploitation of the labourer by the manufacturer ended than he is set upon by the other portions of the bourgeoisie—landlord, shopkeeper, pawnbroker.
Lower strata of the middle class sink into the proletariat. The proletariat goes through various stages of development: at first struggle of individual labourers, then of a factory, then of an entire trade in one locality, against the individual bourgeois who exploits them; destroy imported wares, smash machinery, set factories ablaze—destroy the instruments of production to restore the vanished status of the workman of the Middle Ages. At this stage labourers still form an incoherent mass scattered over the country; their combination not yet the consequence of their own active union but of the union of the bourgeoisie. With industry the proletariat not only increases in number; it becomes concentrated in greater masses, its strength grows, it feels that strength more. Interests and conditions of life within the ranks of the proletariat more and more equalised. Collisions take on the character of collisions between two classes; workers form combinations (trades’ unions) against the bourgeois; clubs permanent; here and there the contest breaks into riots. Now and then the workers are victorious, but only for a time; the real fruit of their battles lies not in the immediate result but in the ever-expanding union of the workers. This union is helped on by improved means of communication. National struggles of the proletarians of different countries are on the point of combination in one national struggle between classes. Organisation of the proletarians into a class, and consequently into a political party, is continually being upset again by competition between the workers themselves, but it ever rises up again stronger, firmer, mightier. It compels legislative recognition of particular interests of the workers (e.g. the ten hours’ bill in England).
The bourgeoisie finds itself in constant battle—with the aristocracy, with portions of the bourgeoisie itself whose interests have become antagonistic to the progress of industry, with the bourgeoisie of foreign countries—and is compelled to appeal to the proletariat, thus dragging it into the political arena and furnishing it with its own elements of political and general education. Entire sections of the ruling class are precipitated into the proletariat; a portion of the bourgeois ideologists who have raised themselves to the level of comprehending theoretically the historical movement as a whole goes over to the proletariat. Of all classes that stand face to face with the bourgeoisie today, the proletariat alone is a really revolutionary class. The lower middle class—small manufacturer, shopkeeper, artisan, peasant—are conservative or reactionary, seeking to roll back the wheel of history; if revolutionary, only in view of their impending transfer into the proletariat. The “dangerous class,” the social scum (lumpenproletariat), may be swept into the movement but is more prepared for the part of a bribed tool of reactionary intrigue.
The proletarian is without property; modern industrial labour has stripped him of every trace of national character; law, morality, religion are to him so many bourgeois prejudices. All previous classes that got the upper hand sought to fortify their already acquired status; the proletarians cannot become masters of the productive forces of society except by abolishing their own previous mode of appropriation and thereby every other previous mode of appropriation. The proletarian movement is the self-conscious, independent movement of the immense majority in the interest of the immense majority. The essential condition for the existence and sway of the bourgeois class is the formation and augmentation of capital; the condition for capital is wage-labour; wage-labour rests on competition between the labourers. The advance of industry replaces the isolation of the labourers due to competition by their revolutionary combination due to association. What the bourgeoisie therefore produces, above all, are its own grave-diggers. Its fall and the victory of the proletariat are equally inevitable.
Chapter II. Proletarians and Communists
Relation of the Communists to the proletarians as a whole: Communists do not form a separate party opposed to other working-class parties; they have no interests separate and apart from those of the proletariat as a whole; they do not set up any sectarian principles. They are distinguished only by: (1) in the national struggles of the proletarians of the different countries, they point out and bring to the front the common interests of the entire proletariat, independently of all nationality; (2) in the various stages of development which the struggle of the working class against the bourgeoisie has to pass through, they always and everywhere represent the interests of the movement as a whole. Practically, the most advanced and resolute section of the working-class parties of every country; theoretically, they have over the great mass of the proletariat the advantage of clearly understanding the line of march, the conditions, and the ultimate general results of the proletarian movement. Immediate aim: formation of the proletariat into a class, overthrow of the bourgeois supremacy, conquest of political power by the proletariat.
Theoretical conclusions of the Communists are in no way based on ideas or principles invented or discovered by this or that would-be reformer; they merely express, in general terms, actual relations springing from an existing class struggle, from a historical movement going on under our very eyes. Abolition of existing property relations is not a distinctive feature of Communism; all property relations have been subject to historical change. The distinguishing feature is not the abolition of property generally, but the abolition of bourgeois property. Modern bourgeois private property is the final and most complete expression of the system of producing and appropriating products that is based on class antagonisms, on the exploitation of the many by the few. In this sense the theory of the Communists may be summed up in the single sentence: Abolition of private property.
Communism deprives no man of the power to appropriate the products of society; all that it does is to deprive him of the power to subjugate the labour of others by means of such appropriation. Objection that upon the abolition of private property all work will cease is answered: if that were so, bourgeois society ought long ago to have gone to the dogs through sheer idleness; those of its members who work acquire nothing, and those who acquire anything do not work. Culture under which the enormous majority have been stunted is, for the bourgeoisie, identical with the disappearance of all culture. Bourgeois notions of freedom, culture, law, &c., are but the outgrowth of bourgeois production and property. Charges concerning the family, education, and the “hallowed co-relation of parent and child” are answered by pointing to the practical absence of the family among the proletarians, to public prostitution, and to the education of children turned into a mere article of commerce. Bourgeois marriage is in reality a system of wives in common; the Communists might be reproached at most with desiring to introduce, in substitution for a hypocritically concealed, an openly legalised community of women—and abolition of the present system of production will abolish prostitution both public and private.
“The working men have no country.” National differences and antagonisms between peoples are daily more and more vanishing; supremacy of the proletariat will cause them to vanish still faster. United action of the leading civilised countries is one of the first conditions for the emancipation of the proletariat. Exploitation of one nation by another will be put an end to with the exploitation of one individual by another. Charges from a religious, philosophical, and ideological standpoint: man’s consciousness changes with every change in the conditions of his material existence; the ruling ideas of each age have ever been the ideas of its ruling class; the Communist revolution is the most radical rupture with traditional property relations and therefore with traditional ideas.
First step in the revolution: raise the proletariat to the position of ruling class, to win the battle of democracy. The proletariat will use its political supremacy to wrest, by degree, all capital from the bourgeoisie, to centralise all instruments of production in the hands of the State (the proletariat organised as the ruling class), and to increase the total productive forces as rapidly as possible. Despotic inroads on the rights of property unavoidable as means of entirely revolutionising the mode of production. In most advanced countries, generally applicable measures:

Abolition of property in land and application of all rents of land to public purposes.
A heavy progressive or graduated income tax.
Abolition of all rights of inheritance.
Confiscation of the property of all emigrants and rebels.
Centralisation of credit in the hands of the state, by means of a national bank with State capital and an exclusive monopoly.
Centralisation of the means of communication and transport in the hands of the State.
Extension of factories and instruments of production owned by the State; the bringing into cultivation of waste-lands, and the improvement of the soil generally in accordance with a common plan.
Equal liability of all to work. Establishment of industrial armies, especially for agriculture.
Combination of agriculture with manufacturing industries; gradual abolition of all the distinction between town and country by a more equable distribution of the populace over the country.
Free education for all children in public schools. Abolition of children’s factory labour in its present form. Combination of education with industrial production, &c., &c.

When class distinctions have disappeared and all production is concentrated in the hands of a vast association of the whole nation, the public power will lose its political character. Political power is merely the organised power of one class for oppressing another. If the proletariat, organised as a class, by revolution makes itself the ruling class and sweeps away the old conditions of production, it will have swept away the conditions for the existence of class antagonisms and of classes generally, and will thereby have abolished its own supremacy as a class. In place of the old bourgeois society, with its classes and class antagonisms, an association in which the free development of each is the condition for the free development of all.
Chapter III. Socialist and Communist Literature
1. Reactionary Socialism

A. Feudal Socialism — Aristocracies of France and England, after July 1830 and the English reform agitation, reduced to literary battle; feudal Socialism half lamentation, half lampoon; waves the proletarian alms-bag but shows feudal coats of arms; French Legitimists and “Young England”; in practice join coercive measures against the working class; barter truth, love, and honour for traffic in wool, beetroot-sugar, and potato spirits. Clerical Socialism hand in hand with Feudal Socialism.
B. Petty-Bourgeois Socialism — In countries where modern civilisation has become fully developed, a new petty bourgeoisie oscillates between proletariat and bourgeoisie (e.g. in France); Sismondi as head of this school in France and England. Dissection of contradictions in modern production; but either wants to restore old means of production and exchange, or to cramp modern means within the framework of the old property relations—both reactionary and Utopian (corporate guilds for manufacture; patriarchal relations in agriculture).
C. German or “True” Socialism — German philosophers and semi-philosophers took French socialist literature without the social conditions of France; French literature stripped of immediate revolutionary significance became pure literature representing the Nature of Man; German Socialism proclaimed the German nation the model nation and the German petty philistine the typical man; became a weapon against the bourgeoisie in the hands of German absolute governments, and an expression of reactionary interests of the German philistine.

2. Conservative or Bourgeois Socialism — Part of the bourgeoisie desirous of redressing social grievances to secure continued existence of bourgeois society: economists, philanthropists, humanitarians, organisers of charity, societies for prevention of cruelty to animals, temperance fanatics, hole-and-corner reformers; Proudhon’s Philosophie de la Misère as example. Desire existing society minus its revolutionary elements; a bourgeoisie without a proletariat. Practical form: depreciate every revolutionary movement by showing only change in material conditions (meaning administrative reforms, not abolition of bourgeois relations of production) can help. Free trade, protective duties, prison reform—all “for the benefit of the working class.” Summed up: the bourgeois is a bourgeois—for the benefit of the working class.
3. Critical-Utopian Socialism and Communism — Not the literature of every great modern revolution that voiced proletarian demands (Babeuf, &c.). The first direct attempts of the proletariat in times of universal excitement necessarily failed; the revolutionary literature that accompanied them was reactionary in content (universal asceticism, social levelling in its crudest form). Socialist and Communist systems properly so called (Saint-Simon, Fourier, Owen, &c.) appear in the first undeveloped period of struggle between proletariat and bourgeoisie. They see class antagonisms and action of the decomposing elements in the prevailing form of society, but the proletariat, as yet in its infancy, offers to them the spectacle of a class without any historical initiative. They want to improve the condition of every member of society, even the most favoured; hence appeal to society at large without distinction of class, and preferentially to the ruling class. They reject all political, and especially all revolutionary, action; wish to attain their ends by peaceful means and small experiments. Critical element: attack every principle of existing society; hence full of the most valuable materials for the enlightenment of the working class. Their positive proposals (abolition of the distinction between town and country, of the family, of the carrying on of industries for private account, of the wage system; proclamation of social harmony; conversion of the functions of the State into a mere superintendence of production) point solely to the disappearance of class antagonisms which were, as yet, only just cropping up. Significance is in inverse ratio to historical development; though the originators were revolutionary in many respects, their disciples form mere reactionary sects.
Chapter IV. Position of the Communists in Relation to the Various Existing Opposition Parties
Section II has made clear relations to existing working-class parties such as the Chartists in England and the Agrarian Reformers in America. Communists fight for attainment of the immediate aims and momentary interests of the working class, but in the movement of the present they also represent and take care of the future of that movement.

France — Ally with the Social-Democrats against the conservative and radical bourgeoisie, reserving the right to take up a critical position toward phases and illusions traditionally handed down from the great Revolution (Engels note: party of Ledru-Rollin, Louis Blanc, Réforme).
Switzerland — Support the Radicals, without losing sight of antagonistic elements (Democratic Socialists in the French sense; radical bourgeois).
Poland — Support the party that insists on an agrarian revolution as the prime condition for national emancipation (the party which fomented the Cracow insurrection of 1846).
Germany — Fight with the bourgeoisie whenever it acts in a revolutionary way against the absolute monarchy, the feudal squirearchy, and the petty bourgeoisie; never cease to instill into the working class the clearest possible recognition of the hostile antagonism between bourgeoisie and proletariat, so that after the fall of the reactionary classes the fight against the bourgeoisie itself may immediately begin. Attention chiefly to Germany, on the eve of a bourgeois revolution under more advanced conditions of European civilisation and with a much more developed proletariat than England in the seventeenth or France in the eighteenth century; the German bourgeois revolution will be but the prelude to an immediately following proletarian revolution.

Communists everywhere support every revolutionary movement against the existing social and political order of things. In all these movements they bring to the front, as the leading question in each, the property question. They labour everywhere for the union and agreement of the democratic parties of all countries. They disdain to conceal their views and aims. They openly declare that their ends can be attained only by the forcible overthrow of all existing social conditions. Let the ruling classes tremble at a Communistic revolution. The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win.
Working Men of All Countries, Unite!
