sources/mayhew-london-labour-london-poor.content:
London Labour and the London Poor, Vol. I: The London Street-Folk
Publication History
First published in single volume form in 1851, covering only the Street-Folk. The enlarged four-volume edition appeared 1861–62. This is Volume I of that enlarged set.
Contents
The Street-Folk
Wandering Tribes in General — Mayhew’s opening classification of nomadic and wandering populations; theoretical framework for studying street folk as distinct tribes.
Wandering Tribes in the Country — Rural wandering populations: hawkers, pedlars, showmen, and travelling labourers; comparison with urban street populations.
The London Street-Folk — General survey of the street population of London: numbers, classifications, and economic conditions; the street-sellers as a distinct class.
Costermongers — The largest and most organized group of London street-sellers. Sub-sections include:

Costermongers Attending the London Markets
Markets on the Surrey Side
Markets on the Middlesex Side
The London Costermonger — detailed portrait of the costermonger’s life, habits, earnings, language, and social organization
The Coster-Girl — female costermongers
The Oyster Stall — specialist oyster sellers

Street Sellers of Fish — Fish sellers in the streets; Billingsgate market; types of fish sold; earnings and conditions.
Street Sellers of Fruit and Vegetables — Green-grocers and fruit sellers; market tables showing quantities of home-grown and imported produce sold throughout the year.
Stationary Street Sellers of Fish, Fruit, and Vegetables — Fixed stalls and shops compared with mobile street-selling.
The Street Irish — Irish immigrants in the London street trade; their concentration in certain occupations; social conditions and earnings.
Street Sellers of Game, Poultry, Rabbits, Butter, Cheese, and Eggs — Sellers of provisions and animal products.
Street Sellers of Trees, Shrubs, Flowers, Roots, Seeds, and Branches — Plant and flower sellers; quantity tables for annual wholesale market sales.
Street Sellers of Green Stuff — Sellers of fresh greens and herbs; includes The Groundsel Man.
Street Sellers of Eatables and Drinkables — Food and drink vendors: baked potatoes, coffee-stalls, pie-men, herbalists; includes The Baked Potato Man, The London Coffee-Stall, The Coster Boy and Girl Tossing the Pieman, Doctor Bokanky the Street Herbalist.
Street Sellers of Stationery, Literature, and the Fine Arts — Print-sellers, ballad-singers, song-sellers, book-auctioneers, street-artists; includes Long-Song Seller, Hindoo Tract-Seller, The Kitchen at Fox-Court, and extensive treatment of street ballads and popular literature.
Street Sellers of Manufactured Articles — Sellers of small manufactured goods: nutmeg-graters, dog-collars, crockery-ware, walking-sticks, boot-laces, lucifer matches, combs, rhubarb and spice, and other articles.
The Women Street Sellers — Women engaged in street-selling across all categories; their particular hardships, earnings, and social position.
The Children Street Sellers — Children working as street-sellers; their earnings, living conditions, and the moral and physical effects of street life on children.
Appendices and Tables
Throughout the volume, Mayhew includes detailed statistical tables showing:

Quantities and values of goods sold in London markets
Earnings of different classes of street-sellers
Capital invested in street-trading
Demographic data on street populations

sources/mayhew-london-labour-london-poor.title: London Labour and the London Poor, Vol. II: The London Street-Folk, Book the Second
sources/mayhew-london-labour-london-poor.content:
London Labour and the London Poor, Vol. II: The London Street-Folk, Book the Second
Publication History
Volume II of the enlarged 1861–62 edition. This volume continues Mayhew’s survey of the Street-Folk begun in Volume I, shifting from street-sellers of goods to street-sellers of services and second-hand articles, the buyers and collectors who form the other side of the street economy, the people who clean the streets, and the street-sweepers. The source file for this volume comes from a Cornell University Library scan (Woodfall and Son imprint) with digitisation by Microsoft.
Contents
Introduction
Mayhew opens the volume with a statistical and philosophical introduction on the proportion of street-traders to the general metropolitan population. He discusses the inadequacy of the 1841 Census (which set down “Hawkers, Hucksters, and Pedlars” at only 2,045 for the Metropolis) and argues for the true scale of the street population.
I. Street-Sellers of Second-hand Articles
Dealers in old clothes, second-hand furniture, and cast-off goods — the vast market in second-hand articles centred on Petticoat Lane and Rosemary Lane.

Petticoat Lane market — scenes, traders, quantities
The Jew Old-Clothes Man — portraits and interviews
Old Clothes Exchange and the “swag-shops”

II. Street-Sellers of Live Animals
Sellers of dogs, birds, caged animals, pigeons, and songbirds. Includes:

The Street-Seller of Birds’ Nests
The Crippled Street Bird-Seller
Dog-sellers and the dog-stealing trade
Sellers of guinea-pigs, rabbits, and other small animals

III. Street-Sellers of Miscellaneous Productions and Natural Curiosities
Hawkers of oddities: shells, fossils, minerals, preserved specimens, and natural rarities. Street-corner museums and portable cabinets.
IV. The Street-Buyers
An unusual category — the buyers who attend street-auctions, buy from street-sellers to resell, and the rag-and-bottle shops. The middlemen of the street economy who collect and redistribute goods.
V. The Street-Jews
A dedicated section on the Jewish population engaged in street-trading, especially the old-clothes trade. Social organisation, religious observance, and economic position of the Jewish street-traders.
VI. Street-Finders or Collectors
The urban scavengers and collectors who make a living from what others discard:

The Bone-Grubber — collectors of bones, rags, and scrap metal
The Mud-Lark — children and adults who scavenge the Thames foreshore at low tide for coal, rope, iron, and copper
The London Dustman — dust-collectors and the dust-yards
The London Scavenger — street-sweeping contractors
The Rubbish-Carter — cartage and disposal of household waste
Street Orderlies — men employed to keep streets clean
The Able-Bodied Pauper Street-Sweeper — paupers put to work sweeping as a condition of relief

VII. The Streets of London
A comprehensive section on the sanitary condition of London’s streets — the filth, the scavenging system, the inefficiency of contractors, and proposals for reform. Subsections include:

The Sewer-Hunter — men who enter and clean London’s sewers
Mode of Cleansing Cesspools — the night-soil trade
Flushing the Sewers — methods and equipment
The Rat-Catchers of the Sewers — the vermin population of the underground drainage system
London Nightmen — the men who empty cesspools at night
Dust-yards and the sorting of London’s refuse

VIII. Chimney-Sweepers
The trade and condition of chimney-sweeps in London. Includes:

The London Sweep — a general profile of the climbing-boy system
One of the Few Remaining Climbing-Sweeps — an interview with a surviving child-sweep
The Sweep’s Home — living conditions
The Milkmaid’s Garland — May-day traditions among sweeps
The gradual reform of the trade after the Chimney Sweepers Act

IX. Crossing-Sweepers
The men and boys (and some women) who sweep street-crossings for alms. Individual portraits include:

The Bearded Crossing-Sweeper at the Exchange
The Crossing-Sweeper that has been a Maid-Servant
The Irish Crossing-Sweeper
The One-Legged Crossing-Sweeper at Chancery Lane
The Boy Crossing-Sweepers
Earnings, rivalries over pitches, and hierarchies among crossing-sweepers

Notes
This volume covers what might be called the “service and waste” side of the street economy — the sellers of used goods, the collectors of refuse, the cleaners of streets and sewers, and the chimney-sweepers. Working conditions are described in extraordinary physical detail, often quoting the workers themselves.
The text is derived from a Cornell University scan with Microsoft digitisation. OCR quality is uneven — the TOC and some section headings are particularly garbled, but interview and narrative passages remain largely readable.

sources/mayhew-london-labour-london-poor.title: mayhew-london-labour-london-poor-vol3
sources/mayhew-london-labour-london-poor.content:
Henry Mayhew — London Labour and the London Poor, Vol. III: The London Street-Folk
Metadata





































FieldValueAuthorHenry MayhewFull TitleLondon Labour and the London Poor: A Cyclopædia of the Condition and Earnings of Those That Will Work, Those That Cannot Work, and Those That Will Not WorkVolumeVol. III: The London Street-FolkEditionFirst edition 1851 (Vol. I only); enlarged edition 1861–62 (4 vols.); new impression 1865PublisherAngell Press (reprint)ISBN978-1-4474-6519-5Raw textmayhew-london-labour-london-poor-vol3.txt (8,995 lines)
Description
The third volume of Henry Mayhew’s encyclopaedic survey of the London poor, covering the “Street-Folk” — those who work and live in the public spaces of the metropolis. This volume examines the street trades and labouring classes of mid-Victorian London through first-hand interviews, statistical analysis, and vivid ethnographic description. It covers the street sellers, performers, artisans, and unskilled labourers who made their living on the streets of London.
Contents
I. The Destroyers of Vermin

The Rat-Killer — sporting rat-catchers in Somers-town, rat-killing at public-houses
Jack Black, Her Majesty’s Ratcatcher — the Queen’s official rat-destroyer at Battersea
“Catch-‘em-alive” boys — lads who catch birds and vermin
Bug-destroyers — Tiffin & Son and the trade in phosphor paste

II. Street-Exhibitors

Punch’s Showmen — the travelling puppet-showmen
Street-Performers on Stilts
Street-Acrobats — performing at fairs
Street-Conjurors — itinerant magicians
Street-Telescope Exhibitors — charging for views through a telescope

III. Street-Musicians

Old Sarah — a street singer
Ethiopian Serenaders — blackface minstrel performers
Italian organ-grinders and street bands

IV. Street-Vocalists

Street ballad-singers and vocal performers

V. Street-Artists

Interior of Photographer’s Travelling Caravan
Street portrait-painters and sketchers

VI. Exhibitors of Trained Animals

Performing dogs, monkeys, and other animal shows

VII. Skilled and Unskilled Labour
Garret-Masters

Cheap Cabinet-Makers — the garret-master system
Home-working artisans in the furniture trade

The Coal-Heavers

The Coalbackers — men who carry coal sacks from ships
The Coalmeters — who measure coal for sale
The Coalporters — who fill waggons at coal-wharves
Conditions of work in the coal trade

Ballast-Men

Ballast-heavers at work in the Pool of London
Meeting of the Ballast-Heavers’ Wives

Lumpers

Discharging timber-ships in the Commercial Docks
The timber trade and its labourers

The Dock-Labourers

Casual labour in the London Docks
The “call-on” system and its miseries

Cheap Lodging-Houses

A dinner at a cheap lodging-house
The lowest class of metropolitan lodging-houses
Conditions, vermin, and overcrowding

The Transit of Great Britain and the Metropolis

London Watermen, Lightermen, and Steamboat-Men — Thames river workers
London Omnibus-Drivers and Conductors
London Cab-Drivers
London Carmen and Porters — street ticket-porters

London Vagrants

The Casual Ward of the Workhouse
The Asylum for the Houseless Poor, Playhouse-Yard
Tables of ages and countries of applicants
The Refuge for the Houseless Poor
Vagrants’ habits and histories

Meeting of Ticket-of-Leave Men

A gathering of convicts released on licence
Their statements and efforts at reform

Notes
The filename labels this as “Vol. 2” but the actual content is Volume III of the 1861–62 enlarged edition. The first edition (1851) consisted only of Volume I; the expanded four-volume set was published 1861–62. Volume I covered the street-sellers; Volume II the street-buyers and street-finders; Volume III (this volume) the street-folk; and Volume IV (published posthumously) additional material on prostitutes, thieves, and the criminal classes, with contributions by John Binny and others.
Many of the sections in this volume originated in Mayhew’s Morning Chronicle letters of 1849–50, but were rewritten and expanded for the book edition.

sources/mayhew-london-labour-london-poor.content:
London Labour and the London Poor, Vol. IV: Those That Will Not Work — Prostitutes, Thieves, Swindlers, Beggars and Vagrants
Publication History
Volume IV of the enlarged 1861–62 edition. Unlike the first three volumes — which are entirely by Mayhew — this volume is a collaborative work. The structure is distinctive: it opens with a substantial essay by the Rev. William Tuckniss cataloguing the religious, charitable, and reformatory agencies operating in London, followed by Mayhew’s general introduction and classification system, and then by extended treatises on prostitution, thieves, cheats, and beggars contributed by associates. The source text comes from a scan of the Griffin, Bohn edition.
Contents
I. Introductory Essay: The Agencies at Present in Operation within the Metropolis for the Suppression of Vice and Crime
By the Rev. William Tuckniss, B.A.
A comprehensive survey of the philanthropic landscape of mid-Victorian London, covering:

Preventive Agencies — Ragged School Union; Society for Improving the Condition of the Labouring Classes; Female Servants’ Home Society; Field Lane Night Refuges; Houseless Poor Asylum; Foundling Hospital; Association for the Relief of Destitution
Curative Agencies — British and Foreign Bible Society; Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge; London City Mission; Church of England Scripture Readers’ Society; Religious Tract Society; Pure Literature Society
Reformative Agencies — Reformatory and Refuge Union; Magdalen Hospital; London by Moonlight Mission; Society for the Rescue of Young Women and Children; London Female Preventive and Reformatory Institution
Repressive and Punitive Agencies — Society for the Suppression of Vice; Society for Promoting the Observance of the Lord’s Day; Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals

Tuckniss discusses the inadequacy of mere palliatives, the doubtful decrease of crime, and the social position of London as a concentration of both vice and charitable effort.
II. Introduction and Classification
By Henry Mayhew
Mayhew’s famous taxonomic system for classifying the metropolitan population:


THOSE WHO WILL WORK

Enrichers (deriving income from rent, dividends, yearly stipends, obsolete offices)
Auxiliaries (trades in which the worker does not appear)
Benefactors
Servitors



THOSE THAT NEED NOT WORK

Those who derive income from rent
Those who derive income from dividends
Those who derive income from yearly stipends



THOSE WHO CANNOT WORK

Those who are provided for
Those who are unprovided for



THOSE WHO WILL NOT WORK

Vagrants or Tramps
Professional Beggars
Cheats and their Dependants
Thieves and their Dependants
Prostitutes and their Dependants



III. The Prostitute Class Generally
By Henry Mayhew and Bracebridge Hemyng
An encyclopaedic survey of prostitution, organised geographically and historically:
Prostitution in Ancient States — The Jews; Ancient Egypt; Ancient Greece; Ancient Rome; The Anglo-Saxons
Prostitution among the Barbarous Nations — African Nations; Australia; New Zealand; Islands of the Pacific; North American Indians; South American Indians; Cities of South America; West Indies; Java; Sumatra; Borneo
Prostitution among the Semi-Civilized Nations — Celebes; Persia; The Affghans; Kashmir; India; Ceylon; China; Japan; Egypt; Northern Africa; Arabia, Syria, and Asia Minor; Turkey; Circassia; The Tartar Races
Prostitution among the Mixed Northern Nations — Russia; Siberia; Iceland and Greenland; Lapland and Sweden; Norway; Denmark
Prostitution in Civilized States — Spain; Amsterdam; Belgium; Hamburg; Prussia-Germany; Berlin; Austria; Modern Rome; Turin; Berne; Paris
Prostitution in London
By Bracebridge Hemyng

General Remarks — statistics and surveys
Seclusives — those who live in private houses and apartments; the Haymarket
Board Lodgers — including autobiographies of prostitutes
Those Who Live in Low Lodging Houses — Swindling Sall; Lushing Loo
Sailors’ Women — Ratcliff Highway; Bluegate Fields
Soldiers’ Women — Knightsbridge
Thieves’ Women — Drury Lane
Park Women — Hyde Park prostitutes
The Dependants of Prostitutes — bawds, procuresses, pimps, panders, fancy men, keepers of accommodation houses, bullies
Clandestine Prostitutes — female operatives, maid-servants, ladies of intrigue and houses of assignation
Cohabitant Prostitutes — narrative of a gay woman
Criminal Returns
Traffic in Foreign Women

IV. Thieves and Swindlers
By John Binny
A systematic survey of London’s criminal classes:
Introduction — Classification of thieves
Sneaks, or Common Thieves

Juvenile Thieves — child stripping
Stealing from the Till

Horse and Dog Stealers

Horse Stealing
Dog Stealing

Highway Robbers

A Ramble among the Thieves’ Dens in the Borough
Narrative of a Burglar

Housebreakers and Burglars

Park Women

Felonies on the River Thames

Mudlarks

Smuggling

Narrative of a Mudlark

V. Cheats
By Several Contributors

Embezzlers

Swindlers

VI. Beggars
By Andrew Halliday
A systematic classification of London beggars:
Disaster Beggars — A Shipwrecked Mariner; Blown-up Miners; Burnt-out Tradesmen; Lucifer Droppers
Bodily Afflicted Beggars — Seventy Years a Beggar; Having Swollen Legs; Cripples; A Blind Beggar; Beggars Subject to Fits; Being in a Decline; Shallow Coves; Famished Beggars
Begging Letter Writers — Decayed Gentlemen; Broken-down Tradesmen; Distressed Scholar; The Kaggs’ Family; Advertising Begging Letter Writers
Ashamed Beggars
The Swell Beggar
Clean Family Beggars
Naval and Military Beggars — Turnpike Sailor; Street Campaigners; Destitute Poles; Negro Beggars
Foreign Beggars — Hindoo Beggars; The French Beggar
Distressed Operative Beggars — Starved-out Manufacturers; Unemployed Agriculturists; Frozen-out Gardeners; Hand-loom Weavers; The Choking Dodge; The Offal Eater
Petty Trading Beggars — An Author’s Wife
Dependants of Beggars — Referees
VII. Vagrants

Origin and History of the Poor Laws
Statistics of the Poor Laws
Report of the Poor Law Board
Street Beggars in 1816
Mendicant Pensioners
Mendicity Society
Examples of Applications
The Low Lodging Houses

Appendix: Maps and Tables
Criminal statistics of each county in England and Wales, including:

Map showing the Density of the Population
Tables of criminal returns

Notes
Volume IV is the most heterogeneous of the four volumes, combining Mayhew’s own work with substantial contributions by associates. The Rev. William Tuckniss’s introductory essay on London’s charitable agencies is a valuable survey of the mid-Victorian philanthropic landscape. The lengthy section on prostitution by Bracebridge Hemyng includes an ambitious comparative survey of prostitution across world cultures. John Binny’s section on thieves and swindlers is among the most detailed contemporary accounts of the London criminal underworld.
The OCR quality is mixed — the Roman-numeral page numbering in the Tuckniss essay is particularly garbled, but the main text of each section is readable.

sources/mayhew-morning-chronicle-survey.content:
Henry Mayhew — The Morning Chronicle Survey of Labour and the Poor: The Metropolitan Districts
Metadata





































FieldValueAuthorHenry Mayhew (with Peter Razzell, ed.)Full TitleThe Morning Chronicle Survey of Labour and the Poor: The Metropolitan DistrictsSeriesRoutledge Library of Sociology (Vol. 20 of a set reprinting the Morning Chronicle letters)EditionFirst published 1981 by Caliban Books; this edition 2017 by RoutledgeISBN978-1-138-20393-8 (Volume 20 hbk)Year1850 (original letters); 1981/2017 (modern compilation)Raw textmayhew-morning-chronicle-survey.txt (3,592 lines)
Description
A compilation of 14 letters from Henry Mayhew’s celebrated series in the Morning Chronicle (January–March 1850), investigating the condition of the labouring poor in the metropolitan districts. These letters, written by Mayhew as Special Correspondent to the Morning Chronicle, formed the raw material for his later, expanded work London Labour and the London Poor (4 vols., 1861–62). The letters present vivid first-hand testimony, statistical tables, and analytical commentary on the social conditions, trades, and habits of the London poor.
Contents
Letters
















































































LetterDateSubjectLetter XXVIIJan 18, 1850Casual wards, vagrancy, the Houseless Poor — the evils of uncertain labour, the system of casual wards in workhouses, and the class of habitual vagrants created by the systemLetter XXVIIIJan 22, 1850Geographical history of vagrancy over 14 years — tables from the Asylum for the Houseless Poor showing numbers by county and country, the effect of the Irish famineLetter XXIXJan 25, 1850Causes of depredation, vagrancy, and mendicancy — drawing on the Constabulary Commissioners’ Report of 1839Letter XXXJan 29, 1850Vagrancy as a source of crime — further investigation into its causesLetter XXXIJan 31, 1850Characters frequenting the low lodging-houses of the Metropolis — first-hand statements from the inhabitantsLetter XXXIIFeb 4, 1850Condition of the artisans of London — begins a series on the Metropolitan Boot and Shoe MakersLetter XXXIIIFeb 7, 1850Earnings of Boot and Shoe makers — the West-end Men’s Trade, with detailed accountsLetter XXXIVFeb 11, 1850Earnings of “men’s-men” in the eastern division of the boot and shoe tradeLetter XXXVFeb 14, 1850The Cheap and Slop Shoe Trade — iniquitous practices, meanness and petty cheatsLetter XXXVIFeb 18, 1850Conclusion of the Slop Boot and Shoe trade investigationLetter XXXVIIFeb 21, 1850Toy-makers — intended to be on Prison labour but deferred for statisticsLetter XXXVIIIFeb 25, 1850Toy-makers continued — makers of playthings for the children of the richLetter XXXIXFeb 28, 1850Doll manufacture — the distinction between “wooden” and “sewed” dollsLetter XLMar 7, 1850Condition, earnings, and treatment of a further trade (continued in subsequent letters, the series continuing beyond this volume)
Notes
This volume is part of the Routledge Library of Sociology reprint series. It collects only those letters from Mayhew’s Morning Chronicle series that relate to the metropolitan districts. The complete Morning Chronicle series ran from 1849 to 1850 and covered both London and the provincial manufacturing districts (which appeared in later volumes of the reprint set). Many of the same subjects and informants reappear in expanded form in London Labour and the London Poor.

sources/mccarthy-history-of-our-own-time.title: McCarthy, Justin — A History of Our Own Times: From the Accession of Queen Victoria to the General Election of 1880
sources/mccarthy-history-of-our-own-time.content:
A History of Our Own Times
Justin McCarthy’s A History of Our Own Times is a political and public narrative of the reign of Queen Victoria from the accession in 1837 to the general election of 1880. This one-volume Burt edition is useful for the 1800–1865 wiki because the first forty-seven chapters carry the story from 1837 through the death of Lord Palmerston in 1865.
For the period requested — from the close of the Crimean War to 1865 — the especially relevant chapters are XXX–XLVII. They cover the Second China War, transportation, the Indian Mutiny and the end of Company rule, the Orsini crisis, the Derby ministry, the Ionian Islands, the French commercial treaty and paper duties, Eastern questions, the American Civil War, the Alabama, Palmerston’s last electoral victory, the ebb and flow of parties, and Palmerston’s death.
Sources
Justin McCarthy, A History of Our Own Times: From the Accession of Queen Victoria to the General Election of 1880. New edition with an appendix of events to the end of 1880. New York: A. L. Burt, [1880s]. OCLC 843529.
The local source file is the Anna’s Archive ZIP titled A history of our own times_ From the accession of Queen -- McCarthy, Justin, 1830-1912_ -- 1880 -- A_L_Burt Co_, [188-] -- oclc 843529 -- faf55b74b31a04c42116ecd940c05e2f -- Anna’s Archive.zip.
Text
raw/mccarthy-history-of-our-own-times-complete-burt-1880.txt — 61,694 lines, extracted by concatenating the page-level text files in numerical order.
Coverage

Chronological scope of the book: 1837–1880, with an appendix to the end of 1880.
Chronological scope relevant to this wiki: chapters I–XLVII, 1837–1865.
Post-Crimean-to-1865 coverage: chapters XXX–XLVII, beginning after the Congress of Paris and ending with Palmerston’s death.
Later chapters: chapters XLVIII–LXVII continue beyond the folder’s terminal date and belong chiefly to the 1865–1919 continuation, but are included in the raw source for context.

Why this source matters for the 1800–1865 wiki
McCarthy gives a continuous Victorian narrative from the beginning of the reign to the end of the Palmerston era. For this folder he is especially useful as a bridge source: he begins after the Reform Act generation, follows the early Victorian crises of Chartism, Ireland, free trade, church controversy, and imperial war, and then carries the story across the Crimean War into the decade that ends in 1865.
The source is particularly strong for:

parliamentary and party politics: Melbourne, Peel, Russell, Palmerston, Derby, Disraeli, Gladstone, Cobden, Bright, and the shifting relation between Whigs, Peelites, Conservatives, radicals, and Liberals;
public agitation: Chartism, Repeal, Young Ireland, the Anti-Corn-Law League, the Ecclesiastical Titles agitation, and the reform issue before the Second Reform Act;
imperial crises: Canada, Afghanistan, China, India, the Ionian Islands, and the Mediterranean/Eastern questions;
mid-Victorian political culture: the Great Exhibition, the literature of the reign, public scandal, press and paper duties, education, divorce reform, and the language of national honour;
1856–1865 specifically: the Arrow dispute, Indian Mutiny, end of Company rule, Orsini crisis, Cobden-Chevalier Treaty, American Civil War, Alabama, and Palmerston’s final ministry.

Detailed chapter breakdown — chapters I–XXIX, 1837–1856
Chapter I — The King is Dead! Long Live the Queen! (starts line 215)

Opens with William IV’s death at Windsor on June 20, 1837, and the summons sent to Kensington Palace for Victoria.
Establishes the transition from the old monarch to the young queen and uses the accession to introduce the political atmosphere of the new reign.
Useful for pages on Victoria’s accession, monarchy at the beginning of the reign, and the ceremonial/political opening of the Victorian period.

Chapter II — Statesmen and Parties (starts line 988)

Surveys the leading statesmen at Victoria’s accession, beginning with Lord Melbourne as first minister.
Introduces the party world of the late 1830s: Melbourne, Peel, Wellington, Brougham, O’Connell, and the parliamentary conditions inherited from the Reform Act era.
Useful for pages on early Victorian parties, Melbourne’s ministry, Peel’s opposition, and the political inheritance of 1832.

Chapter III — Canada and Lord Durham (starts line 1687)

Treats the Canadian rebellion as the first major disturbance of the new reign.
Covers Lord Durham’s mission and the constitutional questions raised by colonial unrest in British North America.
Useful for pages on the Canadian rebellions, Durham Report, responsible government, colonial reform, and empire after 1837.

Chapter IV — Science and Speed (starts line 2740)

Places the opening of Victoria’s reign alongside railways, steam, industrial invention, and new applications of science and commerce.
Presents technological acceleration as part of the public character of the age, not merely a background condition.
Useful for pages on railways, steam power, industrial modernity, and the social perception of speed in early Victorian Britain.

Chapter V — Chartism (starts line 3309)

Moves from technological optimism to domestic unrest and working-class political agitation.
Covers the People’s Charter, the discontents behind Chartism, and the early Victorian fear that political reform had not settled the social question.
Useful for pages on Chartism, working-class politics, suffrage demands, and social pressure in the late 1830s and early 1840s.

Chapter VI — Question de Jupons (starts line 4156)

Covers the Bedchamber crisis and the difficulty of transferring government under a young queen whose household appointments had political meaning.
Shows Sir Robert Peel rebuilding Conservative strength while the Melbourne ministry weakened.
Useful for pages on the queen’s household, monarchy and party politics, Peel’s first attempt at office, and court politics in 1839.

Chapter VII — The Queen’s Marriage (starts line 4631)

Covers Victoria’s announcement of her marriage to Prince Albert and the parliamentary/public discussion surrounding it.
Introduces Albert’s position, public reception, and the place of the royal marriage in the early reign.
Useful for pages on Prince Albert, royal domesticity, the monarchy’s public image, and court culture.

Chapter VIII — The Opium War (starts line 5290)

Narrates the China opium dispute and the outbreak of the Opium War soon after Victoria’s accession.
Places trade, treaty rights, coercion, and British imperial policy in China at the centre of an early Victorian foreign-policy crisis.
Useful for pages on the Opium War, China trade, imperial coercion, and British treaty-port expansion.

Chapter IX — Decline and Fall of the Whig Ministry (starts line 5878)

Follows the weakening of Melbourne’s Whig ministry as public agitation and political pressure mounted around it.
Covers the circumstances leading to the return of Peel and the end of Melbourne’s government.
Useful for pages on Melbourne, Whig decline, Peel’s accession to office, and early Victorian ministerial instability.

Chapter X — Movements in the Churches (starts line 6555)

Surveys church controversies in the early reign, beginning with Oxford and the censure of religious teaching associated with the Tractarian movement.
Covers ecclesiastical agitation, religious controversy, and the political importance of church questions.
Useful for pages on the Oxford Movement, Tractarianism, church politics, religious controversy, and the Anglican establishment.

Chapter XI — The Disasters of Cabul (starts line 7139)

Treats the early Peel ministry’s foreign crisis in Afghanistan and the disaster at Kabul.
Covers the shock of imperial failure after the British retreat and destruction of the Kabul force.
Useful for pages on the First Anglo-Afghan War, Kabul retreat, imperial vulnerability, and the foreign-policy inheritance of Peel’s government.

Chapter XII — The Repeal Year (starts line 8625)

Centres on Daniel O’Connell and the declaration that 1843 would be the great year for repeal of the Union.
Discusses O’Connell’s character, mass meetings, Irish political mobilization, and the British government’s response.
Useful for pages on Repeal agitation, O’Connell, Irish nationalism, monster meetings, and the politics of Union.

Chapter XIII — Peel’s Administration (starts line 9605)

Surveys important domestic measures under Peel, including social legislation and administrative reform.
Uses measures such as restrictions on women and girls in mines to show Peel’s government as more than a Corn Law ministry.
Useful for pages on Peel’s domestic administration, early factory/mines legislation, fiscal policy, and Conservative governance.

Chapter XIV — Free Trade and the League (starts line 10246)

Covers the Anti-Corn-Law League and the intensifying campaign for free trade.
Frames the Corn Law issue as a central political controversy of Peel’s administration and of the 1840s.
Useful for pages on Cobden, Bright, the Anti-Corn-Law League, free trade, political economy, and manufacturing interests.

Chapter XV — Famine Forces Peel’s Hand (starts line 11383)

Connects the Irish famine to Peel’s decision to move toward Corn Law repeal.
Shows the pressure created when humanitarian emergency, food supply, and political economy converged.
Useful for pages on the Irish famine, Corn Law repeal, Peel’s break with Protection, and the fall of his ministry.

Chapter XVI — Mr. Disraeli (starts line 12115)

Introduces Disraeli as the speaker who rose suddenly into prominence during the anti-Peel revolt.
Covers his parliamentary style, personal distinctiveness, and position as a leader of opposition to Peel.
Useful for pages on Disraeli, Young England, anti-Peel Conservatism, and parliamentary rhetoric.

Chapter XVII — Famine, Commercial Trouble, and Foreign Intrigue (starts line 13043)

Covers the Russell ministry after Peel: Russell at the Treasury, Palmerston at the Foreign Office, Charles Wood at the Exchequer, Grey at the Colonies, and George Grey at the Home Office.
Places famine, economic difficulty, and foreign affairs together as the new government’s inheritance.
Useful for pages on Russell’s first ministry, famine administration, commercial crisis, and Palmerston’s return to the Foreign Office.

Chapter XVIII — Chartism and Young Ireland (starts line 13782)

Treats 1848 as the year of European revolutions and follows its British and Irish consequences.
Covers the Chartist demonstration, renewed working-class agitation, and the Young Ireland movement.
Useful for pages on 1848 in Britain, Chartism’s last great demonstration, Young Ireland, revolutionary fear, and public order.

Chapter XIX — Don Pacifico (starts line 15056)

Covers the Don Pacifico affair and the foreign-policy crisis around Palmerston’s defence of British subjects abroad.
Leads to parliamentary confrontation and Palmerston’s famous justification of his policy.
Useful for pages on Don Pacifico, Palmerstonian foreign policy, gunboat diplomacy, and the language of British protection.

Chapter XX — The Ecclesiastical Titles Bill (starts line 16101)

Covers the anti-Catholic agitation after the restoration of a Roman Catholic hierarchy in England.
Explains the Ecclesiastical Titles Bill and the strange intensity of religious-political alarm in 1850–1851.
Useful for pages on papal aggression, anti-Catholic politics, Russell’s ministry, and religious liberty in mid-Victorian Britain.

Chapter XXI — The Exhibition in Hyde Park (starts line 16996)

Treats the Great Exhibition of 1851 as a public landmark of the reign.
Covers the Crystal Palace, international display, industrial achievement, and the association of the Exhibition with Prince Albert.
Useful for pages on the Great Exhibition, Prince Albert, industrial culture, free trade display, and mid-century optimism.

Chapter XXII — Palmerston (starts line 17590)

Gives McCarthy’s extended character treatment of Lord Palmerston after Peel’s death left him one of the most prominent statesmen in Britain.
Covers Palmerston’s self-asserting foreign-policy style and his position within and beyond the cabinet.
Useful for pages on Palmerston, foreign-policy independence, ministerial discipline, and mid-Victorian liberal nationalism.

Chapter XXIII — Birth of the Empire; Death of “The Duke” (starts line 18947)

Places 1852 in a wider imperial and emotional setting, with continental events and British reactions shaping politics at home.
Includes the death of the Duke of Wellington and the public meaning attached to his passing.
Useful for pages on Wellington’s death, imperial expansion, 1852 politics, and the memory of the Napoleonic generation.

Chapter XXIV — Mr. Gladstone (starts line 20114)

Centres on Gladstone’s emergence as a major parliamentary and financial figure.
Covers the rivalry and contrast between Gladstone and Disraeli in debate.
Useful for pages on Gladstone, the 1852 budget debates, Peelites, finance, and parliamentary oratory.

Chapter XXV — The Eastern Question (starts line 20584)

Begins from Britain’s long peace and moves into the diplomatic crisis around Turkey, Russia, and the Eastern Question.
Covers the road toward the Crimean conflict and the assumptions with which Britain approached it.
Useful for pages on the Eastern Question, Ottoman Empire, Russia, diplomacy before Crimea, and Britain’s return to European war.

Chapter XXVI — Where was Lord Palmerston? (starts line 21941)

Asks how Palmerston positioned himself as the Eastern crisis developed.
Covers cabinet tensions, Palmerston’s warlike expectations, and the political meaning of his temporary resignation and return.
Useful for pages on Palmerston and Crimea, Aberdeen’s coalition, cabinet management, and the politics of war.

Chapter XXVII — The Invasion of the Crimea (starts line 23049)

Covers Britain and France entering the war as allies and the appointment of Lord Raglan and Marshal St. Arnaud.
Narrates the expedition to Crimea and the early military conduct of the war.
Useful for pages on the Crimean War, Raglan, St. Arnaud, allied command, expeditionary war, and British military administration.

Chapter XXVIII — The Close of the War (starts line 23996)

Opens with Palmerston’s unexpected arrival at the premiership in 1855.
Covers the last phase of the Crimean War, political pressure over mismanagement, and the movement toward peace.
Useful for pages on Palmerston’s first ministry, war administration, the fall of Aberdeen, and the Congress/Treaty of Paris.

Chapter XXIX — The Literature of the Reign: First Survey (starts line 24914)

Treats the close of the Crimean War as a major landmark in Victoria’s reign and pauses for a literary survey.
Reviews the literary achievements of the reign up to the Crimean-War divide.
Useful for pages on Victorian literature, public culture, and McCarthy’s own sense of periodization at 1856.

Detailed chapter breakdown — chapters XXX–XLVII, 1856–1865
Chapter XXX — The Lorcha Arrow (starts line 26615)

Opens after the supposed settlement of the Eastern Question at the Congress of Paris and shows a post-Crimean lull giving way to new conflicts.
Covers Russell’s national-education proposal, the Wensleydale life-peerage controversy, public frauds and poisoning trials, Cyrus Field’s Atlantic telegraph project, Lesseps’s Suez Canal proposal, and the Arrow dispute at Canton.
Follows the seizure of men from the lorcha Arrow, the expired British registration, Consul Parkes, Sir John Bowring, Yeh, the bombardment of Canton, Cobden’s censure motion, Palmerston’s dissolution, and the election victory of 1857.
Useful for pages on the Second China War, Palmerstonian foreign policy, Cobden and Bright, parliamentary censure, national honour rhetoric, and the politics of empire after Crimea.

Chapter XXXI — Transportation (starts line 27371)

Treats 1857 as the year in which penal transportation effectively ended.
Gives the background of transportation from earlier penal policy to the Australian colonies and explains settler resistance to continued convict arrivals.
Useful for pages on transportation, convict labour, Australian colonies, penal reform, and settler self-government.

Chapter XXXII — The Sepoy (starts line 27917)

Opens from the centenary of Plassey and introduces the Sepoy army as the immediate setting of the Indian Mutiny.
Explains the cartridge grievance, religious anxieties, military conditions, and the deeper fragility of Company rule.
Useful for pages on the Indian Mutiny, Bengal Army, cartridges, Company administration, and British assumptions about Indian loyalty.

Chapter XXXIII — The Hundredth Anniversary of Plassey (starts line 28657)

Follows the shock in Calcutta when news arrived from Meerut and Delhi.
Uses Plassey’s hundredth anniversary as a symbolic frame for the crisis of British rule.
Useful for pages on Meerut, Delhi, Plassey memory, panic in British India, and the symbolic chronology of empire.

Chapter XXXIV — Cawnpore (starts line 29090)

Centres on the events at Cawnpore and the appeals for aid that Sir Henry Lawrence at Lucknow could not answer.
Treats Nana Sahib and the massacres as episodes that shaped British public anger during the Mutiny.
Useful for pages on Cawnpore, Nana Sahib, atrocity narratives, Lucknow, and British revenge sentiment.

Chapter XXXV — Reconquest (starts line 29693)

Begins with the capture of Delhi and follows the transition from imperial crisis to military reconquest.
Covers Delhi, Lucknow, relief operations, command decisions, and the reassertion of British control.
Useful for pages on Delhi, Lucknow, Havelock, Colin Campbell, siege warfare, and the military suppression of the uprising.

Chapter XXXVI — The End of “John Company” (starts line 30114)

Describes British agitation over India while the Mutiny unfolded and news reached England.
Covers the political end of East India Company rule and the transfer of India to the Crown.
Useful for pages on the Government of India Act, East India Company, Crown rule, India Office, and Victorian imperial administration.

Chapter XXXVII — The Orsini Bombs Explode in Paris and London (starts line 30752)

Explains how the Orsini attempt against Napoleon III produced a British political crisis.
Covers French pressure over refugees, Palmerston’s Conspiracy Bill, parliamentary resistance, and the fall of his ministry in 1858.
Useful for pages on political asylum, Orsini, Napoleon III, Anglo-French relations, and Palmerston’s fall.

Chapter XXXVIII — On the True Faith of a Christian (starts line 31585)

Covers Derby’s second ministry and Disraeli’s difficult position leading a minority government in the Commons.
Describes Conservative survival tactics, parliamentary alignments, and the religious-political language of the moment.
Useful for pages on Derby, Disraeli, minority government, Conservative politics, and the post-Palmerston parliamentary balance.

Chapter XXXIX — The Ionian Islands (starts line 32360)

Discusses British possession of the Ionian Islands and the case for union with Greece.
Presents the Ionian question as a test of imperial interest, Mediterranean strategy, and local national feeling.
Useful for pages on the Ionian Islands, Gladstone’s mission, cession to Greece, and liberal imperial policy.

Chapter XL — The Tory Diogenes Rolling his Tub (starts line 32767)

Uses the image of Diogenes to frame Conservative attempts to keep politically active by handling reform.
Covers Disraeli’s reform manoeuvres and the difficulties of a Conservative ministry attempting a reform settlement.
Useful for pages on parliamentary reform before 1867, Disraeli’s tactics, Derby’s government, and party competition over reform.

Chapter XLI — The French Treaty and the Paper Duties (starts line 33558)

Covers Palmerston’s return to office, Cobden’s commercial treaty with France, and Gladstone’s finance.
Follows the struggle over repeal of the paper duties and the constitutional conflict between Commons and Lords over taxation and finance.
Useful for pages on the Cobden-Chevalier Treaty, paper duties, Gladstone’s budgets, cheap press, and Commons financial privilege.

Chapter XLII — Troubles in the East (starts line 34648)

Opens with the Queen’s Speech of January 1860 and renewed disturbances in China after the Treaty of Tientsin.
Covers the Peiho/Peking crisis and wider Eastern and Mediterranean diplomatic complications in Palmerston’s later ministry.
Useful for pages on the Second China War, Treaty of Tientsin, Peking, coercive diplomacy, and eastern policy after Crimea.

Chapter XLIII — The Civil War in America (starts line 35371)

Begins with the outbreak of the American Civil War after Lincoln’s election and Southern secession.
Explains British opinion toward Union and Confederacy, the cotton question, slavery, trade interests, and the official problem of neutrality.
Useful for pages on British neutrality, cotton famine background, slavery and secession in British debate, and Anglo-American relations.

Chapter XLIV — The Cruise of the Alabama (starts line 36111)

Covers the Confederate cruiser Alabama, British shipbuilding, neutrality law, and the controversy that later fed the Alabama claims.
Places the dispute in the wider Anglo-American tension of the Civil War years and links it to Prince Albert’s final counsel for calm in the Trent crisis atmosphere.
Useful for pages on the Alabama, Laird rams, Confederate commerce raiding, neutrality, and Anglo-American diplomacy.

Chapter XLV — Palmerston’s Last Victory (starts line 37174)

Opens with the 1862 International Exhibition after Prince Albert’s death.
Covers Palmerston’s late political strength, public popularity, and last electoral/parliamentary success.
Useful for pages on Palmerston’s final ministry, the 1865 election, exhibition culture, late Palmerstonian liberalism, and public confidence in the old premier.

Chapter XLVI — Ebb and Flow (starts line 38592)

Describes English politics as a recurring movement of action and reaction, with reform energy followed by fatigue and renewed quiet followed by agitation.
Covers the shifting movement of party feeling in the last Palmerston years.
Useful for pages on Liberal cohesion, Conservative recovery, reform fatigue before 1866–1867, and the atmosphere before the post-Palmerston transition.

Chapter XLVII — The Death of Lord Palmerston (starts line 39569)

Closes the pre-1865 sequence with Palmerston’s death and presents it as the end of a political era.
Connects Palmerston’s passing to the coming change in Liberal leadership and the renewed reform conflicts after 1865.
Useful for pages on Palmerston, the 1865 transition, Russell and Gladstone, and the end of mid-Victorian Palmerstonian government.

Later chapters — continuation after 1865
These chapters continue beyond this folder’s main period. They should usually be used in the later United Kingdom 1865–1919 wiki, though they are useful here for tracing transitions out of 1865.
