The 1865 boundary: chapter XLVII closes the period; chapters XLVIII onward belong primarily to the continuation wiki.

sources/mccarthy-history-of-our-own-time.title: McCarthy, Justin — A History of Our Own Times, Vol. II
sources/mccarthy-history-of-our-own-time.content:
A History of Our Own Times, Vol. II
This is the second physical volume of the Belford, Clarke & Co. edition of Justin McCarthy’s A History of Our Own Times. The title page describes the set as “four volumes in two”; this physical volume contains McCarthy’s internal Volumes III and IV, beginning with chapter XXX, “The Lorcha Arrow,” and continuing through chapter LXVII, “The Literature of the Reign: Second Survey.”
For the 1800–1865 wiki, the important part of this volume is its opening sequence, chapters XXX–XLVII. It begins immediately after the Crimean settlement and ends with the death of Lord Palmerston in 1865. The later chapters are included in the raw text but belong mainly to the 1865–1919 continuation.
Sources
Justin McCarthy, A History of Our Own Times. New edition with copious index and an introduction to American readers by Elmo. Four volumes in two, Vol. II. Chicago and New York: Belford, Clarke & Co., 1884. OCLC 20186980.
The local source file is the Anna’s Archive ZIP titled A history of our own times _ By Justin McCarthy_ -- McCarthy, Justin, 1830-1912_ -- Illinois, 1884 -- Belford, Clarke & co_, 1884_ -- oclc 20186980 -- 3cd8f830f423fa0671c38395f8b590b8 -- Anna’s Archive.zip.
Text
raw/mccarthy-history-of-our-own-times-vol2-belford-1884.txt — 32,800 lines, extracted by concatenating the page-level text files in numerical order.
Coverage

Physical volume: Vol. II of a four-volumes-in-two edition.
Internal contents: Volumes III–IV of McCarthy’s work, chapters XXX–LXVII.
Relevant chronological scope for this wiki: from the post-Crimean settlement in 1856 through Palmerston’s death in 1865, especially chapters XXX–XLVII.
Later chronological scope: chapters XLVIII–LXVII continue after 1865 and should be used mainly for the later United Kingdom 1865–1919 wiki.

Why this volume matters for 1856–1865
McCarthy’s second physical volume gives a connected Victorian political narrative for the years after the Crimean War. It is especially useful because it does not treat 1856–1865 as an empty interval between the Crimean War and the Second Reform Act. Instead, it follows a chain of mid-century questions:

the renewed China conflict after the Arrow dispute;
the end of transportation and the colonial rejection of convict settlement;
the Indian Mutiny and the transfer of India from Company to Crown;
the Orsini crisis and the fall of Palmerston’s ministry;
Derby, Disraeli, and the Conservative reform manoeuvres of 1858–1859;
the Ionian Islands and Britain’s shifting role in the Mediterranean;
the French commercial treaty, Gladstone’s finance, and the paper-duties conflict;
the American Civil War, British neutrality, and the Alabama controversy;
the last phase of Palmerstonian politics and Palmerston’s death in 1865.

Detailed chapter breakdown
Volume III — Post-Crimean settlement to Palmerston’s death
Chapter XXX — The Lorcha “Arrow” (lines 148–905)

Opens with the political lull after the Congress of Paris and immediately shows how quickly post-Crimean quiet gave way to new questions in Parliament and empire.
Covers Lord John Russell’s unsuccessful national-education resolutions, including the idea of a school rate for districts deficient in education; McCarthy notes that public opinion was not yet ready for compulsory national education.
Describes the life-peerage dispute around Sir James Parke, later Baron Wensleydale, and the anxieties it raised about the hereditary character of the House of Lords.
Gives character sketches of Sir George Cornewall Lewis and the parliamentary reputation he acquired despite an unattractive speaking manner.
Places the Arrow dispute amid domestic scandals and schemes: the Palmer and Dove poisoning trials, Royal British Bank frauds, Robson and Redpath, John Sadleir, Cyrus Field’s Atlantic telegraph project, and Lesseps’s Suez Canal proposal.
Narrates the seizure of men from the lorcha Arrow by Chinese authorities at Canton, the expired British registration, Consul Parkes’s demand, Sir John Bowring’s escalation, and Admiral Seymour’s bombardment of Canton.
Follows the parliamentary controversy: Lord Derby’s motion in the Lords, Cobden’s motion in the Commons, speeches by Lyndhurst, Gladstone, Disraeli, Russell, and others, the censure vote carried by 263 to 247, and Palmerston’s appeal to the country.
Ends with Palmerston’s electoral triumph, the defeat of Cobden, Bright, Milner Gibson, and other peace-party figures, and the passage of the Divorce and Matrimonial Causes Act before the next ministerial crisis.

Chapter XXXI — Transportation (lines 906–1443)

Treats 1857 as the year in which the old system of penal transportation effectively came to an end.
Gives the long background of transportation from the seventeenth century to the loss of the American colonies and the later use of Australia as a convict destination.
Explains the colonial resistance to continued transportation, especially as settler communities no longer wished to receive convicts from Britain.
Useful for pages on punishment, empire, settler self-government, the transformation of colonial society, and Britain’s shift from dumping convicts overseas to managing punishment at home.

Chapter XXXII — The Sepoy (lines 1444–2177)

Opens with the centenary of Plassey in 1857 and uses it to introduce the fragility of British power in India.
Explains the structure and position of the Sepoy army, the social and religious fears among Indian soldiers, and the immediate role of the cartridge grievance.
Treats the uprising not simply as a military mutiny but as a crisis of imperial rule, communication, suspicion, and misunderstanding.
Useful for pages on the Indian Mutiny, the East India Company army, religious anxieties under empire, and the limits of Company government.

Chapter XXXIII — The Hundredth Anniversary of Plassey (lines 2178–2603)

Follows the first shock of the news from Meerut and Delhi and the atmosphere of alarm in Calcutta.
Frames the rebellion around the symbolic coincidence of Plassey’s hundredth anniversary, a date that had become charged in British and Indian interpretations of rule.
Tracks the widening of revolt from military outbreak to imperial panic, with Delhi as the centre of the early crisis.
Useful for pages on Delhi, the symbolic politics of empire, British public fear in 1857, and the collapse of confidence in Company administration.

Chapter XXXIV — Cawnpore (lines 2604–3193)

Centres on Cawnpore as the most tragic and emotionally charged episode in McCarthy’s account of the Indian Mutiny.
Describes the appeals for help that reached Lucknow while Sir Henry Lawrence was unable to spare assistance.
Covers Nana Sahib, the siege, surrender, massacre, and the way the events at Cawnpore shaped British public feeling.
Useful for pages on Cawnpore, atrocity narratives, British anger during the Mutiny, and the moral atmosphere of reconquest.

Chapter XXXV — Reconquest (lines 3194–3605)

Begins with the capture of Delhi on September 20 and the debate over whether the available British force could safely attempt an assault.
Covers the military movement from defensive crisis to reconquest, including Delhi, Lucknow, relief operations, and the reassertion of British control.
Emphasizes the importance of engineering, siege operations, commanders, and the strain of holding scattered imperial positions.
Useful for pages on Delhi, Lucknow, Henry Havelock, Colin Campbell, military logistics, and the restoration of British authority in India.

Chapter XXXVI — The End of “John Company” (lines 3606–4239)

Describes British public agitation over India while news of the Mutiny and reconquest reached England.
Shows the East India Company becoming politically indefensible after 1857, even though British opinion had long treated India with indifference.
Covers the passage from Company rule to direct Crown government and the creation of a new imperial administrative arrangement.
Useful for pages on the Government of India Act, the end of Company sovereignty, the India Office, Crown rule, and Victorian imperial administration.

Chapter XXXVII — The Orsini Bombs Explode in Paris and London (lines 4240–5049)

Moves from India to Europe and explains how the Orsini attempt against Napoleon III became a British political crisis.
Covers French anger over conspirators and refugees in England, Palmerston’s Conspiracy to Murder Bill, and the suspicion that Britain was yielding to French pressure.
Shows how the bill divided opinion, turned parliamentary feeling against Palmerston, and brought down his ministry.
Useful for pages on political exile, asylum, Anglo-French relations, Napoleon III, Orsini, and the fall of Palmerston in 1858.

Chapter XXXVIII — On the True Faith of a Christian (lines 5050–5826)

Covers Lord Derby’s second ministry and Disraeli’s difficult role as leader in the House of Commons.
Describes a Conservative government with limited numbers, obliged to survive through parliamentary tactics and the divisions of its opponents.
Treats the religious and political language surrounding office, legitimacy, and public confidence.
Useful for pages on Derby, Disraeli, minority government, Conservative strategy, and the party balance after Palmerston’s fall.

Chapter XXXIX — The Ionian Islands (lines 5827–6238)

Follows Lord Stanley’s colonial and imperial responsibilities after the changes caused by the Indian crisis.
Discusses the British protectorate over the Ionian Islands, local discontent, and the growing case for union with Greece.
Presents the Ionian question as an example of a possession whose strategic and diplomatic value had to be weighed against local national feeling.
Useful for pages on the Ionian Islands, Gladstone’s mission, Greek union, Mediterranean policy, and liberal imperial withdrawal.

Chapter XL — The Tory Diogenes Rolling his Tub (lines 6239–7023)

Takes its title from Diogenes rolling his tub while Athens prepared for war, using it as McCarthy’s image for Conservative activity on reform.
Covers Disraeli’s reform tactics and the Conservative attempt to produce a measure that could occupy ground normally claimed by Liberals.
Shows how parliamentary reform remained unresolved after 1832 and could be used tactically by both parties.
Useful for pages on Conservative reform before 1867, Disraeli’s parliamentary method, and the breakdown of Derby’s ministry.

Chapter XLI — The French Treaty and the Paper Duties (lines 7024–8107)

Begins with Palmerston’s return to power amid international commotion: China, Italy after Villafranca, and the unsettled European scene.
Covers Cobden’s commercial treaty with France and the connection between foreign policy, free trade, and fiscal reform.
Follows Gladstone’s budget policy, the attempt to repeal the paper duties, and the constitutional conflict with the House of Lords.
Useful for pages on the Cobden-Chevalier Treaty, Gladstone’s finance, cheap press politics, paper duties, and Commons-versus-Lords finance privilege.

Chapter XLII — Troubles in the East (lines 8108–8820)

Opens with the Queen’s Speech of January 24, 1860, and the renewed disturbances in China after the Treaty of Tientsin.
Covers the British and French mission to the Peiho, the failure of diplomatic settlement, and the renewed military pressure that led toward the occupation of Peking.
Also belongs with McCarthy’s wider account of Eastern and Mediterranean questions during Palmerston’s later ministry.
Useful for pages on the Second China War, Peiho, Treaty of Tientsin, Peking, and Britain’s coercive diplomacy in Asia.

Chapter XLIII — The Civil War in America (lines 8821–9554)

Begins with the outbreak of the American Civil War after Lincoln’s election and Southern secession.
Explains British reactions to the Union and Confederacy, the cotton question, slavery, trade interests, and diplomatic neutrality.
Treats the war as a major test of British public opinion because sympathy, economic pressure, and official neutrality did not always point in the same direction.
Useful for pages on British neutrality, cotton famine background, British views of slavery and secession, and Anglo-American relations during the Civil War.

Chapter XLIV — The Cruise of the Alabama (lines 9555–10599)

Opens with Prince Albert’s death and links his final public counsel to the need for calm in the dispute with the United States over the Confederate envoys.
Covers the Alabama, British shipbuilding for the Confederacy, neutrality law, and the diplomatic controversy that later fed the Alabama claims.
Shows how the American Civil War forced Britain to define the obligations and limits of neutrality in practice, not only in formal declarations.
Useful for pages on the Alabama, Laird rams, Confederate commerce raiding, neutrality law, Prince Albert, and Anglo-American diplomacy.

Chapter XLV — Palmerston’s Last Victory (lines 10600–12017)

Opens with the preparations for the 1862 International Exhibition after Prince Albert’s death.
Covers Palmerston’s late political strength, his continuing popularity, and the electoral and parliamentary setting of his last victory.
Places domestic politics beside the major events of the early 1860s: exhibition culture, foreign affairs, and the continuing prestige of Palmerston’s public image.
Useful for pages on Palmerston’s last ministry, the 1865 election, late Palmerstonian liberalism, and public confidence in the old premier.

Chapter XLVI — Ebb and Flow (lines 12018–12988)

Describes English politics as governed by recurring action and reaction: reform energy followed by fatigue, and quiet followed by renewed agitation.
Follows the movement of party feeling in the last Palmerston years, including the uncertain relation between Liberal reformers, Whigs, Conservatives, and Palmerston’s personal authority.
Useful for pages on party realignment, reform fatigue before 1866–1867, Liberal cohesion, and the political atmosphere immediately before Palmerston’s death.

Chapter XLVII — The Death of Lord Palmerston (lines 12989–13616)

Closes the pre-1865 sequence with Palmerston dying in Hertfordshire after what McCarthy presents as an exceptionally long public career.
Treats Palmerston’s death as the end of a political era and the removal of the figure who had held together much of mid-Victorian public politics.
Provides material for assessing the transition from Palmerstonian government to the renewed reform conflicts under Russell and Gladstone.
Useful for pages on Palmerston, the 1865 transition, the old Whig-Liberal governing style, and the opening of the post-Palmerston period.

Volume IV — Continuation after 1865
The remaining chapters continue beyond this folder’s terminal date. They are listed here to show the shape of the physical volume and to make clear which material belongs mainly in the later United Kingdom 1865–1919 wiki.

Chapter XLVIII — The New Government (lines 13617–14335) — Lord Russell’s ministry after Palmerston and the immediate post-1865 political arrangement.
Chapter XLIX — The Troubles in Jamaica (lines 14336–15188) — the Jamaica controversy and its repercussions in Britain.
Chapter L — Driven Back Across the Rubicon (lines 15189–15894) — the political crisis surrounding reform.
Chapter LI — The Reform Agitation (lines 15895–16416) — popular and parliamentary agitation for reform.
Chapter LII — The Leap in the Dark (lines 16417–17316) — the Second Reform Act.
Chapter LIII — The Fenian Movement (lines 17317–18273) — Irish Fenianism and British responses.
Chapter LIV — Trades-Unions (lines 18274–19241) — trade unions and working-class organization.
Chapter LV — The Example of the New Dominion (lines 19242–19909) — Canadian confederation and imperial lessons.
Chapter LVI — “Begins with Soldan, Ends with Prester John” (lines 19910–20652) — the Abyssinian expedition.
Chapter LVII — The Irish Church (lines 20653–21455) — the disestablishment question.
Chapter LVIII — “Irish Ideas” (lines 21456–22394) — Irish policy after disestablishment.
Chapter LIX — “Reformation in a Flood” (lines 22395–23520) — reform measures in the Gladstone ministry.
Chapter LX — The Black Sea Clause: The Alabama Arbitration (lines 23521–24358) — the Black Sea settlement and Alabama arbitration.
Chapter LXI — The Tide on the Turn (lines 24359–25136) — the waning of Gladstone’s government.
Chapter LXII — The Fall of the Great Administration (lines 25137–26052) — the Liberal government’s fall.
Chapter LXIII — “Conservative Reaction” — Installed in Office (lines 26053–26852) — Disraeli and the Conservative return.
Chapter LXIV — The Eastern Question Again (lines 26853–27841) — the renewed Eastern crisis.
Chapter LXV — The Congress of Berlin (lines 27842–28716) — the Berlin settlement.
Chapter LXVI — The Anti-Climax of Imperialism (lines 28717–29449) — aftermath of imperial excitement.
Chapter LXVII — The Literature of the Reign: Second Survey (lines 29450–32800) — literary survey of the later reign.

Best uses in this wiki

Political narrative, 1856–1865: use chapters XXX, XXXVII–XLI, XLV–XLVII.
Empire and India: use chapters XXXII–XXXVI.
China and coercive diplomacy: use chapters XXX and XLII.
Colonial governance and settler politics: use chapters XXXI and XXXIX.
Finance, trade, and parliamentary privilege: use chapter XLI.
American Civil War and neutrality: use chapters XLIII–XLIV.
Transition to the later wiki: use chapter XLVII as the closing point and chapters XLVIII onward only when tracing events after 1865.

sources/molesworth-history-1830-1874-vol.title: The History of England from the Year 1830–1874, Vol. III
sources/molesworth-history-1830-1874-vol.content:
The History of England from the Year 1830–1874, Vol. III — by William Nassau Molesworth
Vol. III covers the period 1854–1874. This is the most politically eventful of the three volumes, opening in the midst of the Crimean War and closing with the Conservative victory of 1874 that ended Gladstone’s first ministry. Molesworth, writing in the immediate aftermath of these events, was able to consult a wide range of parliamentary papers, contemporary newspapers, published correspondence, and memoirs — the volume reflects a more documentary approach than the earlier two, with extensive quotation from Hansard, state papers, and the leading reviews. The narrative remains firmly centred on Westminster politics and high policy, but Molesworth continues his practice of interspersing chapters on the material, intellectual, and social progress of the period.

Chapter I — Sebastopol
The chapter opens with an extended review of the characteristics of the period — the extraordinary material growth of England since 1830, the advances in science and literature, the changes in manners and opinion — before plunging into the military narrative. The Russian retreat from the Danubian Principalities, the allied landing at Eupatoria, the battle of the Alma (20 September 1854), the flank march and the investment of Sebastopol. The battle of Balaclava (25 October) — the Charge of the Light Brigade, Lord Cardigan’s cavalry, the thin red line of the 93rd Highlanders. The battle of Inkerman (5 November) — “the soldiers’ battle,” fought in a fog. Miss Florence Nightingale’s mission to Scutari, the organisation of the nursing service, the mortality at the Barrack Hospital. The winter of 1854–55 — the hurricane, the destruction of the portable huts and stores, the breakdown of the commissariat, the sufferings of the troops before Sebastopol, the correspondence of W. H. Russell in The Times exposing the mismanagement. On the home front: the session of 1854, another reform bill introduced and withdrawn, Gladstone’s budget increasing the income tax, the Reform Club dinner, the declaration of war, the departure of the Baltic fleet, the Patriotic Fund. The Roebuck committee of inquiry — the mismanagement revelations, the resignation of the Aberdeen coalition, the formation of Lord Palmerston’s first ministry (February 1855), the withdrawal of the Peelites (Gladstone, Graham, Herbert), the death of the Emperor Nicholas. The renewal of the bombardment of Sebastopol, the capture of the Malakoff (8 September 1855), the Russian evacuation of the south side of the fortress, the fall of Kars to the Russians after a heroic defence, and the negotiations leading to the Peace of Paris (30 March 1856). Molesworth closes with the declaration of peace, the subsequent thanksgiving, the territorial settlement (the neutralisation of the Black Sea, the independence of the Danubian Principalities), and the general sense that a new era had opened.
Chapter II — The Indian Mutiny
The chapter opens with the life-peerages debate (the Wensleydale peerage case, the Lords’ refusal to admit a life peer) and the peace rejoicings. The dispute with the United States over Central America and the recruiting question. The Chinese War — the affair of the Arrow, the bombardment of Canton, the debate in Parliament, the defeat of the government on Cobden’s censure motion, the general election of 1857, and Palmerston’s triumphant return. Molesworth then turns to India: the greased cartridges, the growing disaffection in the Bengal army, the outbreak at Meerut (10 May 1857), the seizure of Delhi, the massacre at Cawnpore (Nana Sahib, the surrender, the massacre of the women and children), the sieges of Lucknow (Havelock’s relief, Outram’s defence, Sir Colin Campbell’s second relief), the recapture of Delhi (the assault, the death of John Nicholson), the reconquest of Oude. The reception of the news in England — the shock, the anger, the demand for vengeance, and the debates over the causes of the revolt. Disraeli’s motion, the testimony of Indian witnesses before the Parliamentary committee, the abolition of the East India Company (the Government of India Act 1858, the transfer of power to the Crown, the creation of the India Office and the Council of India). The Orsini attempt on Napoleon III (January 1858) — the bomb thrown by Italian revolutionaries, the discovery that the bombs were made in England, the French colonels’ addresses to Napoleon demanding retribution, the Conspiracy to Murder Bill, Palmerston’s defeat, and the formation of the second Derby administration. The India bills, the competitive examinations for the Indian Civil Service (the Macaulay committee’s report, the introduction of open competition), the final removal of Jewish disabilities (Baron Rothschild at last taking his seat), the purification of the Thames (the continuing stench, the metropolitan drainage scheme), the laying of the Atlantic telegraph, and the renewal of the reform agitation.
Chapter III — The French Treaty
The Conservative Reform Bill of 1859 (Disraeli’s attempt at a Conservative measure of reform, Lord John Russell’s amendment on the franchise, the defeat of the government), the general election of 1859 (the “union of the Whigs and Radicals” under Palmerston), the defeat of Derby’s ministry, and the return of Palmerston with Lord John Russell as Foreign Secretary — the Palmerston-Russell duumvirate. Molesworth traces Richard Cobden’s role in the negotiation of the Anglo-French Commercial Treaty (the Cobden-Chevalier Treaty of 1860), Cobden’s view of free trade as a means to peace, the tariff reductions on French wines, silks, and manufactured goods, the reciprocal reduction of French duties on British coal and iron. The frequent changes of ministries in the 1850s (the “everybody against everybody” period), the Liverpool Financial Reform Association, the St. George’s-in-the-East riots (the ritualist controversy in the London church). The death and character of Lord Macaulay — his History of England, his literary fame, his Whig interpretation of history. Gladstone’s French Treaty budget of 1860 — the abolition of the paper duty (the “taxes on knowledge”), the extension of the income tax, the duties on hops and fire-insurance. Lord John Russell’s Reform Bill of 1860, Mackinnon’s motion on the representation, and the withdrawal of the reform bill. The Paper Duties Bill rejected by the Lords — the Commons’ resolution against the Lords’ right to reject a finance bill, the eventual repeal of the paper duties in the budget of 1861. Lord Palmerston’s reconciliations, the invasion panic (the fortification of Portsmouth, the Volunteer movement, Tennyson’s “Riflemen Form!”), international pugilism, the harvest, the church-rates controversy, the budget of 1861. The American Civil War — the affair of the Trent (Captain Wilkes of the USS San Jacinto stopping the British mail packet and removing the Confederate commissioners Mason and Slidell, the British demand for apology and reparation, Prince Albert’s intervention in the wording of the despatch, the release of the commissioners), and the death of the Prince Consort (14 December 1861) — Molesworth records the universal grief, the Queen’s withdrawal from public life, the debate over the Prince’s constitutional role.
Chapter IV — The Palmerston Ministry
The session of 1862 — the effects of the American Civil War on the British cotton industry (the cotton famine, the distress in Lancashire, the relief committees, the destitution of 500,000 operatives with remarkable patience and order), the new Law Courts project, the church-rate question again, the Exhibition of 1862 (the South Kensington building, the exhibits, the financial failure), Glaisher’s balloon ascent (the scientific exploration of the upper atmosphere), the Roupell forgery case (the exposure of the elaborate forgery by a young solicitor, the flight of the forger), the improvement in the condition of factory operatives under the factory acts, the Alabama claims question (the building of the Confederate cruiser in Birkenhead, its escape, the depredations on United States commerce, the eventual arbitration), and the co-operative movement (the Rochdale pioneers, the growth of co-operative stores). The garrotting panic of 1862–63, President Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation, the marriage of the Prince of Wales (the Princess Alexandra of Denmark, the festivities), Gladstone’s budget (the reduction of the income tax to 4d.), the Polish insurrection (the British and French notes to Russia, the diplomatic isolation of the British government), the Trent mail case and international law, law reform (the fusion of law and equity), the Volunteer corps (the 150,000 volunteers, the reviews at Buckingham Palace and Woolwich), the death of Thackeray. The Schleswig-Holstein question — the Danish war of 1864, the invasion of Schleswig by Austria and Prussia, Lord Russell’s diplomatic notes, the Conference of London, the collapse of Danish resistance, the decline of British influence in Europe. Gladstone on parliamentary reform — his celebrated speech declaring that “every man who is not presumably incapacitated by some consideration of personal unfitness or of political danger is morally entitled to come within the pale of the Constitution.” The Permissive Bill (the temperance movement’s attempt to allow local veto on the sale of liquor), the Sheffield flood (the bursting of the Dale Dyke dam, the loss of 250 lives), Garibaldi’s visit to England (the popular enthusiasm, the quiet discouragement by the government, the withdrawal to Caprera), the murder of Mr. Briggs (the first railway murder, the public excitement, the trial of Franz Müller). The session of 1865 — the union-chargeability bill (reform of the poor law rating), the Irish Church question, Gladstone’s budget (the reduction of the tea and sugar duties), Baines’s motion for reduction of the franchise, the preparation for a general election, the resignation of Lord Chancellor Westbury (the leakage of confidential information, the criticism by the Lords committee), the general election of 1865, Gladstone’s triumph in South Lancashire (his defeat at Oxford, his re-election elsewhere), the death of Cobden, the assassination of President Lincoln, and the death of Lord Palmerston (18 October 1865) — Molesworth closes with an extended character sketch of Palmerston, his long career, his robust patriotism, his popularity with the country, his efficiency as a war minister, his easy-going management of the House of Commons.
Chapter V — The Reform Bill of 1867
Lord Russell’s second ministry (the formation of the cabinet, Gladstone as leader of the House and Chancellor of the Exchequer, the new members, the cattle plague of 1865–66, the limited liability acts, the report of the reform commission, the session of 1866). Gladstone’s Reform Bill — the household suffrage in boroughs coupled with a £14 rating franchise in counties, the bill to reduce the county franchise to £14. The “Cave of Adullam” — the group of Liberal malcontents led by Robert Lowe and Lord Elcho, who opposed any further extension of the franchise, the brilliant speeches of Lowe, the defection of Horsman and others, the defeat of the government on an Adullamite amendment (the “tea-room revolt”), the resignation of Russell (June 1866), and the formation of the Derby-Disraeli ministry. The Reform Bill of 1867 — Disraeli’s “leap in the dark,” his acceptance of household suffrage in boroughs (the compounding question, the registered voters as the sole test), the passage of the bill through the Commons with Hodgkinson’s amendment (the removal of the compound householder clauses, the vast extension of the franchise in towns), the Salford by-election showing the new voters in action, the bill in the Lords, the royal assent. The Scottish and Irish Reform Acts followed. The Abyssinian expedition (Sir Robert Napier’s march to Magdala, the release of the British prisoners, the death of King Theodore), the Fenian outbreak (the rising in Ireland, the rescue of Kelly at Manchester (the “Manchester martyrs” executed), the explosion at Clerkenwell prison, the resulting alarm, the suspension of habeas corpus in Ireland). The resignation of the Earl of Derby (his ill-health), Disraeli’s first brief premiership (February to November 1868), the budget, the general election of 1868 (the first under the new household franchise in the boroughs), the defeat of the Conservatives, and Gladstone’s accession as Prime Minister with a majority of 120.
Chapter VI — The Gladstone Ministry
Gladstone’s first cabinet — “a ministry of all the talents” (Lowe at the Exchequer, Bright at the Board of Trade, Cardwell at the War Office, the Duke of Argyll, Lord Granville, Lord Clarendon, Lord Hatherley, Bruce at the Home Office, Fortescue in Ireland). The Irish Church Act of 1869 — the disestablishment and disendowment of the Church of Ireland, the commutation of the life interests of the clergy, the passage of the bill through the Commons and the Lords (the Lords’ eventual surrender after the Queen’s intervention). The Irish Land Act of 1870 — the three F’s (fixity of tenure, fair rent, free sale), the Ulster custom given legal force, the Bright clauses for the creation of a peasant proprietory. The Elementary Education Act of 1870 — W. E. Forster’s bill, the creation of school boards, the filling up of educational gaps, the Birmingham League (Chamberlain, the demand for compulsory free education), the Cowper-Temple clause (the prohibition of distinctive religious teaching in board schools), the denominational schools controversy, the rates and the school boards. The abolition of purchase in the army — Cardwell’s reforms (the War Office reorganisation, the short service system, the localisation of regiments, the abolition of flogging in peacetime). The Treaty of Washington (1871) and the Alabama arbitration — the British acceptance of the “three rules” of neutrality (the duty of a neutral to prevent the fitting out of cruisers in its ports, the extension of the blockade, the notification to belligerents), the arbitration in Geneva, the award of £3¼ million against Britain. The Ballot Act of 1872 — the introduction of secret voting at parliamentary and municipal elections, the end of the old open system of public declarations in the hustings. The Licensing Act of 1872 — the reform of the liquor licensing system, the regulation of public-house hours, the opposition of the publicans, the “Beer Act” riots in some towns. The Irish University Bill of 1873 — Gladstone’s attempt to create a federal university for Ireland incorporating the Catholic University, Trinity College, and the Queen’s Colleges, the opposition of the Catholic bishops and the Protestant interest, the defeat of the bill by three votes, the resignation of the cabinet, the refusal of Disraeli to form a government, the return of Gladstone to office. The session of 1874 — Gladstone’s proposed repeal of the income tax (his “drowning man” budget), the general election of 1874 (the first by secret ballot, the first major test of the new borough electorate), the Conservative victory (a majority of about 50), the defeat of Gladstone himself in Greenwich, and the close of the Gladstone ministry. Molesworth appends a concluding chapter on the characteristics of the period 1830–1874, surveying the material progress (the growth of railways, the improvements in navigation, the development of the telegraph, the expansion of the coal and iron industries), the intellectual advances (the progress of science, the works of Mill, Darwin, and Herbert Spencer, the development of the periodical press), the moral and social improvements (the reform of the criminal law, the condition of the people, the Factory Acts, the Public Health Acts, the Education Acts), and some concluding reflections on the prospects of the nation.

Sources

Molesworth, William Nassau. The History of England from the Year 1830–1874. Vol. III. London: Chapman and Hall, 1875.

sources/molesworth-history-1830-1874-vol.title: The History of England from the Year 1830, Vols. I & II
sources/molesworth-history-1830-1874-vol.content:
The History of England from the Year 1830, Vols. I & II — by William Nassau Molesworth
Vols. I & II cover the period 1830–1854. Molesworth was a firsthand witness to much of what he records — he sat in the House of Commons as MP for various constituencies from 1853 onwards, and his History of the Reform Bill of 1832 is incorporated into the early chapters. He writes from a Liberal standpoint, sympathetic to the progressive causes of the age — parliamentary reform, free trade, religious liberty, colonial self-government — but with a genuine effort at fairness to his opponents.
The work is structured episodically: each chapter follows a year-by-year (or session-by-session) chronicle, weaving together parliamentary proceedings, foreign affairs, social movements, literary and scientific developments, and the condition of the people. Molesworth is particularly strong on economic legislation, fiscal policy, and the working of the reformed parliament.

Volume I — 1830–1837
Chapter I — Introductory
Molesworth opens with an extended survey of the unreformed constitution, tracing the history of parliamentary reform agitation from the Long Parliament and Cromwell through to the revival of the question in the eighteenth century. He reviews the elder Pitt’s reform proposals, the Yorkshire Association movement under the younger Pitt, the influence of the French Revolution on English radicalism, and the repressive legislation of the 1790s. The chapter covers the long Tory ascendancy under Liverpool, the Six Acts, the Queen Caroline affair, the liberal Tory reforms of Huskisson and Canning, and the crisis over Catholic Emancipation — the Clare election of 1828, O’Connell’s organising of the Catholic Association, the Wellington ministry’s reluctant concession of emancipation in 1829. The chapter closes with the agricultural and commercial distress of 1829–30, the July Revolution in France, and the general election of 1830 that brought the reform question to a head.
Chapter II — First Introduction of the Reform Bill
The resignation of the Duke of Wellington’s ministry (November 1830) after his declaration against any reform, and the formation of Earl Grey’s reform administration — the first genuinely Whig government in over forty years. Molesworth details the composition of the cabinet (Brougham as Lord Chancellor, Lord John Russell as Paymaster of the Forces, Lord Durham, Althorp, Melbourne, Lansdowne, Palmerston, Graham, Richmond). The chapter covers the “Captain Swing” disturbances — the machine-breaking and rick-burning that swept the southern and eastern counties — and the special commissions that tried the rioters. Parliament reassembles in February 1831; Lord John Russell rises on 1 March to introduce the Reform Bill, a speech Molesworth describes as “one of the most remarkable ever delivered in the House of Commons.” The great Commons debate that followed — the speeches of Sir Robert Inglis, Joseph Hume, Hunt, Wetherell, Palmerston, Peel, Stanley, Croker, O’Connell — occupies much of the narrative. Molesworth traces the reception of the Bill by the country: the Political Unions forming in Birmingham (under Attwood) and elsewhere, the press campaign, the public meetings, the addresses to the King, the petitions. The Bill passes its second reading by a single vote (302 to 301) — the famous “strangers’ gallery” night — only to be defeated in committee on General Gascoigne’s wrecking amendment.
Chapter III — Second Introduction of the Reform Bill
The dissolution of Parliament (22 April 1831) by royal proclamation — a dramatic gesture that sent members back to their constituencies with the Reform Bill as the sole question of the general election. Molesworth traces the election of 1831, the return of a great reform majority, and the re-introduction of the Bill by Lord John Russell. He covers the anomalies of the old system exposed by the debate — nomination boroughs (Old Sarum, Gatton), the “Pocket-Borough” system, the electoral influence of the aristocracy — and Alderman Thompson’s notorious “inadvertence” in mistaking which lobby he had voted in. The Bill passes the Commons through all its stages, aided by the Speaker’s casting vote. The coronation of William IV (September 1831) provides a brief interlude of pageantry before the Bill is carried up to the Lords.
Chapter IV — The Reform Bill Carried
The Lords’ rejection of the Bill (8 October 1831) by a majority of 41 — the Bishops voting almost solidly against. Molesworth gives full weight to the popular fury that followed: the Bristol riots (the burning of the Mansion House, the Bishop’s Palace, the Customs House), the breaking of windows of anti-reform peers, the attacks on the Duke of Newcastle’s property at Newark, the grim determination of the Political Unions to march on London if necessary. Lord Ebrington’s resolution of confidence in the ministry carries the Commons. The “Days of May” crisis — the Bill’s third introduction, Lord Lyndhurst’s motion to postpone the disfranchising clauses, the resignation of the Grey ministry, the Duke of Wellington’s unsuccessful attempt to form a government (his “d——d nasty question” of the Speakership), the refusal of Peel to serve with him, and the recall of Grey. The King’s reluctant promise to create enough peers to carry the Bill, the mass abstention of the Tory peers, the passage of the Bill through the Lords, and the royal assent (7 June 1832). Molesworth closes the chapter with a survey of periodical literature of the age and a notice of the death of Sir Walter Scott.
Chapter V — The First Reformed Parliament
The general election of 1832 under the new franchise — nearly 300 seats uncontested, the Conservative (now so called) party reduced to about 150 members, the reformers triumphant. Molesworth devotes careful attention to the first reformed Parliament’s legislative agenda: the Coercion Bill for Ireland, the Irish Church question (the appropriation controversy that would eventually split the Whig party), the Irish Tithe Bill, and the great financial measures of the government — the reduction of the malt-tax and house- and window-duties, the renewal of the Bank Charter, the renewal of the East India Company’s charter. The abolition of slavery throughout the British colonies (the Act of 1833, the £20 million compensation to slave-owners, the apprenticeship system). The Factory Act of 1833 (Lord Althorp’s bill, the limitation of children’s hours, the factory inspectorate). The debate over the ballot, triennial parliaments, bribery and corruption at elections. The session of 1834 — the dismissal of Lord Melbourne by William IV (the King’s resentment over the Irish Church appropriation clause), Peel’s brief first ministry (the “Hundred Days”), the Tamworth Manifesto, the destruction of the two Houses of Parliament by fire (16 October 1834). The chapter closes with the death of Coleridge.
Chapter VI — Corporation Reform
The general election of 1835 — Peel’s appeal to the country fails to produce a Conservative majority, the “Lichfield House compact” between the Whigs and O’Connell’s Irish Repealers, the defeat of Peel’s ministry on the election of the Speaker and again on the corporation reform question, Peel’s resignation, and Melbourne’s return to office. The Municipal Corporations Reform Bill — Lord John Russell’s speech, Sir William Follett’s wrecking motion, the Bill in the Lords, the introduction of the ratepaying franchise for local government. The Irish Church tithe question continues. The Orange Lodges controversy — Joseph Hume’s disclosures, the Commons address against them, the Duke of Cumberland’s role. The Budget of 1836, the registration of births, marriages, and deaths, the reduction of the newspaper stamp duty from 4d. to 1d., the extension of counsel’s right to address the jury in felony cases (the Prisoners’ Counsel Act). The New Poor Law of 1834 (the Poor Law Commission, the workhouse system, the Andover workhouse scandal). The Canadian question — Lord Durham’s mission, the Rebellion Losses Bill. British intervention in Spain (the Quadruple Alliance, the Carlist War). The Westminster election of 1837, and the death of William IV — Molesworth gives a character sketch of the King, his constitutional role in the Reform crisis, his bluff plainness, his conscientious if sometimes capricious exercise of the prerogative.

Volume II — 1837–1854
Chapter I — Victoria Regina
The accession of the young Queen Victoria (June 1837) — Molesworth records the universal goodwill and “almost romantic interest” that greeted the new reign. The dissolution and general election — Melbourne’s Whigs maintain their majority. The Canadian crisis deepens: Lord Durham’s mission, his ordinance, his repudiation, his resignation, his famous Report on the Affairs of British North America (1839) which laid the foundation for responsible colonial government. The Bedchamber Question (May 1839) — Peel’s demand for the dismissal of the Queen’s Whig ladies-in-waiting, the Queen’s refusal, Peel’s resignation, Melbourne’s return. Molesworth covers the social and administrative developments of the early reign: the introduction of penny postage (Rowland Hill’s plan, the Treasury competition for the penny black), the formation of the Committee of Privy Council on Education (the beginnings of state involvement in education), the stock of the British Museum, the trial of Courvoisier for the murder of Lord William Russell. Lord Durham’s death, the coronation (1838), the marriage of the Queen, the birth of the Princess Royal. The Eastern Question — Mehemet Ali’s revolt against the Porte, Lord Palmerston’s robust policy, the Straits Convention of 1841. The session of 1841 — the government’s Irish registration measure, the fixed duties on corn (the Whigs’ gradual conversion to free trade), the sugar duties debate, the timber duties question. The defeat of the government on a vote of no confidence, the general election, the return of Peel, the resumption and conclusion of the Eastern crisis.
Chapter II — The Income and Property Tax
Peel’s ministerial announcements — the resignation of the Duke of Buckingham from the cabinet. The great Corn Law debate of 1842: the fixed duty versus the sliding scale — Peel eventually carried his new sliding scale. The deficiency in the revenue — Peel’s plan to revive the income and property tax (abandoned since 1816) at 7d. in the £. Molesworth traces the debates at length, giving the arguments of all parties. The copyright question — Carlyle’s famous petition to the Commons, in which he described himself as “a writer of books.” The reform of the law of libel, the law of evidence, the Bankruptcy Act. The disaster in Afghanistan — the Army of the Indus, the occupation of Cabul, the rising of the tribes, the retreat from Cabul (January 1842), the destruction of the army at the Pass of Tezeen, the captivity of Lady Sale and the other hostages, Lord Ellenborough’s proclamation restoring the gates of Somnath. The employment of women and children in mines — Lord Ashley’s (later Lord Shaftesbury) revelations before the Mines Commission, the Mines and Collieries Act of 1842. Lord Ashley’s motion on the education of the poor, the government plan of education, Sir James Graham’s factory education clauses. The state of Ireland in 1843 — O’Connell’s monster meetings, the Repeal Association, the Clontarf proclamation. The Braintree Case and the Chartist agitation.
Chapter III — The Sliding Scale
The year 1844 — England at peace with all the world, the war in Scinde (Sir Charles Napier’s conquest, his laconic despatch “Peccavi”), the factory question — Lord Ashley’s Ten Hours Bill defeated in the Commons, the government’s alternative factory bill limiting children’s hours but leaving women’s labour unrestricted. Peel’s budget — the reduction of the tariff on 750 articles, the relaxation of the Corn Law sliding scale, the extension of the income tax to Scotland and Ireland. The Bank Charter Act of 1844 (Sir Robert Peel’s Act) — the separation of the issue and banking departments of the Bank of England, the limitation of the note issue, the beginnings of the modern central banking system. Lady Hewley’s charities — the Nonconformist question, the Dissenters’ Chapels Act. The railway mania — the railway legislation of 1844 (Gladstone’s Railway Act, the compulsory parliamentary train, the provisions for third-class passengers), the speculation and the approaching crash. Modifications of the bastardy clauses of the New Poor Law. The Rebecca riots in Wales (the destruction of toll-gates, the disguise of the rioters).The opening of letters at the Post Office — the Mazzini affair. The Irish crisis: O’Connell’s monster meetings, the indictment and trial of O’Connell, his conviction quashed by the House of Lords on a technical point of procedure. The Tahiti affair (the Pritchard incident, French intervention). The session of 1845 — Peel’s financial statement, the sugar duties debate, agricultural distress, the Maynooth Bill (the substantial increase of the grant to the Catholic seminary, the furious Protestant opposition, the passage of the bill), the “godless colleges” of the Irish universities scheme (Sir Robert Peel’s Colleges Bill). The Oregon boundary question with the United States, the potato disease (the first appearance of the blight), the resignation of Peel, the failure of Lord John Russell to form a government, and the resumption of office by Peel — the turning point that would lead to the repeal of the Corn Laws.
Chapter IV — The Anti-Corn-Law League
The rise of the Anti-Corn-Law League — its origins in Manchester in 1838, the founding of the Anti-Corn-Law Association, the role of Richard Cobden and John Bright, the fundraising of £100,000, the registration campaign (qualifying every freeholder in the manufacturing districts for a county vote), the propagation of free-trade doctrines through lectures, pamphlets, bazaars, and the Economist newspaper. The potato blight of 1845 devastates Ireland — the crisis that made repeal inevitable. Molesworth covers Peel’s recantation of agricultural protection (January 1846), Disraeli’s brilliant speeches rallying the Protectionists around Lord George Bentinck, the measure of compensation to the landed interest, the Irish Arms Bill, the defeat of the ministry on the Irish Coercion Bill, the resignation of Peel, his famous final speech, and the formation of Lord John Russell’s Whig ministry. The Sugar Duties Act, the continuing distress and crime in Ireland, the discovery of anaesthetics (ether and chloroform), the Secularist movement, legislation for Ireland, Fielden’s Ten Hours Factory Act (the limitation of the working day for women and young persons to ten hours), the educational vote, O’Connell’s last speech in the House of Commons, his death at Genoa on his way to Rome, the dissolution of the Anti-Corn-Law League, and the discovery of the planet Neptune.
Chapter V — The People’s Charter
The general election of 1847, the November session, Baron Lionel de Rothschild and the Jewish disabilities question — his election for the City of London and his repeated refusal to take the oath “on the true faith of a Christian,” the successive bills for the removal of Jewish disabilities, the long struggle between Lords and Commons. The suspension of habeas corpus in Ireland, the Encumbered Estates Act of 1849 (the sale of insolvent Irish estates, the transfer of land to new proprietors). The effects of the French Revolution of 1848 in England — the alarm of the propertied classes, the voluntary enrolment of special constables (the Duke of Wellington organising the defence of London), the presentation of the Chartist petition. Molesworth traces the Chartist movement from its origins in the 1838 People’s Charter (six points: universal suffrage, equal electoral districts, abolition of property qualification for MPs, payment of members, annual parliaments, the ballot). The Chartist Convention in London, Mr. Duncombe’s amendment to an address, the formal adoption of the Charter, Feargus O’Connor’s leadership and his oratory, the progress of Chartism, the National Petition with its millions of signatures, the “Sacred Month” (the general strike that never really materialised), the Newport insurrection of 1839 (John Frost, the march on the Westgate Hotel, the trials and transportation of the leaders), the Kennington Common meeting of 10 April 1848 (O’Connor, the special constables, the petition delivered to Parliament with its forged signatures), the Land Scheme of O’Connor, the eventual collapse of Chartism as a mass movement. The chapter also covers Mr. Hume’s motion for financial reform, diplomatic relations with the Papacy, the public health legislation (the Public Health Act of 1848, Edwin Chadwick’s work, the General Board of Health), the death of Lord George Bentinck, the repeal of the Navigation Laws (the opening of the British carrying trade to foreign shipping), Disraeli’s resolution on agricultural distress, and Irish and colonial legislation.
Chapter VI — The Great Exhibition
The year 1850 opens with agricultural distress continuing, the Budget of 1850 (Sir Charles Wood’s financial statement), the window-tax (its unpopularity and the agitation for its abolition), the proposed reductions of official salaries (the “economical reform” movement), the Gorham Judgment (the Privy Council’s decision on baptismal regeneration, the defection of Archdeacon Manning and others to Rome), the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council and its growing role, the university reform movement, the removal of the remaining Dissenters’ disabilities, the Sunday delivery of letters controversy (the Post Office’s attempt to stop Sunday deliveries, defeated by Chartist and working-class protest). Peel’s last speech (the debate on the Greek question, his defence of Lord Palmerston’s foreign policy) and his fatal fall from his horse on Constitution Hill, his death and funeral, the universal tributes to his memory. The Papal Aggression — the restoration of the Roman Catholic hierarchy in England by Pope Pius IX (the “Durham Letter” of Lord John Russell denouncing the “insolent and insidious” aggression), the Ecclesiastical Titles Bill (the prohibition of Catholic territorial titles, its passage and later repeal). Alderman Salomons and the Jewish disabilities question. The Great Exhibition of 1851 — Joseph Paxton’s Crystal Palace in Hyde Park, the machinery, manufactures, and works of art from all nations, the opening by the Queen, the vast crowds, the profit that funded the South Kensington museum complex. The foundation of Owens College, Manchester (the precursor to the Victoria University). A new Reform Bill, the dismissal of Lord Palmerston from the Foreign Office (his unauthorised approval of the French coup d’état), the Derby administration (the “Who? Who?” ministry of 1852, Disraeli’s first budget), the Aberdeen coalition ministry (Lord Aberdeen as Prime Minister, Gladstone at the Exchequer, Palmerston at the Home Office). The session of 1853 — Gladstone’s great financial statement (the extension of the income tax, the reduction of the tea and sugar duties, the succession duty). Molesworth concludes with the prosperous condition of the country, the rise of the Eastern Question (the dispute between Russia and Turkey over the Holy Places, the Menshikov mission, the Russian occupation of the Principalities), the destruction of the Turkish fleet at Sinope, the popular war fever in England, and the decision to send the Baltic and Black Sea fleets.

Sources

Molesworth, William Nassau. The History of England from the Year 1830. Vols. I–II. London: Chapman and Hall, 1873.

sources/overton-church-19th.title: Overton, John H. — The English Church in the Nineteenth Century (1800-1833)
sources/overton-church-19th.content:
The English Church in the Nineteenth Century (1800-1833)
John H. Overton, D.D. (Canon of Lincoln and Rector of Epworth, joint author of The English Church in the Eighteenth Century) writes as a High Church historian who loved and believed in the Church’s system. The materials for this volume accumulated over more than twenty years as a natural outgrowth of his investigation into the eighteenth-century Church, which led him forward into a period he saw as the dawn of a brighter day. The book was put into shape over nearly five years and presented to the public in 1893–94.
The work is a thematic rather than a chronological treatment of the Church of England in the first third of the nineteenth century (1800–1833). Overton’s central argument is that this period has been unfairly neglected or disparaged as one of stagnation, when in fact it was a period of substantial revival and preparation — in Church life, doctrine, education, missions, and relations with the State — for the great movements that followed.
Sources
John H. Overton, D.D., The English Church in the Nineteenth Century (1800-1833). London: Longmans, Green, & Co., 1894.
The work includes a preface (dated Epworth Rectory, Doncaster, 1893), a detailed table of contents, and an extensive index.
Text
raw/overton-church-19th/overton-church-19th.txt — 18,616 lines, ~912 KB. Extracted from the Princeton Theological Seminary copy (bequest of Rev. Louis Fitzgerald Benson, D.D.) via Anna’s Archive zip, with 392 individual page text files concatenated in numerical order.
Contents
Chapter I — The General State of the Church
The condition of the Church of England at the opening of the nineteenth century. The effects of the French Revolution and the long war with France. The low state of morals and religion. The abuse of pluralities and non-residence. Gradual improvement as the years went on. Popular attacks on the Church and clergy and the cry of “The Church in danger.” The Church’s unpreparedness for new emergencies. Special attention to the state of the Church in Wales.
Chapter II — The ‘Orthodox’
The survival of the old High Church or “Orthodox” party, which had not died out as commonly supposed. Key figures: Jones of Nayland, William Stevens, Joshua Watson, J. J. Watson, H. H. Norris, Christopher Wordsworth, C. Daubeny, T. Sikes, Hugh James Rose. Sympathetic prelates and other prominent sympathizers. The distinction between old and new types of High Churchmen.
Chapter III — The ‘Evangelicals’
The Evangelical party within the Church. Charles Simeon and the Cambridge circle — Isaac Milner, William Farish. The Clapham Sect: W. Wilberforce, H. Thornton, Z. Macaulay, J. Stephen, John Venn, Thomas Gisborne. The abolition of the Slave Trade. Evangelicals in London and the country. Evangelical bishops and laity. An assessment of strengths and weaknesses in the Evangelical system: their views of “the world” and “the Church,” alleged degeneracy, attitudes toward human learning, literature and art, and their strong points. Summary of the Evangelical contribution.
Chapter IV — The ‘Liberals’
The Liberal or Latitudinarian party. William Paley, Samuel Parr, Sydney Smith, Henry Bathurst, Edward Stanley. The Oriel Noetics at Oxford. Richard Whately and Thomas Arnold. The lack of united action among the Liberals.
Chapter V — Church Services and Church Buildings
The state of public worship. The administration of Holy Communion. Irregularities tolerated in services. Psalmody and preaching. Sunday evening and week-day services. The want of church accommodation. The pew system and proprietary chapels. The war prevented church-building. State and voluntary efforts. Difficulties about church-building. The ugliness and costliness of new churches. The first free church in England. The squalor of country churches. A clergyman’s work in 1825.
Chapter VI — Church Literature
The literary output of the Church in this period. Evidential writings defending Christianity. Practical and devotional works. Biblical and liturgical literature. The Calvinistic controversy. The debate over Baptismal Regeneration. Biography and Church history. The Roman controversy. Religious periodicals and poetry. General literature. Summary of the literary achievements of the clergy.
Chapter VII — The Church and Education
The Church’s role in education at all levels. Oxford and Cambridge universities. Other institutions and the public schools. Dr. Arnold’s work at Rugby. Elementary education: the Bell and Lancaster controversy. The foundation and work of the National Society for the Education of the Poor. Efforts of the parochial clergy. Sunday schools. The Jesus Lane Sunday school. Training colleges and infant schools.
Chapter VIII — Church Societies
The great Church societies and their work. The Society for the Propagation of the Gospel (S.P.G.). The Church Missionary Society (C.M.S.). Missions in Sierra Leone and India. The “five chaplains.” Alarm about proselytizing. Lord Teignmouth. The renewal of the East India Company’s Charter. Bishop Middleton and Bishop Heber in India. Four lives sacrificed in missionary work. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge (S.P.C.K.). The Society for the Suppression of Vice. Mixed societies. The Church and the Bible Society. Private religious societies.
Chapter IX — Church and State
The political relations between Church and State. Acts of 1801 and 1802 affecting the Church. Acts of 1803 and 1804. The services of Mr. Perceval and Lord Liverpool. Acts between 1811 and 1819. The Roman Catholic Relief Bill. The repeal of the Test and Corporation Acts. The case of Queen Caroline. The recurring cry of “The Church in danger.”
Chapter X — Intercourse with Sister Churches
The Church of England’s relations with other Churches in communion with her. Ireland: the United Church of England and Ireland after the Act of Union (1801), the precursors of the Oxford Movement in the Irish Church, the condition of the Church of Ireland before disestablishment. Scotland: the Scottish Episcopal Church and its distinctive character. America: the development of the Protestant Episcopal Church in the United States, the work of Bishop J. H. Hobart as the epoch-making bishop of the American Church, and the contributions of Bishops Chase, Moore, and White.
Index
A comprehensive alphabetical index covering persons, places, events, doctrines, and institutions from the entire work.

sources/overton-english-church-1800-1833.title: Overton — The English Church in the Nineteenth Century (1800-1833)
sources/overton-english-church-1800-1833.content:
Overton — The English Church in the Nineteenth Century (1800-1833)
John Henry Overton, D.D., Canon of Lincoln and Rector of Epworth — The English Church in the Nineteenth Century (1800-1833). — Longmans, Green, & Co., London and New York, 1894.
The second volume chronologically of Overton’s Church history (following The English Church in the Eighteenth Century, co-authored with Charles J. Abbey), covering the Church of England from 1800 to 1833. The work is thematic rather than chronological, devoting each chapter to a different aspect of Church life across the whole period: the general condition of the Church, the three main parties (Orthodox/High Church, Evangelicals, and Liberals), worship and church buildings, religious literature, education, missionary and charitable societies, Church and State relations, and the sister churches of Ireland, Scotland, and America. Overton writes from a sympathetic High Church standpoint but is notably fair-minded toward the Evangelicals, whom he treats at greater length than any other party.
The text is 18,616 lines (911 KB), OCR’d from a library copy. All ten chapters reported in the Table of Contents are present and complete.
Scope and Approach
Overton observes that the first thirty years of the century divide into two equal parts: the first fifteen consumed by the war with France, the next fifteen by adjustment to peace. He treats the whole period thematically rather than year by year, drawing extensively on contemporary sources — bishops’ Charges, parliamentary debates, periodical reviews, letters, memoirs, and statistical reports. The work was compiled over more than twenty years, beginning while he worked on the companion eighteenth-century volume. Overton sees the period as one of steady improvement from the late-eighteenth-century low-water mark, but also of increasing tension between Church and State that would culminate in the crises of the 1830s.
Content Summary
Chapter I — The General State of the Church (p. 1)
The opening chapter sketches the Church’s condition against the background of the French Revolution and the war. Overton argues that the Revolution exerted contradictory effects: it made men suspicious of any change (branded as “Jacobinism”), yet it also stimulated the Church by revealing how little hold she had on the masses. The war monopolised money and attention. Overton surveys the low state of morals and religion, citing Bishop Horsley’s Charge of 1800 and the famous “Report from the Clergy of a District in the Diocese of Lincoln” (1800). Pluralities and non-residence were endemic — a clergyman might hold several benefices while residing in none, serving them through poorly-paid curates. Improvement set in gradually through legislation (the residence and farming Acts of 1802) and rising standards of clerical duty. The cry of “The Church in danger” became a recurrent political slogan. The Church was unprepared for the new emergencies of peace, especially the need to minister to the rapidly growing populations of manufacturing towns. The chapter closes with the particular problems of the Church in Wales, where the Establishment was especially weak among a largely Nonconformist population.
Chapter II — The ‘Orthodox’ (p. 24)
Overton explains his choice of “Orthodox” over “High Churchmen” — the latter was confused with political “Church and State” men and lacked a natural correlative to “Evangelical” and “Liberal.” The party had not died out before the Oxford Movement revived it, as is often claimed; it had merely been quiescent, holding its principles negatively rather than positively. Overton assembles evidence from Bishop Horsley (who declared High Churchmanship essential to being a Churchman at all), Bishop Van Mildert’s Bampton Lectures (1814) insisting on Apostolical Succession, and Archdeacon Daubeny’s assertion that the title meant “a decided and principled attachment to the apostolic government of the Church.”
The chapter profiles the leading Orthodox figures: Jones of Nayland (the link between centuries), William Stevens (the “Saint of the Nonjurors”), the Hackney Phalanx around Joshua Watson (1771-1855) and J. J. Watson, H. H. Norris, Christopher Wordsworth (Master of Trinity), Charles Daubeny, Thomas Sikes (whose remarkable prophecy of the Oxford Movement was later cited by Pusey), and Hugh James Rose (whose Cambridge sermons on German rationalism awakened English Churchmen). The chapter concludes by distinguishing the old type of High Churchman (valuing the Church as a constitutional bulwark) from the new type (seeing her as a divine society independent of the State).
Chapter III — The ‘Evangelicals’ (p. 51)
The longest chapter, reflecting Overton’s judgment that “regarded purely as a spiritual force, the Evangelicals were undoubtedly the strongest party in the Church.” He opens with the passing of the first generation (Henry Venn, Joseph Milner, Romaine, John Wesley) and the surviving links — Thomas Scott, Isaac Milner, Wilberforce, Hannah More, and above all Charles Simeon (1759-1836). Overton gives an extended biographical treatment of Simeon: his spiritual development through reading The Whole Duty of Man, Kettlewell, and Bishop Wilson; his Easter Day conversion at King’s College; his twelve-year struggle at Trinity Church, Cambridge, where he was opposed by churchwardens and parishioners before winning acceptance; and his enormous influence over generations of undergraduates. Overton candidly quotes contemporaries on Simeon’s defects (“haughty, impatient, impetuous”) while noting that his success proved “pure goodness must tell in the long run.”
From Simeon, Overton moves to Isaac Milner (Dean of Carlisle) and William Farish, then to the Clapham Sect — Wilberforce, Henry Thornton, Zachary Macaulay, James Stephen, John Venn, and Thomas Gisborne — with particular attention to the abolition of the slave trade (1807). He surveys Evangelicals in London (Newton, Cecil, Daniel Wilson, Bickersteth), in the country (Scott, Robinson of Leicester, Legh Richmond), and the first Evangelical bishops (Ryder and Sumner). The chapter offers a balanced assessment of weak points: excessive otherworldliness, minimising the visible Church, suspicion of human learning, and hostility to literature and art. But the strong points are equally acknowledged: spiritual earnestness, practical philanthropy, missionary zeal, and the awakening of the national conscience.
Chapter IV — The ‘Liberals’ (p. 110)
A shorter chapter on those who found both the Orthodox and Evangelical platforms too narrow. William Paley (1743-1805), whose Natural Theology (1802) was the last of his works; Samuel Parr (1747-1825), the greatest classical scholar of his day; Sydney Smith (1771-1845), whose witty advocacy of Catholic emancipation and repeal of the Test and Corporation Acts served religious liberty, even if he was equally intolerant of “Methodism” and “Puseyism”; Henry Bathurst (Bishop of Norwich), unusual among Liberals in recognising Evangelical merits; and Edward Stanley. The chapter concludes with the Oriel Noetics — Richard Whately and Thomas Arnold — who promised to become the dominant party but never achieved united action.
Chapter V — Church Services and Church Rubrics (p. 127)
A vivid account of worship as actually conducted. Four celebrations of Holy Communion per year was the minimum Horsley set in 1800, and this remained the norm in country parishes. The number of communicants, however, was often impressive — Simeon noted a vast increase at Trinity Church, and Sawbridge’s parish of Stretton achieved 153 communicants in a population of 610. Both Evangelicals and High Churchmen laid great stress on the Sacrament.
Overton surveys the tolerated irregularities: clergy who mutilated the Liturgy (especially the Baptismal service to soften the language of regeneration), or who raced through services to serve multiple churches. He examines Psalmody (the slow shift from metrical psalms to hymns), Preaching (long sermons, political content, growing demand for evangelical preaching), Sunday evening services (introduced by Evangelicals, suspected by High Churchmen), and the rarity of weekday services. A substantial portion treats the want of church accommodation in mushrooming industrial towns: the pew system that excluded the poor, proprietary chapels, the war’s prevention of church-building, the post-war Church Building Acts and the million-pound parliamentary grant of 1818, the ugliness and costliness of Commissioners’ Gothic churches, the first free church in England (St. Mary’s, West Brompton), and the shocking squalor of many country churches. The chapter closes with “A Clergyman’s Work, A.D. 1825,” an anonymous contemporary account.
Chapter VI — Church Literature (p. 163)
The period saw a great revival of theological interest but “not an age of great theological writers.” Under Evidential writings, Overton gives a substantial account of Paley’s Natural Theology (1802), defending it against later depreciation, and surveys Horsley, Nares, and the Bampton Lectures. Practical and devotional works include Hannah More’s tracts, Thomas Scott’s Commentary, and Legh Richmond’s phenomenally popular Dairyman’s Daughter. Liturgical literature covers William Palmer’s Origines Liturgicae (1832), which “helped to prepare men’s minds for the reception of Tractarian tenets.” The Calvinistic controversy over election divided the Evangelicals themselves; the Baptismal Regeneration controversy arose from Evangelical scruples about the Prayer Book language. Religious periodicals (the British Critic, Christian Observer, Record, British Magazine), religious poetry (Cowper, Heber, Keble’s Christian Year), and the Roman controversy are all surveyed.
Chapter VII — The Church and Education (p. 219)
Oxford had reached its nadir in the eighteenth century but began reforming with the Examination Statute of 1801 — two men took honours in 1802, 173 by 1832. Yet Overton is candid about persistent shortcomings: “a vast amount of bigotry and obstructiveness which had been dispelled elsewhere still lingered in its cloisters.” Cambridge, more open to Evangelical influence, was not much better. Overton examines Dr. Arnold of Rugby, whose prefectorial system and breadth of curriculum transformed the public schools, though his “Liberal” Church views were controversial. Elementary education is treated through the Bell-Lancaster controversy over the monitorial system, leading to the founding of the National Society (1811), which built thousands of Church schools. Sunday schools had grown enormously since Raikes’s experiment, with hundreds of thousands of scholars by the 1820s; the Jesus Lane Sunday School in Cambridge is singled out. The chapter concludes with training schools and infant schools pioneered by Samuel Wilderspin.
Chapter VIII — Church Societies (p. 253)
The voluntary societies that drove Church renewal. The S.P.G. grew from 197 subscribers and £4,983 in 1800 to seventeen times as much money and thirty-seven times as many subscribers by 1832. The Church Missionary Society (founded 1799) is traced in detail: the Eclectic Society agitation, the Rauceby meeting of 1795, the work in Sierra Leone, the mission to India, the “five chaplains” of the East India Company, the alarm about proselytizing, Lord Teignmouth’s role, the Charter renewal of 1813 permitting missionaries, Bishop Middleton as first Bishop of Calcutta (1814), Bishop Heber’s legendary episcopal tours, and the heartbreaking account of four lives sacrificed in early Indian missions. The S.P.C.K. and the short-lived Society for the Suppression of Vice are examined. The British and Foreign Bible Society (1804) divided the Church — High Churchmen suspecting indifferentism, Evangelicals eager supporters. The chapter closes with private religious societies like the Eclectic Society and local clerical associations.
Chapter IX — Church and State (p. 295)
Overton sees the period as “the history of a growing alienation between the two.” He examines the parliamentary legislation affecting the Church: the Act of 1801 excluding priests from the Commons (aimed at the clerical Radical Home Tooke); the Acts of 1802 (Sir William Scott’s Bills restraining clerical farming and enforcing residence); the Acts of 1803-1804 continuing reform; the services of Perceval and Lord Liverpool as consistent Church supporters. The great political battles of the late 1820s receive extended treatment: the Roman Catholic Relief Bill (1829), passed amid furious “No Popery” agitation; the Repeal of the Test and Corporation Acts (1828), removing the sacramental test for Dissenters; and the case of Queen Caroline (1820-1821), which divided the nation and damaged the established order. The chapter closes with the cry of “The Church in danger” — how it rallied opposition to reform but lost its power as Church and State progressively separated in the run-up to the Reform Bill of 1832.
Chapter X — Intercourse with Sister Churches (p. 313)
Ireland. The Church of Ireland, united with England by the Act of Union (1800), is noted for the remarkable fact that many precursors of the Oxford Movement were Irish: Bishop Percy of Dromore, Bishop Mant (a “Puseyite before Puseyism”), Bishop Jebb of Limerick, and above all Alexander Knox (1757-1831), whose theological writings anticipated Tractarian positions. The general tone, however, was decidedly Evangelical. Overton profiles the leading Irish Evangelicals (Walker of the “Walkerites,” Dr. O’Brien) and notes the learning of Irish divines — Graves, Magee (Archbishop of Dublin), and William Hales.
Scotland. The Scottish Episcopal Church, a “persecuted and downtrodden” remnant since 1689, recovered after the repeal of the penal laws in 1792. Overton profiles the three great Scottish bishops: Jolly of Moray, Gleig of Brechin, and Walker of Edinburgh, whom he judges “ornaments to any episcopate in any age.” The Scottish connection with the Oxford Movement and the consecration of American bishops is noted.
America. Overton writes with some shame of England’s refusal to consecrate bishops for America before the Revolution. He narrates the consecration of Samuel Seabury by Scottish bishops in 1784 (since English law forbade consecration without the oath of allegiance to the Crown), the consecration of Bishops White and Provoost at Lambeth in 1787, and the establishment of the Protestant Episcopal Church. The real reviver of the American Church, Overton argues, was not living English Churchmen but the writings of the great Anglican divines of the past.
