sources/reed-our-iron-clad-ships.title: Our Iron-Clad Ships; Their Qualities, Performances, and Cost
sources/reed-our-iron-clad-ships.content:
Our Iron-Clad Ships; Their Qualities, Performances, and Cost — Edward J. Reed (1869)
Author: Sir Edward James Reed (1830–1906), Chief Constructor of the Royal Navy 1863–1870.
Published: 1869, John Murray, London.
OCLC: 7944535
A thorough examination of every class of British ironclad from the Warrior (1860) through the Devastation-class monitors then under construction, written from the author’s position as the officer responsible for most of those designs. Reed defends his ships against contemporary criticism and provides detailed comparative data on armour, guns, speeds, handling, and cost.
Structure

Dedication: To Hugh C. E. Childers, M.P., First Lord of the Admiralty.
Introduction (pp. i–xxiv): Reed’s defence of the ironclad programme; argument that armour is not yet obsolete and that the gun-armour contest is still undecided; emphasis on the unfairness of judging ships without accounting for crew skill and management.

Chapter I — Varieties of Iron-Clads
Variety in the British ironclad fleet is not a sign of indecision but of necessary adaptation to changing armour and guns. Comparison with French, Russian, Prussian, Italian, Austrian, Dutch, and American ironclads. Summary of the principal changes since Warrior: from partial to continuous armour belts, from uniform to graduated armour thickness, from broadside-only fire to all-round fire, from long to short hulls, from V-shaped to U-shaped sections, from overhanging to upright stems.
Chapter II — Armour of the Iron-Clads
Progressive increase in armour thickness: Warrior 4in → Bellerophon 6in → Hercules belt 9in → Hotspur 11in → Glatton turret 14in. Table of armour and backing of English ships. French ships compared; American laminated armour system examined. Comparative strength tables (square-of-thickness rule). Disposition systems: partial (Warrior), complete (Minotaur), central battery (Enterprise). Breastwork-monitor system.
Chapter III — Armament of the Iron-Clads
Progress from 4½-ton guns of Warrior to 25-ton guns of Monarch/Captain and 30-ton of Thunderer/Devastation. Table of weights, charges, and powers of naval guns. French and American gun progress. Fight between Weehawken and Atlanta. Need for horizontal range of fire.
Chapter IV — Structure of the Iron-Clads
Iron vs. wood hulls: lighter, stronger, more durable, safer. French preference for wood. Bottom-fouling problem. Warrior vs. Bellerophon construction systems compared. Precautions against torpedoes. Reductions in hull weight. Dr. Fairbairn’s remarks.
Chapter V — Steaming of the Iron-Clads
Full-speed and half-power comparisons. Gradual improvements. Summary of speeds attained by British, French, and American ironclads. Coal supply and endurance. Measured-mile trials: objections, abuses, and defence.
Chapter VI — Sailing of the Iron-Clads
Opinions of naval officers from Channel Squadron reports 1864–1868. Voyages of Ocean and Zealous. Ironclads as capable sea-boats.
Chapter VII — Rolling of the Iron-Clads
Popular errors: top-heaviness, low free-board, weight, bottom form. Steadiness comparisons with unarmoured ships. Stowage effects. Theoretical deductions and practical applications. Channel Squadron trial results 1864–1868.
Chapter VIII — Dimensions of the Iron-Clads
Table of dimensions and proportions. Warrior compared with finest wood ships. Minotaur class. Defence, Hector, Caledonia classes. French moderation. Introduction of shorter proportions. Handiness: opinions of Admirals Dacres, Yelverton, Warden. Turning trials. Hercules’s remarkable handiness.
Chapter IX — Forms and Proportions of Iron-Clads
Weight of hull and armour in relation to form. “Constants of performance” for steamships — their use and misuse. Frictional resistance of long ships. Analysis of Warrior, Minotaur, Bellerophon trials. Royal Society paper abstract.
Chapter X — Cost of the Iron-Clads
Dockyard accounting. Costs of completed broadside ships (contract and government-built), unfinished broadside ships, turret-ships. Total expenditure on ironclads 1859–1869. Savings from shorter ironclads.
Chapter XI — Turret-Ships
Fair discussion of the turret vs. broadside controversy. Advantages: small port, great training. Disadvantages: vulnerability of turret ports and glacis, risk of jamming. Captain and Monarch compared. American monitors (Monadnock, Miantonomoh) — sea-going qualities, fights with Confederate ironclads, Mr. Eads’ evidence. Breastwork-monitor system.
Chapter XII — Iron-Clad Rams
Revival of ramming. Special ram classes. American and Austrian (Lissa) experience. Handiness essential. Forms of ram-bow: upright, fore-reaching, spur-shaped. Loss of sloop Amazon. Structural strengthening. Manoeuvring and attack.
Chapter XIII — Conversion of Line-of-Battle Ships into Iron-Clads
Converted ships in the navy. Royal Sovereign turret conversion. Reasons against further conversions: hull weight, low speed, worn engines, poor stability under canvas. Wooden fleet as a reserve.
Appendix
On the stability of Monitors under canvas (technical analysis with diagrams).
Index — 13 pages of index entries.

sources/royal-commission-city-of-london-.title: Royal Commission into the Corporation of the City of London (1854)
sources/royal-commission-city-of-london-.content:
Royal Commission into the Corporation of the City of London (1854)
Commissioners: John Duke Coleridge; Henry Labouchere; Sir John Patteson; Sir George Cornewall Lewis (Secretary: J. D. Coleridge).
Title: Report of the Commissioners Appointed to Inquire into the Existing State of the Corporation of the City of London, and to Collect Information Respecting Its Constitution, Order, and Government, &c. Together with the Minutes of Evidence and Appendix.
Date: Commission under the Great Seal, 22 June 1853; Report presented to Parliament and ordered to be printed 1854. London: Printed by George Edward Eyre and William Spottiswoode for Her Majesty’s Stationery Office, 1854.
Format: Report (pp. i–xl) + Minutes of Evidence (with index of witnesses) + Appendix. The Anna’s Archive extract is a 1,106-leaf page-OCR dump (6.5 MB) of the University of Minnesota copy (class 352.042), identifier member 31951001571865z.
What the report is and how it opens
A Royal Commission appointed in June 1853 to inquire into the existing state of the Corporation of the City of London, its constitution, order, and government, its jurisdictions civil and criminal, its prisons and police, the mode of electing its members and officers, the rights of its freemen and liverymen, its property, revenue, and expenditure — and to consider whether any measures were necessary to make better provision for the future government of the City. The Report opens by addressing the Queen, sets out the terms of the Commission, and records the course of the inquiry: the Commissioners examined first the witnesses who condemned the constitution or administration of the Corporation, and then the principal officers and leading members of the Corporation, whose ready assistance the Report acknowledges. The Report explains the peculiarity of the City’s position, describes its existing constitution and administration, and annexes suggestions for the amelioration of its defects.
The peculiar position of the City of London
The Report first explains why the Corporation of London stood apart from every other municipal corporation in England. When the Municipal Corporations Act of 1835 (5 & 6 Will. 4 c. 76), founded on the first report of the Municipal Commissioners of 1835, reformed the boroughs of England and Wales, the City of London was not included among the enumerated boroughs; the Municipal Commissioners reported upon London only in their second report of 1837, and no legislative measure was founded upon it. The Report notes the grounds of the City’s exemption: the antiquity, extent, and importance of its privileges, the long series of its charters, the large amount of its revenues, its metropolitan position, and its historical associations. It also notes that the Common Council of London had for many years secured an identity of interests between the governing body and the municipal community — distinguishing the City from the close corporations the Act of 1835 was designed to reform.
The City and the metropolis
The Report devotes particular attention to the relation of the City proper to the whole metropolis. The City of London, 723 acres in area, lay at the centre of a metropolis that the Registrar-General’s division made 78,029 acres; its population was 128,833 in 1801 and 129,128 in 1851 (nearly stationary, while the whole metropolis more than doubled from 958,863 to 2,362,236 in the same period); its rateable assessment was £953,110 against the metropolis’s £9,964,348. The Report observes that, as the metropolis grew at its extremities, the City formed a constantly smaller portion of it — a seventh of the metropolitan population in 1801, only an eighteenth in 1851. The City was the only part of the metropolis with a municipal corporation: Westminster, Marylebone, Finsbury, the Tower Hamlets, Southwark, Lambeth, and Greenwich were parliamentary boroughs but not municipal boroughs. The Report argues that an extension of the City boundaries to embrace the whole metropolis was inapplicable and undesirable — London was “a province covered with houses,” whose extremities had few interests in common and whose administration a single corporation could not conduct with the minute local knowledge and community of interest that municipal government required. It therefore recommends, instead, the extension of municipal institutions to the rest of the metropolis and joint action between its parts.
The constitution of the Corporation
The Report surveys the constituent parts of the Corporation of London: the Lord Mayor, the Court of Aldermen, the Common Council, the Sheriffs, the Recorder, and the courts. It examines the mode of election of each, the wardmote elections and the Common Hall, and the qualifications and privileges of the freemen and liverymen. It considers the jurisdictions of the Corporation — the Lord Mayor’s Court, the Sheriff’s Court, the Court of Hustings, the Court at St. Martin’s-le-Grand — and its prisons and police, including the City Police (regulated by 2 & 3 Vict. c. 94) and the question of their incorporation with the metropolitan police. It examines the Corporation’s conservancy of the river Thames, its control of the markets, its collection of the metage duties and the coal duties, the exclusive privileges of the freemen, the Fellowship of Porters, the Company of Watermen and Lightermen, and the other trading restrictions of the City. And it sets out the property, revenue, and expenditure of the Corporation — the fines for leases, the coal duty (4d. and 8d. per ton), the metage duty on corn, the fees on freedoms, the sheriffs’ fines, the rents of the Bridge House estates, the produce of the tolls of Billingsgate market, and the interest on the government securities.
The defects and the reforms recommended
The Report identifies the defects of the existing system and recommends their amendment. Its central conclusion is that, in revising the constitution of the Corporation, the leading provisions of the Municipal Corporations Act should be applied, with due allowance for the peculiar circumstances of London. It then sets out thirty-two numbered recommendations:

Constitution and elections — a new charter consolidating the preservable charters and customs (1); the Lord Mayor elected by the Common Council (2); the aldermen elected by the burgesses of the wards for six years, re-eligible, and justices of the peace during their term (3); the powers of the Municipal Corporations Act for stipendiary magistrates extended to London (4); the Court of Aldermen abolished, its functions transferred to the Common Council (5); the wards reduced to between twelve and sixteen, with area and population made as equal as possible (6); each ward to return one alderman and five common councilmen, with the qualification of the larger class of boroughs (7); the voters in the wardmote elections to be occupiers rated at £10 without additional qualification (8); the elections in Common Hall abolished (9); the sheriffs elected by the Common Council (10).
Courts — the Lord Mayor’s Court and the Sheriff’s Court consolidated, with an appeal to the superior courts at Westminster (11); the Court of Hustings abolished (12); the Court at St. Martin’s-le-Grand abolished (13).
Trade and privileges — all regulations prohibiting persons not free of the City from carrying on trade or handicraft within the City abolished (14); the metage of grain, fruit, and other measurable goods no longer compulsory (15); the Fellowship of Porters dissolved and other privileges of porters abolished (16); the admission of brokers by the Court of Aldermen abolished (17); the street toll on carts not the property of freemen abolished (18).
Police and the river — the City police incorporated with the metropolitan police (19); the conservancy of the Thames transferred to a board of the Lord Mayor, the First Lord of the Admiralty, the President of the Board of Trade, the Deputy Master of the Trinity House, and the First Commissioner of Woods (20); the exclusive privileges of the Watermen and Lightermen abolished (21).
Finance — the accounts of revenue and expenditure consolidated (22); the money and securities lodged in the Bank of England (23); the election of auditors amended (24); the provisions of the Municipal Corporations Acts on mortgaging and annual returns extended to London (25).
Metropolitan government — the Irish Society dissolved and its trusts declared by Act of Parliament (26); the external boundaries of the City unchanged but the municipal connexion with Southwark abolished (27); the rest of the metropolis divided into districts for municipal purposes (28); a Metropolitan Board of Works created, composed of members deputed from the council of each metropolitan municipal body, including the Common Council of the City (29); the coal duties, while they remain in force, under the administration of this Board, and the 4d. duty to cease when the duties expire in 1862 if not renewed (30); the Board empowered to levy a rate, limited to a fixed poundage, for public works of general metropolitan utility (31); and no works executed without the approval of a Committee of the Privy Council (32).

The closing statement
The Report closes by expressing its opinion of the state of the Corporation: it had found much to amend, but nothing to affect injuriously the honour and integrity of the officers. Some of the recommended alterations would reduce the Corporation’s income, but others would relieve its burdens and diminish its expenditure; some would curtail its powers and privileges, but would remove mischievous restraints upon trade and industry and abolish institutions unsuited to modern legislation. The Commissioners trusted that the changes, founded on the recognized policy of the country with respect to municipal boroughs, would place the Corporation on a more solid and enlarged basis, enabling it to continue, under an amended system, to possess abundant means for public usefulness and for a decent hospitality and splendour; and they abstained from recommending an extension of the boundaries to include the whole metropolis, proposing instead an arrangement enabling the Corporation to form part of a general metropolitan system.
Minutes of evidence and appendix
Following the Report are the Minutes of Evidence — the testimony of the witnesses examined, with an index of witnesses (George Appleton Wallis, James Acland, William Delafield and Horatio Nelson Fisher on the metage and porterage suit, John Gellibrand Hubbard, John Dillon, Alexander Pulling on the law, John Remington Mills on the appointment of sheriffs, John Distin Powles on the Corporation’s measures with respect to trade, John Hawkins Elliott, Francis Bennoch, John Cattley, James C. Gooden on the conservancy of the Medway, and many others, including witnesses on the Common Hall elections, the suit of the Crown respecting the bed of the Thames, the Southwark connexion, and the trading companies). The evidence is followed by the Appendix, which prints the supporting documents — the statements and accounts of the revenue and expenditure, the reports on the Bridge House estates, the trusts of the various funds, and the other papers laid before the Commission.

Leaves are numbered 00000001.txt–00001106.txt; the Report proper runs from roughly leaf 5 to leaf 43, followed by the Minutes of Evidence and the Appendix. OCR is page-level and retains running heads and some noise.

sources/second-report-municipal-commissi.title: Second Report of the Municipal Corporations Commission — London and Southwark (1837)
sources/second-report-municipal-commissi.content:
Second Report of the Municipal Corporations Commission — London and Southwark (1837)
Commissioners for Inquiring into the Municipal Corporations of England and Wales. Among the commissioners were Sir Francis Palgrave, Fortunatus Dwarris, Sampson Wilkinson, and Thomas Jefferson Hogg.
Title: Second Report of the Commissioners Appointed to Inquire into the Municipal Corporations in England and Wales — London and Southwark. London Companies.
Date: Ordered by the House of Commons to be printed 25 April 1837; Session 1837, Vol. XXV (Sess. Paper 239). The London report proper is dated pursuant to an address to His Majesty of 3 April 1835.
Format: The Irish University Press reprint (ISBN 9780716508281) of the 1837 Second Report, bound in the British Parliamentary Papers series (“Municipal Corporations” subject set), 930 pages, including the General Report on London and Southwark, the report on the London Companies, the Minutes of Evidence, and the correspondence and protests of the commissioners. The Anna’s Archive extract is a page-OCR dump (~4.4 MB) of this volume.
What the report is and its place
This is the Second Report of the great Royal Commission appointed to inquire into the municipal corporations of England and Wales. The First Report (1835) examined the boroughs generally and led directly to the Municipal Corporations Act 1835 (5 & 6 Will. 4 c. 76); the Corporation of the City of London was deliberately excepted from that Act and from the First Report’s schedule. The Commission reported on London only in this Second Report of 1837, which covers the Corporation of London and Southwark and the London Companies. It is the fundamental contemporary inquiry into the constitution, government, and privileges of the City of London, and it is the document upon which the later Royal Commission of 1854 (also in this wiki) explicitly built — the 1854 Report cites and relies on “the Second Report of the Municipal Commissioners, presented in 1837.”
The peculiar position of London
The Report opens by explaining why London stands apart from the other municipalities. The Municipal Corporations Act of 1835 brought within its provisions the towns enumerated in its schedules, enlarging many of them by the adoption of the parliamentary borough boundaries — Bristol raised from 59,000 to 104,000, Liverpool from 165,000 to 206,000, and so on. But London was not enumerated in the schedules, and the Report examines whether the same reasoning that justified the extension of the other boroughs applied to the metropolis. It sets out how small a proportion of the metropolis was comprehended within the municipal boundary of the City, and it insists that any reasoning founded on the assumption that questions respecting the Corporation relate to the whole town of London is fallacious — a point that was to run through all subsequent discussion of the City and its government.
The limits, territory, and municipal constitution
The Report describes the limits and municipal territory of the City of London. The City, including the Liberties (the districts into which the municipal franchises and privileges extend), is distinguished into London within the Walls and London without the Walls, or the Liberties — a distinction which, the Report notes, then existed only in name, the term “City” being employed to designate the whole of the municipal territory comprehended within the outer frontier of the Liberties. It describes the position of the bars and gates, the line of the walls, the boundary between the Liberties and the county of Middlesex, the ancient London Bridge within the City and the “Bridge Foot” on the Surrey shore, and the Tolls Traverse collected at the bars. It examines the division into wards, the wardmote elections, the Common Council, the Court of Aldermen, the Lord Mayor, the Sheriffs, the Recorder and the officers of the Corporation — their election, their functions, and their privileges.
The governing bodies and officers
The Report surveys the constituent parts of the Corporation and their functions. It treats the Lord Mayor and his office and jurisdiction; the Court of Aldermen, with its judicial and elective powers, including the admission of brokers and the appointment of officers; the Common Council, the popular and representative body of the City, and its committees (the Committee of City Lands, the Thames Navigation Committee, the Bridge committee); the Sheriffs, and the office of the Town Clerk and the Chamberlain. It examines the mode of election of the different members and officers — the wardmote elections of the common councilmen, the election of the Lord Mayor and the sheriffs, and the part of the Livery and of Common Hall in those elections. It describes the courts of the City — the Lord Mayor’s Court, the Sheriffs’ Courts (with the custom of Foreign Attachment), the Court of Hustings, the court at St. Martin’s-le-Grand, the jurisdiction of the Recorder and the Common Sergeant — and the connection with the Central Criminal Court, which had recently been established.
The privileges, franchises, and property
The Report examines the rights and privileges of the freemen and liverymen of the City — the exclusive privileges of trading and exercising a handicraft within the City, the admission to the freedom, and the relation of the Companies to the Corporation. It describes the property, revenue, and expenditure of the Corporation: the Bridge House estates and the tolls of London Bridge, the markets and their tolls (including Billingsgate and the coal market at Blackfriars), the metage duties, the various fines and fees, and the management and application of the corporate funds.
The London Companies
A distinct and important part of the Second Report is the account of the London Companies — the trading and livery companies of the City. The Report traces the rise and progress of the guilds and companies, examines their constitution, their privileges, their relation to the Corporation, and their condition, and sets out the nature of the information obtained concerning them. It notes (as the Report candidly records) that in the case of the Companies information was in some instances altogether refused, and in many others furnished only under exceptions or restrictions, so that the account of the Companies was far from complete. The Companies — such as the spectacle-makers, clock-makers, silk-throwers, distillers, and tobacco-pipe makers mentioned in the report’s contents — form the guild inheritance of the City.
The evidence and the Southwark connexion
Following the General Report is the Minutes of Evidence, the testimony of the witnesses examined before the Commission, with the usual appendix of documents. The Report also treats the connexion of the Corporation with Southwark — the limited and partly nominal municipal relation of the City to a portion of the parliamentary borough of Southwark on the Surrey shore, including the courts leet, the quarter sessions, and the appointment of the judge and prothonotary of the Borough Court by the City. The volume also prints the correspondence and protests from certain commissioners, reflecting the divisions of opinion within the Commission itself.
Raw Text
wiki/raw/second-report-municipal-commission-city-of-london-1837/report.txt — page-OCR text of the 1837 Second Report volume (930 pages; ~4.4 MB; SHA-256 458ca9804df8280f6260841a4b9dc96c1feae10514088160f94c583613b7742a). The OCR retains the facsimile’s running heads and page numbers; the London report body begins around the “GENERAL REPORT LONDON AND SOUTHWARK” section, followed by the London Companies, the evidence, and the correspondence and protests. The scan is a facsimile reprint, so some pages carry broken type and OCR noise.

sources/smiles-engineers-smeaton-rennie.title: smiles-engineers-smeaton-rennie
sources/smiles-engineers-smeaton-rennie.content:
Lives of the Engineers, Vol. II: Harbours, Lighthouses, and Bridges — Smeaton and Rennie
Author: Samuel Smiles
Title: Lives of the Engineers. With an Account of their Principal Works; Comprising also a History of Inland Communication in Britain. Vol. II: Harbours—Lighthouses—Bridges. Smeaton and Rennie.
Edition: New and Revised Edition
Publisher: John Murray, London
Year: 1874
Call number: TA 139 .S64 1874 vol. 2 (University of Michigan)
Raw text: wiki/raw/smiles-engineers-smeaton-rennie.txt (18,135 lines)
Description
The second volume of Smiles’ five-volume Lives of the Engineers, covering the history of harbours, lighthouses, and bridges in Britain through the lives of John Smeaton (1724–1792) and John Rennie (1761–1821). Three introductory chapters on the early history of shipping and harbours, beacons and lighthouses, and bridges are followed by separate biographical sections on Smeaton and Rennie, each tracing the engineer’s life from childhood through their major civil engineering works. Smeaton is principally known for the third Eddystone Lighthouse, his improvement of the Newcomen steam engine, and numerous harbour, canal, and bridge works throughout Britain. Rennie is noted for Waterloo, Southwark, and London Bridge, the London and Liverpool docks, extensive fen drainage in Lincolnshire and Cambridgeshire, and the development of the dredging machine and hollow quay walls.
Chapter Breakdown
Introductory Chapters

Chapter I: Shipping and Harbours — The late development of English commerce; foreign merchants of the Hanseatic League; English merchant adventurers and the Muscovy, Levant, and East India Companies; early harbours at Lyme Regis, Dover, Yarmouth; the development of docks at Liverpool and on the Thames.
Chapter II: Beacons and Lighthouses — The Pharos of Alexandria; Roman lighthouses at Boulogne and Dover; medieval lights at Whitby, Flamborough, and other English headlands; coal-fire lights; the incorporation of Trinity House and the abuses of the lighthouse system.
Chapter III: Early Bridges — Bridges built by the early Churchmen at Burton, Norwich, Rochester, Wakefield, Monmouth, and Llanrwst; Croyland Bridge; Bow Bridge; the fraternity of bridge-builders.
Chapter IV: Old London Bridge — Thames ferries; the first wooden London Bridge and its stone successor; the building and description of the old bridge; Westminster Bridge built by Labelye; Blackfriars Bridge; the Mylnes.
Chapter V: William Edwards, Bridge Builder — Life and self-education of William Edwards; his drystone wall-building; his iron forges; the building of the Old Bridge at Pontypridd.

Part I: John Smeaton

Chapter I: Smeaton’s Early Years — Birth at Austhorpe, Leeds (1724); early mechanical inclinations; childhood contrivances; education at Leeds Grammar School.
Chapter II: Smeaton Learns the Trade of Mathematical Instrument Maker — Placed in an attorney’s office; attends the law courts at Westminster Hall; learns mathematical instrument making; attends meetings of the Royal Society; his paper on the natural powers of wind and water to turn mills; his tour in Holland.
Chapter III: The Eddystone Rock — Winstanley’s and Rudyerd’s Lighthouses — The dangers of the Eddystone Rock; Henry Winstanley’s eccentric character and his first lighthouse, washed away in the great storm of 1703; John Rudyerd’s second lighthouse, destroyed by fire; Smeaton called upon to build the third.
Chapter IV: Smeaton Builds the Eddystone Lighthouse — Smeaton’s design, inspired by the oak tree; his dovetailed granite construction; the building process and the difficulties of working on the exposed rock; the completion and lasting success of the lighthouse (1759).
Chapter V: Smeaton’s Engineering Works — Improvement of river navigations (Calder Navigation, etc.); drainage of the Lincoln and Cambridge Fens; repairs to London Bridge; design of pumping engines; bridges at Perth and Coldstream; Forth and Clyde Canal; Banff, Hexham, and other bridges; harbours at St. Ives, Ramsgate, Eyemouth; use of the diving bell; mills and machinery; improvements in Newcomen’s steam engine (including his separate condenser experiments and the indicator).
Chapter VI: Smeaton’s Private Life — Death and Character — His home at Austhorpe; his study, workshop, and blacksmith; papers contributed to the Royal Society; his tools, lathe, and mechanical contrivances; his character and death (1792).

Part II: John Rennie

Chapter I: Rennie’s Early Years — Birth at Phantassie, East Lothian (1761); early boyhood and education; his mechanical turn of mind; attends the University of Edinburgh; studies under Professor Robison.
Chapter II: Rennie’s Master Andrew Meikle — Fletcher of Saltoun’s introduction of barley-mills and fanners into Scotland; James Meikle; Andrew Meikle’s invention of the thrashing machine; improvements in windmills; drainage of Kincardine Moss.
Chapter III: Rennie Begins Business as Millwright and Engineer — Frequents Meikle’s workshop; begins business as a millwright; attends the University of Edinburgh; prepares designs and estimates; early millwork and factory projects.
Chapter IV: Rennie’s Canals — Rennie’s employment on the improvement of the River Witham; the Horncastle and Sleaford Navigations; the Lancaster Canal (aqueducts); the Crinan Canal; the Rochdale Canal; the Kennet and Avon Canal (Caen Hill locks, the Dundas Aqueduct).
Chapter V: Rennie’s Fen Drainage Works — The East Fen; Sir Joseph Banks and the drainage of Wildmore Fen; the catchwater system; Great Hobhole Drain and its effects on agriculture; improvement of the Witham at Boston; drainage of the Great Level; the Eau Brink Cut; Fen scenery.
Chapter VI: Mr. Rennie’s Bridges — Dr. Robison visits Rennie in London; theory and practice in bridge-building; early bridge designs; Kelso Bridge; Musselburgh Bridge; projected cast-iron bridge over the Menai Straits; Boston Bridge; Waterloo Bridge and its distinctive features; Southwark Bridge; London Bridge.
Chapter VII: Rennie’s Harbours and Docks — The London Docks; the East and West India Docks; his method of working; report on Wick Harbour; the River Clyde improvements; Grimsby Docks; invention of hollow quay walls; Holyhead Harbour; Hull Harbour and Docks; invention of the dredging machine; Leith Docks; various harbour works; Ramsgate Harbour; improvement of the diving bell.
Chapter VIII: Mr. Rennie’s War Docks and Other Government Works — Coast defences; defensive works on the River Lea; the Hythe Military Canal; Fulton’s torpedo; report on the government dockyards; recommended improvements at Plymouth, Portsmouth, Deptford, Woolwich, and Chatham; his plan for a naval arsenal at Northfleet; Sheerness dockyard.

Notes

Volume II of Smiles’ five-volume series. Other volumes: I (Vermuyden, Myddelton, Perry, Brindley, Smeaton — embankments and canals), III (Metcalfe and Telford — roads), IV (Boulton and Watt — the steam engine), V (George and Robert Stephenson — the locomotive).
Rennie’s major bridges (Waterloo 1817, Southwark 1819, London Bridge 1831) and docks (London Docks 1805, etc.) fall squarely within the 1800–1865 period.
Smiles also wrote Self-Help (1859), Character (1871), Thrift (1875), Industrial Biography (1863), and The Huguenots in England.

sources/smiles-engineers-vol1-vermyden-b.title: smiles-engineers-vol1-vermyden-brindley
sources/smiles-engineers-vol1-vermyden-b.content:
Lives of the Engineers, Vol. I: Early Engineering — Vermuyden, Myddelton, Perry, Brindley
Author: Samuel Smiles
Title: Lives of the Engineers. With an Account of their Principal Works; Comprising also a History of Inland Communication in Britain. Vol. I: Early Engineering — Vermuyden, Myddelton, Perry — James Brindley.
Edition: New and Revised Edition
Publisher: John Murray, London
Year: 1874
Call number: TA 139 .S64 1874 v.1 (State University of Iowa)
Raw text: wiki/raw/smiles-engineers-vol1-vermyden-brindley.txt (16,055 lines)
Description
The first volume of Smiles’ five-volume Lives of the Engineers, covering the earliest British engineering works — land drainage, water supply, and canal construction — through the biographies of four engineers. A lengthy introductory section (twenty chapters) provides a general history of British engineering from Roman times to the mid-nineteenth century, covering the reclamation of the Fens, the development of roads, the rise of commerce and manufacturing, the steam engine, railways, and the character of the English engineer as a self-taught practical man. The main body treats four engineers: Cornelius Vermuyden (drainage of the Fens and Hatfield Chase), Sir Hugh Myddelton (the New River water supply to London), Captain John Perry (the Dagenham Breach), and James Brindley (the Bridgewater Canal, the Grand Trunk Canal, and the beginnings of the British canal system).
Chapter Breakdown
Introduction (sections I–XX)
A general history of English engineering from its beginnings through the mid-nineteenth century. Topics include: the early settlement of Britain; the work of the Dutch and Flemish engineers in draining the Fens and embanking the Thames; England’s early dependence on foreign engineers and skilled workmen (German miners, Dutch millwrights, French architects); the poor state of English roads down to the eighteenth century; the development of turnpikes and the improvement of transport after the Union of 1707; the rise of canals and the commercial revolution; the inventions of Watt, Arkwright, and Cort; the coming of steam navigation and railways; the self-taught character of British engineers; colonial expansion and the growth of commerce during the Napoleonic wars; the role of private enterprise (rather than government) in engineering works.
Part I: Sir Cornelius Vermuyden

Chapter I: Introductory — Labour and skill in making modern England; early embankment and drainage works from Roman times; the reclamation of Romney Marsh; embankments of the Thames; the Great Level of the Fens; laws for preserving reclaimed lands; destructive floods; James I encourages drainage works; Vermuyden, the Dutch engineer, employed by the king (pages 1–18).
Chapter II: Sir Cornelius Vermuyden — Drainage of the Fens — Vermuyden’s embankment and drainage works at Dagenham and Windsor; the Isle of Axholme; reclamation of Hatfield Chase; the works carried out by foreign capital and foreign labour; opposition of the native population.

Part II: Sir Hugh Myddelton

Chapter III: Sir Hugh Myddelton — Cutting of the New River — Old London’s water supply by streams and conduits; defective supply; water-works at Hull, Tiverton, and Plymouth (Sir Francis Drake’s leet); the Myddelton family; Hugh Myddelton apprenticed as a goldsmith; his career as merchant, cloth-maker, alderman, and M.P.; appointed to committees on the water supply of London; the difficulty of finding an engineer; Myddelton undertakes the work; the New River; hostility of property owners; King James I assists in the completion; the opening ceremony; benefits of the undertaking.

Part III: Captain John Perry

Chapter: Captain John Perry — The Dagenham Breach — The great breach at Dagenham; futile attempts to stop it; Boswell the contractor; Captain John Perry, his early career as a sailor; employed by Czar Peter of Russia to superintend a canal from St. Petersburg to the Caspian Sea; comptroller of Russian maritime works; leaves Russia without pay; undertakes the stoppage of the Dagenham breach on the Thames; description of his process; opposition of Boswell; completion of the works; Perry a loser by his contract; his subsequent employment as surveyor of harbours.

Part IV: James Brindley

Chapter I: Brindley’s Early Years — The First English Canal Maker — Brindley’s birth and parentage; his unpromising early life; apprenticed to a millwright; mechanical ingenuity; works on the first English canal (the Worsley Canal); his marriage and character.
Chapter II: Brindley as Master Wheelwright and Millwright — The variety of Brindley’s employment; his ingenuity earns him the name “The Schemer”; his memorandum books; employment by Earl Gower at Trentham; improves flint-mills for the Potteries; employed by the brothers Wedgwood; drains drowned mines for John Heathcote at Clifton Colliery; fits up a silk-mill at Congleton; his habits of observation and fertility of resources; improvements in machinery for silk manufacture, mills, and pumps at the Potteries; his original contrivances.
Chapter III: The Duke of Bridgewater’s Canal — The Barton Aqueduct — The Duke of Bridgewater; his desire to open a canal for his coal-mines at Worsley; consults James Brindley; Brindley’s survey and plans; execution of the canal; the Barton Aqueduct pronounced “a castle in the air”; description of the aqueduct and other works; Trafford Moss; subterraneous canal at Worsley; Brindley’s mechanical contrivances; the value of the canal when finished.
Chapter IV: Extension of the Duke’s Canal to the Mersey — Brindley’s survey from Stretford to the Mersey; importance of communication between Manchester and Liverpool; the growth of Liverpool and decay of Chester; opposition to the Duke’s bill in Parliament; Brindley’s efforts and counter-surveys; Brindley examined at the Bar of the House of Commons; the bill passed; the canal completed to Runcorn.
Chapter V: The Duke of Bridgewater — Personal History — Extensive coal workings at Worsley; cost of the canals; reduction in the cost of water-carriage; Brindley’s insignificant remuneration; disputes between the Duke and Brindley; the Duke’s personal interest in his canals, coal-mines, and mills; personal traits and anecdotes; his business habits; his death, character, and public services; benefits of his canal to Manchester and Liverpool; the extraordinary growth of Manchester (pages 217–247).
Chapter VI: Brindley Constructs the Grand Trunk Canal — The Grand Trunk Canal connecting the Mersey with the Trent; Josiah Wedgwood as one of its promoters; Brindley’s level lengths; the canal between Chesterfield and the Trent; the extent of canals laid out by Brindley; his educational disadvantages; his work not duly appreciated in his own day; other canal projects (Leeds and Liverpool Canal, the Thames survey, Lincolnshire drainage); his pupils; his private life, strange courtship and marriage; his home at Turnhurst; illness and death; characteristics; mechanical genius; his studies in bed; his private character; influence of Brindley’s canals on the enterprise and speculation of the time; extent of the canal system in Great Britain.

Notes

Volume I of Smiles’ five-volume series. Other volumes: II (Smeaton and Rennie — harbours, lighthouses, bridges), III (Metcalfe and Telford — roads), IV (Boulton and Watt — the steam engine), V (George and Robert Stephenson — the locomotive).
Volume II (Smeaton and Rennie) is already in this wiki at sources/smiles-engineers-smeaton-rennie.md.
Volume V (the Locomotive) is already in this wiki at sources/smiles-locomotive-stephenson.md.
The lengthy introductory section (twenty sections, pages i–xx) gives a broad but popular view of the history of British engineering, emphasizing the self-taught, practical character of English engineers and the role of private enterprise.
Brindley’s canals (the Bridgewater and Grand Trunk, both completed in the 1760s–1770s) predate the 1800–1865 period but laid the foundation for the inland transport revolution that continued through the early nineteenth century.

sources/smiles-engineers-vol3-metcalfe-t.title: smiles-engineers-vol3-metcalfe-telford
sources/smiles-engineers-vol3-metcalfe-t.content:
Lives of the Engineers, Vol. III: History of Roads — Metcalfe and Telford
Author: Samuel Smiles
Title: Lives of the Engineers. With an Account of their Principal Works; Comprising also a History of Inland Communication in Britain. Vol. III: History of Roads — Metcalfe and Telford.
Edition: New and Revised Edition
Publisher: John Murray, London
Year: 1874 (this copy 1904)
Call number: TA 139 .S64 1874 vol. 3 (University of Michigan)
Raw text: wiki/raw/smiles-engineers-vol3-metcalfe-telford.txt (15,391 lines)
Description
The third volume of Smiles’ five-volume Lives of the Engineers, tracing the history of British roads and road-making through the lives of John Metcalf (1717–1810) and Thomas Telford (1757–1834). Five introductory chapters survey the state of roads and modes of travel from Roman Britain through the eighteenth century, including the manners and customs shaped by poor communications, the state of roads in Scotland, and the era of stage-coaches and mail-coaches. The first biographical section treats John Metcalf (“Blind Jack of Knaresborough”), whose career as road-maker in Yorkshire and Lancashire despite total blindness forms a remarkable story of personal enterprise. The second and longer section covers Thomas Telford, the shepherd boy who became the greatest road- and bridge-builder of his age — his early life in Eskdale, his work as surveyor for Shropshire, his landmark iron bridges (Buildwas, Bewdley), his Highland roads and bridges under the Parliamentary Commission, the Caledonian Canal, his work as a road-maker (including the Shrewsbury and Holyhead road), his presidency of the newly-formed Institute of Civil Engineers, and his death in 1834.
Chapter Breakdown
Introductory Chapters: Early Roads and Modes of Travelling

Chapter I: Old Roads — Roads as agents of civilisation; ancient British trackways or ridgeways; Roman roads in Britain; decay of the Roman roads; early legislation relating to highways; roads near London, the Weald of Kent, hollow ways, Dartmoor, Sussex, Kensington.
Chapter II: Early Modes of Conveyance — Riding on horseback as the ancient mode; Shakespeare’s description of travelling; Queen Elizabeth’s coach; introduction of coaches and waggons; painful journeys by coach; Great North Road under Charles I; stage-coaches introduced; Sobriere’s account of English coaches.
Chapter III: Manners and Customs Influenced by the State of the Roads — Restricted intercourse between districts; local dialects and customs preserved; Camden’s fear of travelling north; imperfect postal communication; hawkers and pedlars; laying in stores for winter; great fairs; primitive manners of Dartmoor district.
Chapter IV: Roads and Travelling in Scotland in the Last Century — Poverty of Scotland; backwardness of agriculture; Andrew Fletcher’s description; slavery of colliers and salters; improvement in agriculture opposed; low wages; state of the Lothians and Ayrshire; wretched state of the roads.
Chapter V: Turnpikes, Stage-Coaches, and Mail-Coaches — The turnpike system; growth of stage-coaching; Palmer’s mail-coaches; improvement in speed and comfort; the coaching inn; the golden age of the road; the coming of railways.

Part I: John Metcalf

Chapter VI: John Metcalf, Road-Maker — Metcalf’s boyhood; his blindness; his boldness as a musician; his travels as a journeyman musician; joins the army in the rebellion of 1745; adventures in Scotland; becomes travelling merchant and horse dealer; begins road-making; builds a bridge; his extensive road contracts in Yorkshire and Lancashire; his manner of making surveys; his skill in road-making; his last road; his death; the Dunstan pillar; rapid improvement in roads; application of steam.

Part II: Thomas Telford

Chapter I (Part II): Eskdale — Eskdale and Langholm; former lawlessness of the Border population; Telford’s birth and parentage; his shepherd boyhood; early education; learns the trade of a mason.
Chapter II: Apprenticed to a Stone-Mason — Telford becomes a stone-mason; his master; works on the building of Langholm Bridge; removes to Edinburgh; his evening studies; becomes a skilful hewer; returns to Eskdale.
Chapter III: Working Mason in London, and Foreman at Portsmouth — Telford a working man in London; obtains employment as a mason at Somerset House; correspondence with Eskdale friends; observations on his fellow-workmen; becomes foreman of builders at Portsmouth Dockyard; continues to write poetry.
Chapter IV: Surveyor for the County of Salop — Superintends repairs of Shrewsbury Castle; appointed Surveyor for Shropshire; superintends erection of new gaol; interview with John Howard; studies in science and literature; poetical exercises; fall of St. Chad’s Church; discovery of the Roman city of Uriconium.
Chapter V: Telford as Engineer — Cast-Iron Aqueducts at Chirk and Pontcysyllte — First employment as engineer; the Ellesmere Canal; the cast-iron aqueduct at Chirk; the still greater aqueduct at Pontcysyllte (the longest and highest in Britain); extension of canal to Ruabon; other canals.
Chapter VI: Telford’s Early Bridges — The bridge at Buildwas (the first iron bridge after Coalbrookdale); cold-blast iron used; iron bridges at Cound, Bewdley, and elsewhere; the style of Telford’s bridges; the suspension bridge over the Menai Straits proposed; difficulties with the Admiralty; the Menai Suspension Bridge built; the Conway Bridge.
Chapter VII: Iron and Other Bridges — Use of iron in bridge-building; the first iron bridge at Coalbrookdale; Tom Paine’s iron bridge; Wear iron bridge at Sunderland; Telford’s iron bridge at Buildwas; his iron lock-gates and turn-bridges; project for a one-arched iron bridge over the Thames; Bewdley stone bridge; Tongueland Bridge; extension of Telford’s business; literary friendships with Thomas Campbell.
Chapter VIII: Highland Roads and Bridges — Progress of Scottish agriculture; Romilly’s account; state of the Highlands; want of roads; use of the cas-chrom; emigration; Telford’s survey of Scotland; Lord Cockburn’s account of the difficulties of travelling the Northern Circuit; Parliamentary Commission of Highland Roads and Bridges appointed; Dunkeld and other bridges.
Chapter IX: Caledonian Canal — Early surveys for a ship-canal across Scotland; Telford’s survey; the great chain of lakes; plan of the canal; the summit level near Fort Augustus; the cutting and works; the earning of wages; the construction of the Caledonian Canal; its limited commercial success.
Chapter X: Telford’s Canals — Construction of the Caledonian Canal works; commercial failure of the canal; Glasgow and Ardrossan Canal; Weaver Navigation; Gotha Canal in Sweden; Gloucester and Berkeley Canal; Harecastle Tunnel; Birmingham Canal; Macclesfield Canal; Birmingham and Liverpool Junction Canal; Telford’s pride in his canals.
Chapter XI: Telford as a Road-Maker — Increase of road-traffic; improvement of main routes; Carlisle and Glasgow road; Telford’s principles of road-construction; Macadam; Cartland Crags Bridge; improvement of the London and Edinburgh post road; communication with Ireland; state of Welsh roads; Shrewsbury and Holyhead road; London and Shrewsbury post road; coast road in North Wales.
Chapter XII: St. Katharine’s and other Docks — Demand for dock accommodation in London; St. Katharine’s Docks; Telford appointed engineer; his design and execution; the dock buildings; working of the docks; improvement of the River Tyne; other harbour works.
Chapter XIII: Telford’s Later Public Works — Improvements of the Carlisle and Glasgow road; roads and bridges in Ireland; Dunkeld and other bridges; canals; harbour works in Scotland.
Chapter XIV: Southey’s Tour in the Highlands — Southey sets out with Telford; Dunkeld; works at Dundee Harbour; Bervie Harbour; Mitchell and Gibbs; Aberdeen Harbour; Banff and Cullen Harbours; the Forres road; Beauly Bridge; Bonar Bridge; Fleet Mound; Southey’s description of the Caledonian Canal; John Mitchell; results of Highland road-making.
Chapter XV: Telford’s Later Years — Death and Character — Telford’s residence in London; leaves the Salopian; first President of the Institute of Civil Engineers; consulted by foreign governments; his views on railways; failure of health; consulted as to Dover Harbour; illness and death; his character; his friends; integrity; views on money-making; benevolence and patriotism; his will; libraries established.

Notes

Volume III of Smiles’ five-volume series. Other volumes: I (Vermuyden, Myddelton, Perry, Brindley — embankments and canals), II (Smeaton and Rennie — harbours, lighthouses, bridges), IV (Boulton and Watt — the steam engine), V (George and Robert Stephenson — the locomotive).
Telford’s Menai Suspension Bridge (1826) and many of his Highland roads and bridges fall squarely within the 1800–1865 period.
Smiles devotes considerable space to the social history of travel and communications before the railway age.
John Metcalf worked entirely in the eighteenth century (d. 1810) but his methods and achievements form the background to later road improvement.

sources/smiles-engineers-vol4-boulton-wa.title: smiles-engineers-vol4-boulton-watt
sources/smiles-engineers-vol4-boulton-wa.content:
Lives of the Engineers, Vol. IV: The Steam-Engine — Boulton and Watt
Author: Samuel Smiles
Title: Lives of the Engineers. With an Account of their Principal Works; Comprising also a History of Inland Communication in Britain. Vol. IV: The Steam-Engine — Boulton and Watt.
Edition: New and Revised Edition
Publisher: John Murray, London
Year: 1878
Call number: TA 139 .S64 1874 vol. 4 (University of Michigan)
Raw text: wiki/raw/smiles-engineers-vol4-boulton-watt.txt (18,083 lines)
Description
The fourth volume of Smiles’ five-volume Lives of the Engineers, tracing the development of the steam engine through the partnership of Matthew Boulton (1728–1809) and James Watt (1736–1819). The first half of the volume follows Watt’s early life and struggles — his upbringing in Greenock, his training as a mathematical instrument maker, his friendship with Joseph Black and John Robison at the University of Glasgow, his experiments with the Newcomen engine model, and his invention of the separate condenser. The second half follows Matthew Boulton’s career in Birmingham, his founding of the Soho Manufactory, the partnership with Watt, the long battle to establish the condensing engine in the Cornish mines, the fight to defend the patent against infringers, the introduction of the rotary engine for mills, and the later prosperity of the firm. The volume concludes with the French Revolution and Birmingham riots, William Murdock’s invention of gas-lighting, and the final years of both men.
Chapter Breakdown
Part I: Early Life of James Watt

Chapter I: James Watt’s Birthplace and Lineage — Birth at Greenock (1736); his grandfather the mathematician; his father’s business; his mother; his fragile constitution; early schooling; first visit to Glasgow; boyish ingenuity; home education; the Rebellion of 1745; his love of scientific pursuits; sent to Glasgow to learn mathematical-instrument making.
Chapter II: Glasgow, London, and the College — Glasgow in 1754; the tobacco lords; early clubs and social habits of the merchants; Watt’s master; leaves Glasgow for London on horseback; placed with a mathematical-instrument maker; danger from press-gangs; returns to Scotland; refused permission to begin business in Glasgow; gains asylum in the College; intercourse with the professors; intimate relations with John Robison.
Chapter III: Early History of the Steam Engine — Early knowledge of the power of steam; Hero’s writings; the Æolipile; Branca; Solomon de Caus; the Marquis of Worcester’s water-commanding machine; Dr. Papin; Thomas Savery; early tin-mining; Savery’s steam engine used to pump water; Thomas Newcomen and his steam engine; Humphrey Potter; Henry Beighton; Newcomen’s engine found wasteful and disused.
Chapter IV: Watt’s Experiments on Steam — Robison and Watt’s conferences on the power of steam; Dr. Black and latent heat; the College model of the Newcomen engine arrives; Watt’s difficulties and perseverance; takes a partner and opens a shop; his marriage; his Sunday walk on Glasgow Green and his first idea of the condensing engine; removes to a cellar and erects a working engine; mechanical and financial difficulties.
Chapter V: Partnership with Dr. Roebuck — The Patent — Watt’s introduction to Dr. Roebuck; begins business as surveyor; partnership with Roebuck in the engine; Watt at Kinneil; a patent determined on; correspondence with Dr. Small; Watt erects a trial engine; Roebuck’s embarrassments; Watt’s despondency; learns German; employed in surveys; designs Hamilton Bridge; supplies plans for docks and harbours; illness and death of Mrs. Watt; Dr. Roebuck’s ruin.

Part II: Boulton and Watt — Birmingham

Chapter VI: Matthew Boulton’s Early Career — Soho — Birmingham in early times; its industrial growth; Matthew Boulton begins business; Snow-hill; aims at excellence; removes to Soho; the Soho Manufactory; the best artists employed; visits of foreigners; Boulton’s scientific pursuits.
Chapter VII: First Meeting of Boulton and Watt — Water- and horse-power at Soho; Boulton’s correspondence with Benjamin Franklin concerning fire-engines; Boulton’s model; Watt visits Soho; correspondence of Boulton, Dr. Small, and Watt; Dr. Roebuck visits Boulton; Watt’s anxiety for Boulton to join him; Watt engineer for the Monkland Canal; terms of proposed partnership; Roebuck’s share transferred to Boulton; Watt’s arrival at Birmingham.
Chapter VIII: Boulton’s Character — The Engine at Soho — Characteristics of Matthew Boulton; contrast between him and Watt; Boulton’s friends; Watt’s engine at Soho; Boulton’s views of the engine business; the Kinneil engine re-erected at Soho; inquiries for pumping-engines from the mining districts; Watt in London; death of Dr. Small; application to Parliament for extension of engine patent; the Act obtained; manufacture of engines begun.
Chapter IX: The First Orders — Watt Marries — Watt’s house on Harper’s Hill; first order for engines; Boulton’s activity; London engineers predict failure; Watt revisits Glasgow; his second marriage; terms of partnership between Boulton and Watt; Watt returns to Soho; orders for Ting-tang and Chacewater mines, Cornwall; Watt and the Shadwell Waterworks Committee; Stratford-le-Bow engine; difficulties with workmen.
Chapter X: Watt in Cornwall — Inefficiency of the Newcomen pumping-engines; mines drowned; Watt and Jonathan Hornblower; Mrs. Watt’s account of Cornwall; Chacewater engine finished; Boulton’s courage and perseverance; fire at Soho; engine royalty on savings of fuel; altercations with adventurers; William Murdock employed; his character and ability; his mode of dealing with the Cornish captains.
Chapter XI: Financial Embarrassments — Lieutenant Henderson in Cornwall; Boulton’s financial difficulties increase; the Soho pictures; Watt’s letter-copying machine; more Cornish engines wanted; engine-dues; Boulton organises the mining business; Boulton’s house at Cosgarne; the engine patent threatened by the Cornish men; the Birmingham Copper Company; Boulton improves engine-boilers by introducing tubes.
Chapter XII: Rotary Motion — The Patent Threatened — Watt again visits Cornwall; the crank-engine at Soho; theft of the invention; Smeaton and steam power; evasions of the engine patent; the Hornblowers’ engine; Watt’s new inventions; the rotary engine; Murdock’s sun-and-planet motion; patent taken for the reciprocating expansive engine.
Chapter XIII: Financial Position — Rotary Engines for Mills — (continued); Watt and Boulton’s financial consolidation; the rotary engine applied to mills; new partnerships and contracts.
Chapter XIV: Commercial Politics — Cornish Riots — Albion Mill — Boulton’s action in commercial politics; Watt on free commerce; combination against patents; the Cornish copper-miners; the Copper Company formed; riots in Cornwall; the Albion Mill scheme; the double-acting engines; Albion Mill burnt down; demand for rotative engines; Boulton’s health fails; his generosity to Watt.
Chapter XV: Friends of Boulton and Watt — The Lunar Society — The Lunar Society of Birmingham; its members — Erasmus Darwin, Priestley, Edgeworth, Wedgwood, Withering, Day, Keir, Galton, and others; the character of the society; its influence on science and industry; social and intellectual life in Birmingham.
Chapter XVI: [Soho Foundry and Later Works] — Establishment of the Soho Foundry; the firm’s expansion; the great engines for London waterworks; steamboat engines; Boulton’s retirement; Watt’s continuing experiments.
Chapter XVII: Prosperity of Soho — Murdock’s Gas-Lighting — Prosperity at Soho; the king’s visit to Windsor; young Boulton returns from Paris; the French Revolution; the Birmingham riots; Priestley’s house destroyed; unpopularity of the “Philosophers”; young Watt and the Jacobins; Watt’s flight from Paris; denounced by Burke; the sons join the partnership; legal proceedings; William Murdock’s services; Murdock invents gas-lighting; his various inventions; his death.
Chapter XVIII: Closing Years of Boulton and Watt — Boulton’s retirement and death (1809); Watt’s later years and continued activity; his inventions after the engine; the sculpturing machine; his death (1819); the national memorial in Westminster Abbey.
Chapter XIX: The Watt Relics — A tour through Watt’s workshop at Heathfield; his tools, lathe, and mechanical contrivances; the governor; the parallel motion; a model of his proposed calculating machine; the library and mathematical instruments; the enduring legacy.

Notes

Volume IV of Smiles’ five-volume series. Other volumes: I (Vermuyden, Myddelton, Perry, Brindley — embankments and canals), II (Smeaton and Rennie — harbours, lighthouses, bridges), III (Metcalfe and Telford — roads), V (George and Robert Stephenson — the locomotive).
Although Watt’s invention dates to the 1760s and Boulton’s Soho Manufactory to the 1760s, the partnership of Boulton and Watt (1775–1800) and the later years of both men extend into the first decades of the nineteenth century, making the volume relevant for understanding the industrial background of the period 1800–1865.
William Murdock’s invention of coal-gas lighting (c. 1792, installed at Soho c. 1802) is covered in detail.
The Lunar Society section provides insight into the intellectual circles that connected engineering with natural philosophy and political thought in late eighteenth- and early nineteenth-century Britain.

sources/smiles-locomotive-stephenson.title: Smiles — Lives of the Engineers: The Locomotive — George and Robert Stephenson
sources/smiles-locomotive-stephenson.content:
Smiles — Lives of the Engineers: The Locomotive — George and Robert Stephenson
Samuel Smiles (1812–1904) — Lives of the Engineers: The Locomotive — George and Robert Stephenson. — Good Press, 2022 (reprint of the 1882 edition).
A single volume from Smiles’ multi-volume Lives of the Engineers series, devoted entirely to the lives of George Stephenson (1781–1848) and his son Robert Stephenson (1803–1859), the two men most closely associated with the development of the railway locomotive and the early railway system. The book traces the Stephensons from their humble origins in the Northumberland coal-fields through their revolutionary improvements to the steam locomotive, the construction of the Stockton & Darlington and Liverpool & Manchester railways, and the extension of the railway system across Britain and the world. The introduction (dated from the 1857 first edition) surveys the extraordinary growth of railways in Britain, Europe, India, Canada, the United States, and the colonies in the decades following the opening of the Liverpool & Manchester Railway.
The text is 13,131 lines, extracted from the Good Press EPUB reproduction.
Content Summary


Introduction — a survey of railway progress from the 1850s to the 1880s: the growth of the British railway network (from 8,300 to 16,000 miles), the spread of railways across Europe (Mont Cenis and Brenner passes linking France and Italy with Germany), the construction of Indian railways (5,000 miles, uniting Bombay, Madras, and Calcutta), the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada and the Victoria Bridge, Australian and South African lines, the vast expansion of railways in the United States (from a few thousand to over 70,000 miles), the unexpected growth of passenger traffic, and the transformation of communication


Chapter I — Newcastle and the Great Northern Coal-Field — the topography and geology of the Tyne and Wear district; the early history of coal-mining in the north of England; the formation of the great northern coal-field and its importance to the region


Chapter II — Wylam and Dewley Burn — George Stephenson’s Early Years — George Stephenson born at Wylam in 1781; his family circumstances; his boyhood as a herd-boy and labourer; the poverty and hard conditions of the colliery districts; his early character and dawning interest in engines


Chapter III — Engineman at Willington Quay and Killingworth — Stephenson’s employment at various collieries; his work as a fireman and engineman; his marriage and early domestic life; his determination to master the principles of the steam engine


Chapter IV — The Stephensons at Killingworth — Education and Self-Education of Father and Son — the family’s removal to Killingworth; George Stephenson’s efforts to educate himself, learning to read and write as an adult; Robert’s schooling and early aptitude for mathematics and mechanics; the father’s determination that his son should have the education he himself lacked


Chapter V — Early History of the Locomotive — George Stephenson begins its Improvement — the early efforts at steam locomotion: Trevithick, Blenkinsop, and Hedley’s “Puffing Billy”; the imperfect state of the locomotive at the time Stephenson took it up; his first attempts at Killingworth to build a more effective engine


Chapter VI — Invention of the “Geordy” Safety-Lamp — the danger of firedamp in the northern coal-mines; the steps leading to the invention of the safety-lamp; the contemporaneous invention by Sir Humphry Davy; the controversy over priority; Stephenson’s character and conduct throughout the dispute


Chapter VII — George Stephenson’s further Improvements in the Locomotive — The Hetton Railway — Robert Stephenson as Viewer’s Apprentice and Student — the continued improvement of the Killingworth locomotive; the Hetton Railway, the first entirely locomotive-worked railway; Robert’s apprenticeship as a viewer and his studies at the University of Edinburgh


Chapter VIII — George Stephenson Engineer of the Stockton and Darlington Railway — the project of a railway between Stockton and Darlington; Stephenson appointed engineer; the survey and parliamentary struggle; the construction and opening in 1825; the first public railway to use locomotives for freight and passengers


Chapter IX — The Liverpool and Manchester Railway projected — the commercial necessity of a railway between Liverpool and Manchester; the opposition of canal and landed interests; Stephenson’s controversial survey; the parliamentary battle and the famous cross-examination by counsel; the eventual Act obtained


Chapter X — Chat Moss — Construction of the Railway — the engineering difficulties of crossing Chat Moss, a vast peat bog west of Manchester; Stephenson’s methods of draining and filling; the construction of the Olive Mount cutting and the Sankey viaduct; the execution and completion of the line


Chapter XI — Robert Stephenson’s Residence in Colombia, and Return — The Battle of the Locomotive — “The Rocket” — Robert’s three years in Colombia as a mining engineer; his return to England; the Rainhill Trials of 1829 and the competition for a locomotive for the Liverpool & Manchester line; the design and triumph of the “Rocket”; the decisive establishment of the locomotive as the motive power for railways


Chapter XII — Opening of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway, and Extension of the Railway System — the grand opening on 15 September 1830; the fatal accident to Mr. Huskisson; the immediate success of the railway; the rapid extension of the system; the locomotive adopted throughout the country; Stephenson’s role as engineer for numerous new lines


Chapter XIII — Robert Stephenson constructs the London and Birmingham Railway — the largest engineering work of its day; the survey and the opposition; the Kilsby Tunnel and the difficulties of its construction; the completion of the line and its opening in 1838; Robert Stephenson’s reputation established


Chapter XIV — Manchester and Leeds, and Midland Railways — Stephenson’s Life at Alton — Visit to Belgium — General Extension of Railways and their Results — George Stephenson’s semi-retirement at Tapton House, near Chesterfield; his engagement in coal-mining; the Manchester & Leeds and Midland lines; his visit to Belgium at the invitation of King Leopold; the general spread of railways through Europe


Chapter XV — George Stephenson’s Coal Mines — Appears at Mechanics’ Institutes — His Opinion on Railway Speeds — Atmospheric System — Railway Mania — Visits to Belgium and Spain — Stephenson’s coal-mining ventures at Tapton; his addresses to working men at mechanics’ institutes; his views on railway speeds (predicting 50 mph as the future limit); the brief trial of the atmospheric system; the Railway Mania of 1845–46; his later travels


Chapter XVI — Robert Stephenson’s Career — The Stephensons and Brunel — East Coast Route to Scotland — Royal Border Bridge, Berwick — High Level Bridge, Newcastle — the rivalry and friendship between the Stephensons and Brunel; Robert’s work on the East Coast main line; the Royal Border Bridge at Berwick and the High Level Bridge at Newcastle; his election as Member of Parliament


Chapter XVII — Robert Stephenson’s Tubular Bridges at Menai and Conway — the conception and construction of the Britannia Bridge across the Menai Strait and the Conway tubular bridge; the experiments on tubular girders; the novel engineering principle; the floating and raising of the tubes; the completion of both bridges


Chapter XVIII — George Stephenson’s Closing Years — Illness and Death — the last years at Tapton House; his declining health; his death in 1848; the public mourning and funeral; his character, habits, and achievements summarised


Chapter XIX — Robert Stephenson’s Victoria Bridge, Lower Canada — Illness and Death — Stephenson Characteristics — the Victoria Tubular Bridge across the St. Lawrence at Montreal; the difficulties of construction in the Canadian winter; the opening by the Prince of Wales in 1860; Robert’s final illness and death in 1859; the character and qualities of both father and son

Thomas Tooke’s monumental two-volume work on prices, currency, and the circulation forms the foundation of the nineteenth-century empirical study of the British economy. The work begins with a theoretical treatment of the forces affecting prices — seasons, war, and currency — and then presents a detailed historical chronicle from 1792 to 1837. Tooke was a leading figure in the Banking School of monetary theory and a key witness before Parliamentary committees on the currency.

The continuation of Tooke’s great work, now with William Newmarch as co-author. Volume III covers the years 1838–1839 in exhaustive detail — the corn trade, prices of other produce, the state of the circulation, and proposed currency reforms. Volume IV extends the chronological treatment through 1847, including a major historical review of the entire currency question from 1797 to the Bank Charter Act of 1844 and its operation through the crisis of 1847. The final volumes of the History of Prices, now entirely under William Newmarch’s authorship though still published under Tooke’s name. Volume V examines the domestic British economy during the nine years after the repeal of the Corn Laws — corn prices under free trade, general produce prices, the railway mania and its aftermath, the progress of free trade since the Merchants’ Petition of 1820, and the operation of Sir Robert Peel’s Bank Charter Act of 1844 through the commercial crises of 1847 and beyond. Volume VI (Parts VI–VII) shifts to international dimensions: the financial policy of France since 1848, the Bank of France and French credit institutions, and the great influx of precious metals from California and Australia (1848–1856). A comprehensive set of appendices and a General Index to all six volumes conclude the work.

sources/wakeman-church-of-england.content:
An Introduction to the History of the Church of England
Henry Offley Wakeman (Fellow of All Souls College, Tutor of Keble College, Oxford) offers a narrative interpretation of the development of the Church of England rather than a mere chronicle. His stated aim is to answer the question “How is it that the Church of England has come to be what she is?” by fixing attention on what has proved permanent and passing quickly over periods of interruption or deterioration.
The book is written from a High Church/Anglo-Catholic perspective, reflecting the Oxford Movement’s conception of the Church of England as a branch of the Catholic Church, reformed of medieval abuses but in continuous historical succession with the primitive and medieval Church.
Sources
Henry Offley Wakeman, An Introduction to the History of the Church of England, from the Earliest Times to the Present Day. Fifth edition. London: Rivingtons, 1898. OCLC 3084052.
The work includes prefaces to the first (September 1896), third (December 1896), and fifth (December 1897) editions. A chronological table (55 BC–1896) precedes the text, and an extensive index follows.
Text
raw/wakeman-church-england/wakeman-church-england.txt — 22,228 lines, ~1.15 MB. Extracted from the New York Public Library copy (NYPL 3 3433 07029946 0) via Anna’s Archive zip, with individual page text files concatenated in numerical order.
Contents
Chronological Table (55 BC–AD 1896)
A detailed timeline from Caesar’s first invasion of Britain through the planting of the Church in Roman Britain, the conversion of the English, the Danish invasions, the Norman Conquest, the Reformation, the Civil War, the Restoration, the Evangelical Revival, the Oxford Movement, and the ritual controversies of the late nineteenth century.
Chapter I — The Church in Britain, A.D. 200–597
Wakeman opens by acknowledging that no one knows precisely when Christianity first reached Britain, though passages in Tertullian and Origen, written between 208 and 240, make it probable that a church existed in the Roman province by the early third century. It may have arrived with Roman soldiers building the roads and camps that still inspire wonder, or more likely in the wake of wealthy Gallic civilians who built villas at Silchester and Verulam, bathed at Bath, or dined on oysters at Chichester and Canterbury. Whatever its origin, it left few traces — enough, however, to sketch a “fairly vivid picture” of an infant Church on the extreme edge of Roman civilisation.
This was a poor and struggling institution, “mainly of the poorer Roman provincials,” deriving its existence, ritual, and orders from its richer neighbour, the Church of Gaul. Over two centuries under the Roman eagles, it produced no great man, built no great building, endured no serious persecution, sent out no missionaries, and was obliged to appeal to Gaul for help in internal difficulties. At the Council of Ariminum in 359, the British bishops were the only ones who accepted the emperor’s expense allowance — a telling measure of their poverty. They could not even overcome the Pelagian heresy by themselves but had to summon Germanus of Auxerre and Lupus of Troyes from Gaul. Nevertheless, it was a duly organised branch of the Catholic Church, possessing bishops at London and York (and probably Lincoln), and sending representatives to the great councils of Arles (314), Ariminum (359), Nicaea (325), and Sardica (347). The proto-martyr S. Alban sealed his faith with his blood in 304 during the Diocletian persecution, though Wakeman wryly notes his martyrdom owed more to “his interference with the course of Roman justice than to his religious opinions.”
Wakeman then turns to the legends that poetry and later ages wove around these scanty facts — S. Paul as apostle of the Britons, Bran the Blessed bringing Christianity from Rome, and above all the beautiful medieval romance of Joseph of Arimathea at Glastonbury, bearing the Holy Grail and planting a staff that burst into thorny blossom each Christmas. These legends, however touching, have “no foundation in fact.” Genuine religious revival came only with the closing years of the fourth century: S. Ninian’s mission in 397 and his stone church at Whithern in Galloway; the anti-Pelagian mission of Germanus and Lupus; and S. Patrick’s labours in Ireland. A new Church grew up in the fifth and sixth centuries, “loose and ill-jointed in organisation and government” but “instinct with personal holiness, inspired by missionary zeal, and imbued with a passion for learning.”
This was the Church that faced the Saxon and English heathen pirates from 449 onward. The Celtic Church could not rise to the task of converting its conquerors; it shrank back into the fastnesses of Welsh and Cornish hills, and over five-sixths of England the worship of Christ gave way to Woden, Freia, and Thor — a fact still stamped on the days of the English week. Only in the unconquered Celtic west and across the water in Ireland did the faith survive, while at Iona the great missionary college of Columba was already founded. The chapter closes with a turning point: the marriage of the Kentish king Æthelbert to Bertha, daughter of the Christian king of Paris, who brought with her the Frankish bishop Luidhard and restored the ancient church of S. Martin at Canterbury. Their presence paved the way, but the initiative for conversion came not from Gaul but from “distant Rome under the humble cowl of a monk.”
Chapter II — The Conversion of the English, A.D. 597–655
The story begins with a famous encounter: in 585, Gregory, abbot of a monastery on the Caelian Hill, saw Northumbrian slave-boys in the Roman market — their “white skins, blue eyes, and flaxen hair” so moved him that he sought permission to missionise the heathen English. His fellow-citizens refused to let him go. Years later, as pope, he could command rather than ask. He chose Augustine, prior of his own monastery, to lead the mission. In 596 the little band set out, but at Aix in Provence they were struck with “sluggish fear” and sent Augustine back. Gregory would not hear of retreat; arming Augustine with abbatial authority and smoothing his path with letters, he drove them forward. In the spring of 597, Augustine landed at Ebbsfleet in Thanet — the very spot where Hengest’s Jutes had first landed 150 years earlier on an errand of “conquest and rapine.”
The meeting with King Æthelbert was staged with memorable theatre: the king sat in the open air under a tree, Teutonic fashion, while a procession of forty men approached chanting litanies, bearing a silver cross and a painted image of Christ Crucified. Augustine, towering over his companions, set forth in simple words “how the tender-hearted Jesus by His own throes had redeemed the sinful world.” The king, a statesman already familiar with Christianity through his wife Bertha, promised protection but refused to convert without more thought. Converts came nonetheless, and by summer Æthelbert himself offered for baptism. Augustine was consecrated archbishop of the English at Arles on 16 November 597, and with that the infant Church of England began.
He established his cathedral in an old Roman church at Canterbury, rebuilding it on the model of S. Peter’s on the Vatican — Christ Church, still the mother church of English Christianity. Outside the walls rose the beginnings of what would become the rich monastery of S. Augustine. Gregory sent reinforcements in 601 — Mellitus, Justus, and Paulinus — along with a pall, that “narrow strip of white woollen material” whose symbolic meaning later tangled English churchmen in questions of papal authority. Gregory’s grand scheme for two archiepiscopal provinces at London and York, each with twelve suffragans, was never realised; stubborn paganism kept the southern see at Canterbury, and the northern province took centuries to gain real weight.
The great missed opportunity was the union with the Celtic Church. Augustine met the Welsh bishops under an oak in 603, demanding they accept Roman customs — the date of Easter, the tonsure, the rite of baptism. The Celts, whose Church had developed wholly apart from Rome and was sending missionaries from Ireland to Burgundy and Switzerland, would not surrender their ancient customs. The conference broke up “amid hot recriminations,” and both sides suffered. Augustine died in 604, having founded the sees of London and Rochester but little more. His work, though narrow, was solid: “nothing that Augustine did had to be undone.”
After his death came crisis. The pagan reaction under Eadbald (who relapsed into heathenism on Æthelbert’s death) was short-lived, and in 625 Paulinus was consecrated missionary bishop for Northumbria, accompanying the princess Æthelburga to her marriage with King Eadwine. The great gemot at Godmundingham in 627 is one of English history’s most famous scenes: the cynicism of Coifi the high priest, the thegnly parable of the sparrow flying through the lighted hall from darkness to darkness, and Eadwine’s baptism on Easter eve. For six years Paulinus evangelised on foot, a gaunt stooping figure with piercing eyes and long raven hair, baptising by the hundred.
Then came Penda of Mercia, the heathen champion who defeated and killed Eadwine at Heathfield in 633. Paulinus fled to Kent, and for a moment Christianity in the north seemed doomed. But Oswald, a nephew of Eadwine educated at Iona, defeated the Celtic king Cadwallon at Heaven-field in 635 and summoned a new bishop from the Scottish monastery. The first monk sent returned discouraged, but a voice cried out from the brethren: “Was it their stubbornness or your severity? Did you forget the apostle’s command to feed them first with milk and then with meat?” That speaker was Aidan, and he was at once acclaimed bishop.
Wakeman draws a masterful contrast: Roman Christianity was the civitas Dei — law, order, territorial organisation — capable of governing but inclined to confine. Irish Christianity was ascetic, personal, monastic, capable of winning souls but not of building institutions. The combination of both was needed. Aidan himself is drawn with evident love — a “second Francis of Assisi,” embracing holy poverty, travelling on foot, founding Lindisfarne as a second Iona, training twelve picked boys, and working in perfect harmony with the king-saint Oswald. Aidan died in 651, his heart broken by the murder of his friend Oswin. Four years later, at the Battle of Winwaed (655), Oswiu defeated and killed Penda. “The Church was everywhere victorious. At once she began to occupy the vacant country.”
Chapter III — The Organisation of the Early English Church, A.D. 655–735
With heathenism defeated, the Church faced a new challenge: unity and organisation.
