The Tracts for the Times, 1833–1840 — The first tract appeared in September 1833, short papers dealing with definite points of Church doctrine and practice. The leading idea: to justify the sacramental side of the Church’s life. The revival of the nineteenth century was to be anti-individualistic, based on the Incarnate Life of our Lord continued through the Church and Sacraments. The power given to all mankind to become the sons of God through His spouse the Church was the leading principle of the revival. The tracts brought men face to face with questions long forgotten: “What is the Church? Has she divine credentials? Has she inestimable privileges at her disposal?”
Accession of Dr. Pusey, 1834 — Pusey, Professor of Hebrew at Oxford and Canon of Christ Church, “the most venerated man in Oxford,” threw the weight of his profound learning into the scale. A character lofty in its ideals and stern even to asceticism. At a university “real profundity of learning and strength of character will always meet with respectful recognition.” Forty-six tracts published in 1833 and 1834. The collected volume with Newman’s introduction spread the doctrines among all the parsonages in England. Success among younger men at Oxford was most marked. Newman’s afternoon sermons at St. Mary’s — severe in tone, searching in thought, insisting upon conduct as the evidence of faith — made the movement recognised as a great effort after moral perfection.
The Hampden controversy, 1835 — The ill-judged appointment of Dr. Hampden as Regius Professor of Divinity united the university against the government. Hampden had laid down principles in his Bampton Lectures that seemed subversive of the Christian faith. The Tractarians, as the most earnest and able of Oxford theologians, appeared as leaders of a united university in protest.
Leadership of Newman, 1835–1841 — Insensibly Newman stood out as the real leader. It was round his personality that the younger men gathered. His quick intellect gauged the trend of thought and saw what positions needed fortifying.
The Roman controversy and the Via Media, 1836 — Newman was obliged to deal with the Roman controversy. The claim of the Church of England to be the true Catholic Church was met by the more imposing claims of Rome. Newman’s Lectures on Romanism and Popular Protestantism enunciated the theory of the Via Media: the Church has lost its unity of government but below the surface there is real unity — a unity of faith in the creeds, of liturgical worship, of apostolic episcopate. The surface is broken into three great pieces owing allegiance to Rome, Constantinople, and Canterbury. The duty of English Churchmen is to vindicate the true character of their Church, trusting that her central position between Rome and Protestantism, especially with the world-wide extension of the Anglo-Saxon race, might make her “the pivot round which the ultimate reunion of Christians would turn.” At the time (1837) the theory met the strongest opposition from the popular religion of the day. In 1839, while studying the Monophysite question, a “terrible doubt” came to Newman: was the parallel between the Monophysite and Anglican positions too close to be agreeable? He recovered his equilibrium and prepared Tract XC.
Tract XC and the storm, 1841–1845 — The publication of Tract XC was the turning-point. Newman subjected the Thirty-Nine Articles to a severe analysis to ascertain the irreducible minimum of statement against Roman doctrine to which subscribers could be legally bound. His argument: no Catholic doctrine, and hardly any theological Roman doctrine, was condemned by the Articles — only popular exaggerations current when the Articles were drawn up. All Protestantism flew to arms. The Heads of Houses condemned the tract as a dishonest evasion. The issue of the tracts was stopped at the request of the Bishop of Oxford. Bishop after bishop condemned them in their charges. Newman bowed to the storm and withdrew to Littlemore.
The Roman party — W. G. Ward of Balliol, combining extraordinary dialectical skill and love of paradox with boisterous capacity for fun, threw himself into the fray with more zeal than discretion. He boldly claimed the right to hold all Roman doctrine and remain in the Church of England. He became the centre of Faber, Dalgairns, Morris, Oakeley — men with little affection for the Church of England, powerfully attracted by the logical system of Rome. A rift appeared: Ward’s party drifting Romewards, Keble and Pusey’s remaining firmly Anglican.
Newman’s secession, 1845 — The doubt from the Donatist controversy returned and did not pass away. The Jerusalem bishopric scheme (1841) — a joint bishopric with Prussian Lutherans — seemed to demonstrate hopeless want of principle. Pusey’s unjust suspension for preaching a sermon on the Eucharist (1843). Ward’s condemnation by the university (1844). The knowledge that only the veto of the proctors prevented Newman’s own condemnation. In the summer of 1845 Ward, Dalgairns, Faber, Oakeley, and Christie seceded. In October the long-impending blow fell: “Newman was lost to a communion, the vitality and truth of which he had done more than any man to prove.”
The widening of the movement into a general High Church revival, 1845–1865 — The catastrophe of 1845 shattered the Tractarian party but did not stop the Oxford movement. The staunch fidelity of Pusey, Keble, Isaac Williams, J. B. Mozley, and Dean Church reassured the timid. The movement changed character: it lost its intellectual and academical stamp, ceased to be concentrated round a few persons at Oxford, became less argumentative and more occupied with practical Church work and the training of souls. Men like Dr. Hook at Leeds, Gladstone in Parliament, Roundell Palmer at the bar, Justice Coleridge on the bench, though not wholly accepting all Tractarian teaching, threw themselves into the work of spreading its principles. The Guardian newspaper was started in 1846. Samuel Wilberforce as Bishop of Oxford began to organise his diocese and set an example of episcopal activity possible only in one who believed strongly in episcopacy and the Church. Churches were cleaned, services multiplied and made brighter with music. The Eucharist was celebrated more frequently and with greater reverence. Devotional meetings for clergy were held. New parishes were formed, new churches built and endowed. The rising appreciation of Gothic art was pressed into the service of the Church.
Church reform and the Ecclesiastical Commission, 1836–1850 — The Church Discipline Act of 1840 introduced simpler procedure into ecclesiastical courts. The Ecclesiastical Commission of 1836 fixed and equalised episcopal and capitular incomes, freeing funds for new parishes and poor benefices. Legal obstacles to colonial bishoprics were removed: Selwyn to New Zealand (1841), Gray to South Africa (1847), Broughton to Australia (1836). In 1850 Convocation was finally permitted to meet regularly — the wrong of 1717 redressed.
The Gorham case, 1850 — The Privy Council’s decision in the Gorham case was understood to declare that the Church of England did not teach baptismal regeneration. A fresh batch of secessions followed, including that of Archdeacon Manning. Wakeman’s analysis: the court had not gone that length, and if it had, it was only a parliamentary court with no authority to bind conscience in matters of faith. The trend of affairs more than the facts of the case brought about crucial decisions.
Difficulties of the High Church revival — Englishmen became possessed with the belief that every attempt to raise the Church above customary tradition was a step towards popery. High Churchmen lived in an atmosphere of suspicion. The revival of carved figures, the symbol of the cross in decoration, coloured altar frontals — all denounced as disloyal. The wearing of the surplice in the pulpit instead of a black gown caused disgraceful riots in different parts of the country.
The Eucharistic controversy, 1856–1871 — Opposition centred upon efforts to surround the Holy Communion with dignity and splendour. The doctrine of the Real Presence had never died out but had ceased to influence official theology. Dr. Pusey devoted his massive learning to its vindication. In 1856 proceedings against Archdeacon Denison of Taunton for two sermons on the subject; the condemnation was set aside as irregular. In 1871 the Rev. W. J. E. Bennett was attacked for unguarded language on the Real Presence; both the ecclesiastical court and the Privy Council found his language not punishable as inconsistent with the formularies.
The Ritualist prosecutions, 1850s–1890s — After the Bennett decision, it became clear that prosecuting High Churchmen for heresy was useless; it was easier to punish them as law-breakers for ceremonial. The ornaments rubric was invoked to justify Eucharistic vestments and other ceremonial. Bishops, mostly Evangelicals or Latitudinarians, declared war on ceremonial. A series of Privy Council decisions in every point adverse to the High Church party followed. Many decisions were based on historical blunders later exposed by scholarship. Archbishop Tait’s Public Worship Regulation Act (1874) established a new parliamentary court. Conscientious clergy refused to acknowledge it. Five were actually imprisoned. The scandal of sending clergy to prison for refusing to acknowledge the State’s right to enforce decisions in matters of faith became unbearable. Tait himself saw his mistake; on his deathbed in 1882 he left a legacy of peace and toleration. The Lincoln Judgment (1892) reconsidered and partially overruled earlier decisions. Since then no fresh ritual prosecution occurred.
The Church’s defence of the faith — The Church’s response to mid-century intellectual challenges: the scientific spirit, the critical study of other religions, the higher criticism of the Bible, the utilitarian spirit. The Cambridge school of biblical scholars and the Oxford school of historians provided the defence. Wakeman’s conclusion: future investigation is unlikely to impair the conclusions of the Cambridge school on the authenticity of early Christian documents, or the evidence for the Church’s regenerating influence brought into prominence by the Oxford historians.
Estimate of the High Church revival — The High Church revival brought to English religious life “largeness of view.” It sought to take the whole of man — intellectual, moral, aesthetic, social, as well as spiritual and humanitarian. It restored the true conception of the Church, laid the basis of Church order on historical fact, claimed the witness of the ages for its defence. It welcomed knowledge from whatever quarter as a further revelation of the mind of God. It consecrated the beautiful and ennobling in the arts. Wakeman’s historical judgment: the Church revival of the nineteenth century is seen to be “nothing more than the complete reaction against the Protestant movement of the sixteenth century” — a reaction that began with Hooker and Bancroft, was developed by Andrewes and Laud and Jeremy Taylor, and reached its full expression in the Oxford Movement.
Notes C, D, E
Three special notes following the text:

C. The Eucharistic Controversy — More detailed treatment of the doctrinal disputes over the Eucharist in the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries.
D. The Royal Supremacy — The historical and legal development of the Crown’s authority over the Church.
E. English Orders — The question of the validity of Anglican holy orders, written with the assistance of the Rev. F. E. Brightman of Pusey House.

Index
A comprehensive alphabetical index covering persons, places, events, doctrines, and institutions from the entire work.

sources/walpole-history-of-england-vol4.title: A History of England from the Conclusion of the Great War in 1815, Vol. IV
sources/walpole-history-of-england-vol4.content:
A History of England from the Conclusion of the Great War in 1815, Vol. IV — by Spencer Walpole
Vol. IV covers domestic history from the fall of the Whig Ministry (1841) to the triumph of Free Trade (1853), and foreign affairs to the Peace of Paris (1856). The volume contains six chapters (XVII–XXII) and continues the numbering from Vol. III.

CHAPTER XVII — The Effects of the Reform Act of 1832 (text starts line 1565)
Period: c. 1833–1841 (the post-Reform decade)
Walpole opens this volume with a sweeping reflection on the Reformed Parliament a decade after the Reform Act of 1832. He examines whether the fears of Tories and the hopes of Radicals had been fulfilled, concluding that both had been equally disappointed. The convulsion of 1832 subsided quickly; reformed Parliaments were not revolutionary. The characteristic features of the reformed House of Commons included: longer debates (the House sat 1,270 hours in 1833 vs. under 1,000 before reform), multiplication of Parliamentary papers (252 volumes in 1825–32 vs. 400 volumes in 1833–41), increased petitions (from 5,000 to 20,000 per year), and procedural reforms to limit debate on petitions.
Walpole provides a statistical tour of the period: Hansard swelled from 52 volumes for 1820–1830 (Series 2) to 59 volumes for 1830–1841 (Series 3). He discusses oratory in the reformed House — Peel, Russell, Stanley, Macaulay, O’Connell — and the changes in Parliamentary manners and private business. The chapter then broadens into the economic and social conditions of the time: extravagant speculations, joint-stock banks, limited liability, the commercial crisis of 1836, the general fall in prices after 1815, the distress of the working classes, the abject poverty aggravated by the Corn Laws, and the prevalence of disease in the slums.
Walpole describes the Poor Law of 1834 and the fierce agitation against it (Tory rural paternalism vs. Liberal Malthusianism), the rise of Robert Owen and his New Lanark model, Chartism in all its phases (the Charter, People’s Charter, Bull Ring riots, Newport march, Frost trial), and the Corn Law agitation. He examines the humanitarian reforms of the decade: mitigation of the criminal code, prohibition of dogs drawing carts (a reform for animal welfare inspired by Martin’s Act), prison reform, transportation reform (the probation system of 1842, modified 1847, abandoned), counsel for prisoners, abolition of imprisonment for debt, the soldier’s and sailor’s lot (distribution of medals and prize money, flogging, press gang abandoned). The chapter closes with a reflection on duelling — the decline from Lord Cardigan and Captain Tuckett’s affair through the legal and social repression of the duel — and a summary of the general characteristics of the period: “perhaps the most remarkable decade in English history” for humanitarian progress.

CHAPTER XVIII — The Formation of Peel’s Second Administration (text starts line 7598)
Period: 1841–1845
Walpole details Peel’s return to power in 1841, the difficulties he faced, and his first measures. The session of 1842 saw the renewal of the Income Tax (a temporary measure to cover the deficit), the relaxation of Protection, and the first of Gladstone’s budgets at the Board of Trade. Debates on the Budget revealed the growing divide between Protectionists and Free Traders.
The distress of the people in 1842 — strikes, the summer’s effects on prices, shrinking revenue — forced Peel to defend his policies against Tory attack (the Canada Corn Bill) and Liberal assault. Peel’s successive budgets (1842, 1843, 1844) show the gradual conversion to free trade. The conversion of Three-and-a-Half Per Cent. Stock, the alteration of Sugar Duties, and the pivotal Bank Charter Act of 1844 are examined in detail.
Walpole provides a history of banking in Great Britain: joint-stock banks, the Committee of 1836 on banking, the crisis of 1836, Peel’s views on banking, the Bank Charter Act (separating Issue and Banking Departments), the Act of 1845 for Ireland and Scotland, and the purging of the tariff (glass, auction duty, cotton, wool, sugar). The chapter documents Disraeli’s first attacks on Peel and the increasing distrust of the Prime Minister within his own party.
The second half of the chapter turns to infrastructure and invention: the railway mania and its consequences, the development of steam at sea, the tool-makers of the nineteenth century, the democratic effects of steam power, and the electric telegraph (from Thales and the Leyden jar through Galvani, Volta, Oersted, Ampère, and Faraday to the commercial telegraph). Walpole then returns to Ireland — the Poor Laws, bastardy, settlement, the employment of women and children in mines, the Factory Bill of 1843, the Factory Act of 1844, and the Ten-Hours Clause.

CHAPTER XIX — Ireland (text starts line 12926)
Period: 1841–1846
A focused chapter on Ireland, examining the English and Irish views of the Irish Question, the characteristics of English legislation towards Ireland, and the consequences of Catholic Emancipation. O’Connell’s Repeal Association, the “monster meetings,” the treatment of O’Connell in London, and the poverty of the Irish people — attributed to population increase, the absence of coal, the Relief Act of 1793, the potato, and absentee landlords.
Walpole covers the disfranchisement of the 40s. freeholders, the revival of Repeal agitation in 1842, the doctrine of nationality, Father Mathew’s temperance crusade, Peel’s Irish policy (Sugden and the Irish magistrates, the Arms Bill, coercion), Smith O’Brien, the prohibition of the Clontarf meeting, O’Connell’s trial and conviction (reversed by the Lords on a technicality), O’Connell’s death and character.
Peel’s constructive Irish measures: Irish railways, Charitable Bequests Act, changes in Irish government, and the Maynooth Grant. The chapter describes the anger of the country at the increased grant to Maynooth and Gladstone’s resignation over the issue. Middle-class education in Ireland, the Devon Commission on land tenure, Stanley’s abortive Irish Land Bill of 1845 (withdrawn in the Lords). The potato disease of 1845, its consequences, Peel’s conversion to repeal of the Corn Laws, the Cabinet meeting, the Edinburgh Letter, Peel’s resignation, Russell’s failure to form a ministry, Peel’s resumption of office, the mutiny of the Dukes, the fury of the Protectionists (led by Lord George Bentinck), obstruction in the House of Commons, the passage of the Corn Bill, and ultimately Peel’s fall.

CHAPTER XX — The Formation of the Russell Administration (text starts line 17368)
Period: 1846–1852
Russell’s administration formed June 1846. Its composition, the alteration of Sugar Duties, and the condition of Ireland form the opening. The Famine: measures for dealing with it, their failure, the discontinuance of relief works, the organisation of relief committees. The Famine in Western Scotland and the Western Highlands. The Irish Poor Law, the Encumbered Estates Act, and Bentinck’s proposal for assisting Irish Railways.
The Budget of 1847, the dissolution of Parliament, and the Commercial Crisis of 1847 — the Bank Charter suspended. Renewed outrages in Ireland, fresh Coercion measures, Somerville’s Irish Land Bill. The chapter then shifts to the European Revolutions of 1848: Smith O’Brien’s abortive rising in Ireland, suspension of Habeas Corpus, the rebellion’s collapse. Chartism in 1848: Feargus O’Connor, the collapse of the Chartist movement.
The financial and legislative history of 1848: the Panic of 1848, four successive budgets, the Disabilities of the Jews, Disraeli becoming leader of the Protectionist Party, Bentinck and the Sugar Duties. Returning prosperity, the state of Ireland in 1849 (the Battle of Dolly’s Brae, the Queen’s visit), the Rate in Aid Bill, the Irish Poor Law Amendment Bill, differences between Lords and Commons.
The Navigation Acts — their repeal in 1849. Agricultural distress in England, the Budget of 1850, Peel’s support of the ministry, and Peel’s death (after a fall from his horse on Constitution Hill). Walpole’s assessment of Peel’s character closes the chapter.

CHAPTER XXI — Religious Movements (text starts line 22525)
Period: c. 1800–1850
A thematic chapter surveying the religious history of the nineteenth century. Walpole opens with the functions of history and traces the religious movement to pre-existing causes. The effects of the Reformation comparable to Constantine’s conversion — Christianity and Paganism, Milton and Homer. The growth of doubt as the chief consequence of the Reformation, the rise of Rationalism, Galileo, the telescope enlarging man’s ideas of space, Kepler and Newton, Descartes, doubt and Deism in the eighteenth century.
The Church of the eighteenth century, the effects of the French Revolution on religion, jealousy of Rome in England, the Bible Society, geology’s challenge to Scripture (the attack on the Establishment).
Walpole then examines the parties within the Church: the Party of Resistance and the Party of Reform. The Ecclesiastical Policy of Peel: the wealth of the Church and its unequal distribution, the Bishops and their patronage, non-residence, the Ecclesiastical Commission, pluralities, the Ecclesiastical Courts, Church discipline, the Nonconformists, the Universities, Church Rates (the Braintree Case), Unitarian Chapels, the controversy between Freethought and Religion.
The Oxford Movement: Oriel College, Newman, Richard Hurrell Froude, Wilberforce, the origin of the movement, Keble’s Assize Sermon (1833), the Tractarians, Tract XC and its condemnation, the Jerusalem Bishopric, Ward’s “Ideal of a Christian Church,” Pusey, the secession to Rome, excitement and agitation in the country. The Broad Church: Hampden — his appointment as Regius Professor and as Bishop of Hereford, the Gorham Judgment, the Durham Letter (Russell’s response to Papal Aggression). Convocation. General effects of the Oxford Movement: the observance of Sunday, Sunday travelling, Sunday letters, theatres in Lent.
The Scottish Disruption: The resemblance between the Ten Years’ Conflict in Scotland and the Tractarian Movement — the history of the Reformation in Scotland, the claim of the Scotch Church, Episcopacy in Scotland, patronage, persecution, scepticism, the Act of 1712, Robertson and Chalmers. Chalmers’ views on pluralities, the effect of the Reform Act, the Call, the Veto, the Chapel Act, the Auchterarder Case, Aberdeen’s Non-Intrusion Bill, the Marnoch Case, the Duke of Argyll’s Bill, the change of ministry in 1841, the Claim, Declaration, and Protest, and the Secession of 1843. Walpole closes with the connection between the Tractarian and Disruption controversies, noting that the Scotch Movement was marked by greater earnestness.

CHAPTER XXII — Foreign Affairs (text starts line 28047)
Period: 1841–1856
Walpole surveys Britain’s foreign relations from Aberdeen’s tenure at the Foreign Office (1841–1846) through Palmerston’s return (1846–1851). The United States: the boundary dispute and the award of the King of the Netherlands (rejected by the US and ultimately by England), the arrest and release of Greely, the Caroline affair, McLeod’s Case, the Right of Search, Palmerston succeeded by Aberdeen, Lord Ashburton’s Mission, the Ashburton Treaty (1842), the Oregon Dispute.
France: the Tahiti Incident — Thouars and Queen Pomare, Thouars’ action ratified by France, Pritchard restores Pomare’s authority, the annexation of the Society Islands, Pritchard’s arrest, excitement in England, the settlement. Algiers — French ill-success in Morocco, the bombardment of Tangiers, the Entente Cordiale.
Spain and the Spanish Marriages: The mission of M. de Salvandy, the British Minister at Madrid, the candidates for the Queen’s hand, Bulwer and Bresson, Guizot’s Memorandum of 27th February, Aberdeen’s Despatch of 22nd June, Palmerston’s return and his Despatch of 19th July, the marriages celebrated. Cracow and its annexation to Austria. Portugal: the revolt of 1846, Saldanha’s coup d’état, Wylde’s Mission, Dom Miguel, Palmerston’s offer to interfere.
Switzerland: the Jesuits, the Sonderbund, the victory of the Diet. Italy: the Election of Pius IX, his liberal policy disliked by Metternich but supported by Palmerston, Lord Minto’s Mission, disturbances at Milan.
The Revolutions of 1848: the fall of Louis Philippe — reform in France, the political banquet forbidden, Lamartine, the February Revolution, the fall of Guizot, Bugeaud in command, the abdication, the provisional government, the flight of Louis Philippe. Effects of the Revolution in England and in Austria and Italy. Austria’s overtures to England, Italy’s difficulties, the Reconquest of Lombardy by Austria, Piedmont’s appeal to France, British and French mediation.
The Hungarian Revolution: Revolution in Hungary, Magyar and Slavonic jealousy, the second Revolution in Vienna, the accession of Francis Joseph, increasing excitement in Italy (war resumed), Palmerston’s Italian Policy, Russia interferes in Hungary, the Hungarians defeated, Palmerston’s policy towards Hungary, Austrian reprisals. Hungarian refugees in Turkey, the demand for their extradition. Greece: the Greek Revolution of 1843, Mr. Finlay’s Claim, other claims, Don Pacifico, the British fleet sent to Greece, its operations, the mediation of France, the renewal of coercive measures and their success, Drouyn de Lhuys recalled. The Lords censure Palmerston, the Commons approve his policy. The Great Exhibition closes the volume.

sources/walpole-history-of-england-vol5.title: A History of England from the Conclusion of the Great War in 1815, Vol. V
sources/walpole-history-of-england-vol5.content:
A History of England from the Conclusion of the Great War in 1815, Vol. V — by Spencer Walpole
Vol. V covers the period 1850–1878, continuing from Vol. IV. The volume contains six chapters (XXIII–XXVIII), combining domestic political narrative, foreign affairs, the Crimean War, India, and the colonies.

CHAPTER XXIII — 1850–1852 (text starts line 1264)
Domestic political crisis, Papal Aggression, and the fall of Russell
Circumstances in 1850 had strengthened the Whig ministry: Palmerston’s bold foreign policy was popular in the country, and Peel’s accidental death (from a fall from his horse) removed the only Conservative leader who might have threatened Russell. Yet the session brought new storms.
Papal Aggression (1850): In the autumn of 1850, Pope Pius IX issued a Bull restoring the Roman Catholic hierarchy in England, dividing the country into territorial dioceses with English bishops holding their titles from English sees. The public reacted with fury. Lord John Russell’s “Durham letter” denounced the measure as “an insolent and insidious attack” on the Protestant establishment. The government introduced the Ecclesiastical Titles Bill (1851), prohibiting Roman Catholic prelates from assuming territorial titles — though the Act was never seriously enforced and became a dead letter.
Ministerial Crisis of 1851: Russell’s government was defeated on the county franchise question. Russell resigned; Lord Stanley (the future Earl of Derby) tried but failed to form a ministry; Lord Lansdowne declined. Russell was compelled to resume office, weakened and with diminished prestige.
Palmerston’s Dismissal (December 1851): Palmerston, as Foreign Secretary, had long acted independently of Cabinet control. When Louis Napoleon’s coup d’état of 2 December 1851 occurred in France, Palmerston expressed approval to the French ambassador without consulting the Queen or the Prime Minister. Russell dismissed him — a step the Queen had long desired. Palmerston retaliated in the following session by moving an amendment to the Militia Bill, defeating the government and bringing down Russell’s ministry.
Lord Derby’s First Ministry (February–December 1852): Derby became Prime Minister with Disraeli as Chancellor of the Exchequer and Leader of the House of Commons. The Duke of Wellington died in September 1852. Parliament was dissolved; the new House saw a bitter contest over Disraeli’s Budget. Disraeli’s proposed increase in the House Duty and changes to the Income Tax were attacked from all sides. Gladstone delivered a devastating reply. The government was defeated and resigned.
Aberdeen’s Coalition Ministry (December 1852): A coalition of Peelties and Whigs under Lord Aberdeen. Gladstone’s first Budget (1853) extended the Income Tax for seven years for gradual abolition, reduced duties on 133 articles, and proposed the extension of the Succession Duty to real property (settling the battle with the landed interest that had raged since 1851). The Budget was received with extraordinary enthusiasm.

CHAPTER XXIV — The Crimean War (text starts line 6123)
Period: 1853–1856
Walpole’s account of the Crimean War is notable for its scepticism. He begins with the Russian Empire’s perennial drive toward the Bosphorus — the vast power “which frowns over Eastern Europe” with difficult access to the ocean. The Ottoman Empire was weak and corrupt, “encamped for centuries on the soil of the rich provinces.”
Origins: The war began in a dispute over the Holy Places in Palestine — Roman Catholic vs. Greek Orthodox claims to the custody of Christian shrines. Napoleon III, seeking prestige, asserted French claims; the Czar Nicholas I countered with Russia’s right under the Treaty of Kainardji (1774) to protect Orthodox Christians in the Ottoman Empire.
Menschikoff’s Mission (February 1853): Prince Menschikoff was sent to Constantinople as special envoy. He demanded a sened (imperial decree) and a treaty recognising Russia’s protectorate over Orthodox Christians. The British Ambassador, Lord Stratford de Redcliffe (Stratford Canning), counselled the Porte to reject these demands. The Czar ordered the occupation of the Danubian Principalities (Moldavia and Wallachia) in July 1853.
The Vienna Note: The four Powers (Austria, France, Prussia, Britain) drafted a compromise — the Vienna Note. Russia accepted it; the Porte, on Stratford’s advice, rejected it. Walpole is sharply critical of Stratford, arguing he “fulfilled his instructions to the letter, but he so contrived that his employers were constantly getting deeper into a war policy.”
War: The Turkish fleet was destroyed at Sinope (November 1853). Britain and France declared war in March 1854. The allied armies landed in the Crimea in September 1854. Battles of the Alma, Balaclava (the Charge of the Light Brigade), and Inkerman. The Siege of Sebastopol (winter of 1854–55, with its terrible suffering from cold, disease, and mismanagement). The death of Lord Raglan (June 1855). The fall of Sebastopol (September 1855).
Peace: Austria’s intervention; the Congress of Paris (March 1856). The Treaty neutralised the Black Sea, guaranteed the integrity of the Ottoman Empire, and opened the Danube to free navigation. Walpole’s famous verdict: the war’s result was “setting back the clock for some fourteen years.”

CHAPTER XXV — The Supremacy of the British in India (text starts line 10870)
Period: c. 1750–1835
A long historical survey of British India from the earliest East India Company adventurers through the Governors-General up to 1835. Walpole argues that the story of British India is “the most thrilling story in British history,” yet one that “has never been told by a competent writer.”
From trade to empire: The first object of the early adventurers was trade, not conquest. Rival European powers in India (French and English competition extended to India), both combatants seeking native help. The condition of the Native States. The Company’s servants in India and its Directors at home. The monopoly of Indian trade destroyed.
Governors-General: Lord Cornwallis (permanent settlement of Bengal), Sir John Shore, Lord Wellesley (subsidiary system, war with Tippoo Sultan, the Nabob of the Carnatic), Zemaun Shah, Wellesley’s treatment of Oudh. The Mahrattas: Scindia, Holkar, the first Mahratta War, the war of 1804 with Holkar, the retreat of Monson, the siege of Bhurtpore. Wellesley’s operations disapproved in England; he was superseded by Cornwallis (who died soon after arrival).
Lord Minto (north-western frontier policy), Lord Moira (Marquess of Hastings — the Nepaulese War, the Pindarees, the third Mahratta War, the results of the war, the cholera). Lord Amherst (the first Burmese War, Bhurtpore), Lord William Bentinck (Batta, abolition of suttee, suppression of thuggee, assessment in the North-West, flogging in the Indian army).

CHAPTER XXVI — Afghanistan, Scinde, and the Punjab (text starts line 16486)
Period: 1835–1849
Bentinck resigns (1835); Metcalfe temporarily succeeds. The press in India under Wellesley, Hastings, and Adam; Silk Buckingham’s case; Metcalfe and Macaulay establish a free press. Education. Lord Heytesbury appointed but not sent; Lord Auckland made Governor-General.
The Afghan Disaster: Russian influence in Persia, the Euphrates route to India, the siege of Herat by Persia, Alexander Burnes at Cabul, Vicovitch’s mission, Auckland at Simla and his decision to dethrone Dost Mahommed, Macnaghten’s mission to Lahore, the Tripartite Treaty (June 1838), the Proclamation of 1st October 1838. The advance of the Army of the Indus, the fall of Ghuznee, the occupation of Cabul, the unpopularity of the war in England. The Russian expedition to Khiva, the surrender of Dost Mahommed. Macnaghten succeeded by Burnes, Cotton by Elphinstone. The cantonments, the effects of retrenchment, the rising (November 1841), the murder of Burnes and Macnaghten, the disastrous retreat from Cabul (January 1842), the annihilation of the army. Sale’s defence of Jellalabad, Pollock’s advance, the relief of the prisoners, the destruction of the bazaar at Cabul.
Scinde: Ellenborough as Governor-General, his policy, the conquest of Scinde by Sir Charles Napier (Meeanee, Hyderabad), the annexation and its controversy, Napier’s “Peccavi.”
The Sikh Wars: The death of Runjeet Singh, the disorders in the Punjab, the Sikh Army supreme, the first Sikh War (Moodkee, Ferozeshah, Aliwal, Sobraon), the Treaty of Lahore. The Lawrences. Lord Dalhousie becomes Governor-General. The murder of Vans Agnew and Anderson at Mooltan; Herbert Edwardes; the second Sikh War (Chillianwalla, Gujarat), the annexation of the Punjab.

CHAPTER XXVII — Dalhousie and Canning (text starts line 22665)
Period: 1849–1856
Walpole opens with the annexation of the Punjab concluding a distinct period in Indian history. For eleven years Indian statesmen had been concentrated on the north-western frontier; that dread was now temporarily removed.
Burma: The second Burmese War (1852), Lambert’s mission, the Court of Ava yields, the new Governor of Rangoon refuses to receive Captain Fishbourne, Lambert’s stringent measures, the Burmese fire on H.M.S. Fox, Dalhousie’s ultimatum, the expedition, the annexation of Pegu.
Oudh: The state of Oudh, Wellesley’s policy, the Nawab’s loans to Hastings/Amherst/Bentinck, Bentinck’s threat of interference, Auckland’s policy, the treaty of 1801, the treaty of 1837 (its abrogation not communicated), Hardinge’s warning, Sleeman’s tour, Outram’s report, the manner of interference, the claims of Oudh on British forbearance, Dalhousie’s opinion and his Council’s decision, the decision of the India House, Dalhousie’s ultimatum, the annexation of Oudh (1856). The policy of the annexation and its real motives.
Dalhousie’s reforms: Retirement of Dalhousie, his positive legacy (railways, telegraph, canals, education, postal system). Succeeded by Canning.
Persia and Herat: Yar Mahommed Khan, the Persians occupy Herat, fresh arrangements between Persia and Britain, Meerza Khan at Shiraz, Murray strikes his flag, the Persian Manifesto, the Persian Mission to Constantinople, the Persian War of 1856 and its termination.
The Coming of the Mutiny: The state of India, European and Native troops, the services of the Native Army, the Mutiny at Vellore (1806), the Mutiny of the 47th Regiment (1824), the Mutiny of the 34th at Ferozepore, the Mutiny at Rawul Pindee (1840), the Order of 1844 and its modification, Napier suspends the modified order, his controversy with Dalhousie, the refusal of the 38th to embark for Burma, Canning’s General Service Order of 1856, the Sepoys’ objection to it.

CHAPTER XXVIII — British Colonies (text starts line 29170)
Period: c. 1800–1870
Walpole argues that while the British in India provide a romantic episode, the true monument of British greatness lies in the growth of the Colonial Empire. At the beginning of the century, the colonies were almost exclusively possessions conquered from other Powers, and the colonial system was based on monopoly and restriction.
The Old Colonial System: The Navigation Acts, the mercantile theory, the gradual relaxation of monopolies. The slave trade — abolition in 1807, emancipation in 1833, the apprenticeship system (abolished 1838), the decline of the West Indies after emancipation. Free trade and British capital favouring new fields.
Population and Emigration: The enormous growth of British population, Malthus’ theory, the poor harvests of the 1840s (the Hungry Forties), the pressure of population relieved by emigration. The colonies as an outlet.
South Africa: The Cape Colony, the Boers, the Great Trek, Kaffir Wars, Sir Harry Smith, the Orange Free State and the Transvaal, Governor Sir George Grey.
Canada: The rebellion of 1837, Lord Durham’s Report, the union of Upper and Lower Canada (1840), the achievement of responsible government under Lord Elgin (Rebellion Losses Bill, 1849, the burning of the Parliament House at Montreal).
Australia: Cook’s discovery, the first convict settlement at Botany Bay (1788), the wool industry (John Macarthur, Samuel Marsden), exploration (Blaxland, Wentworth, Lawson crossing the Blue Mountains), the Wakefield theory of systematic colonisation, the abolition of transportation, the discovery of gold (1851), the Eureka Stockade, the achievement of responsible government.
New Zealand: Captain Cook, the Maoris, the missionary efforts of Marsden, the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), colonisation (the New Zealand Company under Wakefield), the Maori Wars, the problem of extinguishing native title.
Transportation (the last convicts sent to Western Australia). The achievement of self-government in the major colonies. Walpole closes with the question whether the colonies would eventually separate from the mother country, an issue then unresolved.

sources/walpole-history-of-england-vol6.title: A History of England from the Conclusion of the Great War in 1815, Vol. VI
sources/walpole-history-of-england-vol6.content:
A History of England from the Conclusion of the Great War in 1815, Vol. VI — by Spencer Walpole
Vol. VI, from the expanded 6-volume edition (1905), covers the period 1853–1880. The volume contains five chapters (XXIV–XXVIII), focusing on the Crimean War, India, and the growth of the British colonial empire.

CHAPTER XXIV — The Crimean War (lines 1163–4311)
Period: 1853–1856
The Origins — The Holy Places and the Eastern Question: The war originated in a dispute between Russia and France over the custody of the Holy Places in Palestine — churches, shrines, and the keys to the Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem. Russia claimed the right to protect Orthodox Christian subjects of the Ottoman Empire under the Treaty of Kainardji (1774). Napoleon III, seeking prestige for his new regime, challenged this by asserting French claims on behalf of Latin Christians.
Menschikoff’s Mission (February 1853): Prince Menschikoff was sent to Constantinople as a special envoy. He demanded a sened (imperial decree) and a treaty recognising Russia’s right to protect Orthodox Christians throughout the Ottoman Empire. The British Ambassador, Lord Stratford de Redcliffe, counselled the Porte to reject these demands. The Czar Nicholas I, convinced that Britain would not fight, ordered the occupation of the Danubian Principalities (July 1853).
The Vienna Note: A compromise was drafted by the four Powers (Austria, France, Prussia, Britain) and accepted by Russia but rejected by the Porte on Stratford’s advice. Walpole is sharply critical of Stratford, arguing that he “fulfilled his instructions to the letter, but he so contrived that his employers were constantly getting deeper into a war policy.” The Czar’s interpretation of the Note, leaked through a Prussian newspaper, further inflamed tensions.
The War: The Turkish fleet was destroyed at Sinope (November 1853). Britain and France declared war on Russia (March 1854). The allied armies landed in the Crimea. Battles of the Alma, Balaclava (including the Charge of the Light Brigade), Inkerman. The Siege of Sebastopol, winter 1854–55. The sufferings of the army: disease, cold, mismanagement. Florence Nightingale and the sanitary commission. The death of Lord Raglan (June 1855). Sardinia joins the allies. The storming of the Redan and the Malakoff (September 1855). The Russians evacuate Sebastopol.
Peace: Austria’s ultimatum to Russia; the Congress of Paris (February–March 1856). The Treaty of Paris neutralised the Black Sea, guaranteed the integrity of the Ottoman Empire, opened the Danube to free navigation, and admitted Turkey to the European concert. Walpole’s verdict: the war set back European progress by fourteen years. The only permanent result was the freeing of the Danube and the weakening of Russia’s position in the Near East.

CHAPTER XXV — The Supremacy of the British in India (lines 4312–8001)
Period: c. 1750–1835
A historical survey of the rise of British power in India. Walpole argues that the growth of the British colonial empire is the “most striking and lasting monument of Anglo-Saxon supremacy,” but that the conquest of India provides the more thrilling story.
The Foundations: The East India Company’s early struggles against French competition (Dupleix, Clive). The Battle of Plassey (1757). The administration of Warren Hastings. The Regulating Act and Pitt’s India Act. Lord Cornwallis and the Permanent Settlement of Bengal. Sir John Shore. Lord Wellesley and the Subsidiary System — the war with Tippoo Sultan, the annexation of the Carnatic, the conquest of the Mahrattas.
The Early Governors-General: Lord Cornwallis (second term), Lord Minto, Lord Moira (Marquess of Hastings — the Nepaulese War, the Pindarees, the third Mahratta War), Lord Amherst (the first Burmese War), Lord William Bentinck (financial reforms, abolition of suttee, suppression of thuggee, educational reforms, Macaulay’s Minute).
The Civil and Military System: The Company’s army, the Civil Service, the administration of justice, the Ryotwaree system (Munro), the Land Settlement of Bengal, the sale of offices, the institution of a police force.

CHAPTER XXVI — Afghanistan, Scinde, and the Punjab (lines 8002–12027)
Period: 1835–1849
Bentinck’s Successors: Bentinck’s resignation; Metcalfe’s interim administration. The free press in India — Silk Buckingham’s case, Metcalfe and Macaulay’s reforms. Lord Auckland as Governor-General.
The Afghan Disaster (1838–1842): Russian influence in Persia, the Euphrates route to India, the siege of Herat, Alexander Burnes at Cabul, Vicovitch’s mission, Auckland’s decision to dethrone Dost Mahommed. The Tripartite Treaty with Ranjeet Singh (1838). The Army of the Indus advances, Ghuznee falls, Cabul is occupied. The unpopularity of the war in England. The disastrous winter of 1841–42: the rising, the murder of Burnes and Macnaghten, the retreat from Cabul and annihilation of the army. Sale’s defence of Jellalabad. Pollock’s and Nott’s advance. The destruction of the Cabul bazaar. The release of the prisoners.
Scinde (1843): Lord Ellenborough as Governor-General. The conquest of Scinde by Sir Charles Napier — the battles of Meeanee and Hyderabad. The controversy over Napier’s “iniquitous” annexation. Operations in Gwalior.
The Sikh Wars (1845–1849): The death of Runjeet Singh. The Sikh Army becomes supreme in the Punjab. The first Sikh War: Moodkee, Ferozeshah, Aliwal, Sobraon. The Treaty of Lahore. Sir Henry Hardinge as Governor-General. The Lawrences and the administration of the Punjab. The second Sikh War: the murder of Vans Agnew and Anderson at Mooltan, Herbert Edwardes, the battles of Chillianwalla and Gujarat. The annexation of the Punjab under Lord Dalhousie.

CHAPTER XXVII — Dalhousie and Canning (lines 12028–16374)
Period: 1849–1856
The Second Burmese War (1852): Lambert’s mission to Rangoon, the Court of Ava yields, the refusal of the new Governor to receive Captain Fishbourne, Lambert’s stringent measures, the Burmese fire on H.M.S. Fox, Dalhousie’s ultimatum, the expedition, the annexation of Pegu. The cost and controversy of the war.
Oudh and the Doctrine of Lapse: The State of Oudh, Wellesley’s policy, Bentinck’s threat of interference, Auckland’s treaty of 1837 (abrogated without notice to the Nawab). Hardinge’s warning. Sleeman’s tour and recommendations (1849). Outram’s report. Dalhousie’s ultimatum. The annexation of Oudh (February 1856). Walpole’s treatment reveals the moral and legal controversy: the British case for annexation (misgovernment, duty to the people) and the Indian case for forbearance (the treaty of 1801 constituted an independent state; earlier governors-general had accepted the Nawab’s sovereignty). Dalhousie’s own ambivalence.
Dalhousie’s Reforms: Railways, the electric telegraph, the Ganges canal, the postal system, educational policy (Wood’s Despatch of 1854). His retirement and death. Lord Canning succeeds him.
Persia and Herat (1856): The Persian occupation of Herat, the British demand for its evacuation, the Persian War (1856–57), its rapid termination. The difficulty of fixing India’s north-western frontier.
The Eve of the Mutiny: The state of the Indian army. The grievances of the Sepoys: the General Service Order of 1856, the refusal of the 38th Regiment to embark for Burma, the greased cartridge question (foreshadowed). The European and Native troop ratio.

CHAPTER XXVIII — Greater Britain (lines 16375–18929)
Period: c. 1800–1870
The Colonies and the Mother Country: Walpole argues that Britain’s colonial empire is the true monument of British greatness, though at the beginning of the century the colonies were conquered possessions governed by the restrictive mercantile system.
The Old Colonial System and its Fall: The Navigation Acts, the monopoly of colonial trade, the relaxation after 1822 (Huskisson’s reforms), the triumph of free trade, the repeal of the Navigation Acts (1849). The colonial system transformed: from monopoly to freedom.
The Slave Trade and the West Indies: Abolition of the slave trade (1807), slave emancipation (1833), the £20 million compensation, the apprenticeship system (1834–1838), the decline of the West Indian colonies after emancipation. The rise of alternative supplies of sugar from Cuba and Brazil.
Emigration and the Growth of Population: Malthus’ theory, the pressure of population in the British Isles, the famine in Ireland and the Highlands, the great emigration of the 1840s and 1850s. The colonies as the safety-valve.
South Africa: The Cape Colony (acquired 1806, ceded 1815). The Boers and their trek (the Great Trek, 1835–37). The conflicts with the Zulus and the Kaffir wars. The annexation of Natal (1843). The Orange Free State and the Transvaal. Sir Harry Smith and the Battle of Boomplaats (1848). Governor Sir George Grey. The problem of native policy and race relations.
Canada: The Constitutional Act of 1791. The rebellion of 1837 (Papineau, Mackenzie). Lord Durham’s Report (1839) — “two nations warring in the bosom of a single state.” The union of Upper and Lower Canada (1841). The achievement of responsible government: Lord Elgin, the Rebellion Losses Bill (1849), the burning of the Parliament House at Montreal. The Reciprocity Treaty with the United States (1854). Confederation: the Quebec Conference (1864), the British North America Act (1867).
Australia: Discovery by Captain Cook (1770). The first convict settlement at Botany Bay (1788). The crossing of the Blue Mountains (1813). John Macarthur and the wool industry. The Wakefield theory of systematic colonisation. The abolition of transportation to New South Wales (1840). The discovery of gold (1851, Bathurst and Ballarat). The Eureka Stockade (1854). Responsible government granted to New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia, Tasmania, and Queensland. The exploration of the interior: Burke and Wills, Stuart, Macdouall.
New Zealand: Discovery by Tasman (1642) and Cook (1769). The Maoris — their character, capacity for civilisation. Samuel Marsden’s missionary work, the Treaty of Waitangi (1840). The New Zealand Company under Edward Gibbon Wakefield. Colonisation of the North and South Islands. The Maori Wars (the Flagstaff War, the Taranaki War, the Waikato campaigns). The problem of native title and race relations. Self-government granted (1852).
Transportation: The history of convict transportation to Australia. The last convicts sent to Western Australia (1868). The end of the system.
Conclusion: Walpole closes with the achievement of self-government in the colonies and the question of whether they would eventually separate from the mother country. These issues, he notes, remain open. The volume closes with Britain at the height of its imperial power but facing new questions of colonial relationship and responsibility.
